** iiij

**Louis** <note>original: "Loys," an archaic spelling of Louis</note>, by the grace of God King of France & Navarre, To our beloved and faithful Councilors, the members of our Courts of Parliaments in Paris, Toulouse, Rouen, Bordeaux, Dijon, Aix, Grenoble, & Brittany: Bailiffs, Provosts, Seneschals <note>Bailiffs, Provosts, and Seneschals were various types of local judicial and administrative officials in pre-revolutionary France</note>, or their Lieutenants, and to all our other Justices and Officers whom it may concern, Greetings. Our well-beloved Pyramus de Candole, merchant Bookseller, has represented to us that he recently recovered a book titled the *Treasury of Languages*, composed by the late Claude Duret, who during his life was our Councilor and President at the Presidial Court <term>Presidial Court: A middle-level court established to handle cases that were too important for local courts but not significant enough for the high Parlements.</term> of Moulins in Bourbonnais. Since this book is worthy of the light and of being shared with the public, he wishes to have it printed; however, as he fears that after incurring the expenses to support the said printing, other Booksellers or Printers of this our Kingdom might do the same, he would be deprived of the profit he expects from it. He has very humbly petitioned us to allow him the sale and distribution of the said books in this our Kingdom, with prohibitions against all Booksellers or Printers from selling or printing them without his acknowledgement and consent, and to this effect, to grant him our necessary letters. For these reasons, inclined toward the prayer and petition of the said de Candole, we have permitted and granted to him, and do permit and grant by these presents, that after having the aforementioned book printed, he may have it sold and distributed in this our Kingdom, lands, and territories under our obedience, by such Merchants, Booksellers, or Printers, or such others as he sees fit, without any other of the said Booksellers or Printers being allowed for six full and consecutive years—counting from the day that the said printing is finished—to print, sell, or distribute the said books without the express permission of the said de Candole, upon pain of confiscation of all copies found, and for all costs, damages, and interests, and a fine of five hundred livres <term>Livres: The primary currency of France from the Middle Ages until 1795.</term>. We therefore command you, and enjoin each of you, each in your own right, that you allow the said de Candole, whether widow or heirs, to enjoy and use our present permission, privilege, and grant, along with everything contained within it, fully and peacefully during the said time, without allowing any hindrance or obstacle to be placed against him; for such is our good pleasure, notwithstanding any edicts, ordinances, mandates, or prohibitions to the contrary.

Given at Paris the ninth day of May, the year of grace one thousand six hundred thirteen:
and of our reign the third.

->By the King in his Council,<-

Signed
->DERDIN.<-

Collated with the original.

<meta>The catchword "PRE" suggests this page serves as a preface or preliminary approval (Approbation) for the following work. It continues the formal front matter of the book.</meta>

One may extract and most abundantly draw out, as if from the richest mines of the Indies, the purest gold: the examples of magistrates, the foresighted counsels of governors, and the illustrious deeds of princes. By the brilliance of this work, my mind was so refreshed and moved that I did not hesitate to examine it more diligently; and having scrutinized it accurately with the sharp edge of my mind and read it through by day and by night, I have given it my approval. I decided that my approval (which I hope will not be unwelcome to you) should be sent; I send it therefore and come to an end, and I earnestly pray to the Lord, the Creator of all things, that He may preserve you long in safety and health, and adorn you with His heavenly gifts. For it is God who heals all things, not with herbs or poultices, but with His Word <note>original: "sermone"</note>, and bestows the grace of health through His singular goodness.
->At Bourges <note>original: "Auarici Biturigum," the Roman name for the city of Bourges</note> on the 2nd day of June 1607.<-

# APPROVAL.

*I, Claude Feydeau, Doctor of Theology and Canon Law, Theological Canon and Grand Penitentiary <term>Grand Penitentiary: a senior priest in a cathedral responsible for matters of penance and confession</term> in the Archiepiscopal Church of Bourges, certify that I have seen and read this Treasury of Languages <term>original title: "Thresor des Langues"</term> composed by the Noble Claude Duret, President at the Presidial Court <term>Presidial: a type of mid-level royal court in Renaissance France</term> of Moulins in Bourbonnais. I have found nothing contrary to the Catholic religion; therefore, I have judged it worthy of being printed, as being useful and necessary to demonstrate and teach the antiquity, dignity, and variety of languages.*
->*Done at Bourges this 2nd of June 1607.*<-

->CLAUDE FEYDEAU.<-

->On the tower of Babel and the city of Babylon.<-

### C H A P T E R  I I I.

The great and admirable Prophet Moses, after having described in his history of Genesis, chapter 10, very particularly the generations of the children of Noah, and the division of the Isles and the nations by their regions, each one in his own language, according to their children and families among their people, writes in the following chapter 11 as follows: At that time, the whole universal earth was of one same language and speech, and it happened as they departed from the East that they found a plain in the land of Shinar <note>original: "Sennaar"</note>, and they dwelt there and said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and bake them in the fire." So they had bricks instead of stones, and clay <note>bitumen or mortar</note> instead of cement; then they said, "let us build ourselves a tower, the top of which reaches to heaven; let us make ourselves a name <note>renown</note>, so that perhaps we may not be scattered over all the earth." Then the Lord came down to see the said tower that the sons of men were building. For he said, "behold," and the great Origen in his 11th homily on the book of Numbers dared to write that various Angels operated various languages for each of the men who worked on the construction of this tower. Josephus in book 1, chapter 4 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, St. Augustine in his *Questions on Genesis*, and Paul Orosius in his writings, assure us that in the very place where the said Tower of Babel was constructed and built by Nimrod <note>original: "Nembrot"</note> and his followers and underlings (of which the heathens and pagans Hestiaeus, Eupolemus, the Sibyls, Alexander Polyhistor, Abydenus, and others mentioned in Eusebius book 9, chapter 4 of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, and after him in P. de Mornay chapter 26 of *The Truth of the Christian Religion*, all speak), the great and populous city of Babylon, also named in the Hebrew language בבל <gloss>Babel</gloss>, was afterwards built and constructed there upon the river Euphrates, from which the surrounding lands and regions named Chaldea and Mesopotamia took their names and titles. The Hebrews write that the word Babel is derived from the root בלל <gloss>Balal</gloss> <note>meaning to mix or confuse</note>.

Now, this speech assisted by reason is within us what the first eternal emanation is in the divinity: namely, the Word or Wisdom, which *came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the first-born before all creatures* <note>original: "ex ore altissimi prodiuit primogenita ante omnẽ creaturã"; a quote from Ecclesiasticus 24:3 in the Vulgate</note>. Moreover, it is double: the one animated by the living voice, proceeding from the chest <note>original: "estomach"; in this period, the "stomach" or "breast" was often viewed as the physical seat of thought and internal speech</note> through the tongue in articulate and distinct words; and the other, namely writing, which performs the office of speech as if mute and silent, separated apart from us, for which the hand is the instrument. Both serve to express the inner conceptions of our soul, upon which depends the knot and principal bond of human society, which could not be preserved without a well-ordered governance, nor could governance be established except by means of reason. For though reason is the lady and mistress of all things, without the benefit of speech which casts it from potentiality into action, it could not achieve its effects; thus it would remain as if uselessly buried apart within the chests of individuals. But then again, what would either of them do without the help of writing, their common assistant? Writing cannot be restricted by any boundaries, spreading everywhere. Certainly, little could be achieved without it, as can be seen among the savages of the **West Indies**, who are so barbarian, uncivilized, and beast-like, being deprived of its use. Indeed, when the **Spanish** conquered them, the natives held writing in such admiration and respect—seeing that by its means they could make their thoughts understood from one place to another, regardless of the distance—that they thought there was a demon or familiar spirit enclosed within these characters. One could hardly prevent them from worshipping the packets and dispatches placed in their hands to carry. This served greatly to keep these barbarians in obedience and subjection, and to dissuade them from all enterprises, conspiracies, and revolts. Furthermore, as *Pierre Martyr* <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an Italian-born historian of Spain's explorations</note> recounts in his *Decades*, if it was a question of discussing something secret among themselves, they took great care not to approach a tree that grows in their region called the *Copei* <note>The Copey tree (*Clusia major*), known for its thick leaves that can be written upon</note>, because for lack of paper, the **Spanish** were accustomed to writing to one another on the leaves with a stylus; these leaves are very large and thick, like those of a water lily. What is said above is in some way represented to us by the law given by word of mouth to the Prophet **Moses**, and the written law, which is like the soul of the other, holding the place of the body. For the law given by word of mouth—so say the Hebrew sages in their most secret Theology—has no foundation nor authority except the written law, no more than the moon has any light except what it receives from the Sun. *Plato* calls this the clarity transmitted and infused by the divinity into our souls to lead and elevate them to the knowledge of the intelligible world; and he calls that of the moon the instinct and natural discourse of reason, by means of which, depending on how it is exercised, we acquire the science of celestial and elementary things in the sensible world. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]

For there is not a single small point or accent in the Torah <term>Torah: the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, also known as the Pentateuch</term> that does not signify some great mystery. It was written (so they say) expressly as one continuous sequence, without any separation of words or clauses from the beginning to the end; so much so that the whole work appeared to be only a single word, if it could indeed be that long. This was done so that the common people—even though everyone had it before their eyes and knew it by heart—could not understand its secret significance for fear of it being held in contempt. Instead, it was understood only by those of the council to whom Moses communicated what was necessary for them to exercise their duties, according to what their capacity could handle. Moses reserved for himself the remainder of the sacred secrets, especially those concerning the Trinity. He never wished to reveal these to the Israelites except in veiled words, for fear of leading them into idolatry, to which they were quite inclined because they could not comprehend the high mystery of a plurality of persons in such a perfect union. However, he did share these secrets with Aaron and the seventy of the Sanhedrin <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</note>, and they with their successors in like manner, as I will describe more particularly hereafter. From this has come the name Kabbalah <note>original: "cabale"; meaning "received tradition"</note>, which is to say a tradition received by ear without anything being committed to writing. The Pythagoreans and the Druids later followed this same practice, according to the words of Julius Caesar in book 6 of his *Commentaries*.

But these Kabbalistic mysteries proceeded from the written law and did not consist so absolutely in a verbal tradition that the Scripture did not contain the better part of them—whether in the form of the characters, their points, accents, order, sequence, and arrangement, or in the transposition, commutation, and pairing of letters. These are what the Hebrews call *Ethbas* <note>original: "Ethbas" (Atbash); a substitution cipher where the first letter is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc.</note>, *Tmurah* <note>original: "Tmurah" (Temurah); the process of exchanging letters to find hidden meanings</note>, and *Ziruph* <note>original: "Ziruph" (Tziruf); the art of combining and permuting letters</note>, as well as *Notariacon* <note>original: "Notariacon" (Notarikon); a method of forming new words from the initial or final letters of phrases</note>, numerical equivalences, and *Ghematrie* <note>original: "Ghematrie" (Gematria); a system where letters are assigned numerical values</note>, along with other such devices and observations. Among all authors, a certain Spanish Jew named Rabbi Joseph Cicatilia <note>Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a famous Spanish Kabbalist</note> from the city of Salamanca has composed three large volumes on this, titled **גנת אגוז** <note>original: "Ghinat Egoz," which translates to "Garden of the Walnut Tree"</note>. The first volume treats words; the second, letters; and the third, points and accents, as I shall clearly demonstrate hereafter. 

Furthermore, just as writing is more spiritual than the spoken word (which relates more to the body because it falls under the sense of hearing, which is coarser and more material than the sense of sight, upon which writing consists), secret notes or ciphers are also more spiritual than common writing. Therefore, they relate to the mystical sense of the law, hidden beneath the "bark" or shell of the literal letter. Regarding this, the same aforementioned Rabbi, in the first book of the *Gates of Light*, discusses the difference between these two words: **אמירה** <note>original: "Emirah," meaning speech or word</note>, which comes from the verb **אמר** <note>original: "Amar," to say or speak</note>, and **דבור** <note>original: "Daberah," from "Dibur," meaning reasoning or discourse</note>. He posits that the first denotes the law given by mouth to Moses, which is represented by the divine name **אדני** <note>original: "Adonai," meaning "My Lord"</note>; and the other, namely the utterance (*Daberah*), as when one finds in the Hebrew Scripture **מדבר** <note>original: "Medhaber," meaning "He spoke"</note> (it must be understood that God spoke), signifies the written law, denoted by the sacred and holy Tetragrammaton **יהוה** <note>The four-letter name of God, often transliterated as YHWH</note>. Furthermore, the written law, being more spiritual and mysterious, is explained by the law given by mouth, which is the temple and tabernacle of the written law—just as *Adonai* is for the ineffable four-letter name. And just as there is no other access to reach that sacred name except under the guidance and direction of *Adonai*, which draws all blessings and effects from it, so too there is no other way...

By the letters, therefore, are represented all the parts of composite things, and they are like their matter; by the points, all the kinds of forms that vivify them; and by the accents, all the proper operations of matter and form joined together in the constitution of a body, corresponding to their celestial principles and their divine ideas. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

Because such a one undoubtedly exists—that is, one beloved both above and below, inheriting two worlds, the present world and the world to come—for this reason, the Talmudists and Kabbalists are divided into two branches, although both arise and emanate from the same transmitted traditions. For both place their faith in the traditions of their ancestors, even when no rational explanation is given. But they are distinguished by this arrangement of their purpose: the happy and blessed Kabbalist transfers and translates all study, effort, counsel, labor, and diligence—indeed, the entire intention of his mind—from the sensible world <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses.</note> finally to the intellectual world.

The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universe. If he occasionally proceeds freely toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God Himself as immanent and absolute, but rather as the Architect and Cause of things, occupied with His creations. He assigns angels to daily ministries and to carry out the effects of the divine will, always relating the contemplation of the highest things back to this lower world. Nevertheless, one of these branches often borrows the insights of the other and draws them toward its own desires.

Indeed, Talmudists and Kabbalists sometimes exchange their studies back and forth, much like the active and contemplative lives. Though they often use the same context of Sacred Scripture, one invites toward "servile fear" and the other toward "filial love" <note>original: "timorem servilem... amorem filialem"; a distinction between fearing God as a slave fears a master versus loving God as a child loves a parent.</note> through their own pleasant persuasions. For that Talmudist will be seen residing with sharp study over the precepts and mandates of the Law, explaining them, arranging and directing them, venerating and kissing them. Thus, we might correctly define the Talmud as nothing other than an explanation of the Law according to the author's intention.

Hence the Talmudists are called "Expositors" and Pharisees, who, from the pulpit and the chair of Moses, are always intent on their work, preaching and exhorting the common people, saying with the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>: *Serve the Lord in fear*, and with Joshua: *Fear the Lord and serve Him.* Furthermore: "Do this in such a way, and omit that with such-and-such moderation," from which they have reduced the 613 commandments—summed up in the single word <gloss>Taryag</gloss> <insert>תריג</insert> <note>The Hebrew letters Tav, Resh, Yud, and Gimmel add up to 613 in gematria.</note>—into two headings: "Do" and "Do not do," which you are accustomed to calling affirmative and negative commandments, which are very helpful to know and quite necessary in practice.

The Kabbalists, however, although they are men who piously observe the Law (as truth bears witness), lean more toward contemplation; therefore, they are called "men of speculation" among the masters of the Law. These men leave to the Talmudists the care of the state and private affairs at home, the rituals and customs of war, and judicial and moral matters along with their history. They have reserved for themselves only those things which pertain to the peace and tranquility of the soul and to the love of God. For they say: "The intention of the entire Law consists of two things: the good disposition of the soul and the good disposition of the body." For the whole Law tends primarily toward the perfection of man, and according to it, we attain two perfections: one of the mind and the other of the body. Truly, that which helps the soul and perpetuates life is far worthier and of a higher preeminence, even though a suitable condition and proper composition of the body comes first in time and nature. Therefore, the Kabbalists must be held in a higher place and a worthier degree, as they follow that exposition of the Law which, through certain symbols, most powerfully impels the elevation of the mind toward the heavens and toward divine matters. The Greeks call this <term>anagogical: a method of spiritual interpretation that seeks to lead the mind from the literal text to a higher, mystical meaning</term> instruction, which not only...

HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

The second, called <term>Masekhet Ketubot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת כתובות; the title refers to "written contracts," specifically the marriage contract.</note></term>, meaning the treatise on contracts, is divided into 13 chapters. These discuss marriage contracts, dowries, and the legal obligations that a husband must observe toward his wife, and a wife toward her husband.

The third, called <term>Masekhet Nedarim<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נדרים; "Tractate on Vows."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on vows, is divided into eleven chapters, which discuss the vows made by women.

The fourth, called <term>Masekhet Nazir<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נזיר; "Tractate on the Nazirite."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on the Nazirite, is divided into nine chapters. These discuss the vow of the Nazirites—those who "separate" themselves from the vanities of the world. During the term of their vow, they were not permitted, among other things, to drink wine or taste any liquor or product of the vine, nor to cut their hair, nor to touch any dead body.

The fifth, called <term>Masekhet Sotah<note>original Hebrew: מסכת סוטה; historically referring to a woman suspected of adultery.</note></term>, meaning the treatise on diversion or divorce, is divided into 9 chapters. These discuss the diversion or divorce involving a woman and her husband when she marries another. <note>The author uses the term "diversion" (diuersion) likely to describe the legal deviation from a marriage or the specific ordeal described in biblical law for a suspected wife.</note>

The sixth, <term>Masekhet Gittin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת גטין; "Tractate on Bills of Divorce."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on legal documents of divorce, is divided into nine chapters, which discuss the documents of repudiation and the dissolution of marriage.

The seventh, <term>Masekhet Kiddushin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת קדושין; "Tractate on Betrothals."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on betrothals, is divided into 4 chapters, which discuss betrothals and matters pertaining to them.

### THE FOURTH PART of the aforementioned Talmuds, named the *Order of Damages*, is likewise divided into seven books.

The first of these is called <term>Masekhet Nezikin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת נזיקין; "Tractate on Damages."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on dangers and nuisances; this section is itself divided into three <term>Bavot<note>original Hebrew: בבות; literally "Gates." The author translates this as "positions."</note></term>.

The first of these is called <term>Bava Kamma<note>original Hebrew: בבא קמא; "The First Gate."</note></term>, meaning the first position; it is divided into ten chapters, which discuss all the dangers and nuisances typically caused by both men and brute beasts.

The second is called <term>Bava Metzia<note>original Hebrew: בבא מציעא; "The Middle Gate."</note></term>, meaning the middle position; it is also divided into ten chapters, which discuss lawsuits, rights, usury, and rentals.

The third is called <term>Bava Batra<note>original Hebrew: בבא בתרא; "The Last Gate."</note></term>, meaning the final position; it is likewise divided into ten chapters, which discuss sales, shared fields, partnerships, and heirs and inheritances.

The second book is called <term>Masekhet Sanhedrin<note>original Hebrew: מסכת סנהדרין; referring to the High Court of ancient Israel.</note></term>, meaning the treatise on Ordinary Judges, and is divided into 14 chapters. These discuss at length the ordinary judges, judgments, and other matters pertaining to legal trials. It also discusses those who have a portion in the world to come under the Messiah, specifically in <term>Perek Helek<note>original Hebrew: פרק חלק; "Chapter Portion."</note></term>—that is, the chapter that begins with the word *Helek*, which means "portion."

The third, called <term>Masekhet Shevuot<note>original Hebrew: מסכת שבועות; "Tractate on Oaths."</note></term>, meaning the treatise on oaths, is divided into 8 chapters, which discuss oaths and especially the guardianship of property.

# History of the Origin of the...

...to be received.

The **ESSENES**, distinguished practitioners of piety and not much unlike Christian monks, bound themselves by these laws and sanctions:

<margin>1</margin> All things are governed by fate—that is, by the will of God—and nothing happens to men except by the determination of fate.

<margin>2</margin> Souls are immortal, and after this life, rewards and punishments are repaid for one’s deeds: for the good, indeed, beyond the ocean, where there is a region pressed neither by cold nor heat, but made pleasant by the breathing West Wind <note>original: *Zephyrus*</note>; for the wicked, however, in the underworld, where there are places of hardship and full of lamentations.

<margin>3</margin> Every oath is to be avoided as if it were perjury: because whatever a perfect man says should have the force of an oath; and that man is condemned as if guilty of a lie who is not believed unless God is called as a witness.

<margin>4</margin> The greatest reverence, after God, must be shown to the lawmaker **Moses**, whom if anyone blasphemes, he shall be condemned to death.

<margin>5</margin> Principal study must be applied to the divine scriptures and the writings of the ancient fathers, and from there one must seek what may relieve the cares of the soul.

<margin>6</margin> The leader of the common fellowship must be obeyed in such a way that nothing is permitted to be done without his command.

<margin>7</margin> To lead a continent and celibate life, and to abstain entirely from all marriage throughout one’s whole life.

<margin>8</margin> All resources are to be held in common, and there is one estate for all, which is dispensed by common stewards.

<margin>9</margin> Nothing is to be bought or sold among themselves, but it is free for all to receive whatever is needed from whomever they please.

<margin>10</margin> White garments are to be used, and the clothing and shoes are not to be changed unless they are either completely torn or consumed by long use.

<margin>11</margin> Such care for cleanliness must be maintained even in natural waste, that each person should daily dig a trench for himself in the most secret places with a small axe <term>dolabella: a small pickaxe or tool used by the Essenes for hygiene and work</term>, in which he may relieve his bowels, first having lowered his garment all around for the sake of covering the body, and then returning the earth he had dug out to its place, so that, of course, no injury is done to the brightness of the divine light.

<margin>12</margin> Before the rising of the sun, the author of the dawning light must be celebrated with public praises; after that, however, each must proceed to his own arts and studies.

<margin>13</margin> At the fifth hour of the day <note>approximately 11:00 AM</note>, they must gather in a common dining room, clothed in sacred garments—that is, linen coverings—and there they are to eat sitting in silence from the same bread and food <note>original: *pulmentum*, a thick porridge or pottage</note>; nor is it lawful for anyone to taste anything unless a public prayer precedes and follows the meal, which praises God, the giver of food, both before and after the meal.

<margin>14</margin> After the meal, having laid aside the sacred garments, each must return to his own work until evening.

<margin>15</margin> Those recently approaching the worship of the Essenes are not to be admitted immediately into the fellowship, but, clothed in a white garment and a loincloth <note>original: *perizoma*</note> and girded with a small axe, they are to be tested by their curators for three full years, until they have given proof of their tried virtue.

**Epiphanius** <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note>, in Book 1 *Against Heresies*, says that the "traditions of the elders" are four Jewish expositions of the divine law, devised by certain Hebrew masters: namely, by the Prophet **Moses**, by **Rabbi Akiba**, by **Rabbi Ida**, and by the sons of **Asamoneus** <note>The Hasmoneans</note>, who derived constitutions from the aforementioned expositions.

HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

of the Holy Hebrew Scriptures was formerly hidden beneath various layers of code, much like a kernel within multiple husks, skins, and shells. Thus, the matters now seen contained within the **Talmuds** <term>Talmud: The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</term> were not committed to writing in ancient times, nor was any part of the commentary or explanation of the law recorded. Instead, the Hebrews passed these down to one another by word of mouth and through tradition, as he <note>Referring to Maimonides, mentioned later as "Rabbi Moses the Egyptian."</note> confirms in his *Exodus* on *Deuteronomy*. This was done because of the difficulties that arose until one hundred and twenty years <note>original: "six vingts ans"</note> after the second destruction of the temple, which occurred in the time of the Emperors Vespasian and his son Titus; this brings us to approximately the Year of Grace 190. At that time, the same Rabbi Judah <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the redactor of the Mishnah.</note> was the first to arrange that same *Mishnah* <term>Mishnah: The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions.</term> into a compendium or summary. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note> discusses this at length in Book 2, Chapter 5 of *The Faith Against the Jews*. The aforementioned Rabbi Judah taught and left the explanation and interpretation of this law—arranged in his own compendium and summary—to another, Rabbi Johanan. Three hundred years after the destruction of the aforementioned Temple of Jerusalem, Johanan, along with his companions Rav and Samuel, expanded and increased that compendium or summary of the aforementioned *Mishnah*. He did so with a clearer and more eloquent style, composing another volume called the **Jerusalem Talmud**. In its beginning, this work was quite small, as asserted by Victor of Carben <note>A 15th-century Jewish convert to Christianity.</note> in his book *On the Life and Customs of the Jews*, Chapter 9 and those following. This Rabbi Johanan had as colleagues and companions Rabbi Rav and Rabbi Samuel; their student was Rabbi Rav Huna, who had as a student Rabba; he in turn taught Rabba Ravan, whose student was Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Assé). Rav Ashi, who excelled in great erudition, modesty of life, and worldly honor and glory, was the first to begin—along with Rabina in the year 436—to compose the **Babylonian Talmud**. It was so named because of the Rabbis who assembled in the city of Babylon to create it. This is confirmed by Elias Levita <note>A 15th-century Hebrew scholar and grammarian.</note> in the preface to his Chaldaic lexicon; by Jerome in Book 2, Chapter 5 of *The Holy Faith Against the Jews* (cited above); and by Guillaume Postel in Book 1, Chapter 3 of *The Concord of the Whole World*. The aforementioned Rabbi could not entirely finish this Talmud because he was overtaken by death before doing so. However, after his death, his son named Mor, with his colleague and companion Moreuar, finished it completely. This is likewise confirmed by Pietro Galatino <note>Petrus Galatinus, a Franciscan theologian.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 5 of *The Truth of the Catholic Faith*, and Sixtus of Siena in Book 2 of his *Holy Library* (both cited above). This Talmud contains the glosses and commentaries on the aforementioned compendium or summary of the Mishnah, along with all the other laws, ordinances, and new constitutions that have been made and promulgated at various times and places. It also includes many secrets and mysteries of the holy Hebrew language, as well as other reveries, fables, wickednesses, and impieties of the Talmudists. All the Jews who are currently scattered throughout every province of this universe receive, hold, and keep these Talmuds with careful observation and veneration, as they are—according to them—filled with wisdom that is at once divine, natural, legal, and political.

The aforementioned Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> counts and numbers forty generations from Moses until the Talmud was committed to writing in his preface to *Deuteronomy*. A certain modern Jew, in a book of his titled,

Genesis <note>The first book of the Bible</note> has hitherto been considered more noble. For just as it is necessary for that work to exist before the things themselves, so it is established that nature was prior to grace, although the latter is more noble; yet grace would have had no place anywhere unless nature had been prior. Thus, unless there had been *Yetzirah* <note>The world of "Formation" in Kabbalistic thought; original Latin: "Iezira"</note>, there could never have been *Beriah* <note>The world of "Creation"; original Latin: "Beriah"</note>.

The learned Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and noted Hebraist</note>, in book 2 of his *Chronography*, speaking of Ezra and his writings, said:

> He restored the Scriptures, which had been burned by the Babylonian leader of the army Nabuzardan <note>Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard under Nebuchadnezzar</note>, and returned them to this order which the Hebrews for the most part maintain today. Of him, Rabanus Maurus <note>A prominent 9th-century Carolingian theologian</note> writes in *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 54: "Inspired by the divine spirit, he repaired all the ancient sacred books when the Jews had entered Jerusalem, and corrected all the volumes of the Prophets which had been corrupted by the Gentiles; and he organized the entire Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters [in the Hebrew alphabet]." Otherwise, it was not within the power of Nebuchadnezzar to destroy all copies, especially since ten tribes were already in the East, outside his jurisdiction. For some make him [Ezra] the author of the points and accents <note>The vowel markings and musical notations used in Hebrew</note> with which the Hebrew Bibles are marked today. But they err, since it is clear from the books of Saint Jerome himself that none existed in his time. They were, however, invented shortly after the time of the Emperor Honorius, in the year 436 from the destruction of the Temple, which is the year 476 from the Passion of Christ, in the city of Tiberias in Galilee. The leaders of this were Aaron ben Asher and Jacob ben Naphtali <note>Famous 10th-century Masoretes who standardized the Hebrew text</note>, who, while they disagreed among themselves regarding the points of certain words, divided the Jews into two parties. For the Easterners, and those who inhabit Babylon by the River Nearda, follow the reading of the latter, while the Westerners follow the former. Forty-one years earlier, the Babylonian Talmud <term>Talmud: the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishna and Gemara</term>, or book of doctrine, began to be collected from the writings of the ancient masters by Rabbi Hina and Rabbi Ashi, and was later completed by Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Ashi's son. It contains the Jewish canon law, which in the time of Christ had not yet been committed to a full writing, but was preserved partly from fragments and partly from oral traditions. It began to be written down by Rabbi Hakkadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, also known as "The Holy Rabbi"</note> in the times of the Emperor Antoninus, in that shorter form called the *Mishna* <term>Mishna: the first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions</term>. And that is regarding the Babylonian Talmud: for the Jerusalem Talmud was written in the year of Christ 300, and the Babylonian about a hundred years later.

The same author, afterwards treating the ruin of Jerusalem that occurred under the Emperor Vespasian, says:

> During the destruction, there flourished Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai and his disciple Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who wrote the book *Pirke* <note>The *Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a work of biblical interpretation and astronomy</note>, concerning the arrangement and influences of the spheres of the earth and all the wonders of astronomy; his disciple Rabbi Ishmael the High Priest, Rabbi Joshua, Rabbi Gamaliel, and his son Rabbi Simeon, who was the father of Rabbi Judah Hakkadosh, [author of the] *Cozri* <note>Likely referring to the *Kuzari*, though historically it was written later</note>, and in the treatise *Berakhot* <note>Blessings</note> the final chapter. After the destruction, Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiba [flourished]. Following them, after the Emperor Hadrian, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Jose, Rabbi Simeon ben Azzai, and Rabbi Hananiah. Under Antoninus [reigned] the second Rabbi, Rabbi Hakkadosh, or Rabbi Judah; Rabbi Nathan, Rabbi Joshua ben Gotha. Soon after were the *Tannaim* <term>Tannaim: Rabbinic sages whose views are recorded in the Mishna</term>, the authors of the *Mishna*, or the Talmudic context; and finally the *Amoraim* <term>Amoraim: Jewish scholars who commented upon the Mishna</term>, the authors of the *Gemara* <term>Gemara: the portion of the Talmud that analyzes the Mishna</term>, or the Talmud itself. As for what the Jews did after the exile from Rome, and how the *Talmud*, *Gemara*, *Midrashim* <note>Original: "Derasim"</note>, *Gaonim* <note>Original: "Ghernim"</note>, etc., conducted themselves up to the year 1108 from that same destruction, in which Maimonides—Rabbi Moses ben Maimon—was writing (which is the year of Christ 1148), consult his preface to that book and the Kabbalistic history of Rabbi Abraham the Levite <note>Abraham ibn Daud</note>. And these things indeed concern the ancient people.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

From Zerubbabel to Simeon the Just. Second, the **Tannaim** <note>original: "Tannaim", the rabbinic sages whose views are recorded in the Mishnah</note>, the authors of the **Mishnah** or the Talmudic foundation, from Simeon the Just (whom they establish as the first of them) to Rabbi Judah the Holy <note>original: "Rabbi haccados", also known as Judah the Prince</note>, who was the last, when that first part of the Talmud was published in 180 AD under the Emperor Antoninus.

Third, the **Amoraim** <note>original: "Amoraim", the "speakers" or interpreters who commented on the Mishnah</note>, authors of the **Gemara** <note>original: "Ghemara", the rabbinical analysis and legal decisions completing the Talmud</note>, or the completion and decision of the Talmud; from Rabba (who appeared immediately after Rabbi Judah the Holy), the first doctor of that kind, until the death of Ravina, and Rabbi Sama the son of Rabba, and Rabbi Ashi, who finished the latter part. All of these flourished for 827 years. For they count that many years from Zerubbabel until the death of Ravina.

Fourth, the **Savoraim** <note>original: "Seboraim", the "reasoners" or scholastic doctors who followed the Amoraim</note>, who were the speculative, scholastic doctors; the first was Rabbi Jose, and the last was Rabbi Isana, lasting 187 years.

Fifth, the **Geonim** <note>original: "Gheonim", the heads of the great Babylonian academies who acted as supreme religious authorities</note> (corresponding to Practical Jurists); the first was Rabbi Hanina, and the last was Rabbi Hai, up to the year of our Lord 1121. Sixth, the **Rabbis**, who thereafter exercised themselves in the treatment of the Bible and other theological books. And the same [lineage is found in] the **Kabbalah** <note>here meaning "tradition" or "chain of succession"</note> of the *Kuzari*, and the *Tishbi* by Elias Levita.

Around the year 1127, the book of Jewish annals was written, which we have translated, titled **Seder Olam**, that is, the **Order of the World**; it is of the highest authority among the Jews. For this reason, Rabbi Solomon <note>likely Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note>, Rabbi Kimhi, and more recent Hebrews are accustomed to citing it quite often.

Likewise, there is the *Book of Tradition* <note>original: "liber Cabbalæ", specifically the Sefer ha-Qabbalah</note> by Rabbi Abraham Levita the Spaniard, written during the time of King Alfonso VII, who was called the Emperor of the Spains, a man so famous for heroic praise that this Rabbi Abraham called him the "King of Kings." For he frequently triumphed over the **Saracens** <note>original: "Saracenis", a medieval term for Muslims</note>, took Cordoba from them, etc.

At that time, the heresy of the **Sadducees** <note>a sect that rejected oral tradition and the Talmud</note> was troubling the Jews in Castile; for a certain Abben Altras had written a book.

The **Book of Abu Alfaraj** (Abu Alfaraj was his teacher), in which he taught that the Talmud and Mishnah and the other constitutions of the fathers were empty, and that the true Synagogue existed within his own party.

Against him, the aforementioned Rabbi dictated his *Kabbalah* <note>his work on tradition</note>, proving the truth of his Synagogue or Church <note>The author uses "Church" (Ecclesia) here to refer to the established Jewish community</note>, first from **succession**. For he traced his accounts back through 36 generations—all holding the same view—to the Prophets: the last being Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, whose succession could easily be traced back to Moses. For there were ten generations of the Great Synagogue from them to Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai, who was among the remnants of the Great Synagogue under Vespasian. Then, under the **Tannaim**, the doctors of the Mishnah or Talmudic text, five generations followed; then seven under the **Amoraim**, the doctors of the Gemara or Talmudic decisions; then another five under the **Geonim**, the interpreters of the Talmud; and from the Geonim until his own age, three generations, which makes 36 in number since the Prophets themselves.

Second, [he proves it] from **communion** <note>universal agreement</note>, since Synagogues throughout the whole world feel the same way: in Spain, Africa, Egypt, Palestine, Arabia, Babylonia, Persia, Elam, Greece, Germany, Italy, and Gaul (for our Gaul then abounded with Jews). They commonly receive the Talmud and Mishnah and the remaining traditions of the fathers. Furthermore, he proves this communion from the fact that the fathers and masters never disagree on the **root** of a commandment, but only on the appendices and circumstances. For example, they do not argue whether a lamp should be lit on the Sabbath or not, but rather with what oil it should be lit, or with what it should not...

Secondly, because they have few of their own communion, having only one synagogue in the deserts of Spain, and a few in Egypt and Palestine, who are not received by others but are excommunicated <note>original: "anathematizentur"</note>. "When the city of Jerusalem was captured, the Temple destroyed, the Jews driven out, and captives led away, and no end to their captivity and misfortune could be found, Rabbi Judah the Prince <note>original: "Rabbi Iuda Hannasi"; a 2nd-century CE rabbi and chief editor of the Mishnah</note> (who because of his humility, piety, and holiness was called our holy Master <note>original: "Rabbenu Haccadosch"</note>) found such great favor and kindness in the eyes of Emperor Antoninus, to whom he was very dear and intimate, that by his majesty's permission he gathered the most learned of the Jews from all parts of the empire to deliberate on what should be done. This was so that while the misfortune of the Jews increased more and more, the wisdom of the Jews and their learned men would not be killed or driven into exile, or the law itself perish utterly, but rather be preserved safe among the people. Although the *Kabbalah* or oral law <note>The term here refers to the "received" oral tradition, not the later mystical movement</note> was among them, because it was not lawful to commit the oral law <note>original: "Thorah scebealpe"</note> to writing, yet in consideration of the great misery of the Jews who were scattered throughout the entire world, he wrote down into a certain book everything that had remained in memory concerning the oral law from before and after Christ until his own time. This book is called the **Mishnah** <note>original: "Mischna"</note>, that is, the repeated or second law, called in Greek *deuterosis* <note>original: "δευτέρωσις"</note>, comprising six *Sedarim* <note>original: "sedarim"; the "Orders" or primary divisions of the Mishnah</note> or summaries, subdivided into sixty *Masikhtot* <note>original: "Massichtos"; the individual tractates or chapters</note>, or lower parts, or individual treatises. And thus again up to here these things have been recited by Rabbi Niccotzi <note>Likely referring to Moses ben Jacob of Coucy, author of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol</note>, etc."

To conclude this chapter, we will say that there are several kinds of Talmudists: namely, those who preceded the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and those who were after the said coming until the time the Babylonian Talmud <note>original: "Thalmud Babylonien"</note> was composed, which was in the year of Salvation 477. Both are called Talmudists because the Talmud was woven and composed from their writings. For this reason, the ancient Hebrew doctors were also not inappropriately called by this name, Talmudists; but the recent or younger doctors have been commonly named Talmudists, who, having lived a long time after the others, tried to pervert and destroy the testimonies of the law and the Prophets concerning the Messiah against the Christian law, so that they might retort against the opinion of the aforementioned ancient Talmudists. And it is very certain that these recent or younger Talmudists can easily be convinced of falsehood, both by the aforementioned ancient Talmudists who preceded the coming of our said Lord Jesus Christ, and by those who lived after the aforementioned...

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE...

André Osiander <note>A 16th-century German Lutheran theologian</note>, in chapter 15 of his *Evangelical Harmony*, speaks of seven types of Pharisees according to the Jewish Talmud. The author of *The Bundle of Time* <note>original: "Faiſceau des temps," referring to the *Fasciculus temporum*, a popular world history by Werner Rolevinck</note> also adds the Arboneans and Genistes, as confirmed by François de Belleforest in book 2, chapter 4 of his *Universal History*. Carlo Sigonio, in book 5, chapter 11 of his *Republic of the Hebrews*, provides a list of other sects among the said Hebrews, distinct from those previously mentioned. A certain individual named Otthon Henonius, in his *Antiquities of Barbarian Philosophy* (the treatise titled *Indicus*, chapters 21 through 25), discusses this quite extensively, even speaking of the Rechabites <note>original: "Recabees"</note> and their successors the Essenes or Hossians; Gilbert Génébrard does the same in book 2, pages 197 and 198 of his *Chronography*.

As for the Hebrew Rabbis, we learn that the Hebrews have always named those of the greatest and most eminent knowledge among them Rabbanim <note>original: "רבנים"</note> or Rabbis, which is to say masters or persons of great dignity. In fact, he among the Hebrews who possesses great learning in the Holy Scripture is always called Rabbi <note>original: "רבי"</note>, meaning master, and among the Chaldeans, Rabbon <note>original: "רבון"</note>, which means the same. These words come from the root *Rab* <note>original: "רב"</note>, which in Latin means "great" or "much" <note>original: "multus"</note>. The power and virtue of this word is explained in several places in the Talmud, in the *Tishbi* of Elias Levita <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note>, and in the discourse of Angelo Canini on the explanation of passages from the New Testament.

For a specific explanation of the words mentioned above, we refer to the statement of Porchetus <note>Salvagus Porchetus, a 14th-century Genoese monk who wrote against Jewish doctrines</note> in part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*, where he notes that Rabbi Nathan says the following in the Talmud: "The word Rabbi is attributed to the Sages of the land of Israel, upon whom hands were laid in the assemblies and councils of the Hebrews." This is said because of the "imposition of hands" by the elders and ancients, who place their hands upon someone and name him *Rabbi*, "my master." These Hebrews grant power to this created and initiated Rabbi to judge cases that deserve punishment—a ceremony which is still practiced today in the promotion of Jewish Rabbis.

Furthermore, we find in the same Talmud the terms *Rabban*, *Rabbana*, and *Rabbó*. The word *Rabbó*, which is pure Syriac, does not merely signify a simple master or Lord, but one who is called by the Greeks *Kyrios* <note>original: "κύριος"</note> <gloss>Lord <note>original: "x κύριος"</note></gloss> and by our legal scholars "he who possesses absolute power" <note>original: "ille qui habet merum imperium"</note>. Indeed, when the Hebrews mention God in the Mishnah, they use the word *Ribbon* <note>original: "ריבון"</note>. This is why Mary Magdalene saluted our Lord Jesus Christ, raised from death to life, by the name *Rabboni* in chapter 20 of the Gospel of Saint John; in the Syriac language, this carries the weight of "My Lord who knows God." Before the resurrection, no one had called him *Rabboni*, but only *Rabbi*. Be that as it may, one finds in some parts of the Talmud that *Rabbi* is a more excellent title than *Rab*, and *Rabbá* or *Rabbó* is more excellent than *Rabbi*. For this reason, it is said that our Lord Jesus Christ forbade Christians from calling any mortal by the name *Rabbon*.

Many great and curious investigations worthy of note on this matter are recited by Sebastian Münster in his Hebrew and Chaldean dictionaries and in his annotations on chapter 21 of Genesis; by Sante Pagnini in his *Hebrew Treasure* under the word *Rabbi*; by Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie in his preface to the Syriac New Testament and in his Syro-Chaldean dictionary under the words *Rab*, *Ebed*, and *Ray* <note>original: "רב עבד ריי"</note>; and also by Johannes Mercerus in his booklet on abbreviations.

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

Priests and Levites for spiritual matters only—though the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council or court of justice in ancient Israel</note> were not excluded from it either—which one should in no way doubt was the same script we have today. This is evidenced by these two Hebrew letters, **ס**, *Samech*, and **ם**, *Mem* finals, which were preserved whole within the fragments of the first tables of law that were broken because of the Golden Calf <note>According to Jewish tradition, because these letters are closed loops, they were held in place miraculously when the Ten Commandments were engraved through the stone</note>. This writing was afterwards released indifferently to the public by Ezra upon the return from the Babylonian captivity. The other set of characters, which are said to be those of the Samaritans, served for profane <term>profane: here meaning secular or non-religious</term> purposes, such as justice, civil administration, trade, and similar worldly affairs. Consequently, the script used by the ancient Chaldeans was vulgar and used by all the Jewish people; it was later shared with the Phoenicians. Just as Syriac and Arabic arose from Hebrew, the Greek script was born from the Phoenician, and consequently the Latin script, which consists entirely, or nearly so, of Greek capital letters, as we shall demonstrate hereafter.

Berossus and Saint Jerome, in his prologue to the Galatians and on Chapter 9 of the Prophet Ezekiel, and in his preface to the Book of Kings, along with the Hebrew author of the *Massekhet Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Masechet Sanhedrin" — a tractate of the Talmud dealing with the law and the priesthood</note>, write that after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple under Zerubbabel, Ezra found the Hebrew letters which the Jews and we ourselves still use today. This seems to be confirmed by Philo the Jew in Book 2 of *The Life of Moses*. Some modern scholars agree with this more readily than with all that has been said above, seeing as the Hebrews and Jews before this Ezra used Samaritan characters, which I treat at length hereafter in a separate chapter on the Samaritan language. Some among the Rabbis themselves agree with this, holding for a certainty that these Samaritan characters were the first in the world. They allege certain reasons for this, among others that these Samaritans always possessed the Torah, or Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>, in this, their own particular Samaritan script. Furthermore, the most ancient medals and coins of gold, silver, and other metals—which have been found from time immemorial in the ruins and countless locations of Jerusalem and Palestine—were inscribed and engraved with Samaritan letters. This is confirmed by Benito Arias Montano in Volume 3 of the *Apparatus*, in the chapter on the Shekel near the end, and after him by François Louis in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, Chapter 1. This is a thing which denotes that the Hebrew letters of today are not the same as the first and most ancient ones.

So it was that the Hebrews or Israelites, during the revolt of the ten tribes when they split from the crown of Judah under Rehoboam, son of Solomon—with whom only Judah and Benjamin remained—went to establish themselves under Jeroboam in the midst of Judea, in the region of Samaria at Shechem, the capital city of their entire state. They declined into idolatry, and because they kept the ancient Hebrew characters, Ezra (or Jeshua his son, the High Priest) and the other Jews who had remained in the true religion of the Great God, wishing to have nothing in common with them, chose to use and serve other letters and scripts that were entirely different, which they invented from that time on. The Samaritans, together with their descendants and posterity until today, have always kept the ancient characters of their fathers and ancestors.

It is true that this Kabbalistic method, insofar as it does not stop at the letter—which of itself can only be dead and unable to supply or furnish us with living intelligence—but instead rises up to make a display of all nature, can easily be subdivided into those senses mentioned above. However, it is one degree inferior to the anagogical and divine sense, which perfects and accomplishes all the others and in which all of them are comprised. This is something I could easily and readily prove with great deductions of words if time and leisure permitted. 

But passing further, I will say that under allegory, some have included and numbered the "typical" sense, upon which allegory depends. This figure has divisions and parts which are as follows: the first and oldest in terms of history, but of lesser extent than any of the others, is **The Equal** or **Judaic**, because its limits do not go beyond the enclosure of the synagogue. The second, already much more embracing, is named **Christian** or **Evangelical**. The third, which surpasses the second as much as the second surpasses the first, is called **Spiritual**. The fourth, which brings the Hebrew people back into the Greek Church, is rightly called by a name mixed of two: **Greco-Jewish**. The fifth, which considers in the cloudy mirror of the Hebrew people the pure, shining, and transparent crystal of the Latins, can be named **Latino-Jewish**. The sixth is called the **Christian Spiritual**. And the last, which contains the other six, deserves the title of **New Jerusalem**, seeing as in it the others come to complete their course and revolution.

Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism.</note> celebrate the letters of this word מלח *Malach* <note>original: מלח (*Melach*)</note>, which signifies salt, for rising in the calculation of their numbers to 78. For *Mem* is worth 40; *Lamed*, 30; and *Het*, 8. Now, divide these 78 in whatever way you wish, and there will always result some number that represents a mystery of the divine names. For example, half is thirty-nine, as much as the letters of כוזו *Chuzu* <note>original: כוזו (*Kuzu*), a protective name of God often written on the back of Mezuzah scrolls.</note> amount to—the "sheath" or "scabbard," as they interpret it, of the Great Name—namely *Kaph* twenty, *Vav* six, *Zayin* seven, and *Vav* again six. If divided into three parts, each will amount to twenty-six, which is the number of the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton|The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</term> יהוה: in six parts, they will be thirteen, which are equal to the measure of piety <note>The Hebrew word for "One" (*Echad*) also totals 13.</note>; in thirteen parts, they will be six, which is the value of the *Vav*, a letter representing the life from above, and six is the first perfect number. In twenty-six parts, it will be the number of the most holy and sacred Trinity, three; in thirty-nine parts, two, which is the value of the *Beth*, a symbol of the Word, or the second person and the "house of ideas" of the Archetype; and finally, the seventy-eight denote as many units, each of which represents the unity of a single God.

It is exactly the same with the word לחם *Lechem* <note>original: לחם</note> meaning bread, which is an anagram of the preceding word, whereby the letters similarly yield seventy-eight: *Lamed* thirty, *Het* eight, and *Mem* forty. But יין *Iain* <note>original: יין (*Yayin*)</note> or wine is worth only seventy, a number proceeding from the multiplication of ten by 7, which concerns the soul, which has its seat in the blood, into which wine is very easily converted. By this means, the Divinity has always taken great delight in these two substances of bread and wine, both for the mystery they denote of His Church—composed of many souls united in a common consent of belief, in imitation of how bread is made of many grains of wheat kneaded together, and wine is pressed from clusters of grapes—and because of the incorruptibility in which they participate more than any others, arising from the quintessence <term>quintessence|In alchemy, the purest "fifth element" or essence of a substance.</term> of the "water of life" <note>likely referring to alcohol or spirits</note> which resides there in great abundance. They are also coupled in the first book of Esdras, chapter six, with salt and oil as the four most useful and necessary things that Nature produces.

To make it short, Gematria <term>Ghematrie|Gematria; the system of assigning numerical value to a word or phrase.</term> is a circular revolution and a square and cubic multiplication containing many devices that depend principally on formal Arithmetic and Geometry employed in the profound meditations of the Hebrew Cabala. The aforementioned J. Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>, in the place cited above, says these words:

> The Cabalistic Art consists of three principal things: first, the calculation of numbers which is named Geometry <note>meaning Gematria</note>, as if it were a numerical dimension of earthly characters, which nonetheless depends on that Arithmetic which, due to its abstract simplicity, is not manageable by any senses, and therefore is not subject to a crude or novice craft. Thus, the first part was called Geometry rather than Arithmetic, although both actually count as one and the same in this art. Then, syllables are sometimes transmuted, so that there is a transformed word, or a word is simply inverted. Secondly, a letter is put for a word, and it is called *Notariacum* <note>Notarikon</note> from the shorthand of Notaries, since there every letter is noted at the top so as to be a sign of some whole word. Thirdly, this art consists in the change of letters, when one is ingeniously placed for another, and it is called commutation <note>Temurah</note>, which is why Rabbi Joseph the Younger of Salerno called the books he wrote on this art "The Garden"—

> -> ...[know] because of the three letters of this word ת <note>original: *Tav*</note>, as each of them designates one of the three portions of the Cabalistic art. For *Gimel* signifies *Gematria*, *Nun* signifies *Notaricon*, and *Tav* signifies *Temurah*. Thus, these are the parts of the entire art: *Gematria*, which is Arithmetic; *Notaricon*, as it were a system of shorthand; and *Temurah*, which is the transposition of elements, etc. <note>original Latin: *...nauerit.i.n. ת propter ternas huius dictionis literas...*</note> <-

In short, from what we have deduced above, we shall learn that the mystery or artifice of the aforementioned Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, called *Gematria*—a word undoubtedly corrupted from that of *Geometry* as I have already stated—by which they also understand *Arithmetic*, without which Geometry cannot exist, nor can measures and figures exist without numbers. Arithmetic, which is simpler and more formal, does quite well without Geometry, which is more material and coarse, just as figures are more material than numbers. Indeed, just as speech and writing cannot exist without some premeditation of thought, whereas thought can certainly exist without speech or writing. 

They might also, perhaps, have been moved to give these two sciences, joined together, the name of the second—namely Geometry—for it is a modern term, rather than that of the first, Arithmetic, because Plato magnifies it so much in the seventh book of the *Republic*, calling it the knowledge of *That which always is*. <margin>For geometrical knowledge is of that which always exists. <note>original Greek: *τῆς γὰρ ἀεὶ ὄντος, ἡ γεωμετρικὴ γνῶσίς ἐστιν* (Plato, Republic 7.527b).</note></margin> And in another place, according to the citation by Plutarch in the second question of the eighth book of the *Symposiacs* <note>Also known as *Table Talk* (*Quaestiones Conviviales*).</note>, he posits that God practices it continually. On this, he discourses that Lycurgus banished Arithmetical proportion from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note> in order to introduce Geometrical proportion. By the former, he denoted a tumultuous confusion of the Common People, which consists in number, and consequently concerns equality, where everyone is the master "like rats in straw." By Geometry, he denoted reason; because it lies in the difference of lines, longer or shorter. This denotes the authority that the great, and people of virtue, honor, counsel, and foresight, must have over the ignorant and brutal Common Populace—the majority of whom are also vicious, debauched, reckless, and hasty, seeking nothing but equality, than which there is nothing more unjust or pernicious in a state. 

By this means, God, in all things, insofar as they permit and as it can be done, withdraws equality from the world; he observes in its place merit geometrically, and dignity, concluding everything according to reason. Plato, therefore, by "the greater" and "the lesser," describes not only matter, as Aristotle would attribute to him, but forms as well, together with all the compounds of these two, according to the degrees of their essence and perfection—neither more nor less than Pythagoras before him had done through the even and the odd number, and Empedocles through the *Dense* and the *Rare* <note>original: *l'Espoix & le Rare*</note> which he established among the Principles. 

In imitation of this, the Cabalists have constructed systems of occult writing through the path of the aforementioned *Gematria*, established on the number of points on one hand, and lengths on the other, which they afterwards disguise in several ways. As I have already remarked above regarding this, B. de Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat and cryptographer famous for the "Vigenère cipher."</note> in his treatise on ciphers—wishing not to enter into too long an extension of these lines—contented himself with deducing eight differences, each of which serves reciprocally for two letters. These are discerned by certain small marks and secret notes difficult to perceive, for fear of engendering some suspicion of the ruse; thus does this figure particularly deduce it...

So it is that both the figures and the numbers of these three letters אמת *Emet*, truth, are, in whatever way one may take them, always solid; and those of falsehood, שקר *Secher* <note>Sheker</note>, on the contrary, are weak and wavering, following the proverb, *That a lie has short heels*, as presupposing that it is very easy to overturn. He invites us enough to apply our understanding there, especially since from this arises one of the most secret and ingenious modes of secret writing or ciphers, which consist of characters that are all equal, without any difference in form, quantity, or color: such as a sky all strewn with stars, a tree clothed in its leaves, a sea agitated by waves, or points and lines all alike. In short, it includes everything that nature produces that is perceptible to our eyes, or that we can imagine in our thoughts, as we have clearly shown above; so that this entire universe seems like a book, in which the wonders of the Creator are written, incessantly announcing His praises to those, at least, who know how to read it.

For it is a cipher, and a very hidden one for the most part, for those who contemplate the celestial bodies no differently than they would a great number of burning lamps in a Jewish synagogue or a Muslim mosque, or even—according to the philosopher **Xenophanes** <note>Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570 – c. 475 BC) was a Greek philosopher who proposed naturalistic explanations for celestial phenomena, such as stars being clouds of fire or burning coals.</note>—as many large coals lit at night and extinguished by day, without looking further into their order, placement, and arrangement. We leave aside the "intelligences" <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "intelligences" refers to the angelic beings believed to guide the movements of the celestial spheres.</note> that invisibly assist them, and I restrict myself to what can be perceived by the senses, upon which all efficacy in this case depends. This is what the <term>Gematria</term> <note>original: "Ghematrie". A Kabbalistic method of interpreting Hebrew scriptures by calculating the numerical value of words.</note> of the Hebrews reveals to us—the source of all secret ways of writing and ciphers that must be taken into account. And it introduces us through true <term>Arithmetic</term> and <term>Geometry</term>—which **Pythagoras** calls the "concordances and proportions," the principles of all things according to him—to infinite revelations of the secrets of the three uncommon sciences attributed, as has already been said, to the three worlds <note>The "three worlds" typically refer to the Elemental (Earthly), Celestial (Starry), and Intellectual/Supercelestial (Angelic/Divine) realms.</note>.

For just as in a beautiful palace, where there was first on the lowest floor a large quantity of exquisite utensils and furniture, such as wooden household goods, linens, and tapestries, and other such conveniences for human life; then above, in some secret wardrobe, many buffets of gold and silver plate, vases, and cups; and at the very top, a cabinet of jewels—of these three rooms, locked with strong padlocks and ironworks, one would need to have the keys to see with one’s own eye what is there. The same is true of the three worlds, for which the three occult sciences are the true keys, which alone can unlock for us the secret treasures within, as is said in **Isaiah 29**: *The vision of all these things will be to you like a sealed book, which, when presented to one who knows letters to read it, he will answer that he cannot, because it is closed; and the ignorant person will say the same.*

-># HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF<-

...heretical, a false and erroneous understanding that leads it to perdition. Similarly, there have never been lacking anywhere, nor in any profession or doctrine, strayed minds who have wandered from the straight path and perverted all this beautiful knowledge into vain abuses, illicit curiosities, and impious superstitions. Some have done so under the cover and name of **Kabbalah**; others under the title and quality of **Magic**. This science was once so honored that **Plato**, in the *Charmides* <note>A dialogue of Plato concerning temperance and the "medicine of the soul."</note>, calls it the true medicine of the soul, through which the soul acquires perfect tranquility and the body a healthy state. And in the *First Alcibiades*, he notes that it used to be taught to the children of the great Kings of Persia by their theologians and philosophers called **Magi** <note>Zoroastrian priests of ancient Persia, whose name became the root for the word "magic."</note>, in order to teach them how to shape their empire and rule upon the pattern and model of the order and governance of the universe.

And others finally have slandered all the third science, called **Chemistry** or **Alchemy**, viewing it merely as the lures and false baits of a heap of riches born in an instant through imaginary metallic transmutations. These worthy individuals, who so carefully applied their study to it, never aspired to such things. Rather, they sought through it remedies more sovereign than common ones against the accidents to which the weakness of the flesh subjects us, and wished by the same means to smelt metals—the most beautiful, permanent, and admirable substance that nature produces. For besides the diversity of ornaments coming from them, with which a person may adorn and deck themselves, and besides the many conveniences human life receives from them in agriculture, navigation, and in all kinds of arts and trades (which without them would remain incomplete), and finally the medicines made from them, for both external and internal use, their wonder in all this is that they can be metamorphosed in infinite ways without losing their specific form. They always restore themselves to their original state—unless by a very ingenious artifice and very long preparations—notwithstanding their having been reduced to impalpable powder, lime, salt, water, oil, glass, enamel, and similar alterations.

Their intention was as stated above, and not a vain and frivolous greed: to discover through this elementary science the hidden progress of nature, which is nothing else—according to **Empedocles** <note>A Greek philosopher who proposed that all matter is composed of four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> and **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that nature is a mixing and un-mixing of eternal substances.</note>—than the mixing and separation of elements. It is around this that **Chemistry** or **Alchemy** revolves, which is why it is called <term>Spagyric</term> <note>A term likely coined by Paracelsus, from the Greek words *spao* (to separate) and *ageiro* (to combine).</note>, as it separates and rejoins substances. And in the revelation of these beautiful secrets, the glory of Him who is their first author is manifested, taking His delight therein, just as we His creatures do in the pursuit of their hidden and latent causes, with their properties and effects. This is one of the most favorable nourishments for the soul; for it serves us as a ladder to climb on high and an elevation of our thoughts out of the sensuality of this human husk, which seeks only—by a troublesome counterweight—to pull them down and keep them submerged in idle pleasures and beastly concupiscences. 

This is aided by that false and treacherous deceiver, our inveterate adversary and cursed ancient serpent, named by the Kabbalists <term>Hazael</term> <note>Often associated in mystical texts with fallen spirits or the "shadow" side of the elemental world.</note>, father of <term>Tamah</term> <note>A Hebrew term meaning "impurity."</note> and <term>Lilith</term> <note>In Jewish folklore, a female demon and the "first wife" of Adam, representing night and impurity.</note>, who are pollution and filth. This being, as the <term>Zohar</term> <note>The foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah.</note> says, is the final end of all flesh where he predominates, and in the blood, as they are of the earth. As it is written in Genesis 3: *You shall eat dust all the days of your life* <note>original: "Terram comedes cunctis diebus vitae tuae"</note>. From which he does not stray...

These two numbers, three and four, which when added together make 7, if you multiply them by each other, will produce 12—exactly as many as there are signs in the Zodiac. By this, one sees the great affinity the planets have with them. It is the same from 7 to 12 as it is from 6 to 8. For 2 and 4 make 6, and 2 times 4 gives 8. These signs serve as houses <term>domiciles: In astrology, the specific zodiac sign where a planet is said to be "at home" and most powerful</term> for the planets, in the manner of the 64 black and white squares on the back of a game board <note>The author compares the arrangement of the cosmos to the strategic layout of a chessboard</note>, for the different positions of the pieces in a game of chess, and their various arrangements and aspects toward one another. There is nothing more suitable than this to represent the movements of the celestial bodies. The same is true for the multiple combinations of letters, both in general in all kinds of writing, and particularly in square ciphers <note>Likely referring to "magic squares" or cryptographic tables used in mystical traditions</note>, which have several meanings beneath the same character. For the aspects and habits of the planets in the signs, when joined with the four elements from which all bodies are produced, symbolize the characters of writing that constitute words. 

Furthermore, these 12 signs, which Plato calls the "gates of Heaven"—of which Capricorn is called the *Ascendant* <note>The rising point</note> because the Sun begins to climb again within it, and the Crab <note>The sign of Cancer; original: *l'escreuice*</note> the *descendant* because, having arrived there, it declines once more—denote the 12 gates of the Holy Celestial City described in Revelation 21. To these are assigned as many Angels who assist there, divided three by three as guards for each of the four regions of the Heaven: East, West, South, and North, in the exact same way that astrologers distribute them. To each of these signs is assigned one letter from the "twelve simples" <note>In the *Sefer Yetzirah*, a foundational text of Jewish mysticism, the Hebrew alphabet is divided into 3 "mothers," 7 "doubles," and 12 "simples," the latter corresponding to the zodiac signs</note>, so called because they are always pronounced in the same way, just as the signs, for their part, always remain in the same property and virtue.

Thus our Savior, who participates in both of these two natures <note>The divine and the human</note>, held this number of twelve in high regard, as one can see in many places in the Gospel. It is seen again in Revelation concerning the aforementioned Holy City, all divided by 12, just as Plato organized his worldly city in the 5th and 6th books of his *Laws*. They are so in agreement with one another that it would not be possible to be more so; from this, one clearly sees the great sympathy and connection that exists between superior things and inferior things.

In the first place, it was not permitted to anyone except the King and the President of the Consistory <note>The Sanhedrin, the supreme judicial and religious council</note> to interrogate or inquire of God through this means of the Urim and Thummim, and even then only in matters of great importance: such as for undertaking a war, or if the Consistory—namely the Court that administered Justice—could not properly decide a case, nor offer any resolved opinion. In these cases, the King or the Judge who was inquiring turned his face toward the Priest he was questioning, while the Priest kept his own gaze fixed straight toward the Urim and Thummim, and the *Shem HaMephorash* <note>original: "Schemhammaphoras"; the explicit or hidden Name of God</note> underneath, being in the aforementioned ornament <note>original: "affiquet"; a decorative fastening or breastplate</note> on the breast of the Pontiff. Furthermore, the voice of the one who inquired had to be soft and quiet, and not loud or haughty, but only enough to be barely understood by the Priest in distinct words; and one must not ask two things at once, but only one, unless by chance necessity pressed. For even if two were proposed, the response was nevertheless given only for one, and then the letters from which it was to be formed, by the power of the great name Jehovah <note>original: "Iehoua"</note>, would begin to brighten and rise above the others. So that the Priest, having a good way to notice them, gathered in his mind what he saw represented there. But if he were incapable or unworthy, they did not illuminate or rise at all, and he drew no response to his request. Some have written that these Urim and Thummim were nothing other than the letters of the name *Shem HaMephorash*, nor any stones added to the twelve of the ornament, but only those [twelve stones] which shone almost like fire, if the Divinity admitted the request; otherwise they remained in their original state. Indeed, *Ur* signifies fire; and as for Thummim, which comes from <term>תם</term> *Thom* <note>Hebrew root for completeness or integrity</note>, integrity or perfection, this denoted that these gemstones, as true and exquisite paragons of their kinds, without any flaw or defect, together gave off a brilliant luster, intermingled with various colors such as one sees in opals or in the rainbow, from which the Priest, inspired by a divine enthusiasm <note>meaning a state of being filled with the spirit</note>, came to understand and conjecture what the Divinity portended.
