### C H A P T E R X X I I.

IN the preceding chapter, we spoke in passing of visions and divine dreams without explaining them particularly, reserving the full treatment of them for this chapter. To enter into the matter, we must say that we must turn to the Hebrew prophets to find the true sources of all philosophy and the occult sciences. This is because they read (according to St. Augustine in the first book of *On Free Will*) in the "Book of Life." Because of this, Eusebius, in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, not only prefers them to the Greek philosophers, but even prefers the simple Hebrew theologians. In comparison to the Hebrews, he says, the others—though there are some very excellent ones among them, even admirable for a superficial subtlety of understanding—appear very insignificant regarding the solid foundation. Such was the foundation upon which the visions of the Hebrew prophets were placed and established: they gazed without any obstacle or hindrance, as if in a very certain mirror, at the first model and original of all created things in their real and true existence. Whereas the reasonings of the natural philosophers depend on the bodily senses, which are most of the time uncertain and deceptive; this is what moved Democritus to speak of a certain deep well where he said truth was hidden.

Some serve the office of simple vowels, nine in number: *Pathath*, *Cametz*, *Tzere*, *Segol*, *Scheua*, *Sirec*, *Solem*, *Schurec*, and *Meloppé*. The compounds are three in number: *Hateph-pathath*, *Hateph-cametz*, and *Hateph-segol*. Others do not signify or denote any vowels but suggest the qualities of the letters in a dual way, by moving and changing the natural voices of the letters, or demonstrating how they should be taken and pronounced. The diversity of these cannot be known by the varied shape of the figures, but by the property of the places where they are placed and located. They are four in number: namely *Dagesch*, *Raphe*, *Holem*, and *Mappic*, as can be seen in the Hebrew grammars of Clenard, Quinquarbre, Cornelius Bertramus, and others cited below. As for the Hebrew accents, they are commonly distinguished into two orders: some are named "Kings," fifteen in number, and the others "Ministers," seven in number, according to Elias Levita in his Hebrew grammar and *Book of Canticles*, and Sebastian Münster in his Hebrew grammar. Some modern authors assert that up to 34 are found, specified in this fashion: *Dagges*, *Rebia*, *Tebir*, *Zakef*, *Little Zakef*, *Great Zakef*, *Segolah*, *Macaf*, *Rafé*, *Pessif*, *Legarme*, *Meteg*, *Gaiah* with *Sheua*, *Sof*, *Passuf*, *Gheress*, *Gheressin*, *Meaielah*, *Simple Merca*, *Double Merca*, *Tifca*, *Pasta*, *Ietif*, *Mahpach*, *Munach*, *Hilni*, *Mercabel*, *Iarcah ben Iomo*, *Athnach*, *Darga*, *Zarchaz*, *Salseceleth*, *Talissa*, *Talfa*, *Carne*, *Parah*, *Pazer*. The discourse above must be considered all the more marvelous and admirable considering that in what remains to us of so many works or books that can be seen or read today in any language whatsoever, we can only observe seven primary and principal very ancient languages: namely Hebrew, Assyrian, Egyptian, Chaldean, Arabic, Greek, and Latin. This moved Raphael Volaterran <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar from Volterra</note> in book 33 of his *Commentaries* to write these words: "Therefore, seven dialects <note>original: 'catalecti'</note> and as many types of letters are found. The Assyrians or Babylonians are the oldest; then the Arabs. The Jews do not differ much from the Arabs in their characters and language. The Egyptians and Ethiopians, though very ancient, used figures of animals and other things more truly than letters, which they call hieroglyphs <note>original: 'hieroglypha'</note>—no one has yet understood them. The Ethiopians, however, have used Babylonian letters until the present day. After these came the Greeks, then the Latins, and finally the Dalmatians from corrupted Greek. The Saracens today, as well as the Tartars and Turks, although their dialects differ slightly among themselves, all use Arabic letters; the Turks also use the Greek letters of those they rule." <note>original: 'Igitur catalecti septem... quibus dominantur'</note>. Just as all things that can be spoken and written are comprised and contained within these 22 letters, so too are there 22 divine books in which are comprised all things that can be known and proclaimed. This was the view held among Christians by Origen, Epiphanius, Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, Saint Jerome, and Rufinus. Some among the aforementioned Hebrews—namely Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra and Rabbi David Kimchi—count 24 books according to the same 22 letters of the said Hebrew alphabet, adding to them three times the letter י [*Yod*] in honor of the four-letter name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>. Out of reverence for this name, these Hebrews have the custom of expressing it only in writing and not by voice or word, using three *Yods* in the manner of the Kabbalists <note>Mystics of the Jewish tradition</note> in this way: ייי. This division was followed by some of the ancient Greeks, as it was very suitable for the 24 letters of their Greek alphabet; it was also adopted by some ancient and modern Latins, based on the mystical number of the 24 elders worshiping the Lamb who opens the book sealed with seven seals, which no one could open in heaven or on earth, as mentioned by Saint John in Revelation, chapter 5. Some other Hebrews count 27 books, equal to the number of characters resulting from the 22 simple elements that make up the whole Hebrew alphabet, plus the five final letters <note>Known as *sofit* letters, which change shape at the end of a word</note> repeated or doubled from it, which are formed differently at the beginning, the end, or the middle of Hebrew words. On this subject, one may specifically consult Saint Jerome in his prologue to Galatians, Epiphanius in his books on weights and measures, Abulensis <note>Alonso Tostado</note> on Galatians, Rabbi René Benoist in books 1 and 2 of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "stromates"</note> on the Bible, Sixtus of Siena in his *Library*, book 1, section 1, and Brother Louis in book 1, chapter 3 of his *Globe of the Canons of the Holy Language*.

Concerning all this, the same Gregory the Theologian wrote in Greek hexameter and pentameter verses in his book of poems. <note>original Greek: "Δέχουσο τῶν ἐμῶν τ' ἔγκριτον..." These verses are from Gregory's poem *Concerning the Genuine Books of Inspired Scripture*.</note>

> Accept, my friend, the approved number of my books:
> The historical books of ancient Hebrew wisdom are twelve in all.
> First Genesis, then Exodus, and Leviticus,
> Then Numbers, then the Second Law [Deuteronomy].
> Then Joshua, the Judges, and Ruth the eighth.
> The ninth and tenth books are the Acts of Kings,
> And the Chronicles; finally, you have Ezra.
> There are five metrical [poetic] books, of which Job is first,
> Then David, then three of Solomon:
> Ecclesiastes, Song, and Proverbs.
> And likewise five of the prophetic spirit.

The same Hebrews call all these same books *Magdaffa* in their language—that is to say, "sanctification"—otherwise written as מקדשיה *Macdescya* <note>original: "Macdescya"</note>, "Holy thing of God," according to P. Galatin in book 1, chapter 1 of *The Secrets of the Catholic Faith*. This is because it makes its readers holy and enemies of all injustice, as well as despisers of this world who desire nothing other than eternal bliss. The Greeks name them in their language βιβλία <note>original: "βιβλία"</note>, which is to say "Books," *κατ' ἐξοχήν* <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν," a Greek phrase meaning "par excellence" or "preeminently."</note>, because these books alone are such that there are no others like them on the whole earth, and because within them the voice and word of the living God are contained and comprised, according to Porchetus in chapter 8, part 1 of his *Victory Against the Jews*. The aforementioned Hebrews have constantly held that the great Ezra—called *Josedech* the Priest in the first book of the Sacred Annals <note>original: "Annales sacrees"</note> and *Malachias* by the said Hebrews—was the last of all their Prophets. Upon his return from the Babylonian Captivity, being illuminated by the Holy Spirit, he dictated two hundred and forty books of words that were contained in the Holy Scriptures which had been burned during the destruction of Jerusalem. These books were set down in writing on boxwood tables by five excellent and swift scribes during forty entire days, just as this figure dictated them from his mouth. Of these books, he brought 126 to light; the others, composed of secret wisdom and more excellent science, he gave to be read only by the sages and doctors of the law. This is amply witnessed by the said Ezra in book 4, chapter 14 of Ezra in the Bible, and by Rabanus Maurus in *On the Institution of Clerics* <note>original: "de insti. Cleric."</note>, chapter 54, as cited above. On this subject, Friar Sixtus Senensis writes in book 2 of his *Holy Library* <note>original: "bibliotheq. saincte"</note> that in his time there was in his monastery at Bologna the Pentateuch of this Ezra, written on a single but very long membrane or sheet by his own hand, without any points or vowels according to the word of those Hebrews. Shalmaneser <note>Shalmaneser V, King of Assyria</note> therefore, coming to the aid of the King of Judah, defeated the King of Israel: and nevertheless led away with him a great number of Jewish prisoners, to whom he gave the Region of Itene <note>This likely refers to Halah or Gozan, regions of Assyrian exile</note> to inhabit, and this was the first captivity and dispersion of the Jews since they miraculously left Egypt: indeed, a short time after that, the Assyrian King constrained the Kings of Israel to pay him a tribute every year. In that time, the Prophets Hosea, Isaiah, Amos, Micah, and Jonah were in power.

After the death of the unfortunate Ahaz, Hezekiah his son succeeded to the crown. This Prince was quite different from his father, for he was prudent, just, religious, and God-fearing. Thus Jerusalem regained its former prestige in his time: for he so reformed the government and restored the service of God to such perfection that, as the Holy Scripture bears witness to him, the Kingdom of Judah never had such a King; he also lived in great prosperity and obtained great victories.

This Prince, not content with uprooting all idolatry—to which he saw the people strongly inclined—and wishing to fully restore the service of God, summoned the other ten tribes of Israel to live according to the Law that God had given them by the hand of Moses. To this several condescended, coming to sacrifice in Jerusalem and celebrate the Passover according to the ordinance of Moses; and nevertheless, according to what one can see in the holy writings, the others persevered in their idolatry and mocked his summons, despite whatever warnings the Prophets gave them. Because of this, they were often punished by the rods of God, both by Shalmaneser and by Sennacherib, who greatly oppressed them. In the first year of the reign of Hezekiah—even the fourth year of the reign of Hoshea <note>original: "Osias"</note>, King of Israel—this Assyrian Prince waged such a strong war against the seven <note>The text specifies seven tribes here, though traditionally ten tribes made up the northern kingdom</note> tribes of Israel for the space of three years that he constrained them to abandon their homeland and go to live as slaves among the Medes. And that is how the Jews were dispersed here and there among foreign nations, without ever returning to their homes, so that one cannot say what became of them afterward; this was the ruin and the end of the Kingdom of Israel, which had lasted three hundred and seventy years.

Shalmaneser, on the contrary, sent Assyrians to Samaria to inhabit it; these people, seizing all the country formerly inhabited by the Israelites, took the name of Samaritans. Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note>, however, takes this name as essential <note>meaning inherent to their nature</note>, but his opinion does not seem acceptable to the most learned and scholarly, who hold that they were called Samaritans for and because of Samaria, the capital city of that region. These Assyrians mixed the law of the Jews with their idolatry; thus, they were held in abomination as excommunicated people.

After the defeat and ruin of the Israelites, the Kingdom of Judah alone remained standing: for the good King Hezekiah, to save his people from the fury of King Shalmaneser and to maintain his people in peace, gave him great sums of gold, buying by this means peace for a long time. However, this unfaithful King broke his word to him and came with a large army with the intention of ruining the Kingdom of Judea as he had done that of Israel: but God, wishing to preserve his people, sent the

The Prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah to comfort him (for this Prophet lived at that time), and in one night the Angel of the Lord destroyed one hundred and eighty <note>original: "octante," a regional term for eighty</note> thousand men in the Assyrian camp; this carnage forced the others to retreat. And thus Hezekiah, having escaped this peril along with his people, lived the rest of his days peacefully in his kingdom. And after God had clearly demonstrated great miracles for the sake of the said King, he died peacefully, leaving Manasseh his son and successor to the kingdom.

This Prince did not follow the path of his father, but instead gave himself over entirely to all forms of idolatry, committing several abominable things against the law of God, into which he also led the people. Because of this, God was offended and stirred up the Assyrians against him, who chastised him so thoroughly that, besides the defeat of his men, he was made a prisoner and led captive to Babylon. However, he repented of his sin, which caused God to deliver him from the hands of the Assyrians, such that he returned to his estates and died there peacefully. Amon his son succeeded him, who, being wicked and iniquitous, was miserably killed; in his time lived the Prophets Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk. After him succeeded Josiah his son, who was a God-fearing Prince and very vigilant in the reformation of his people. For he drove all idolatry out of his kingdom—which was nonetheless deeply rooted in the hearts and souls of men—and repaired the temple, performing several other acts worthy of a holy and just king.

Despite this, the wrath of God could not be appeased against the Jews because of the idolatries committed during the time of Kings Amon and Manasseh. Nevertheless, for the sake of Josiah (who died poorly through his great folly <note>Josiah was killed at the Battle of Megiddo after intervening in an Egyptian military campaign that did not concern him</note>), God deferred the punishment of the Jewish people, as He did afterward. This King died of a wound he received on the day he fought against Necho <note>Pharaoh Necho II</note>, King of Egypt; in fact, this was well-deserved, for Necho asked nothing of him, but rather sought his friendship as much as he could, having no other intention than to employ his forces against the King of Assyria. Nevertheless, Josiah went against him out of a certain recklessness of heart, which cost him his life. His death was greatly regretted, even by the Prophet Jeremiah, who composed his *Lamentations* because of it.

Jehoahaz his son succeeded him, who was given to all iniquity and wickedness; therefore God did not permit him to reign more than three months. For Necho, who had already defeated his father, deprived him of his kingdom, making the land of Judea tributary for one hundred talents of gold and one of silver every year <note>Biblical accounts in 2 Kings 23 usually cite 100 talents of silver and one of gold; the author has likely inverted the metals</note>. Jehoahaz thus being deprived of his estates and led prisoner to Egypt, where he died, Jehoiakim his brother was installed in the kingdom, where he behaved very badly; for he was entirely given to idolatry and induced the people to do the same. Because of this, God raised up as an enemy against him King Nebuchadnezzar, who had already reigned 44 years in Babylon. This King, having obtained victory over the Jewish people, led away as slaves the greatest men of the whole country and carried off the vessels of the temple. The cause of this was that Jehoahaz <note>The author likely means Jehoiakim here, based on the context of the 11-year reign</note> gave aid to the King of Egypt against Nebuchadnezzar, against the advice of Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, having then reigned 11 years and remained a prisoner for three years, died in great poverty. He was succeeded by Jehoiachin, or Jeconiah, who followed the path of his father, being wicked like him; also in his time God began to deploy the very rigorous rods prepared by Him long ago against Jerusalem and deferred for the sake of Josiah.

just as the Prophets had predicted, for Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonofer," referring to the Neo-Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar II</note> came in person with a great army to besiege the city of Jerusalem. King Jehoiachin <note>original: "Ioachin"</note>, being unable to resist him, submitted to his will along with his mother, his wife, and the principal members of his household. Furthermore, he presented him with the vessels and treasures that were still in the temple; by which means this King Jehoiachin and the principal members of his court were led captive to Babylon. But Nebuchadnezzar, taking all the assurances and oaths of loyalty he could from Mattaniah <note>original: "Mathatias"</note>, uncle of King Jehoiachin, appointed and constituted him King of Judah and named him Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedechias"</note>. This King was one of the most iniquitous and wretched Princes there ever was; for not only was he ungrateful toward God for the great graces He had shown him—turning his back on Him and refusing to listen to what the Prophet Jeremiah <note>original: "Hieremie"</note> predicted to him—but he also broke his promise to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had installed him in the Kingdom, by denying him his friendship.

And if this King was worthless, the Priests were even worse, and the common people still more so, such that all manner of abominations and idolatries reigned in Judah, even to the point of profaning the temple, which was held sacred. And despite whatever remonstrances the Prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and others made to this King, his obstinacy nonetheless continued to grow. For this reason, God raised up King Nebuchadnezzar, who, to take vengeance upon this Zedekiah in the ninth year of his reign, came to overrun the land of Judah with a great and powerful army, and held Jerusalem under siege for the time and space of two years, where King Zedekiah had retreated for his safety.

But the besieged, pressed by famine and plague, and unable to endure the siege any longer, were constrained to put themselves at the mercy of the enemy, who, entering the city, put it to fire and blood. King Zedekiah was captured as he fled and, being brought before King Nebuchadnezzar, he had his children slain before his eyes, and afterward had both his eyes put out, leading him captive in this manner to Babylon. After his return, he sent Nebuzaradan <note>original: "Nabuzardã," the captain of the guard</note> to Jerusalem, who was one of his principal Captains, with the charge to ruin the temple. This occurred 400 years after the building of the temple by Solomon <note>original: "Solomõ"</note>. He did the same to the fortresses and buildings of Jerusalem, tearing down the walls of the city and ruining the palaces of the Kings of Judah. He also carried away all the metal that was in the temple and led away the priests and all the principal people, both of Jerusalem and of the entire country, with their wives and children, who remained captive in Babylon for 60 years.

This Babylonian captivity was the one so often spoken of in Holy Scripture and in the writings of the Jews, which occurred approximately 600 years before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. As for the common people, they were left in the country to cultivate the land under the charge of Gedaliah <note>original: "Godolias"</note>, the appointed governor in Judah. But this people mutinied and killed Gedaliah, because of which the remaining Jews, fearing the fury of Nebuchadnezzar, went to live in Egypt, leaving Jerusalem deserted and depopulated. St. Jerome <note>original: "S. Hierofme"</note>, in his book *Hebrew Questions* <note>original: "quest. Hebraiques"</note>, writes that since the capture and sack of Jerusalem, a full 50 years passed without man, beast, or bird entering it. In this, one could clearly recognize the great punishment deserved by this people, once so cherished and privileged by God. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]

Thereafter, it was not Hebrew, or Canaanite, but rather its closest dialect; for Syriac <note>Often used at this time to refer to Aramaic</note> approaches it more closely than the others. This is noted by Elias <note>Elijah Levita, a renowned 16th-century Hebrew scholar</note> in his preface to *Methurgeman* <note>A dictionary of the Aramaic translations of the Bible</note>, by the Talmudists, and by Friar Louys Portuguais <note>Luis de Sotomayor</note> in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Tongue and Divine Scripture*, Book 1, Chapter 1. The Canaanites and Arphaxadites—from whom, just as the Hebrew language came from Heber, so that same language is called "Canaanite" in Isaiah—although Adam <note>likely referring to the commentator Adam Sasbout</note> understands it there as Syriac. B. Arias Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano, a Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note>, in his *Canaan, or of the Twelve Peoples or Nations*, treating this question very extensively, states that the name of the Canaanites was common to all other nations, received from their father, and preserved for the sake of maintaining kinship, society, and providing mutual aid; the entire land was called Canaan, and the common language of all inhabitants, which others call Hebrew, was called the "Language of Canaan."

Regarding the Canaanite language used by the Tyrians, Sidonians, and other Phoenicians, it is nothing other than Arabic or Punic, spread and expanded by the ancient Phoenician colonies in Numidia, Mauritania Caesariensis, and Tingitana <note>Ancient regions of North Africa</note>, even in Spain, which was inhabited centuries ago by Phoenician colonies. And it is more likely that these wandering and vagabond Moors whom we commonly call *Cinganos* <note>An early term for the Romani people, often confused with "Gypsies" or "Egyptians"</note>—the Germans call them *Zegeiner*—first seen in our Europe in the time of our ancestors, were called *Gingan* from the province of *Canaan*, rather than *Vzies* or Egyptians from Egypt. Furthermore, it is very certain from the memoirs of the ancients that the Canaanites once took refuge in Mauritania and Numidia, from where this foreign race and nation first came to move into Europe when the Israelites, under the leadership of Joshua their General, drove them from their first seats and dwellings. This was verified by the statue that was formerly found both in the city of Tingis <note>modern-day Tangier</note>, the first and capital city of Mauritania Tingitana, and by the tablets commonly found in Numidia, of which the inscription on the statue and tablets was such or similar:
> We are the Canaanites whom Joshua the Robber has driven out. <note>original Latin: "Nos sumus Chananæi quos eiecit Iosua Latro."</note>
Which Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> also mentions under the word <term>Canaan</term> <note>original Greek: Χαναάν</note>: that is to say, *we are Canaanites, whom Joshua the Robber has driven from their country*, which Suidas repeated under the Greek word *Canaan*. See what Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss linguist and reformer</note> writes on this question in his commentary on the common reasoning of all languages and letters, and what we have deduced hereafter in the chapter on the Punic and Carthaginian language. Many other things worthy of great consideration on this matter are deduced by B. Pererius <note>Benedict Pererius, a Jesuit scholar</note> in his second volume of commentaries on Genesis, Book 15, marginal number 126, and in his select disputes on Exodus Chapter 3, and 15, dispute 10, citing the opinion of Andreas Masius in his commentaries on Joshua. We speak even more extensively of this question in the subsequent chapter on the Syriac language.

And since we have spoken above of the wandering and vagabond Moors, commonly called *Cinganes*, otherwise *Vzies*, or Egyptians of Egypt, we will now report what Abraham Ortelius <note>The famous Flemish cartographer and creator of the first modern atlas</note> writes of them in his *Geographical Treasury*.

According to Pliny, that part of Africa which is called "Proper" <note>Africa Propria, roughly modern-day Tunisia</note> is named Zeugitana. Aethicus calls it Zeugin. Marius Niger thinks that from this part of Africa emigrated that vagabond race of men, in the manner of Nomads, [wandering] across our Europe

wandering through various regions, whom the Italians call *Zingani* and *Zingari*; the High Germans call them *Zigeuner*; and the Low Germans call them *Egyptenaren* and *Heylieden* <note>original: "Egyptenaren, & Heylieden" — meaning Egyptians and Heathens or Gentiles</note>. We call them Egyptians because they claim to be exiles from "Minor Egypt" <note>A legendary or poorly defined region often cited in the Middle Ages as the home of the Romani people; the author admits he does not know its location</note>. Although Egypt is known to everyone, I have not yet learned from any trustworthy author that it is divided into a "Greater" and a "Lesser" part. Pierre Belon <note>A 16th-century French naturalist and traveler</note> testifies that the French call them *Baumiens* or *Bohemiens* (Bohemians). Pope Pius II writes that they came from the region of Zogoria, located near the Caucasus. Belon says they originate from Bulgaria and Wallachia, where the *Sicynni* once lived—a name not unlike *Zigeuner*. He also adds that he encountered the same people on the journey from Cairo to Macarea, as well as in some places along the banks of the Nile, but there they are considered foreigners. André Thevet <note>A French Franciscan explorer and writer</note> says that in those parts, the Arabs and Moors call them *Rasol heramy* <note>original: "Rasol heramy" — meaning "chief of robbers" or "highwaymen"</note>. The same Belon relates that this class of women has a house near Constantinople, in the city of Pera, divided into many small rooms, where they prostitute themselves to both Christians and Muslims; he says this is permitted to them by a privilege of the Turkish Emperor. Leo Africanus <note>A famous traveler and geographer of North Africa</note> also mentions that these *Zingavi* live in certain places in Africa, such as in Agadez and the borders of the Kingdom of Nubia. It is clear from historians that this nation first became known to our Europeans around the year 1417. They are a race of men living in extreme poverty under the open sky, filthy and sun-burnt. Their exotic appearance remains the same everywhere. They profess to be Christians, but they seek their livelihood through theft and fortune-telling—for they all wish to appear as <term>chiromancers</term> <note>palm readers</note>—by which they deceive common women and children. They have a leader chosen from among their own dregs, whom they obey. They use a peculiar and private language among themselves which no one else understands, though Aventinus asserts he has learned through experience that it is <note>original: "vindicam"</note> Wendish <note>likely referring to a Slavic dialect, though the Romani language is actually Indic in origin</note>.

> » <note>original: "lib.Panor.capit.13." — Referring to the *Panarion* by Epiphanius of Salamis.</note> (Book 1, Chapter 13) they rejected the Prophets, and some of them took only a single wife, and after her death, they fled marriage forever; others, entirely averse to marriage, embraced lifelong virginity. There also thrived among the Jews another kind of men, which, having borrowed some things from the Pharisees and others from the Sadducees, had fashioned a kind of monster. For in other matters, the followers of this sect agreed with the Pharisees, but with the Sadducees they denied the resurrection of the dead. The main point of their practice was that in Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter, they were baptized daily, thinking that men could not live unless they were immersed in water every day and by that means sanctified. For this reason, according to the same Epiphanius (Book 1, Chapters 17 and 18 of the *Panarion*), they were called **Hemerobaptists** <note>From the Greek for "daily baptizers."</note>, to whom were added the **Nazareans**, who neither accepted the books of Moses nor held sacrifices in common with the rest, and avoided the eating of living creatures as if they were unclean.

Those who have traveled to the Levant <note>The Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East.</note> know well enough that there are today Jews in that country who possess very ancient medals and gold and silver coins engraved around the edges with Samaritan letters praising the city of Jerusalem. These represent, on one side, a vessel full of manna with the inscription in Samaritan letters *Sekel Israel* <note>original Hebrew: "Shekel Israel," meaning Shekel of Israel.</note>, and on the other side, the rod of Aaron, with the inscription *Ierusalem Kedusa* <note>original Hebrew: "Yerushalayim Ha-Qodeshah," meaning Jerusalem the Holy.</note>, as things greatly memorable in the divine law. These Jews maintain that these pieces are a very great treasure, even though they hate the Samaritans and their memory more than the plague. This is because, through the mere sight of these coins, they contemplate their ancient characters and letters, which their first and most ancient Fathers used from the beginning of the world. **Rabbi Moses of Gerona** <note>Also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270).</note> in his *Commentaries* near the end of the Pentateuch, asserts that he saw and handled one of these coins in the Holy Land in his time, as is recounted at length by **Benedito Arias Montano** in his *Apparatus* for the Bible in the chapter on the Shekel. What is more, among those Samaritans currently in the Levant, there are some called *Chus* or *Chussebarich*, who are Samaritans in name only, being descended from the people of the ancient colony sent from **Cuthah** and Babylon into Samaria some years after the destruction of Samaria, according to the 4th Book of Kings, Chapter 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 17.</note>, and Book 9, Chapter 15 of the *Antiquities* <note>Referencing Flavius Josephus.</note>. For this reason, they are Samaritans only by their religion, but Cuthites by their nation, as reported by **Elias Levita** in his *Tishbi* in the interpretation of the word *Cuth*, **Gilbert Génébrard** in Book 1 of his *Chronography*, and **Joseph Scaliger** in Book 5 of *The Emendation of Time* in the chapter on the first year of the Samaritans. These Cuthites or Samaritans assert that, commonly, when digging the earth around Jerusalem, such coins are often found, bearing the aforementioned words in Samaritan letters as a mark of great antiquity. Now, it should be noted that the Samaritans have not entered the city of Jerusalem at all since the time of King Solomon, and they have not deigned to call it by the title "Holy," because they worshipped idols as semi-Jews and Gentiles on a mountain outside the aforementioned city; they would have been very far from wanting to honor that city with their own letters, as they regarded it as their adversary and enemy. To finish, [the reading] was not interrupted by the Jews; rather, after the lesson of the Law and <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible, the Torah</note>, they have always added some passages from the Prophets that are most consistent with and approaching the subject of the <term>Parashah</term> <note>The weekly Torah portion read in the synagogue</note>. To this conforms our own manner of employing, in our lessons of Matins for the extension of the Gospel text cited there, the singing of one of the Homilies of the ancient Fathers. A great figure of this time, interpreting the Greek word *archipheréktai* <note>original: α’ρχιφερέκται; literally "chief of the sections"</note> which the Emperor Constantine used in his decree—*that it be permitted for the Hebrews, according to the handed-down law, to read the scriptures in Latin or Greek, or another language, etc.* <note>original: "vt liceat Hebræis ſecundùm traditam legem ſcripturas Latinè vel Græcè, vel alia lingua legere &c."</note>—wrote the following: *The word is a hybrid, partly Greek and partly Hebrew; their duty was to read and interpret those sections of the Law or Prophets which the Hebrews call Parashiot and Perakim, and to adapt to them the sub-divisions of the greater treatises of the Talmud, which the same Jews call Perakim. For what our fifty books of the <term>Pandects</term> <note>The Digest of Roman Civil Law compiled under Justinian</note> are, so are the sixty greater treatises of the Talmudists; as many as we have Titles, they have Perakim. Therefore, these archipheréktai are like masters of the titles, to whom the titles of the Talmud are known to a hair.* <note>original: "Vox eſt hybrida, partim Græca... ad vnguẽ noti Thalmudis tituli."</note>

With these remarks made, we shall say that the ancient Chaldean language was the Babylonian tongue—Babylon being, according to the Prophet Jeremiah in chapter 21 and Ezra in book 1, chapter 5, at that time the head of the entire dominion of the Chaldeans. In this regard, Berosus <note>An ancient Babylonian priest and historian</note> attests that a short time after the universal deluge, there were several books written in this language concerning the state and disposition of the world, and the various columns and cities that were constructed before said Deluge. This is confirmed by Sebastian Münster in his *Chaldean Grammar* and Guy le Fèvre de la Boderie in the preface of his *Chaldean Grammar*. 

Regarding the characters of the letters of this language, some hold that they were the Samaritan characters previously represented in the figure in the preceding chapter; others hold that they were those said to have been given to Abraham at the crossing of the river when he left Chaldea to come to the land of Canaan—since called Palestine, Judea, and the Holy Land—which are also represented in the figure in the preceding chapter on the origin of the Hebrew language and its characters. Some Hebrews do confess that the Chaldeans had letter characters proper to themselves, which the Prophet Daniel seems to declare in his works when he says that Ashpenaz taught him and his companions the letters of the Hebrews and the Chaldean tongue. Indeed, the Hebrew <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Mystics following the Kabbalah tradition</note> have assured that over the characters of the letters and the Chaldean language presided what they call *Bat Kol* <note>original: Bat hcol; literally "daughter of a voice," often referring to a divine echo or heavenly voice</note>, the universal voice, which the *Zohar* and other most distinguished Kabbalists interpret as the mediating and moving power of this universe—namely, the intellect of the Messiah or of the Word, the "mind of minds" <note>original: mens mentium</note> as they call it, through whom the sovereign Father moves everything. 

Even Saint Jerome, in his preface to the Book of Kings, held that the Chaldeans had twenty-two letter elements with the same sound as those of the Hebrews, but diverse and dissimilar, as I will show hereafter. But to say and affirm in truth what these letter elements were is entirely impossible to do, because the Jews themselves, before the time of the same Saint Jerome, were accustomed to writing and copying Chaldean books in Hebrew characters. This is believed to have been done and practiced in the books of Daniel and Ezra which are in our hands.

But regardless of that, it is a very certain thing that both this language and the ancient writing have suffered several mutations and changes. For during the seventy years that those Hebrews remained captive in the city of Babylon, there occurred a mixing and commingling of the Hebrew and Chaldean languages, such as we can visibly see through the writings of the Prophet Daniel, which are woven from both the Hebrew and Chaldean languages. This was well noted in his time by Saint Jerome in his preface to this Prophet, as well as in the Writings of Ezra—which nonetheless closely approach the dialect of the Syriac language—along with the writings of Tobit and Judith, as the aforementioned Saint Jerome confirmed in his prefaces to them. 

This is seen even better and more clearly in the **Targums** or Chaldean Paraphrases of **Onkelos**, who is held to have been the son of the daughter of the Emperor Titus. This Targum was first translated into the Latin language at Strasbourg in the year 1546 by Paul Fagius. It is also seen in the Targums or Paraphrases of **Jonathan son of Uzziel**, one of the disciples of **Hillel** (the great Hebrew teacher) and a fellow student of **Simeon the Just** (who received our Lord Jesus Christ in his arms). Regarding him, the Jews in the *Bava Batra* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning civil law and the history of scripture</note> assert that while this Jonathan was composing that Targum, if a fly or any other bird happened to fly over him or his paper, it was immediately burned and consumed by fire from Heaven, without any damage to the said paper. 

One finds this also in the other Targums or Paraphrases by the Chaldean translators or **Talmudists** of the books of the Hebrew Bible, regarding whom one should consult **Lyranus** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose literal biblical commentaries were highly influential</note> in his commentaries on the eighth chapter of the Prophet Isaiah, and Paul Fagius in his versions of these Targums or Paraphrases. He translated the sense of the passages and explained all the most obscure words, so that whatever was doubtful or hiddenly written concerning the Messiah, he rendered certain and very clear. Indeed, his edition seems not so much a translation as a gloss and exposition, which the Hebrews call a **Targum** <note>Hebrew: תרגום</note>, that is, a translation. ...no one would dare [to challenge him]; but rather, all people everywhere should accord no less faith to his work than to the text itself, both because of the man’s sound judgment and skill, and especially because of the truth of his interpretation and exposition. Therefore, whenever they find anything ambiguous and difficult to understand in the text of the Holy Books, they always recur to this same translation and clarification.

Hence, regarding this same *Jonathan*, as is read in the *Bava Batra* <note>A tractate of the Talmud; original: "baua bathra"</note>, the masters have said that during the hour in which he was occupied with this edition and exposition, if a fly or any winged creature flew over him or over the parchment, it was immediately consumed by fire from heaven without any damage to the parchment itself. From this they infer that *Jonathan* did not produce the entire *Chaldean* Bible.

Without doubt, *Jonathan* translated the entire Bible into *Chaldean* (as I said before, and I think it is not unknown to you). But his translation of the *Pentateuch* is extremely rare, and for that reason it is denied by those who have not seen it. I, however, saw it once, and it begins thus: *The Lord created the heavens and the earth* <note>original Aramaic in Hebrew script: ברא יי ית שמיא וית ארעא</note>. That of *Onkelos* begins thus: *In the beginning, from eternity, He created the heavens and the earth* <note>original Aramaic in Hebrew script: בקדמין מן אדלא ברא ית שמיא וית ארעא</note>.

Here also, *Onkelos* translated and explained the entire Bible in *Chaldean*. His edition and exposition, although now (except for the *Pentateuch*) it is hardly found anywhere, is nevertheless of no less value among the Jews than that of *Jonathan* which we mentioned. They also call it the *Targum*, because it is also in *Chaldean*, just like the other; even if both are written in Hebrew characters. Furthermore, the edition of *Jonathan* himself on the Psalter is in the possession of very few people. Those who have it hide it to the best of their ability because of the mysteries of the Christian faith which it contains.

Finally, Simeon, the son of *Hillel*, whom the *Talmudists* surname *Tzadic* <note>The Righteous; original: צדיק</note> because of his exceptional holiness—in whom (as it is said in the *Pirkei Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers; original: "Pirke auoth"</note>, that is, the Chapters of the Fathers) the scepter of the academy of the Great Synagogue failed—said many things about the *Messiah*. And at last, when in his final old age he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless his eyes saw the *Messiah*, the Son of God, he took Christ himself in his arms; being present, he confirmed those things which he had taught after being instructed by the Holy Spirit. His excellent sayings are found scattered in the *Talmudic* books. From the sayings of all these men, therefore, and many others who at that same time wrote upon the Law and the Prophets and openly showed that our Lord *Jesus Christ* was both the only almighty Son of God and the true *Messiah*, almost the entire *Talmud* is composed.

Paulus Fagius <note>A 16th-century German scholar and Hebraist</note> in his preface to the Chaldean paraphrase <note>original: "paraphrase Chaldaïque"; here "Chaldean" refers to Aramaic</note> writes: "First is antiquity itself, which certainly adds no small majesty to these matters. For it is established from both Hebrew and Latin writings that our Chaldean Paraphrast, whom they call Onkelos—to whom the translation of the Pentateuch is ascribed—was the son of the sister of Emperor Titus, and that he wrote his Paraphrase not long after the devastation of the second temple. The other Paraphrast, whom they call Jonathan son of Uziel, to whom they attribute the Prophets, wrote his works before the devastation of the temple; although there are those who would have it that both translated the entire Bible into the Chaldean language. A second reason is that almost all passages in the Hebrew Bible which seem to have some obscurity and difficulty are beautifully explained in the Chaldean Paraphrase, with all obscurity removed, especially where there are prophecies concerning the kingdom of Christ. For wherever in the Hebrew truth <note>original: "veritate hebraica"; a term used by scholars of this era to mean the original Hebrew source text</note> Christ is dealt with under a hidden name, there in the Chaldean truth the name of the Messiah is always expressed in plain terms, as is easily seen by those inspecting and comparing both original texts. The third reason is the authority it holds even among the Jews themselves, who have no less faith in the Chaldean than in the Hebrew text; so much so that their errors can be proven by no other means more effectively than from the Chaldean Paraphrases, as Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prominent 14th-century Franciscan exegete</note> testifies, who possessed knowledge of both languages. He writes in his commentaries on Isaiah, chapter 8: 'The Hebrew translation [Targum] among the Jews is of such great authority among them that no one has dared to contradict it. It is also a declaration of the Hebrew truth in obscure passages.' Fourthly, this Chaldean Bible should be highly commendable to us because this language, which is the same as Syriac, was the mother tongue in the time of Christ and the Apostles, which both He and the Apostles used, as can be seen from many passages in the New Testament. Indeed, even today, the writings of the four Evangelists exist in this language; of which I offer as a most faithful witness the most famous and learned man, Master Albert Widmanstadt <note>The scholar who produced the first printed Syriac New Testament in 1555</note>, counselor to the Illustrious Prince Duke of Bavaria, who keeps this treasure hidden away for himself. Through very affectionate letters he sent to me, he gave me hope that this Treasure might one day come to light. I wish with all my heart, night and day, that this happens soon, doubting not that great light will also be added to the writings of the Evangelists." See what F. Lucas writes on this matter in his *Treatise on the Chaldean Paraphrase of Scripture*, placed at the end of the Greek and Latin New Testament newly printed at Antwerp by C. Plantin <note>The famous printer Christophe Plantin</note>.

All that is said above is verified even better in the Babylonian Targum, the <term>Mishnah</term> or <term>Mishneh</term>, that is to say the Talmudic Context, from its first composition and edition, otherwise called *Repetition of the Law* by Epiphanius in his Greek language *Deuterosis*, saying these words: <gloss>The Deuterosis <note>original: "Δευτέρωσις"; Greek for "repetition" or "seconding"</note> is the tradition of the elders; there are four: one called by the name of Moses, the second by the one called Rabbi Akiba, the third Adda or Judah, and the fourth the sons of the Hasmoneans.</gloss> Regarding this, we shall remark that Saint Jerome and other Greek and Latin ecclesiastical Doctors call it by this same name. This moved a great personage of this time to write what follows in his works:

In the New Constitutions, constitution 146, regarding the Hebrews <gloss>the one called among you the second [tradition]? <note>original: "☩ παρ' υμῖν λεγομένω δευτέρωτω"; this refers to the *Deuterosis* or Mishnah, which the Byzantine Emperor Justinian regulated</note></gloss>.
The old translation says, "truly that which is called by them the second edition." Alas, what a meager explanation! "Second edition" and *Deuterosis* <note>The Greek term for the Mishnah, meaning "repetition"</note> differ by the whole of heaven. The "second edition" is nothing other than the version of the Bible produced by Aquila <note>A 2nd-century convert to Judaism who made an extremely literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> which in Greek is called the "second edition" <note>original: "δευτέρα ἔκδοσις" (deutera ekdosis)</note>; but *Deuterosis* is a part of the Talmud. When I name the Talmud, I mean the civil law of the Hebrews, which has two parts: the **Mishnah** and the **Gemara**. The Mishnah in Greek is called *Deuterosis*, which the Emperor forbade entirely; it contains many obscenities, and many things that are old wives' tales and fables, as Jerome testifies in his *Letter to Algasia*, question 10, writing thus: "I cannot unfold how great the traditions of the Pharisees are, which they today call *Deuteroses* <note>original: "δευτερώσεις"</note>, nor how many old wives' tales they are; for the size of the book does not allow it, and many things are so foul that I am ashamed to speak of them. I will, however, say one thing to the shame of this enemy nation: they have the wisest men appointed to the synagogues for a loathsome task—to taste the blood of a virgin or a menstruating woman if they cannot discern it with their eyes." Let it be noted here that the Pharisaic traditions are called *Deuteroses*; and *Deuterosis* is the tradition of these things, like a body and a compilation <note>original: "σύσταλμα" (systalma)</note>. 

Nor will it be out of place to bring forward the proper word in this matter, which Jerome mentions in the same place: whenever on certain days they explain their traditions to their disciples, they are accustomed to say *the wise men teach the second traditions* <note>original: "οἱ σοφοι δευτεροῦσιν" (hoi sophoi deuterousin)</note>, that is, the wise men teach the traditions. *The wise men teach the second traditions*, that is, *Shano Hakhamim* <note>original: "Sanu Hahachamim"; Hebrew/Aramaic for "The wise have taught"</note>: which in the Syrian <note>Aramaic</note> language they more frequently say *Theno Rabbanan*, *our teachers teach the second traditions* <note>original: "οἱ διδασκαλοὶ ἡμῶν δευτεροῦσιν"</note>: from this verb the Pharisees were called *Deuterotae* <note>Students or teachers of the Mishnah</note>. Jerome in his tenth *Commentary on Isaiah* says: "It seems to us that the prophetic word cries out against the judges of the tribes of Judah and Jerusalem—namely, the scribes and the *Deuterotae*." I know nothing if he does not mean the Pharisees; the following makes it clear: for God saying, "Honor Father and Mother," they on the contrary warned sons to say to parents, "Whatever gift is from me shall profit you." <note>A reference to the 'Corban' practice criticized in the New Testament, where resources were dedicated to the Temple to avoid using them to support parents</note>. 

Elias Levita in his book *Thesbite* under the word *Thana*: From *Thana*, a legal verb which in Greek is *deuterein* <note>to repeat or teach</note>, they call the wise men *Deuterotae*, or *Tannaim* <note>The rabbinic sages of the period of the Mishnah</note>. The first of these was Simeon the Just, and the last was Rabbenus Hakkadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, that is, our holy teacher, so named for the sanctity of his life, otherwise called Judah by his proper name. They were followed by the *Amoraim* <note>Sages of the Talmudic era who commented on the Mishnah</note>, whose leader was Rabba; and later Rabbina and Rabbi Ashi, who composed the Talmud. See on this subject Rabbi Moses son of Maimon <note>Maimonides, the great medieval Jewish philosopher</note> in his *Massekhet Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note>, or the prologue to the *Seder Zeraim* <note>Order of Seeds</note> which is a part of the Jewish Talmud. 

Some of the Talmudists hold that this *Mishnah* was first begun and published by one Meir <note>Rabbi Meir</note>, who, from being an Idumean necromancer, was made a Jewish proselyte; and that it was afterwards illustrated and augmented with several volumes by Rabbi Monoa, according to James of Valence in his commentaries on Psalm 81. It was finished by Rabbi Judas, or Judah ben Simon, son of Gamaliel, disciple of Simeon the Just—otherwise surnamed Rabbi Hakkadosh, the "Holy Doctor"—around the Jewish year 3949 or 3952, which corresponds to the year of salvation 188. This *Mishnah* was forbidden by the Emperor Constantine <note>Though citing Justinian's Novel 146 earlier, the author here names Constantine</note> cited above in his "Authentic" <note>A collection of laws</note>, so that it might be permitted for the Hebrews, according to the handed-down law, to read the sacred scri[ptures]...

Following him, one may consult Elias Levita in his *Tishbi*, and Guy Lefèvre de la Boderie in his *Syro-Chaldean Dictionary* on this word *Gemara*.

In conclusion, this Chaldean language <note>Early modern scholars often used "Chaldean" to refer to Aramaic</note> is even better deduced and described in the two Talmuds, both the Jerusalem and the Babylonian. The first was begun since the Year of Salvation 300, according to common opinion, and according to the Dionysian calculation from the Year of Salvation 372, or rather 370, by Rabbi Yochanan, assisted by some other Rabbis, and finished in the Year of Salvation 436 with its perfect and entire completion. However, this one is more corrupted than the Babylonian. The second, namely the Babylonian, was begun according to common opinion in the Year of Christ 400 by Rabbi Ashi from the digests of Rabbi Simeon the Just and Rabbi Yochanan named above, one hundred years after the start of the first; and according to the aforementioned Dionysian calculation in the Year of Christ 508 by the aforementioned Rabbi Ashi, and was entirely perfected and finished by Rabbi Mor and Maremar in the Year of Christ 605 or 606, according to Porchetus in his preface to the first book of his *Victory against the Jews*, Pietro Galatino in book 1, chapter 5 of the *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*, Johannes Reuchlin (also called Capnio) in his *Eye-Mirror* and in his defense against his calumniators, Paulus Burgensis in his addition to chapter 34 of Isaiah and in his book titled *Scrutiny of the Faith*, Alfonso the Jew (who became a Christian) in his book *The Wars of God*, Peter Niger in his books on the Messiah, the author of the book titled *Fortress of Faith*, Jean de Podio, and Master Raymond in his *Dagger [of Faith]* <note>The *Pugio Fidei*, a famous 13th-century polemical work by Raymond Martini</note>, Jerome...

The great and admirable Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494) known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note>, in a letter of his written and sent to Marsilio Ficino <note>An influential scholar and priest who led the Florentine Academy.</note>, speaks thus of certain Chaldean <note>In this context, "Chaldean" often referred to Neo-Babylonian or Aramaic sources, often associated with magic and ancient wisdom.</note> books he had in his hands:

<margin>cc</margin>
> The Chaldean books I have are these: <note>original: "Chaldaici libri quos habeo, hi sunt..."</note> first, the oracles of Ezra, Zoroaster, and Melchior the Magi, in which even those parts that are circulated among the Greeks in a corrupted and mutilated state are read here as whole and complete. Then, there is a brief and rugged Interpretation by the Chaldean Sages, yet one full of mysteries. There is likewise a small book on the dogmas of Chaldean Theology, as well as the most rich and divine exposition of the Persians, Greeks, and Chaldeans.

<margin>cc</margin>

Stephanus also calls it **Adiabene** <gloss>Adiabene</gloss> <note>original: "ἀδιαβηνὴ"</note>. There is also a prefecture of Mesopotamia which, according to Pliny in Book 5, chapter 24, draws its origin from the Syrians. It appears from Book 6 of Tacitus's *Annals* that the same area is inhabited by Macedonians; for the cities of **Anthemusia** and **Nicephorium**, which Tacitus ascribes to the Macedonians, Pliny attributes to this prefecture. See also the entries for **Plaga** and **Osrhoena**, as well as **Messana**, which it is also called.

**Assyria** <gloss>Assyria</gloss> <note>original: "Ἀσσυρία"</note>, a region of Asia which was later called **Adiabene**, according to the testimony of Pliny; likewise according to Theodoret in his *History of the Saints*. Niger writes that it is called **Adrinza** by the natives; Girava calls it **Acimia**; Pinet calls it **Mosul**; and Castaldo calls it **Arzerum**. Mercator calls it **Sarh**. Suidas writes that the Assyrians were called Persians. The Assyrians were those who were later called Syrians, as Trogus says in Book 1. Xenophon, in Book 4 of the *Cyropaedia*, places the Assyrians as neighbors to the Hyrcanians.

**Euphrantis**, a region identical to Syria according to Stephanus, named thus after the nearby Euphrates river; it is the same as **Comagena** <note>Commagene, an ancient kingdom in south-central Turkey.</note>.

->*Of the Syrians.*<-

The Hebrew authors write that the word **Aram**, which is the proper name of one of the children of Shem in Genesis 10, signifies in the Hebrew language—just as it does in French—height, elevation, or sublimity. > The name of Syria is sometimes used by Geographers and other authors, both Greek and Latin, to designate the largest tract of the Eastern region. Such it appears to be when starting from the **Desert of Shur** <note>original: "Sur deserto." A biblical wilderness between Egypt and Palestine.</note> (which lies between Egypt and Assyria at the limits of the Ishmaelite territory), measuring westward through Palestine, it enters toward the North the Mediterranean Sea and the Island of **Cyprus** (once torn away from the upper continent); then, crossing the sea again, it traverses all of **Cilicia** and all of **Cappadocia**, and finally flows down into the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea.</note>. From there, having crossed the Euphrates and Tigris to the East, it permeates all of **Assyria** and ends at **Persia** and the Persian Gulf itself; to the south, it skirts **Arabia**. At other times, however, it is used to signify any one of these regions included in that upper tract. The origin of the name is variously handed down. Some believe Syria was named after **Syros**, an island of the Mediterranean Sea; others from a certain **Syrus**, son of Apollo; others from **Mount Hermon**, which is called **Sirion** <note>original: "Schirion."</note> by the Phoenicians, who were certainly among the most principal and ancient Syrians. To me, however, the name of Syria seems to be derived from the same source where we traced the beginnings of that region in the description above: namely, from the **Desert of Shur**, for the very same reason that **Assyria** is named after **Assur**. Certainly, the ancient Hebrews do not use the name Syria, but in its place they use **Aram** <note>original: "ארם"</note>, from which they name many of the regions and languages of that upper tract. Therefore, to them, the Region of Aram in that tract is said to be that which stretches straight from **Antilibanus** toward the Euphrates, and having crossed it, skirts the Tigris, and [includes all of] Mesopotamia.

» traversed entirely as far as the borders of Damascus, and ending at Arabia Petraea itself, all that Royal land, I say, is called **Aram** by the Hebrews in the Holy Scriptures: yet in such a way that different locations within that region are distinguished by various additions.

» **Mesopotamia**, therefore, the greatest and oldest of them all, is sometimes even called simply **Aram** *preeminently* <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (kat’ exochēn), meaning "par excellence" or "by way of distinction"</note>, and the inhabitants of that region are called **Arameans**. Sometimes it is called by a more proper and peculiar name, **Paddan Aram** <note>Hebrew: ארם פדן</note>, that is, the **Yoke of Syria**, as if you were to say Syria joined under a yoke—meaning placed under the "yoke" of two rivers. For this reason, it is also sometimes called **Aram Naharaim** <note>Hebrew: ארם נהרים</note>, or "Syria of the two rivers," or "between the rivers." Indeed, it is even sometimes signified by the addition of **Paddan** alone.

» The region which is first at the river Eleutherus is called **Aram Zobah** <note>Hebrew: ארם ציבא</note>, which is perhaps Sophene <note>An ancient province of the Armenian Kingdom, later a Roman province</note>. In this tract there appears to be **Lower Hamath**, which is called by the name **Hamath-Zobah** in 2 Chronicles 8. David seems to have conquered Hadadezer <note>original: Adarezer</note> there in 1 Chronicles 18, and thus achieved the limits of the land promised by God, which are commonly placed at **Lebo-Hamath** <note>Hebrew: חמות לביא</note>, that is, "the entrance to Hamath"; for the lower tract of that region is thought by some to be Iturea.

» In the vicinity of that tract, it is certain there was **Aram Beth-Rehob** <note>Hebrew: ארם בית רחוב</note>, located not far from that place on the Euphrates called **Rehoboth** <note>Hebrew: רחובות</note> in Genesis 36:37.

» The fourth Aram, which is called **Aram Maacah** <note>Hebrew: ארם מעכה</note>, was not so far from those areas, as appears from the second book of Samuel <note>original: "Schem," for the Hebrew Shemuel</note>, chapters 8 and 10.

» The fifth Aram is called **Aram Damascus** <note>Hebrew: ארם דמשק</note>, which is enclosed by the territory of Damascus, that is, between Lebanon and Arabia: or as others (who suggest the Anti-Lebanon and Lebanon ranges end in Arabia) advise, it is situated between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon: that is, **Coele-Syria** or "hollow Syria," as if bounded by the valleys of those two mountains. And these five regions are explicitly called by the name of Aram in the Holy Scriptures.

» Furthermore, there is a certain sixth Syria, which although not so explicitly called Aram by the sacred writers, there is nevertheless no doubt that the name Aram—by which secular writers honor it—passed from the former to the latter. Thus **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC – 24 AD)</note> testifies that the inhabitants of **Commagene Syria** or **Antioch** were called **Arimi** (that is, Arameans) by ancient writers, saying: *The Armenians, Syrians, and Arabs are very closely joined, whether you consider their language, their rites of living, or the features of their bodies.* And a little later: *For they call those Arameans whom we call Syrians.*

» Certainly, the Scripture makes honorable and magnificent mention of this Antiochian Syria. It calls such territory the **Land of Hamath** <note>Hebrew: חמת</note>. It attributes to it a distinguished kingdom among others conquered by the Assyrian Monarch: indeed, even a metropolitan city, which they call **Hamath the Great** <note>Hebrew: חמת רבה</note> or the Greater. Some also add that this same city is called **Riblah** elsewhere. Therefore, this part of Syria also deserves the name Aram, not only for those names we designated above, but especially for this grace: that in later times, such a region brought the six upper regions under its yoke, and ennobled them with its privileges and even its language; which, before we demonstrate it, seems necessary to define entirely, from where it was derived...

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.
Yy 2

...first came to be known in this Europe in the time of our fathers were thus named Gypsies of Canaan <note>original: "Cinganes de Chenaan"</note>, rather than Uzians or Egyptians, as I shall deduce more fully hereafter in the subsequent chapter on the Punic and Arabic languages.

Therefore, we shall learn that the Syriac language of the present day—which some call "of Jerusalem" <note>original: "Hierosolymitaine"</note> because it consistently retains the name of Chaldean and participates in both Hebrew and Chaldean, yet possesses characters distinct from those of the Hebrews—is nothing other than a notable alteration, corruption, or mutation of the Hebrew and Chaldean languages. This Syriac language is specific and separate from the two aforementioned languages of Hebrew and Chaldean, as is clearly and openly proven in the 4th Book of Kings, chapter 18; in the 1st Book of Ezra, chapter 4; in the book of Isaiah the Prophet, chapter 36; in the second book of Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipom."</note>, chapter 32; and in the book of Daniel the Prophet, chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8. After these, one must see what has been written by Elias Levita <note>A prominent Jewish grammarian and scholar (1469–1549)</note>, a Jew by nation, in his preface to the *Meturgeman* <note>An Aramaic dictionary; original: "Meturgheeman"</note> following the Hebrew Talmudists; by Sebastian Münster in his Chaldean Grammar; and by Cornelius Bertram in the preface to his Grammar of the Hebrew and Aramaic languages; as well as Theodore Bibliander in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*; and Andreas Masius in the introductory epistle of his grammar of the Syriac language. A certain Hebrew Rabbi named Judah, in the treatise *Sanhedrin*, said these words concerning this Syriac language: "The speech of Adam was Aramaic, that is, Syriac" <note>original Latin: *Adę sermo fuit Arameus id est Syriacus.*</note>. Indeed, some ancient Hebrew Kabbalists were moved to write that it is credible that the great Patriarch Abraham the Chaldean—a contemplator of the heavens and the stars—used these Syriac characters and this same language before he departed from Ur in Chaldea. They also suggest that the Prophet Moses likewise used these characters, which were given to him from Heaven by the mouth of Gevurah <note>A Kabbalistic term for Divine Strength or Judgment, often associated with fire</note>, which is the element of fire, along with the tables of the Divine Law written by the very hand of the Eternal on Mount Sinai. This is confirmed by Theseus Ambrosius in his *Introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian Languages*, chapter nine, and by Andreas Masius <note>OCR: "André Magius"</note> in his Chaldean Grammar. This Syriac language was written in the time of our Lord Jesus Christ in Hebrew characters, just like the Chaldean language; but since then, it has had its own characters, unique and particular to itself. Although these characters are read from right to left like those of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs, they are nonetheless not written by the Syrians from right to left as those of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs are, but from top to bottom toward the stomach, as this Latin verse denotes:

->From heaven to the stomach, Chaldea reads its strokes.<-
<note>original Latin: *E cœlo ad stomachum relegit Chaldæa lituras.*</note>

This seems to have moved Festus Pompeius to call this sort of writing <term>flowing downwards <note>original Greek: κάτω χέουσα</note></term>, meaning "downwards" just as we now write "rightwards"—as if, so to speak, falling upon and striking; for the letters seem to fall and sit upon other letters, and one carries the other on its back, while they are applied in the order of the alphabet or the composing of a word, such as:

<note>The following section is translated from the author's Latin citation.</note> The language of the Arameans is not only called <note>original: "ארמיא"</note> Aramaic: but is also called <note>original: "לשון כשדים"</note> the language of the Chaldeans. One might rightly doubt whether the use of the Aramaic language began among the Mesopotamians or the Chaldeans; but if conjecture from the above holds weight—and from the fact that the first mention and traces of the Aramaic language appear in the history of Laban the Mesopotamian or <note>original: "ארמי"</note> Aramean—it seems to have reached the Chaldeans and Assyrians toward the East from Mesopotamia through the descendants of Nahor <note>The brother of the patriarch Abraham.</note>. Whether it was first carried Westward through the same descendants of Nahor to other tracts of Aram across the Euphrates is not equally clear for all. Certainly, in later times, with the expansion of the Chaldean Empire, their language not only pervaded all those regions of the Aramaic tract but also Judea itself, Palestine, and Phoenicia: so much so that the Aramaic language seems to have antiquated and almost obliterated Hebrew in some way—not just once, but quite often, and with its various dialects.

For the Aramaic language and its dialects made marvelous progress: for, having spread from Mesopotamia among the Chaldeans, it was so refined in Babylon among the Babylonian nobles and philosophers that it achieved the greatest possible purity there. Rightly, therefore, we make the first and principal dialect of the Aramaic language the **Babylonian**: in which Daniel, and likewise Ezra, being educated, wrote several pages of their writings. We shall call its second dialect the **Chaldaic or Syriac**, which the earlier Paraphrasts <note>Scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic to make it accessible to the common people.</note> of the Bible used, such as Onkelos in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, and Jonathan in both the former and latter Prophets. We establish the third dialect as the **Jerusalem** dialect, in which the later paraphrases of the Law and the book of Esther were written. This is called the "Jerusalem" dialect because the common people of the Israelites returning from the Babylonian exile mixed many Ammonite, Moabite, Persian, and Greek words into the Chaldean language. We make the fourth dialect of the Aramaic language a certain **middle** dialect between that second Chaldaic one and this third Jerusalem one: in which were written the paraphrases or <term>Targumim <gloss>Aramaic translations or interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term> of the five volumes, as they are called: the Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. And from this difference between the aforementioned Aramaic dialects, a double Targum is established by the doctors of the Hebrews: the Babylonian and the Jerusalem. They call both by these names, not because the former was written in the Babylonian language, but because...

For besides the various uses it has in common with all those others, it provides certain specific and proper ones necessary for a Christian Theologian. No one surely doubts that there are very many places in the context of the Bible that have exercised the wits of many, either because of the various meanings of words or even the ambiguities of sentences. The Syriac dialect can explain all these so sincerely that you would require nothing else for its interpretation.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

the ancient Egyptians did not use letters and distinct writing as we do, but only certain signs that represented a whole meaning, according to the two examples he <note>Likely referring to a previously mentioned author like Horapollo</note> provides: the **Vulture**, which signified nature, because among this kind of bird no males are found, but only females, who at a certain season of the year are impregnated by the wind; and the **Honeybee** denoted the King, together with the two conditions he ought to possess: one of kindness and sweetness, conforming to the honey, and the other of severity and vigor, represented by the sting.

T. Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander (1506–1564), a Swiss orientalist and linguist</note> in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*: <note>original Latin: "Porrò quod Volaterranus negat Hieroglyphica nulli adhuc cõperta..."</note> Furthermore, regarding what Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), also known as Volaterranus, a humanist scholar</note> denies—claiming that Hieroglyphics have not yet been understood by anyone—this, in my judgment, conflicts with published books in which authors of no small repute describe what the sacred letters of the Egyptians were like and what their use was. Furthermore, Diodorus in Book 4 of his *Fabulous Deeds* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian; the reference likely refers to the *Bibliotheca historica*</note> testifies that the Egyptians received the forms of their letters from the Ethiopians—namely those that were commonly used. Since that language has been completely destroyed in Egypt, first by the Greeks, then by the Romans, and later by the Saracens and Arabs, and since few words remain in literary monuments, it cannot be easily judged, nor can anything be pronounced with certainty concerning the language of the Egyptians. Nevertheless, from those things which have come to our knowledge—from the origin of the people of *Mizraim* <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt, often used in a biblical-genealogical context</note>, which was common with the Ethiopians and the descendants of Nimrod in Babylon, and from the proximity of the Edomites and Israelites and the commerce among these peoples—it can be gathered that it was no less related to the **Hebrew** dialect than the Ethiopian, Chaldean, or Phoenician languages. Even if it were as remote as Latin or Scythian, it could still be compared in each of its parts with Hebrew, and therefore fit the same standard of art and science.

Of these Hieroglyphics, one sees more than enough remains even now on large and small obelisks, bases, sphinxes, and other marbles brought from Egypt to Rome, of which **Pliny** makes ample mention in the 36th book, chapter 9, of his *Natural History*; and likewise **Ammianus Marcellinus**, in the previously cited passage, inserted in Greek letters and language the explanation of the largest one, under the name of the aforementioned **Rameses**. With regard to the common speech or language and the writing, we have nothing certain. Consequently, these two Alphabets attributed to these Egyptians have made the most curious scholars of antiquity uncertain and suspicious; moreover, the first seems to hold some trace of that <term>Capreolatin</term> <note>Likely referring to a convoluted or "goat-like" script style mentioned by Renaissance occultists</note> of **Apuleius**, and the names of the letters conform to it, such as you see hereafter, twenty-four in number, just as there are in the Greek Alphabet. Nevertheless, **Plutarch** in his treatise *On Osiris* puts them at 25, according to the square multiplication of five <note>5 x 5 = 25</note>, which is the number of years he <note>Apis, the sacred bull</note> lived. Here are the two Egyptian Alphabets represented in figures by **Theseus Ambrosius** <note>An Italian linguist and author of the first comprehensive work on non-Latin scripts, *Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam* (1539)</note> in his appendix on the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages.

If the two Alphabets above are somewhat suspicious and doubtful, those that follow should be no less so: for it has been well known for a hundred years now what the true Characters of the **Abyssinian Ethiopians** are (whom some call **Indians** and **Nubians** <note>In the 16th century, the term "India" was often used broadly to include Ethiopia, which was frequently referred to as "Middle India."</note>), as well as their manner of writing, which goes from left to right like our own. However, this first Alphabet assigned to the said Indians in the **Grimani Library** <note>The famous library of Cardinal Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), a major center for humanist research in Venice.</note> proceeds in reverse from right to left, just as Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic do. It is indeed true that the Ethiopian, Abyssinian, Indian, or Nubian language is almost entirely derived from those languages; nevertheless, it cannot be their script, nor that of **China** or **Cathay** <note>An archaic name for northern China, popularized by Marco Polo.</note>, who write from top to bottom, as we shall discuss hereafter. Nonetheless, the names of the letters of this Alphabet conform to those of the other which follows, specifically assigned to the said Abyssinian Ethiopians by the Author of the *Voyages Overseas* <note>Likely referring to Bernhard von Breydenbach's "Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam" (1486), which included some of the first printed alphabets of non-European languages.</note>, where he asserts he obtained it from their Embassy when they came to offer obedience to the Holy Apostolic See under **Sixtus IV** around the year 1482.

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE [RELIGIONS]

Oriental history speaks of it differently, saying that the Turks hold that God the Creator—after man whom he had created and his posterity had forgotten Him—gave a law to the Jews mixed with two opposites: of good and evil, of great pain and reward, which they did not wish to observe, but instead committed idolatry. Then, He sent another via the greatest of the Prophets, formed of the Holy Spirit, who is Issa, or Jesus Christ (for so Muhammad calls Him in his Alcoran or *Alphurcan* <term>Alphurcan: From the Arabic "Al-Furqan," meaning "The Criterion" between right and wrong, another name for the Quran</term>). This law was filled with sweetness and ease, yet men still did not wish to keep it. For this reason, He willed to send Muhammad, who came with a sword and rigor to make the Peoples and Nations believe in God by force, or else put them to death or make them Tributaries. 

It is a most marvelous thing that the largest and most significant part of the peoples of Asia, Africa, Europe, and several others now embrace the damnable and abominable errors of this wicked and cursed Alcoran. This is detailed by Theodore Bibliander in his *Apology for the Quran*, Guillaume Postel in his *Treatise on the Twelve Languages* and in his *History of the Turks*, Gilbert Génébrard in books 3 and 4 of his *Chronographia*, André Thevet in book 6, chapter 5 of his *Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest in book 2, volume 2, chapter 8, and book 3 of the same volume, chapters 33 and 34 of his *Cosmography*. 

The reason why this Alcoran has been and still is so widely embraced as a religion among so many peoples and nations of Asia, Africa, and Europe, is that it is woven and composed of all sorts and species of religions, sects, and opinions; it permits all effeminate soft living of the flesh and all pleasure, and has loosened the bridle for all its Muhammadans to every corruption of debauchery, as Guillaume Postel confirms in his treatise *On the Configuration of the Celestial Signs*. It is true and certain that there are in Asia and Africa twelve times more Idolaters than Muhammadans, according to the report of André Thevet in book 6, chapter 5, and book 11, chapters 6, 7, and 8 of his *Cosmography*, and Antonio de Torquemada in the second day of his *Hexameron*. 

So that we leave nothing worthy of remark in this place, we shall say that the books of the *Zuna* <term>Zuna: Referring to the Sunnah, the body of traditional social and legal customs and practices of the Islamic community</term>, which we mentioned above in this same chapter, were composed by the disciples of Muhammad after his death. As these books passed through many hands, some added to them while others removed from them as they saw fit, so much so that one finds such great confusion and contradiction in the said books that what Muhammad had said affirmatively was stated negatively. Such division arose in his sect that it became necessary for the *Alcaliph* <term>Alcaliph: Caliph, the supreme religious and civil leader of a Muslim state</term>—that is to say, the King or Pontiff who ruled at that time over this people called by history the Saracens—named Muawiya <note>Muawiya I (r. 661–680), the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate</note>, living (according to Spanish history) in the year of Salvation 674, to command all Muhammadans that wherever learned men of the Quran were found (called *Alfaki* <term>Alfaki: An expert in Islamic law/jurisprudence</term> in the Arabic tongue), they should come to the city of Damascus to hold a Council, and bring all the writings they could recover. 

Once this was done, the said *Alcaliph* or King, out of the two hundred who had come there, chose six *Alfacis* or scholars. Of these six, one named Muszlin <note>The scholar Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj</note> was chosen first, Bochari <note>Muhammad al-Bukhari</note> second, Buhorayra <note>Abu Hurairah</note> third, Annecey <note>Al-Nasa'i</note> fourth, Aternindi <note>Al-Tirmidhi</note> fifth, and Dend <note>Abu Dawood</note> sixth.
