# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

Among the **Mohammedans** <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note>, prayers and orisons would be made in the month of **Ramadan** <note>The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, observed as a month of fasting, prayer, and reflection</note>, in March, and in each month the entire **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> would be read. In this regard, I remember having read in the *History of the Saracens, and the origin, customs, religion, deeds, order, policy, and discipline of the Christians*, chapter 20, these words worthy of being reported in this place:

> Among other particular divisions concerning the ceremonies of the law of the Turks, their rites, institutions, and worship, there are four solemn opinions regarding the matter of salvation, distinct from one another. Each group <note>original: "generatio"</note> of that sect holds to one of these firmly and follows it, so that not only does one not agree with the other, but one even persecutes the other by force of arms and the fortification of camps. Thus, the entire kingdom is often disturbed, and unless the king intervenes, these disputes could by no means be settled. 
> 
> The first group is that of the **Priests** <note>original: "Sacerdotum"; referring here to the *Ulama* or the legalistic religious class</note>, who are held in great reverence among them as rulers of the people, executors and dispensers of the law, doctors, and judges. They preside over spiritual benefits, churches, and **Gymnasia** <note>original: "Gymnasiis"; religious schools or madrasas</note>. Their opinion is that no one can be saved except through the law of Muhammad. They teach and persuade everyone of this, and though they cannot prove it by any reason, authority, or example, they nevertheless strive to resist those who contradict them in every way possible. They have many among the people who agree with them, especially among the princes and nobles. 
> 
> The second group consists of those called **Dervishes** <note>original: "Deruischler"; Sufi practitioners known for their asceticism</note>, who are religious men held in much veneration, seen as survivors and successors of the saints, and as it were the conservators of the entire kingdom and friends of God and Muhammad. They do not base their opinion on any reason or authority, but try to prove it through wonders and signs, as was shown above in chapters 14 and 15. These also have many supporters and those who agree with them, especially among those who are more spiritual, devout, and humble in their lives. 
> 
> The third group consists of those called **Sufis** <note>original: "Czofilar"; possibly a variation of *Sofi* or *Sufi*</note>, who are meditative or given to spiritual exercises. They are held in high reputation as the successors of the Prophets and the Fathers who founded this sect, and they claim to have greater authority than the others. They have no foundation for their opinion except what they say has been handed down from ancient times. Their opinion is that everyone must be saved through merit, and that this suffices for salvation without grace or law; they call this **Pere Ketallach** <note>original: "Pere Ketallach"; likely *Barakatullah*, meaning the Blessing of God</note>. These are very diligent in private prayers and spiritual exercises, in vigils and meditations. Indeed, they never cease from continual prayer, which they call **Chillar ait mach** <note>original: "Chillar ait mach"; likely referring to the *Chilla*, a forty-day spiritual retreat, and the Turkish *etmek*, to do or perform</note>. 
>

After this, they say **Lahu** <note>original: "Lahu"; Arabic for "to Him"</note>, repeating it in the same way, and finally they say **Hu, hu** <note>original: "Hu, hu"; "He" (God)</note>, repeating it again, until they fall down and sleep as if breathless. Thus, these three generations, with their opinions, are manifest to all people, and they engage in many dissensions among themselves both in private and in public; nevertheless, because they are valued equally by all people, none can prevail over the others, but they are continually brought back to peace and concord. However, the fourth generation is called in their language *Horise* <note>original: "Horise"; likely a corruption of a term for "heresy" or perhaps referring to the Kharijites</note>, which sounds like "heresy"; their opinion is that every person is saved in their own law, and that a law was given by God to every tribe or nation in which they must be saved, and that all laws are equally good for those who observe them, nor should any be preferred as if it were better than others. These are accepted by the Turks and are held as Schismatics, and if they are found, they are burned. For this reason, they do not hold their opinion openly, but secretly. I found one of this generation while I was in Chios, who entered the Church of the Christians, and marked himself with the sign of the Cross, and sprinkled himself with holy water, and said openly: "Your Law is as good as ours," which no Turk of another opinion would do for his life.

he won the day, and Ali <note>original: "Haly"</note> having been fraudulently slain, he was elected by all as monarch of the Saracens. This Mu'awiya <note>original: "Muhauie," referring to Mu'awiya I, founder of the Umayyad Caliphate</note> made an agreement with the Emperor Constans in the year 658, that the Arabs would be tributary to him. From this time, sects began to emerge among the Muslims <note>original: "Mahometifnes"</note>, such that Mu'awiya, favoring the Himyarites <note>original: "Himafites"</note>, drove out and humbled those who were in Persia. According to some authors, it is believed that from these people proceeded the foolish opinion of the Sophis <note>likely referring to the Safavids or proto-Shi'ite Persian factions</note>, condemning the similar heresy of the Arab Hishamites <note>original: "Hifamites"</note>. The Emperor, seeing the strength of these Saracens, was constrained by agreement to relinquish the right he claimed over Damascus and Syria to Mu'awiya, for him and his descendants in perpetuity. And it must be noted in this place that the Emperors, having left Syria, imposed the name of **Romania** <note>The term "Romania" or "Rum" was used to describe Byzantine territories in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)</note> upon Asia Minor; and to this effect, the city of Apamea is placed within "Roman" territory by the *Annals of Constantinople*, because this province remained under the obedience of the Roman Empire. Likewise, since that time, Thrace and part of Macedonia received a similar name when the Greek Emperors were dispossessed of Italy; for not wishing to lose the title of Roman Monarchs, they named Thrace "Roman," Constantinople "New Rome," and their soldiers "Romans," as Gregory, Choniates, and Chalcondyles certify in their works. 

Therefore, against this "Romania" in Asia, the Saracens of Syria conducted raids, and there they were also beaten; for although Yazid <note>original: "Gefid"</note>, son of the said Mu'awiya, had crossed into Phrygia with several troops, he was forced to return, having lost fifty thousand men from his army. Later, in the year of grace 670, the Saracens crossed into Africa for the second time, from where they led away 80,000 men as captives. Two years later, Mu'awiya sent two of his captains, Mahumat and Caïse, who raided the coasts of Lycia and Cilicia; then, sailing as far as the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, they took the city of Cyzicus (now Chizico), where they spent the winter. From there forward, they conducted raids and destruction as far as Constantinople. This war lasted for the space of seven years, during which the Saracens did not gain much, although they occasionally scoured the sea; in these raids, they took, pillaged, and usurped the island of Crete <note>original: "Candie"</note>. 

But they were forced to retreat because their ships were burned by one Callinicus, a Syrian who had fled to the Christians <note>Callinicus of Heliopolis is credited with inventing "Greek Fire," a combustible weapon that devastated the Arab fleet</note>. The Saracens, fearing their utter ruin, departed and abandoned part of the country they had usurped in Phrygia. Meanwhile, the Mardaites—an Eastern people—coming to attack Syria, overstepping Lebanon and raiding as far as Jerusalem, astonished Mu'awiya. Already terrified by the loss his army received by sea in Phrygia, and seeing that many Syrians as well as slaves had retreated toward these Mardaites, he resolved with his council to ask for peace from the Emperor Constantine, nicknamed "the Bearded" or **Pogonatus**. The Emperor granted this to them in the year of grace 677, with the conditions that follow: namely, that the Hagarenes <note>original: "Agarenes," a medieval term for Arabs, referencing their traditional descent from Hagar</note>, wrongly called Saracens, would swear to pay the Emperor of Constantinople every year the sum of 3,000 pounds of gold and 50 slaves, recognizing themselves as subjects and tributaries of the Empire; and that this peace would remain firm and stable for thirty years. Believing this, the foolish Arab set himself to persecute the images <note>this refers to the Iconoclastic movement</note>, in which he gratified the Emperor, but he was deceived in his hope: for he lived as King for only four years.

This so irritated Mahdi the Great Admiral <note>term: "Admiral" here is a translation of "Amir" or "Amir al-Mu'minin" (Commander of the Faithful)</note> that he sent great forces into Asia Minor under the leadership of Asach, governor of Mesopotamia. But having made no progress on this journey, he sent his son against Asia Minor and went himself to Jerusalem: while there, he dispatched letters patent, giving full power to one of his captains or Admirals named Thesian to compel the slaves of the Christians to become Mahometans <note>Muslims</note>, and furthermore to ruin the churches. This wicked man came to Homs <note>original: "Eme" or "Emesse," the ancient city of Emesa</note>, and there feigned that he only wished to compel those who had recently converted; but after he had the census of the Jews and Christians, he began to vomit his most furious rage that a man could imagine, torturing those who refused to deny their faith and baptism, and ruining the churches and monasteries he found in Syria and Mesopotamia. This Mahdi sent his younger son Aaron <note>Harun al-Rashid</note> against Leo, Emperor of Greece, and as he overran Asia, he forced the Greeks to sue for peace, which he granted them, seeing that his father was sickly and that he did not know how his brother Moses <note>original: "Moyse" or "Mose," referring to Al-Hadi</note> would act toward him. And during this, Mahdi or Muhammad died, and had Moses as successor, who held the lordship for only one year, and consequently could not make great journeys; rather, dying, he left the monarchy of Egypt, Arabia, Syria, Mesopotamia, and Persia to the aforementioned Aaron, his younger brother, who was the 22nd Great Admiral of the Saracens <note>original: "Sarrafins"</note>, and a mortal enemy of the Christians, to whom he did infinite evils, there being almost no one to stand against them. This was because the Empress Irene was in a quarrel with her son Constantine <note>Constantine VI</note>, so that their private discord brought a strange prejudice to the entire Christian Republic. This gave Aaron leisure to send his forces to Cyprus, to overrun the island, and there massacre those who would not renounce the faith of the Gospel; and because the Greek Emperor had refused the promised pay <note>original: "soulde," meaning soldier's pay or subsidy</note> to the Armenians, they, in their spite, betrayed and delivered the castle of Amach to the Arabs, which could serve them as a free—

They even took the horses from the stables of the Emperor Constantine <note>Constantine VI</note>, which were on the side of Chalcedon in Asia, in a place called Malagina <note>original: "Malagme," a major Byzantine military camp and staging area</note>.

It was during this season, and in the year of grace 800, that this Harun, having heard tell of the strength and valor of the great Charlemagne, King of France—who had recently been elected and made Emperor of the Romans—sent him an elephant <note>This was the famous elephant named Abul-Abbas</note> and other great presents. To please him, he released several Christians whom he held in servitude, according to the account of Paolo Emilio <note>original: "Paule Emile," an Italian historian who wrote the *De rebus gestis Francorum*</note> in the third book of the *Annals of France*. 

Nicephorus <note>Emperor Nicephorus I (r. 802–811)</note>, having succeeded Irene as Emperor of Constantinople, made an agreement with the aforementioned Charlemagne so that he could defend himself against the aforementioned Harun, who was making war upon him. Harun defeated him in the land of Phrygia and placed him in such distress that, had Nicephorus not saved himself by a very sudden flight, he would have served as prey to Harun, King of Persia, who had just come from his Persian kingdom to settle some discords that had arisen there. After this, Harun, with 300,000 combatants, entered Asia Minor and took the city of Tyana <note>original: "Thiane"</note>, where he had a mosque built for the exercise of his impiety <note>The author uses "impiety" here from a 16th-century Christian perspective to refer to Islamic worship</note>. He forced the surrender of the castle of Heraclea and several other very strong and well-supplied places, and came as far as Ancyra, which is now called Ankara <note>original: "Angoury"</note>. Having seen the city, he withdrew without otherwise trying to besiege it or take it by force. This was because Nicephorus sent to beg him for peace, which he accepted from the infidel at the price of 300,000 gold crowns paid once, and a certain annual tribute <term>jizya|a poll tax paid by non-Muslim subjects</term>, both for the head of the Emperor and for his children. This gave a marvelous satisfaction to Harun, who thereby glorified himself for having subjected the Roman Empire, having made a tributary of the man who bore the title of its sovereign. 

But after Nicephorus fortified some places ruined by the Arab, Harun cast them down again; breaking the peace, he came to Cyprus, where he ruined the churches, drove out the islanders, and did infinite evils to the Christians throughout Asia. After this, in the year of our Lord 807, he sent one of his captains named Humayd <note>original: "Chumeid," likely Humayd ibn Ma'yuf al-Hajuri</note> against the island of Rhodes. Landing there, he pillaged it and greatly impoverished it, but he did not take the fortress. Returning, as he touched upon the city of Myra, he saw himself punished by its patron, namely Saint Nicholas, so that he repaired the damages he had done there. Meanwhile, this sovereign Prince of the Arabs died in Khorasan <note>original: "Corasan"</note> in the Kingdom of Persia. 

He had as a successor Muhammad <note>Caliph al-Amin</note>, against whom his brother Abdallah <note>Caliph al-Ma'mun</note> rose up. From this followed a division among the Arabs and the diminishing of their power, which caused both ruin among themselves and great persecution for the Christians subject to their rule. From this it happened that the churches in the Holy City were both ruined and deserted, and the monasteries scattered throughout Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and the surrounding places felt the fire of this storm. This division lasted five years, until the death of Muhammad; then Abdallah his brother was created general and great King of the Arabs. Under him, the Arabs who were in Africa crossed into Italy and plundered everything from Ostia to the Vatican and the Church of Saint Peter in Rome. In that same season, and in the year of grace 826, the Hagarenes <note>original: "Agarenes," a medieval term for Muslims, referring to their traditional descent from Hagar</note> crossed into Crete <note>original: "Candie"</note>, plundered it, overran it, and made it their home. Under him, the affairs of the Hagarenes did not go very well in Syria, inasmuch as the Emperor Theophilus beat them several times and conquered several cities from them. 

So it was that as the glory and strength of the Hagarenes vanished in the East, they regained vigor in Africa—as we shall say at another time, for fear of confusing the order of history and mixing the African Saracens or Hagarenes with those of Syria, Egypt, Arabia, Mesopotamia, or Persia. In short, this Muhammad was the last of the Admirals descended from the lineage of the four Captains and Impostors who followed the Pseudo-Prophet Muhammad <note>original: "Mahometh"</note>, when he planted his Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> and his doctrine with the sword. These lineages held their Monarchy for the space of about 250 years, from the false Prophet until the end of the reign of this Muhammad, successor to Abdallah. It seems that this Monarchy was greatly shaken because suddenly the Turks began to raid, the Egyptians to establish their Sultanate, the Persians their empire, and the Arabs strove to remain free, with every city in Syria seeking to have its own Prince. 

To Muhammad succeeded Amer <note>Umar al-Aqta, the Emir of Melitene</note>, but the histories make no mention to assure you of which lineage he came from; nonetheless, it is likely that he was of an illustrious house, since that people then accepted no one unless he was among the greatest and most distinguished of the men of war. He was attacked by the Emperor of the Greeks, Michael <note>Michael III, r. 842–867</note>, son of Theophilus, who went to besiege the city of Samosata. But the Hagarenes, feigning fear, made no show of defending themselves, but kept themselves closed inside their city. This gave the Greeks too much confidence, so much so that they no longer bothered to keep watch, nor set up guard posts or sentinels, but went wandering aimlessly here and there through the countryside. Seeing this, the Hagarenes fell upon them with such vehemence that, putting them to flight, they ruined the entire army, and the Emperor himself narrowly escaped being among the prisoners. Twice this Emperor was handled by the Arabs in this manner. But at the third time Petronas, his uncle, undertaking the charge of the war, thrashed those Hagarenes so well that Amer their Prince was slain there, and the rest put to flight. [an]cient language is spoken there, or if it is used, it is only with a corruption as great as that seen when the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards corrupted the natural languages of the nations they conquered, or as the Romans practiced in the past in the lands they subjected. Now, whatever alteration of faith there may have been, both in the time of the Arians <note>A group of early Christians who held specific beliefs about the nature of Jesus that were later declared heretical by the mainstream Church.</note> and in the time of the Arabs and Mohammadans <term>Mahometistes: an archaic term for Muslims</term> in Africa, God always left himself some chosen and elect families who followed the ancient faith of the Church. 

Such was the case in Morocco, where there was a race of Christian gentlemen called *Farfanes*, good knights, who came to King John I of Spain while he was at Alcalá de Henares, as is recounted in Book 15, Chapter 27 of the history of Spain. In our own time, there were still seen in Tunis, when the Emperor Charles V <note>The Holy Roman Emperor who captured Tunis in 1535.</note> went there, certain Christians who had their church separate from those of the Moors; they were called Rabatins. So that they might more freely devote themselves to divine service and enjoy the holy Sacraments of the church, this great Emperor had them move to Naples, granting them great favors and privileges.

In the year of grace 707, Abdemelic <note>Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan</note> having died, Walid <note>original: "Vlid"</note> was called to the crown under the name of Walid I, issued from the blood of Muhammad and the family of Aben Humcia. His lordships were so great that he commanded all of Africa, from the Strait of Gibraltar to the Red Sea, and even extended into the East, striking great fear into everyone. But from where he drew his greatness, he also saw its diminishment and decline. 

For it happened in the year of our Lord 712 or 718, according to Esteban de Garibay (Book 16, Chapter 16 of the history of Spain), that Roderic, the Visigoth King in Spain, seduced Cava, the wife <note>Though historical legends often identify Florinda "La Cava" as the daughter of Count Julian, this text identifies her as his wife.</note> of the Count of Ceuta <note>original: "Septe"</note> called Julian. He, grieved by such an insult, prompted Musa <note>original: "Muça"</note> Aben Zair, an Arab by nation and Lieutenant of Walid in Africa, to cross into Spain. Having informed his Master and Lord Walid, he was given permission to give a light troop to the Count to raid the lands of Spain and Portugal. 

Seeing that matters were succeeding as desired, he sent greater forces, and finally Aben Zair crossed himself with more power than ever. These Mohammadans conquered Seville and forced the Christians to retreat to Asturias and Biscay, where the Spanish nobility preserved themselves for many years for the defense of the Christian faith and the repopulation of the Spains. Inasmuch as the Arabs call their Kings Miramolins, that is to say, "the greatest of the believers." 

The histories of the Saracens state that a certain Saracen person named Abd al-Rahman <note>original: "Abedramon"</note>, descended from the ancient Caliphs of Damascus, was the first among his people who, having retired to Mauretania Tingitana <note>A Roman province located in what is now northern Morocco.</note>, had himself named and called *Miralmumin*, which is to say in the Arabic language, "Prince of the Believers." The Christians, unable to suffer this insult, took up arms and began the war, which did not cease until our time, when the Mohammadans were entirely driven out of Spain.

This Ayyub lived five years in his principality, and was succeeded by a Mohammadan Lord called Alhor <note>Al-Hurr</note>, who, while practicing his grandeur, saw the death of Suleiman <note>original: "Culema," likely referring to Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik</note>, who ordained as his heirs two of his cousins called Omar <note>Omar II</note> and Yazid <note>Yazid II</note>, sons of the King Walid <note>original: "Vlid"</note> mentioned above. Upon his death in the year of grace 720, the two aforementioned came to the Crown, and when Omar died, Yazid (or Gizid), second of the name and third Moorish King over Spain, held the whole empire. He sent Adha as governor to Spain, whom some call Al-Samh <note>original: "Azá"</note> and others Abraham son of Melit. Being the third Prince and governor of Cordoba, he built there the bridge that is seen today over the River Baetis <note>original: "Bethis"</note>, which is now called the Guadalquivir; and it was also he who, first among the Moors, began to raid the Gauls <note>Modern-day France</note>, and who tried to make himself Lord of the lands the Goths had possessed in Languedoc and Gascony. But before arriving there, being at Tortosa, a city seated on the River Ebro in the country of Catalonia, he died. He was substituted in the government by Zaman <note>As-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani</note>, who crossed the Pyrenees mountains and, taking the city of Narbonne, dared not rush upon Toulouse, which had been the royal seat of the Gothic Princes. In this war Zaman died, and in his place was put one whom Yazid sent, called Abderrahamen <note>Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi</note>, otherwise Abdirame. At this time, which was the year of grace 722, Pelagius <note>Pelayo, founder of the Kingdom of Asturias</note>, a Christian King in Spain and of the blood of the Goths, conquered the city of Leon. Two years later died Yazid, sovereign King of the Moors, succeeded by Hisham <note>original: "Hiscan"</note>, who was the most powerful King who had yet been among the Mohammadans, as he had under his Empire part of Asia Minor, Syria, the Medes, Hyrcanians, Persians, all the Arabias, Judea, Egypt, some part of Ethiopia, then Africa, Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria, and many lands in Gaul, and all the Spains, so well that he could boast of being the greatest Prince in the world. And of this lineage was a man named Abd-ar-Rahman <note>original: "Abderrahamé"</note>, of the Umayyad line <note>original: "Abé Humeya," referring to the Banu Umayya</note>, who came to Spain with the intention of making himself King there and standing against the Abbasid lineage <note>original: "race d'Alabeci," the dynasty that overthrew the Umayyads in the East</note>. No sooner had he arrived in Spain than he made war against Joseph <note>Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri, the last governor of Al-Andalus</note>, and he did not cease until he had put him to death and made himself King of Spain. Thus was the Muhammadan Empire divided: there was one King over the Arabs <note>The Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad</note>, another over the Africans, and the third in Spain.

Abd-ar-Rahman, therefore, the first King of Cordoba and the tenth in number among the Muhammadan usurpers of Spain, resolved to keep his court at Cordoba. But because Toledo was, as it were, the capital of the Spanish kingdom, he desired that his son Sulayman <note>original: "Culema"</note> of the Umayyad line should be governor there. He then set about making war against the Christian King of Spain, against whom he gained nothing but blows, and worse still befell him: for as soon as he called himself the Prince of the Believers <note>original: "Miramomelin" or "Miramolin," a corruption of the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*</note> of Spain, the Moors who were in Valencia refused to obey him, saying instead that they were subjects of the Abbasid blood. This was the reason he came to France to see Charlemagne <note>original: "Charles le grād"</note>, who restored him to his kingdom in the year 778, on the condition that the Christians would live in freedom of conscience and have the free exercise of their religion in his lands.

Abd-ar-Rahman having died in the year 780 <note>Modern historians date his death to 788</note>, he had as successor Hisham <note>original: "Hisé"</note> his son, the first of that name. Although he was a younger son, he usurped the state, which gave occasion for another division in the Kingdom, as most of the neighbors gave their obedience to Sulayman, who established his royal seat at Toledo and had himself called Prince of the Believers. It was from this that the kingdom of Toledo took its beginning, just as the rest of the kingdoms in Spain have their foundation in the divisions of the Moors. The two brothers went to war together and fought near Vilches, where King Hisham was victorious. From there, he went to besiege Toledo, which surrendered by agreement without a blow being struck. Sulayman, despairing of recovering his heritage, went to Africa to draw help from there and recover his losses. Hisham <note>original: "Hisen"</note> then made war to retake Languedoc, which had been conquered by some of his predecessors; but having performed some successful exploits there, in the end, by the help of the Emperor Charlemagne, this Moorish King was so thoroughly defeated that most of his cities paid tribute to the aforementioned Emperor, from which Hisham died of vexation in the year 794.

To this valiant King succeeded his eldest son Al-Hakam <note>original: "Hali Hatā" or "Alhacan"</note>, who was the first to order a guard of renegade Christians at his gate; he kept five thousand of them as a regular force to be near his person, just as the Grand Turk currently does with the Janissaries <note>The author compares the elite guard of Cordoba to the Ottoman Janissary corps familiar to 16th-century readers</note>. While he was occupied with his grandeurs, his cousin Sulayman plotted with the citizens of Toledo, and passing with forces from Africa into Spain, he made himself lord of Valencia and regained Toledo. But his joy was not great, for Al-Hakam went to meet him and they came to blows; Sulayman lost both the battle and his life. His brother Abdallah, whom he had brought from Africa, was taken and well-treated by Al-Hakam, who was nine years without being able to recover the city of Toledo. But in the end, he took it by a clever ruse, pretending to want to make peace and offer good treatment, but finally putting to death five or six thousand of the principal citizens <note>A reference to the "Day of the Foss" in 807</note>. During that time, the Christians, aided by the French, were making great conquests in Catalonia <note>original: "Cathelogne"</note>. Abd-ar-Rahman <note>original: "Abderahamen," referring to Abd-ar-Rahman II (r. 822–852)</note>, the second of that name, marched upon Barcelona and took it from the Christians. However, he did not enjoy it for long. During the reign of Louis the Pious in France, Aymon, the Governor of Guyenne <note>Aymon of Aquitaine, who rebelled against Louis the Pious</note>, revolted against his King and joined this Muhammadan King. Together, they besieged Barcelona once more, but it was in vain; they were forced to retreat without achieving anything. He also witnessed the revolts of Zaragoza and Toledo. Thus, the King of Toledo continued <note>The text implies a period of independent rule for Toledo</note>, and a Moor named Musa ibn Hazm <note>original: "Muca Aben Heazin," likely referring to Musa ibn Musa of the Banu Qasi family</note> was made King, being the second ruler of that seat. Leaving his son to govern his lands, he went to wage war against the Christians in Navarre and on the side of Catalonia. However, he was so thoroughly beaten there that, losing his army, he was mortally wounded. He left his son, Lubb ibn Musa <note>original: "Aben Lopé"</note>, as the third King of Toledo, who, fearing Abd-ar-Rahman, formed an alliance with Ordoño, King of Galicia and the Asturias <note>Ordoño I (r. 850–866)</note>.

Upon the death of Abd-ar-Rahman, his son Muhammad succeeded him, the second of that name if one includes the false Prophet Muhammad in the count. He felt the revolt of his subjects against his Kingdom, who were aided by the Christians. However, this cunning Muhammad defeated them by a ruse, killing thirteen thousand Moors and eight thousand Christians. Being unable to take Toledo, he placed garrisons at Coria <note>original: "Corite"</note>, Alcalá de Henares, Talavera, and Calatrava. Finally, he held the city so pressed by famine that it surrendered by agreement in the year 844. Then, giving himself over to pleasures, he died in the year of grace 874 <note>Historical records typically date Muhammad I's death to 886</note>, having reigned for thirty-five years.

Al-Mundhir <note>original: "Almudir"</note>, the first of that name and son of this Muhammad, came to the crown, obeyed by those of Cordoba, Seville, and all of Andalusia. This Al-Mundhir was devoted to pleasures and bodily filth, leaving several sons and daughters, though none succeeded him. He waged no war against the Christians, just as he was never attacked by them, and he died in the year 876. He had as his successor Abdullah <note>original: "Abdalla"</note>, the third of the name and seventh King of Cordoba, who was his brother, or, as others say, his nephew. He also passed his time in peace with the Christians and died in the year 889.

He was succeeded by Abd-ar-Rahman III <note>r. 912–961</note>, whom some call Almanzor <note>original: "Almançor," meaning "The Victorious"; a title later famously used by the vizier Ibn Abi Amir</note>, the son of Abdullah. As soon as he became King, he took the title in his records of *An-Nasir li-Din Allah* <note>original: "Ananzer Ledin Alla," meaning "Defender of the Religion of God"</note>. In his time, the Christians laid siege to Talavera in the Castilian kingdom of Toledo. He sent reinforcements which the Spaniards defeated, taking the city and the general of the Muhammadan army. This so incited and moved the heart of this King that he sent to Africa to King Al-Mutarrif <note>original: "Almotaraph"</note>, who commanded over the <term>Tingitane</term> <note>Referring to Mauretania Tingitana, the Roman name for the region of Morocco</note>, namely over Fez and Marrakesh, who sent forces. There, the Muhammadans were defeated, and the generals of the two Moorish armies were slain in the year 894.

Then King Ordoño <note>Ordoño II</note> abruptly entered the Moor's lordships and, crossing the Tagus <note>original: "Tajò"</note> and Guadiana rivers, came as far as Badajoz. Abd-ar-Rahman crossed into Galicia, and the Christians followed him, where the battle was cruel and bloody, lasting from morning until evening without anyone knowing who had the upper hand, and each of the Kings boasting of victory. This Abd-ar-Rahman tormented the Christians more than any of the Muhammadan Kings of Spain, for he overran as far as Navarre, and afterwards Castile, which was then only a County. He was succeeded by Hisham II <note>original: "Hiſen"</note>, the second of that name, whom others call Yxecà. Passing through, they reached Compostela and tore down part of the Church of Saint James <note>The Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela was famously raided by Al-Mansur in 997.</note>. However, at that hour his troops were struck by strange diseases, so that he returned without achieving anything. Nonetheless, there was later a general for the same King Hisham who overran the country of León and Galicia, performing great feats of arms and making himself terrifying to all those Christians, whose private hatreds were the cause of these disasters. Consequently, the greater part of Catalonia was once again subjected to the Muhammadans.

Among the Moors, divisions also arose following the example of the Christians. There was a Moor named Sulayman <note>original: "Culema," referring to Sulayman al-Musta'in</note> who seized the kingdom from Hisham, whom he put in prison, and made himself <term>Miramomelin</term> <note>From the Arabic *Amir al-Mu'minin*, or "Commander of the Faithful," a title for the Caliph.</note> of Córdoba, having come there from Barbary <note>North Africa</note>, from whence he drew support. But another powerful lord opposed him, drove him out, and usurped the lordship; he was called Muhammad <note>Muhammad II al-Mahdi</note>. As he persecuted the friends of his predecessor, some revolted, including a Moor from Toledo named Abd Allah, who restored the royalty in the city of Toledo in the year 993, 149 years after it had last been subjected to the Kings of Córdoba. From then on, it had its own kings, and it never again returned to the hands of the Kings of Córdoba. This King of Toledo allied with the Christians to gain advantage against the forces of the King of Córdoba. Meanwhile, Sulayman, having been driven from his kingdom and favored by the Christians, made war on King Muhammad, whom he defeated, and returned to his seat. This caused him to release Hisham—whom we said above had been driven from his kingdom by Sulayman—who, as the legitimate king of the succession and royal family, was also received by his subjects. He took several cities of Andalusia which, during the civil wars, had been usurped by tyrants and rebels, and he waged war against the Africans <note>The Berbers</note> who defended the party of his adversary Sulayman.

He also had war against Ubayd Allah <note>original: "Obeydalla"</note>, King of Toledo, in which the Toledan was defeated and killed; he was succeeded by Hayrà, the seventh King of Toledo. But just as Hisham thought to enjoy his states peacefully, he saw himself attacked worse than ever by a Moor named Ali <note>Ali ibn Hammud al-Nasir</note>, favored by the Africans, who also deprived him of his seat in the year 1011. But he was not King for long, for another, Al-Hakam <note>original: "Halyhatan"</note>, unseated him and had him treacherously massacred in the year 1031. This angered the Moors, so that they elected as king a cousin of Ali named Al-Qasim <note>original: "Cacin"</note>, having on his side the Moors of Africa called <term>Berberuzes</term> <note>Berbers</note>. <meta>This page continues the historical account of the Moorish presence in the Iberian Peninsula, focusing on the transition from the Caliphate of Córdoba to the Taifa kingdoms and the rise of the Almoravids.</meta>

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

It had happened quite a long time ago that his son, named Muhammad <note>original: Mahomet</note>, the fifth of that name and the last Moorish King of Córdoba, [reigned]; this kingdom came to an end in the year of our Lord 1027, having begun in the year 758. Following the decline of this kingdom, the kingdom of Toledo gained strength, which we must discuss, since reason dictates that having removed the Moors from Africa, we now see them withdrawing back there again. The downfall of the house of the kings of Córdoba was the reason that the Christian kings of Spain extended their borders and recovered many lands from the Muslims <note>original: Mahometans</note>, especially on the side of Portugal, Galicia, and Catalonia. The kingdom of Castile was established in the year 1034, having previously been only a County; its king was Ferdinand, son of Sancho, King of Navarre, surnamed "the Great," who married the heiress of León and sister of King Bermudo. In this season, a Moorish king named Al-Mamun <note>original: Almenon or Aly Maynon</note> reigned in Toledo, the ninth in the number of kings who commanded in this city, against whom the aforementioned King Ferdinand I waged such violent war that, by taking the towns of Talamanca, Uceda, Guadalajara, Alcalá, Madrid, and others, he so stunned the Moor that he surrendered as his vassal and did him homage for his possessions in Toledo.

This Al-Mamun was succeeded by a son named Hisham ibn Umayya <note>original: Hisé Aben Humeya</note>, under whom very learned men flourished in Toledo, as did many Christians living in liberty of conscience, who were called Mozarabs <term>Mozarabs: From the Arabic 'musta'rib', meaning 'Arabized'; these were Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule and adopted Arabic language and culture while maintaining their Christian faith</term>, just as I have fully described previously. During the final years of Ferdinand, this Toledan king and several other kinglets <note>petty kings of small territories</note> who held the kingdoms of Aragon and Valencia were constrained to return to their former obedience. While these things were passing thus in Spain, there was great division in Africa between the Kings and Princes; for just as those of the blood of Umayya <note>Humeya</note> held Spain (as we have seen), and those of the house of Al-Alawi <note>Aben Alaueci</note> were lords of Africa—both families having descended from two daughters of the impostor Muhammad—there arose a very rich and powerful family of Moors in Africa bearing the name of the Almoravids <term>Almoravids: An imperial Berber Muslim dynasty that emerged in the 11th century</term>. This family drove those of the Al-Alawi race and the blood of the false Prophet out of the African kingdom. The leader of these Almoravids was named Yusuf ibn Tashfin <note>original: Joseph Aben Tesfin</note>, after whom a river in Barbary <note>North Africa</note> is named, in the land and kingdom of Tlemcen. The Spanish and African Moors who did not like the races of Umayya and Al-Alawi placed themselves under the power of this Almoravid. Upon the death of the King of Toledo, Al-Mamun, his only son Hisham succeeded him, which occurred in the year of Grace 1074; those of Córdoba made war against him, but he, aided by his friend the King of Castile, punished them so well that they no longer had the boldness to overrun his lands to harm him.

Now, not to leave out the rest of these Muslims, at that time there were kings in Seville named Al-Mu'tamid <note>original: Almucamuz Aben Amet</note>; in Granada, Al-Muzaffar <note>original: Amundafar</note>; and Abu Bakr in Valencia. However, this last one was a subject of the King of Toledo. Against these, the Cid <note>original: Gid</note>, the great Spanish Captain and pillar of the Christians, fought successfully several times and conquered a good number of places from Al-Muzaffar, who bore the title of King of Zaragoza. Meanwhile, Hisham, King of Toledo, died, leaving as successor his brother Yahya <note>original: Hiaya</note>, surnamed Al-Qadir <note>original: Alcadurbilé</note>, a vicious and dissolute man and the last of the Princes of Toledo, being hated by his subjects because of his youthful excesses, cruelty, and follies. This caused the governor of Valencia, named Abu Bakr, to revolt, and led both the Mozarab Christians of Toledo and the Moors to pray—some to King Alfonso of Castile, the most powerful of the Christians—[for aid].

## **Monarchy of the Moors.**

This young man was of humble origin and the son of a potter, though he possessed a noble heart and a drive reflecting the ambition that smoldered in his soul; he was named Abdelmon <note>Abd al-Mu'min (r. 1130–1163), the first Caliph of the Almohad Empire</note>. He placed such faith in the words of this philosopher, Thumert <note>Ibn Tumart, the spiritual founder of the Almohad movement</note>, that he addressed himself to a Muslim cleric highly learned in the Quran. He revealed Thumert's prediction to him and begged him to provide help and aid, promising that if the affair succeeded as the stars promised, he would make him the greatest among the followers of Muhammad. Almohadi <note>Likely referring to Ibn Tumart's claim to be the 'Mahdi' or 'Guided One'</note>—for so this Muslim cleric was called—resolved to help him. He could find no finer or faster way to sow novelties in their religion than by beginning to interpret the Quran against the sense of all the other doctors of law, adapting everything to the temperaments of the Africans. These people, astonished by this doctrine, gave him their ear and accepted it, holding this man in great reputation for holiness.

Seeing that his plan was progressing according to his desire, he moved further and proposed that Abdelmon was a person chosen by God, who intended to plant His holy Al-Furqan law <note>The author uses "Alphurcaniste," derived from *Al-Furqan*, an Arabic name for the Quran meaning "The Criterion" between right and wrong</note> throughout the whole world. This was the reason that this same Abdelmon was honored and respected as something sent by God. It was then that Almahadi began to reveal himself and to preach against the race of the Almoravids <note>The ruling dynasty prior to the Almohads</note>, calling them tyrants and usurpers, as those who had chased away the family of Alabeci <note>The Abbasids</note> and the blood of their prophet Muhammad.

Going further, he attacked the person of the Caliph of Baghdad <note>Original: "Baldac"</note>, the sovereign pontiff of their law, and spoke against the rest of the *Alfaquis* <note>term: Faqih; an Islamic jurist or expert in religious law</note> and ministers of their sect. In short, by saying that Abdelmon was of the blood of Muhammad, he won over the greater part of the nobility. In this, he was greatly favored by Aben Thumert with his predictions and astronomical figures. With such forces, this son of a potter became great and fought often against the sovereign King of Africa and the Moors of Spain <note>Original: "Hespagne"</note>. Thus was the African state divided into Almoravids and Almohads. It was necessary to recite this history here in order to clear up several doubts that are commonly found in the histories of Africa and Spain.

The matter went so far that when King Albo Aly Aben Tesfin <note>Ali ibn Yusuf ibn Tashfin</note> was killed in battle, this noble potter Abdelmon was made King and *Miramomelin* <note>term: Miramomelin; a European corruption of the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*, or "Commander of the Faithful"</note> of Africa. The Almohad heretics held the Lordship and government over everything, since the King was of their sect and had been advanced by them; this occurred in the year 1147. During these divisions, Alfonso, the first King of Portugal, won several places that the Moors held in Lusitania <note>The Roman name for the region comprising most of modern Portugal</note>, as did the Count of Barcelona, knowing well that it was good to fish in troubled waters. 

But Abdelmon, not content that Africa obeyed him, prepared also to pass into Europe and subjugate the Moors of Spain who obeyed the Almoravids. However, it was Almohadi who made this journey, while Thumert stayed with the King. Through the diligence of this preacher, Abdelmon was made monarch of the Moors of Africa and Spain. There, these Almohads began to use strange tyrannies and cruelties, as much against the Christians as against the Muslims who were not of their opinion. This was done by Abdelmon, who, forgetting his origins, practiced insupportable insolence against the Christians, over whom he made great conquests. After these were put into effect, he returned victorious to Africa, where he established his seat...

royal <note>The catchword from the previous page was "royal," completing the description of the court in Marrakesh.</note> court in Marrakesh, governing as a gentle and gracious Prince by the counsel of Thumert and Almohadi <note>The author refers here to Ibn Tumart (c. 1080–1130), the spiritual founder of the Almohad movement. The text treats "Almohadi" as a title or a second person, likely referring to the Mahdi.</note>, who died in the year 1150. His funeral rites were performed by the King with as much honor as if he had been the Monarch of the Muslims himself; his tomb was honored and visited just as if it were the sepulcher of a holy man, everyone holding him to be a Prophet, though the devil worked great illusions there. When Abdelmon <note>Abd al-Mu'min, the first Almohad Caliph</note>, the first Almohad King, came to die, he had as his successor his son Aben Jacob <note>Abu Yaqub Yusuf (r. 1163–1184)</note>, who, like his father, held the Muslim Kingdoms of Africa and Spain. Having a mortal hatred for the Portuguese, he crossed the sea and came to Spain in the year 1184; giving battle against the Christians, he was mortally wounded there. He was succeeded by his brother <note>Historically his son</note> Joseph, surnamed Mamezuth or Mazemuth <note>Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur</note>, who brought great ruin to Spain. However, he was forced to return to Africa because of the divisions and factions that were already beginning to rise there. Having put an end to these, he returned to Spain and laid siege to the city of Toledo, something no other had done since the time the Christians had reconquered it. He gained nothing there, however, and was forced to retreat, wasting the countryside as far as Andalusia, hoping to take the aforementioned city of Toledo the following year. But he profited as little then as the first time; for this reason, he took and pillaged Vera and Plasencia, Santa Cruz, Trujillo, and Montánchez. In short, he left no corner of the Kingdom of Toledo where he did not exercise his fury and rage. Then, passing into Portugal, he took the city of Silves and Alcácer do Sal, and destroyed Sesimbra, Palmela, and other fortresses. Then he went to Andalusia and from there to Africa to his city of Marrakesh, where he died full of riches and victories in the year of our salvation 1200. He had as his heir his son called Muhammad the Green <note>Muhammad al-Nasir, known as 'the Green' (En-Nasir), likely due to his standard or attire</note>, because he ordinarily wore a green wig. He passed into Spain in the year 1210 and made great conquests over the Christians, and again crossed back in the year 1212 with more forces than ever. The Miramomelin <term>Miramomelin: A corruption of the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*, meaning "Commander of the Faithful"</term> came to Spain, and it is held that he had 80,000 horses, a great number of Moorish Kings, and an infinity of footmen. Against him marched the Christian Kings of Navarre, León, and Castile, and the battle was furious and bloody on all sides <note>This refers to the pivotal Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), a turning point in the Reconquista</note>. But in the end, the Muslims had the worst of it, losing 200,000 dead men and a great number of prisoners. Aben Muhammad and his brother Abu Zayd escaped by the speed of their horses; fearing to lose Marrakesh, he recrossed the sea as soon as he possibly could, leaving the miserable Moors of Spain so discomforted that they did not know "from which wood to make their arrows" <note>A French idiom meaning they were at their wits' end or had no resources left</note>. This rout greatly diminished the authority and credit of Aben Muhammad the Almohad; whereas many had previously feared and respected him, they now left him. Among others, his own brother Zayd Abu Zayd seized Valencia and made himself its King and Lord. Aben Muhammad, his cousin, called himself King of Baeza and usurped Córdoba and the lands of the domain of Toledo and Andalusia. At Seville, there was also a Moor named Abd Allah who held the rest of the people of Andalusia, holding more land than any of the others. Sometime later, Ibn Hud arose, descended from the blood of the Kings of Zaragoza, and made himself King of Granada. These usurpations brought an end to the Muslim Princes of the blood of Abdelmon, and...

In the year 1252, four years after the capture of this city <note original="cefte cité">Referring to Seville, which fell to the Christians in 1248.</note> which had remained for 534 years under the subjection of the Moors, Mahomet <note>Muhammad I ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid dynasty.</note>, King of Granada, renewed the peace and alliance with Don Alphonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, known as "The Wise."</note>, King of Castile, whom he went to visit as far as Toledo. All of Andalusia did not obey this King Mahomet, for there was a King in the Algarve named Aben Mosad; and without fail, if the Moors had not thus divided their power, the Christians would hardly have so quickly regained possession of the Kingdom lost by the Goths. <note>A reference to the Visigothic Kingdom, which fell to the Umayyad conquest in 711 AD.</note> In Jerez and Niebla there was another petty king named Aben Amet, both vassals of the King of Castile, who in the year 1261, along with the King of Granada, revolted against the Castilian and took several towns and fortresses from him. To support this King, Mahomet summoned a thousand horses <note original="mille cheuaux">Meaning a thousand cavalrymen.</note> from Morocco, the soldiers who came upon them calling themselves ***Merins*** or ***Marins*** <note>The Marinids, a Zenata Berber dynasty that replaced the Almohads.</note>, all from the same family and sent by Iucep <note>Abu Yusuf Yaqub.</note>, King of Morocco. These were so well favored by Mahomet that his subjects, feeling envy and spite, revolted and caused much harm to the lands subject to their Princes. I have spoken here of Iucep, King of Morocco, descended from Jacob <note>Yaqub al-Mansur.</note>, and father of this Mahomet surnamed "the Green" <note>Muhammad al-Nasir, who wore a green caftan; he was defeated at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa.</note> who was defeated in Spain. Upon his death, his nephew Caid Arrax <note>Likely referring to the Almohad Caliph al-Murtada.</note> reigned in Morocco, the fifth of the Almohad race in Africa, governing the whole country from the Atlantic Ocean as far as Egypt. Among other governors, he had one at Tlemcen named Gomarança Aben Zien <note>Yaghmurasen ibn Zyan, founder of the Zayyanid dynasty.</note>, of a race called Abdalnés <note>The Abdalwadids.</note> subject to the Almohads, who, because he did not conduct himself as he should in his government, fell into the enmity of King Caid Arrax, who went to besiege him in a castle called Tremezezic. But a cousin of the besieged man, feigning surrender to the King and offering to show him the weakest points of the place, treacherously slew him; and while the soldiers were troubled and astonished by the death of the King, Gomarança emerged from the castle, attacked them, made a great massacre, and made himself King of Tlemcen, whose lineage lasted a long time. At the same time, there was a lineage or family in Fez called ***Merins***, from a powerful citizen named Merin, who was initially a Christian, but his successors became Moors. One of this race named Bucarben Merin <note>Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Haqq.</note>, being governor of Fez for Caid Arrax, hearing of the success of the Almohads at Tremezezic and how the fugitives had been defeated by his own people, named himself also King of Fez; and another brother of his named Aben Iucep was made lord of Rabat, not without great astonishment to the Almohads. The Almohads then made Almorcada <note>Abu Dabbus al-Wathiq.</note>, a relative of the deceased Caid Arrax, King of Morocco, who immediately made war on the Marinids of Fez. They defeated him, and from then on, the Lordship of these two cities was separated. Aben Bucar Merin, dying, left a son of young age named Hiaya, who was placed under the guardianship of his uncle Aben Iucep. But the child dying, the uncle was made King of Fez and highly esteemed among the Africans, so that he was called "the Great Old Man of the Marinids." To him retired a cousin of King Almorcada of Morocco named Budebus, revolting against his Prince and begging for aid from this Marinid, promising him a great extent of land for the enlargement of the Kingdom of Fez if he would help him obtain the lordship of Morocco. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the various peoples and languages of the Levant and the Middle East, specifically focusing on the Syrian Christians and the intellectual contributions of the Arabic-speaking world.</meta>

->LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.<-

Pierre de Vitry <note>original: "Pierre de Vitriaco," a 13th-century historian and bishop of Acre</note> in his history of Jerusalem.

The Syrians or Surani lived in Syria, from which they were named, or from Sur <note>The ancient city of Tyre</note>, which was a famous city of Syria; they follow the religion and rite of the Greeks for the most part. They deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as he does from the Father <note>A reference to the "filioque" theological dispute between Eastern and Western churches</note>. They do not allow fourth marriages and do not recognize the Roman Church as supreme over all others. They regard the excommunications and sentences of the Roman Prelates as nothing. They feel all Latins <note>Western Christians</note> are rightfully excommunicated. They wash the altars on which Latins have performed their rites. They show no reverence to the sacraments of the Latins, nor do they stand for one carrying the consecrated host to the sick. They perform the sacrament with leavened bread; priests keep the wives with whom they contracted marriage before taking holy orders. They do not consider the subdiaconate among the holy orders. Their small children, immediately after baptism, are sealed with chrism by a simple priest, without waiting for a Bishop. They judge the Sabbath day <note>Saturday</note> so solemn that it is permitted to fast on it, except for the Sabbath of Easter. On that day they celebrate divine rites and eat meat. They delight in the Saracenic <note>Arabic</note> language; they keep their wives secluded in a similar manner as the Saracens, and emulate other customs of theirs; they do not shave their beards, in the manner of Easterners.

J. de Mandeville, knight, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>Old Catalan/Provencal in this excerpt</note> in the year 1322.

Also there are other Christians named Syrians, and they hold a middle belief, which is between our law and that of the Greeks; and they all wear beards just as the Greeks do, and they perform the sacrament with leavened bread, and in their languages they use Saracenic <note>Arabic</note> letters, but for the mystery of the Church <note>liturgy</note> they use Greek letters, and they perform their sacrament just as the Jacobites <note>Syriac Orthodox</note> do.

### On the comparison of Arabic and Saracenic knowledge with Egyptian, Chaldean, Persian, Greek, and Latin or Roman.

As the knowledge of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks, and Latins or Romans increased with their force and power, so too did that of the Arabs and Saracens. For when they were the strongest and most powerful in the world, they became highly learned and very scholarly, principally in the astrological and demonstrative sciences, as is deduced by the author of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* <note>original: "Chronique Cassinense"</note>, book 3, chapter 34. Among them, Avicenna and Averroes (mentioned above), Albumasar, Geber, and countless others acquired the highest praise. Avicenna was the most universal of them all in Philosophy, Mathematics, and in Arabic Theology and Poetry; he also wrote on Medicine, treating very well—in the judgment of the most learned in that art—the signs and causes of diseases, applying to them several remedies neither understood nor practiced by the Greeks, Latins, or Romans. Averroes subtly explained the works of Aristotle in their entirety. As for Albumasar, he perfectly understood the celestial movements and their effects, having discovered the great conjunctions <note>The alignment of planets used in historical astrology</note> and several other fine things that had remained unknown until his time. Geber, a very expert Mathematician, found faults in the demonstrations of the Al- <note>The text likely intended "Almagest," the influential astronomical treatise by Ptolemy</note>

majesty of Ptolemy: several others of theirs like Avempace <note>original: "Auenpace," the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajja</note>, Al-Ghazali <note>original: "Algazel"</note>, Ibn al-Baitar <note>original: "Benbitar," a famous botanist and pharmacist</note>, Al-Battani <note>original: "Abaten," the astronomer Albategnius</note>, Ishaq <note>original: "Siphac," likely referring to the translator Ishaq ibn Hunayn</note>, the Philosophers. Mesue, Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"</note> otherwise known as al-Mansur, Serapion, Zoar, nicknamed the wise, the Physicians, Aonias, Avenzoar, Al-Farabi <note>original: "Alpharas"</note>, Al-Farghani <note>original: "Alphragan"</note>, Haly, Ridwan <note>original: "Rodoan"</note> and other Astrologers, cited by me in my discourse on the *Truth of the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics* printed in 1598. All of these figures flourished at nearly the same time, having invented many beautiful things in doctrines and sciences, or improving upon those previously invented; composing their works in the Arabic language, and occupying the schools of the West before the restoration of the Greek and Latin languages. Because of this, these Arabs or Saracens acquired such a reputation in Mathematics that when Alfonso, King of Castile <note>Alfonso X "The Wise," who reigned 1252–1284</note>, undertook the preparation of his Astronomical Tables, he had his primary recourse to them, since they alone in that season could teach and restore such disciplines. To them he gave great gifts amounting to four hundred thousand crowns <note>original: "escus"</note>, imitating in this the liberality of Alexander the Great, who spent a similar sum to have the natures of animals truly represented to him by Aristotle.

But the Arabic Caliphs, seeing that their people were too devoted to Philosophy and Mathematics and cared very little for their Mohammedan Law <note>The author refers here to Islamic Sharia or religious practice</note>, founded colleges for the maintenance of those who would teach and learn the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> of their Prophet, and in some Universities they transferred, or rather transmitted, the lectureship of Philosophy into that of their said law, ordering that whoever from then on studied the Quran would in no way occupy themselves with Philosophy or Astrology. This caused the practice of the other sciences to cool in some places, though not everywhere, considering that in Persia there are to this day very learned Philosophers and Astrologers. 

Regarding the comparison of the Arabic and Saracenic language with Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, we learn that when the Greeks and Romans were in their greatest prosperity, ruling many countries, they extended these two languages along with their Empires and Lordships. Many people and nations studied to understand and speak them, either to please them or to trade with them; then the Christian religion, using these languages, preserved and spread them in many lands and regions. However, these were never understood and spoken in as many places as the Arabic language is now, which is common to almost all the inhabitants of Asia, Africa, and a third part of Europe, as I have remarked previously. Affairs of the Quran are handled in it, along with all other disciplines, just as we use Latin here, separated from the common tongues and understood only by those who have learned it in schools. This language resembles (as I remarked before) Hebrew, Syriac, and Chaldaic, in that it is written like them from right to left, with points in place of vowels, and has several names and words in common, and a phrasing very similar to them; but it has its own letters and characters specific to it alone. In this, it is very different from the Greek and Latin languages, which are also written from left to right, as I demonstrate hereafter in this discourse.

### Concerning the region of the Turks.

Abraham Ortelius, in his geographical synonyms and treasury <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous Flemish cartographer who created the first modern atlas.</note>, speaking of the region of the Turks and their various names and titles, says that Aria <note>original: "Ἀρὶα"</note> is a region of Asia. According to Ptolemy and others, they are the Arii <note>original: "Ἄρειοι"</note>; they are the Arrhiani according to Arrian, and the Ariei according to Curtius—or "Arsi," as the edition by Aldus Manutius has it. They are called Arienses by Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary.</note>, and they appear as the Arieni <note>original: "Ἀριηνοὶ"</note> in the works of Dionysius. The merchant [Pierre] Servere calls it Turkestan; Pinet calls it Hetia eirauæ. According to Giacomo Gastaldi, the region is Khorasan <note>original: "Corafan"</note>, and Garcia de Orta reports that its inhabitants are called the Corasones. According to Pomponius Mela, it is an island in the Black Sea <note>original: "Ponti Euxini"</note>, while Pliny testifies it is called by another name, Chanceritis. Pinet interprets Farnasia as Areos Nesos <note>original: "ἄρεως νῆσος"</note>, that is, the "Island of Mars," which is the name Stephanus gives it. The location of the region of Aria is found in Ptolemy; it seems to me, from the Asian tables of Abulfeda <note>A 14th-century Arab geographer and prince.</note>, to be called Burgiam. Aria is also the name of a city in this region, as well as a river, the Arius <note>original: "ἄρειος"</note>, mentioned by Polybius in Book 10 and by Arrian in his *Life of Alexander*.

The Turks call themselves Muslims <note>original: "Mufulmannos"</note>, as Hugo Favolius writes in his *Byzantine Itinerary*. And Leunclavius <note>Johannes Leunclavius, a 16th-century historian specializing in Ottoman history.</note> notes this in his *History of the Muslims*: their seat is described by Pomponius and Pliny as being near the Sea of Azov <note>original: "Paludem Meotidem"</note>. In the *Miscellaneous History*, they are located near the Caspian Gates. Eustathius writes that the Huns are called "Turks" by the Persians; Hermolaus [Barbarus], in his corrections of Pliny, teaches that they are also called Thunni. According to Scylax, as reported by Theodore Gaza, the Turks are those whom Strabo calls the Cyrtians <note>original: "κύρτιοι"</note>; the Romans called them Curcians, or "Curti" for short. The same Gaza cites Gemistus Pletho, who suggests they are the Paropamisadae, though Gaza admits he does not agree with this. Nearly all authors seem to agree with one voice that their origin is drawn from the Scythians who inhabit the Caucasus mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Laonikos Chalkokondyles reports that "Turk" signifies a man who follows a more rustic way of life. Guillaume Postel thinks they are named Togarmah <note>original: "Togarma"</note> by the Hebrews; Benjamin of Tudela says the same. Mention is made of them in Ezekiel 27 as Togarmah <note>original: "Thogorma or θόργαμα"</note>. I must not omit here that Pintianus, in his corrections of Pomponius Mela, strikes out the name of the "Turks" from Pliny and Mela and substitutes "Iurcae" <note>original: "Ἰούρκαι"</note> in its place, based on Herodotus' *Melpomene*—though by what right he does this, he himself should see. He would certainly have driven them out of our Europe with greater applause than he did from these historical writings. Suidas mentions the Turks, saying that iron is not easily prepared among them. Much more can be found concerning them in the works of Emperor Leo, chapter eight, paragraph forty-five. See also: Huns, Unni, Jaxartae, Sarmatia, Khazars <note>original: "Cafari"</note>, and Hungarians.

The Huns or Unni <note>original: "Οὗννοι"</note> are a people called Thunni <note>original: "Θοῦννοι"</note> by Eustathius, and also by Pliny, as Hermolaus testifies. They are placed after the Scythians by Eustathius. Theophylact Simocatta, as reported by the same, states that they are called "Turks" <note>original: "τούρκοι"</note> by the Persians. The Huns are also called Sabiri <note>original: "σάβειροι"</note>, according to Nicolaus Callistus and Suidas. The same Callistus says the ancients called them Nebrus. They are called Onogurs by Agathias. The Unni, Huns, and Avars are the same people according to Widukind and Eginhard, as are the Hungarians today. The same author also calls the Hungarians Ugrians <note>original: "Vgros"</note> and Magyars <note>original: "Magores"</note>. Jordanes calls them the Aviri. The Huns are also called Chunos...

Thus, by a double exit, they were led out for the punishment of the world, without them even thinking of it.

...having Bactria <note>An ancient region in Central Asia, south of the Oxus river.</note> and Margiana towards the North; the region of the Parthians to the West; desert Caramania and Drangiana to the South; and the country of the Paropamisadae <note>A region in the Hindu Kush, centered around modern-day Kabul.</note> to the East, who are subjects of **Turkestan** under the obedience of the Tartars. **André Thevet**, in Book 9, Chapter 3 of his *Universal Cosmography*, speaks thus of the Turks and their country: "From **Turkestan** in former times the Turks emerged; now the province which is still called **Turkestan**, quite near the Caspian mountains and those named **Tapuris** <note>The Tabaristan mountains.</note> joining the **Emodes** <note>Part of the Himalayan range.</note>, and consequently in **Northern Scythia**, is not far from the **Parthians and Hyrcanians**, along the great river **Chesel** <note>original: "Chesel", likely referring to the Jaxartes or Syr Darya river.</note>, which comes from the rising sun and flows into the Caspian Sea at the borders of the country of **Hyrcania**." Here it must be noted that the Turks have no difficulty confessing their origin to be from that country. However, because this country has changed its name at present—especially since the Eastern Tartars came to attack it in the time of **Ogedei Khan** <note>original: "Occatam Cam", the second Great Khan of the Mongol Empire and son of Genghis Khan.</note>, whereas previously they were in full liberty under the title of **Turkestan**—it is necessary to show by what means the said Turks left their infertile land to find new seats. This occurred at the time when the great overflows of the Northern peoples took place for the ruin of the world: namely, some were **Huns**, who were also **Scythians, Europeans, and Asians**; the **Goths, Visigoths, and Ostrogoths**; the **Alans and Vandals**, having passed their fury; and the **Lombards** afflicting Italy in the time of **King Pippin**, father of **Charlemagne**. It was then that these Turks passed the **Caspian Gates at Derbent** and occupied **Armenia** in the year of salvation 764. They were not yet so powerful as to be able to wage war or establish a state against neighboring princes; rather, they kept to the mountains and the depths of the woods and forests, not daring to attack the armies of their neighbors in an open field, but only lying in wait to pillage and sack places they saw without great defense, etc. See what the same **Thevet** continues to write in the subsequent Chapter 4 concerning these Tartars, and in his Book 11, Chapter 1, on the origin and success of the Turks. **Gilbert Génébrard**, in Book 4 of his *Chronography*, says: "Those who are well-versed in the knowledge of the most ancient languages know well enough that this word 'Turks' signifies in the **Hebrew** language: Cursed people, excommunicated, detestable, exiled, driven away, and banished." This word is held by the **Mahometans, Muslims, and Turks** of today—as I have already remarked—in great contempt and hatred, and they even consider it an atrocious and execrable insult. This has some appearance of truth, inasmuch as their Prophet **Muhammad**, in order not to offend them—and the **Tartars** who began to awaken around the year of salvation 1200—retained in his **Alcoran** or **Al-Furqan** <note>Another name for the Quran, meaning "The Criterion."</note> circumcision, purifications, and ceremonies of the Law of **Moses** for the reasons previously deduced by us. **Sigismund von Herberstein** <note>original: "Sigismūdus Liber"</note> in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs* says: <note>original: "Turcas se vocari ægrè ferunt, probrique loco ducunt, sed Besermani appellari gaudent, eoque nomine & Turcæ se appellari volunt."</note> "They take offense at being called Turks and consider it a disgrace, but they delight in being called **Besermani** <note>A corruption of "Muslims."</note>, and they wish to be called by that name." **Johannes Leunclavius**, in his *Turkish Onomasticon*, states: <note>original: "Iurki, Tzurki, Zurki Turki nomen idem quod Nomades siue Pastores vagabũdi significabuntur."</note> "**Iurki, Tzurki, Zurki, Turki**: the name signifies the same as **Nomads** or wandering **Shepherds**." In the beginning, the Turks lived like the **Nomads**, and even in **Anatolia** <note>original: "Natolie"</note> those who lead cattle are called **Turcomanleri** <note>Turcomans.</note> at present. The authority and power of the Sultans of Egypt and the Mamluks began at the time when King Saint Louis was captured at Damietta <note>King Louis IX of France was captured during the Seventh Crusade in 1250.</note>. Furthermore, *Mamluk* <note>original: "Mammeluz"</note> in the *Syrian, African, and Moorish* languages signifies servants or soldiers who lived according to the manner of their religion without marriage, in the fashion of the <term>Knights of Rhodes</term> <note>A Catholic military order, also known as the Knights Hospitaller.</note>. And just as there were four *Vizier Pashas* <note>original: "Viſi Baſchas"</note> serving the Great Turk, so too the Sultan had four *Emir Kabir* <note>original: "Emir Quibir"</note>—that is to say, Great Emirs or Admirals—under them; besides these, there was a Great Constable whom they called *Dawadar Kabir* <note>original: "Derdard Quibir"</note>, named by <term>Paolo Giovio</term> <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and historian.</note> the "Great Diadoro." The said Sultan was elected by the Mamluks from among their own number, and most often from among the Emirs. All of these Mamluks, moreover, were renegade Christians or the sons of Christians, like the *Janissaries*. For they would under no circumstances receive a *Turk, Moor, or Jew* into their company. They were almost all *Liveroya*—the name given by the Turks to those anciently called *Iberians and Circassians*, now simply *Circassians*—and those who were *Colchians, Georgians, and Albanians*, and other *Jacobite and Nestorian* Christians living near the river *Baso*, anciently called the *Phasis* <note>The Rioni River in modern-day Georgia.</note>. These people were taken by the *Tartars* and brought in troops to be sold to the Emirs, who bought them, raised them, and made them *Mamluks*, as is confirmed by *Chalcondyles* in the third book of his history of the Turks; *Friar Antoine Geuffroy*, Knight of Malta, in his book on the conquests of the Turks; the aforementioned *Paolo Giovio* in his book on the Turks and in books 17 and 18 of his histories; and *Giovanni Maria Angiolello of Vicenza*, who also affirms having read (like Paolo Giovio) what a *Kazasker* <note>original: "Cadileſcher," meaning a military judge or chief justice.</note>—that is to say, a sovereign Pontiff or Bishop in the *Mahometan* superstition—had written about it, having accompanied the Great Turk *Selim* on the journey he made to ruin the authority and power of *Tuman bay* <note>original: "Tomumbey"</note>, the last of the Sultans of the said Egypt. All the above has been transcribed and repeated by *André Thevet* in book 8, chapter 12 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

Those who wish to see who the *Beylerbeys* <note>original: "Beglierbeys," high-ranking provincial governors.</note> or Lieutenant Generals of the Provinces subject to the domination of the Great Turk are, should read the aforementioned *André Thevet*, book seven, chapter ten of his aforementioned *Cosmography*, and even better, book nineteen, chapter 2 of the same *Cosmography*.

As for the word *Muley*, it signifies in the *Arabic, Turkish, and Moorish* languages "King" or "Lord." From this word, the Kings of Africa have in these times carried the title of *Muleys*, just as the *Arabs and Saracens* from their beginning used that of *Admiral*, and later *Sultan*, which signifies (as has been said) Lord and Prince. But it must be noted that the first *Mahometan* Kings of Africa did not take the names of *Muleys* or *Sultans*; rather, to show themselves devoted to the foolish persuasion of the *Alcoran* <note>The Quran.</note>, they called themselves *Miramolins* <note>A corruption of "Amir al-Mu'minin," meaning Commander of the Faithful.</note>, which signifies defenders of the law, or Princes of the believers, in the said *Arabic* language.

Regarding the Caliphs, it must be known that among the <term>Mahometists</term> <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note> they formerly held such authority and veneration as the Popes do among Christians. They made their residence in the city of <term>Babylon</term> <note>The author uses "Babylon" to refer to Baghdad, a common geographical conflation in early modern European texts.</note>, called by the Persians *Boughedot* or *Baldac* <note>original: "Boughedot ou Baldac"</note>, and were for this reason called the Caliphs of Baghdad throughout the East. But since the Mamluks mentioned above held the Empire of the Levant under the power and authority of a Sultan elected from among them, and had seized Egypt, Arabia, Palestine, and Assyria, they deprived the Caliph of his patrimony and temporal power, leaving him simply the authority in spiritual matters. This method was followed by the Great Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan.</note> when he defeated the Sultan of Egypt, and by the <term>Sophy</term> <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia.</note>, who drove the Caliph of Baghdad from his seat more discourteously than the Saracens ever did—except for that great and valiant Prince <term>Saladin</term> <note>The 12th-century founder of the Ayyubid dynasty.</note>, who slew the Caliph of Baghdad to take his treasures and invested himself with the possession and lordship of Babylon, transporting the seat of these Caliphs to the city of Aleppo.

It is true that <term>Paolo Giovio</term> <note>original: "Paule Ioue", a famous 16th-century Italian historian and physician.</note>, in the seventeenth book of his histories, speaks of it differently, saying that the Caliph who lived in the time of Amalric <note>original: "almaury"</note>, successor to Baldwin, King of Jerusalem, called for help to defend himself against the said Amalric who was making war on him. He called a very renowned Captain named <term>Shirkuh</term> <note>original: "Sarraco", the uncle of Saladin.</note> who was in the service of the Sultan of Syria. This Shirkuh, having resisted the war efforts of the said Amalric, seized the aforementioned Caliph, put him in prison, and occupied his state. Since that time, the Caliphs lost their power and Empire and thereafter concerned themselves only with spiritual things and the confirmation of the Sultans. From this Shirkuh came Saladin, who in his time waged war for so long against the Christians who had gone to the conquest of the Holy Land. Whoever wishes to see the genealogies and successions of the Caliphs after the false prophet Muhammad should read <term>Johannes Leunclavius</term> <note>original: "I. Leuntclauius", a German scholar known for his histories of the Ottoman Empire.</note> at the beginning of his Turkish Muslim history.
