The Maurusians, who are none other than Moors, live at present in Mauritania in Africa, so named from the Greek word <note>original: Μαυρὸς (Mauros)</note> **"black"**, which signifies black according to some authors, because these people are colored with this tint. I do not wish to doubt this, although it seems to me that the entire stretch of the country named Mauritania does not have black people, and that the Nigritians rather deserve such a name; but let us move on, and grant to the ancients what is neither honest nor fitting to deny them through contradiction, since the word has such a meaning that it carries not only blackness, but an obscurity and dark color. Thus, one should not draw a conclusion if there are white people in Mauritania, since we know there are several kinds of Moors. Modern navigators and travelers who have described in detail the Cape of Good Hope and the countries in Ethiopia toward the Indian Sea have written the following regarding the doubt so much debated by many over the matter of the color of these Moors or Negroes. There are those who hold that the heat of the Sun is the cause of this blackness, whereas **Strabo** in book 15 seems to be of the contrary opinion when he says that heat is not the cause of the blackened color; for those who are in their mothers' wombs, even though the Sun has not spread its rays upon them, are nevertheless born black and <term>swarthy <note>original: "bazanez" — tanned or dark-skinned</note></term> upon the earth. He then adds that they become such by the force of their fathers' seed, whom they are made to resemble. Those who attribute and report the cause to the Sun, such as **Alexander of Aphrodisias** in book 1 of *Problems*—who, inquiring why the Sun blackens a man, whitens linen, softens wax, and hardens mud, responds also that the aptitude of the affected matter is the cause of this; for, he says, the materials of our body, except for the <term>phlegm <note>original: "pituite" — one of the four humors</note></term>, whenever they are too heated, they cause the hide and the skin to blacken. With this author agrees **Albert the Great** in his book *On the Nature of Places*, when he says that Southern men, and those who stay in hot and meridional parts, and above all the Ethiopians, are black as much for the heat of the Sun in the places where they stay as for the heated disposition of their bodies. This is because, in the first place, the seed of generation in them is hot, and the <term>womb <note>original: "matrice"</note></term> of the women who receive this seed is also very hot and very dry; from which it happens that the seed of the man, once conceived, being digested by a violent <term>concoction <note>An archaic term for the "cooking" or processing of nutrients and fluids by internal body heat</note></term>, the blood of the formed fruit becomes <term>adust <note>original: "adufte" — a medical term for substances scorched or parched by internal heat</note></term> and burnt. The more subtle moisture being driven out by the humor of the place, that which is coarse and earthy, and is also burnt, remains and causes the blackness in the body and the skin of men. Thus, the more earthy parts are also very strong, and the bones very white, as can be seen in the teeth of Moors; whereas their flesh, tinted by the burnt blood, is blackish and swarthy. Because it stays parallel to the Equator, it is also more bearable for those who dwell beneath it, even though twice a year it is perpendicular to them and reflects back upon itself. It does not remain fixed in the same place, for its circle is wide, and with a nearly straight course it departs from the Equinox, to which it does not return without passing through a barrier of four of the lesser signs <note>This refers to the signs of the Zodiac. The author is explaining that the Sun's movement prevents it from dwelling too long over one specific spot, which would otherwise "burn" it.</note>. This is the reason that the heat and its intensity do not remain in one place and do not easily burn it, considering the span of time during which the Sun's heat is rising, and the heat it produces while moving back. It happens that one heat does not meet the other, and consequently, it is impossible for the heat there to be as vehement and increased as was formerly believed. Thus, men of good wit recognize how much those people err who—basing their ideas on the reflection and striking of perpendicular rays upon the inhabitants of the lands beneath the Equator—estimate that they are burned by it. Consequently, they infer that this part of the world is uninhabitable. However, the equality of the days and nights is the cause for this violence of heat being tempered, just as it is also corrected by the deep entry the Sun makes below the Horizon. Thus, the heat increased somewhat by the twelve-hour daily course is tempered by the equal length of the night, making the volatility and haste of the rays' course less vehement. Now, that this solar course passing through the Equinoctial line <term>Equinoctial line: The Equator.</term> is as temperate as we say can be drawn from this: when the Sun is there, it makes its course very sudden, whereas it is more sluggish when passing through the lesser signs of the Zodiac. One cannot accept the opinion which says there is nothing temperate between two very hot things, especially since we cannot agree (without failing colossally) that both Tropics are very hot at the same time. It is impossible for them to enjoy the presence of the Sun in the same season; and it is known by experience that as the Sun moves away from any part of the earth, it also causes a cooling there by the upper hand gained by the lower elements. And not to enter into too long a discourse, since reason shows that the regions beneath the Equator are also temperate, it would be folly to call them uninhabitable—especially since the discovery made in our own time has shown us the contrary. It is known by the true reports of those who have traveled both this side and that of the line dividing the Hemispheres, that between the two Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, one does not feel a continual alteration of heat except in the manner we have described: namely, when the Sun is perpendicular there. For at that time, in the part where it passes, for a month before and a month after, the air is cloudy and hot. This has been assured by the aforementioned navigators and travelers in their voyages, saying unanimously that the inhabitants are troubled by this heat, and that hardly a day passes without it raining for two or three hours. They say the water of this rain, or rather this misty drizzle, is warm, salty, and bad-tasting, which is likely true given the attractions of the Sun. These rains are hardly less sickly than those of a summer storm, when from the vehemence of corrupted vapors we see it rain toads and frogs <note>A common early modern belief that heavy storms could "spontaneously generate" small animals or lift them into the clouds to fall elsewhere.</note>. ...as we have said, is the winter of the Equinoctial <note>The regions located on or near the Equator.</note> lands. However, as the Sun moves further away, the season there becomes mild and temperate, without any sign of drought, nor scorching, nor lack of fruits, grasses, and greenery—contrary to what the ancients tried to prove with arguments that lacked any truth. Furthermore, we find in the logs and journeys of the aforementioned modern navigators and travelers that the inhabitants of **Quilao** <note>Kilwa, located on the coast of modern-day Tanzania. In the 16th century, the "Indies" often broadly referred to lands across the Indian Ocean.</note>, a country of the Indies, are diverse in color (which contradicts those who attribute the darkness of the complexion to the heat of the country). For they are usually olive-colored, neither white nor black; others there are white like those of Barbary, and others black like the darkest people of Ethiopia. On the **Island of Saint Thomas** <note>São Tomé</note>, situated directly under the Equator, the children of Europeans are as white as in Europe, unless their white wives die and they marry daughters of the Ethiopians <note>The author uses "Ethiopian" as a general term for Black Africans.</note> who have become Christian and live in our fashion; for the children who come from them are no longer white, but rather blackish. This is evident proof that the Sun is not the cause of men being black in Ethiopia and other places, but that this comes from the disposition of the seeds <note>An early reference to the concept of heredity rather than environmental conditioning.</note>.

To conclude this matter, we shall inform the readers that according to the accounts of modern writers who speak of the Negroes, Blacks, or Moors of Africa: after one has passed the land of the **Bazanez** <note>Likely the Sanhaja, a Berber tribal confederation.</note> people, now called **Azanaghes**, who are tawny in color and live on this side of the river **Niger** or **Senegal**, one comes to the land of those Negroes, Blacks, or Moors living beyond the aforementioned river Niger or Senegal. The separation between the said Bazanez and the said Negroes, Blacks, or Moors is formed by the said river Niger, otherwise called the Senegal, the source of which is held to come from the same place as that of the Nile. It has a similar ebb and flow to the Egyptian river, watering and enriching the lands through which it passes in the same way, and nourishing crocodiles and other beasts or aquatic monsters that are commonly seen in the Nile. Because of this river, the whole country is named **Senega** <note>Senegal</note>; looking toward the West is the Great Ocean Sea, to the South is the kingdom of **Gambre** <note>Gambia</note>, and toward the North is this great river which separates (as has been said) the aforementioned Bazanez from the said Negroes, Blacks, or Moors, and marks the beginning of the country called in these times **Lower Ethiopia**. These Negroes, Blacks, or Moors of Senegal are at present **Mahometans** <note>Muslims</note>, though they are not as sophisticated or fixed in their superstition as the white Moors, especially since they have no one to instruct them, and they do not pay much heed to it, particularly since Christians have begun frequenting their lands. These Black people go about entirely naked, except for some coverings of goat skin or cotton to cover their private parts. In this country, though outside the power and jurisdiction of the King of Senegal, are the **Barbarins** and **Seretes** <note>Likely the Berbers and the Serer people.</note>, who are as black as the others. Past this country, one goes to the kingdom of Gambia where the inhabitants are also black, partly idolaters and partly Mahometans. Following this coast, hugging Africa and rounding the **Cape of Palms**, you enter the kingdom of **Guinea**, in which are **Molegete**, **Benin**, and **Manicongre** <note>The Kingdom of Kongo</note>, where there are also many Black people, partly idolaters—changing their gods every day first thing in the morning—and partly Mahometans, as is amply described by **John Leo** <note>Leo Africanus (c. 1494–1554), a famous traveler and geographer whose descriptions of Africa were the primary source for Europeans for centuries.</note>.

Which, remaining at the parallel of the Equator, is also more supportable for those who dwell beneath it, although twice a year it is perpendicular to them and reflects back upon itself; not that it stays fixed in the same place, for its circle is extended, and in a nearly straight course it departs from the Equinox, toward which it does not return without interposing something like an interval <note>original: "barbarie." This likely refers to a transitional period or an astrological irregularity.</note> of four of the lesser signs <note>These are the zodiacal signs where the sun's declination changes more rapidly.</note>, which is the cause why the heat and its vehemence do not stop in one place and do not burn it easily, considering the span of time—that is, the heat of the Sun as it rises and that which it creates while moving backward—and it happens that one heat does not meet the other. Consequently, it cannot be that the heat there is as vehement and increased in the way that was formerly estimated. Thus, people of good mind recognize how much those are mistaken who, based on the reflection and rebound of perpendicular rays upon the inhabitants of the lands beneath the Equator, estimate also that they are burned by it, and consequently infer that this part is uninhabitable. On the contrary, the equality of days and nights is the reason why this violence of heat is tempered, just as it is also corrected by the Sun's deep descent below the Horizon: so that the heat, increased somewhat by the twelve-hour daily course, is tempered by the equal length of the night, and makes the speed and haste of the rays' course less vehement. Now, that this solar path passing through the Equinoctial line is as temperate as we say can be drawn from this: that when the Sun is there, it makes its course very sudden, whereas it is slower when passing through the lesser signs of the Zodiac. One cannot accept the opinion which says there is nothing temperate between two very hot things, especially since we cannot agree—without failing grossly—that both Tropics are very hot at the same time, seeing as it is impossible for them to enjoy the presence of the Sun in the same season. And it is known by experience that as the Sun moves away from any part of the earth, it also causes cooling because the lower elements <note>Referring to the classical elements of Earth and Water, which were thought to be naturally cold.</note> gain the upper hand. And so as not to enter into too long a discourse, since reason shows that the regions beneath the Equator are also temperate, it would be folly to call them uninhabitable, especially seeing that the discovery made of them in our time has also shown us the contrary. It is known by the true reports of those who have traveled both here and there across the line dividing the Hemispheres, that between the two Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, one does not feel a continual change of heat except in the manner we have described—namely, when the Sun is perpendicular there—because at that time, in the part where it passes a month before and a month after, the air is cloudy and hot. This has been assured by the aforementioned navigators and travelers in their navigations and journeys, saying unanimously that the inhabitants are much troubled by this heat, and that hardly a day passes without it raining for two or three hours, and that the water of this rain, or rather drizzle <note>original: "broüage." An archaic term for a thick mist or foul-tasting water.</note>, is warm, salty, and of bad taste. This is plausible, considering the attractions of the Sun, and these rains are hardly less sickly than those of some summer storm, when, due to the vehemence of corrupt vapors, we see it rain toads and frogs. <note>A common early modern belief that heavy rains could spontaneously generate small animals or carry them from other places.</note> As for the rest of this rainy and heavy weather, which we...

The Portuguese say that in the city of Canton, one of the largest cities in the great Kingdom of China, the natives and those along the coast are of an olive color, like those of Fez and Barbary <note>Referring to the North African coast</note>, being under the same parallel. ### Of the Kingdom of Ethiopia.

We read nothing in all of Holy Scripture, and even less in the secular histories of the ancients, that provides any certain memory of the race, succession, and lineage of the Kings of Ethiopia. It is true, however, that we find it written in ancient histories that Cush <note>In the Bible, Cush is the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, traditionally considered the ancestor of the Ethiopian people.</note> was the first who founded the kingdom of Ethiopia, which still endures to this day, as Marino Sanuto <note>Original: "Marin Romain." Likely referring to the Venetian geographer or a similar chronicler of the era.</note> deduces in his *History of the Ethiopians*, based on the reports from the histories of the Abyssinians. This seems to be what the poet Homer intended to denote when speaking of the great antiquity of this kingdom. These histories of the Abyssinians or Ethiopians state that after this Cush, the first King of Ethiopia, died, six other Kings, his successors, reigned after him. There is no memory of their names in the histories, and it is certain that one cannot truly determine how long they reigned, nor in which city or town of Ethiopia their principal residence was located, until, after these six Kings, the seventh retired to the city of Axum <note>Original: "Caxumo," referring to Aksum, the ancient capital of the Aksumite Empire.</note>. In this city, the principal royal seat of the Ethiopian Kings was established until the time of Jesus Christ, as the aforementioned Marino Sanuto deduces. He states that the greatest certainty we have regarding the lineage of the aforementioned Ethiopians is that Makeda, otherwise known as Nicaula, Queen of Ethiopia and Egypt—as Josephus writes in Book 8 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*—came from Saba, an island of the Nile later called Meroë by Cambyses. She traveled to the great King Solomon in the eleventh year of his reign, had acquaintance with this great King, and had by him a son first named Melich <note>Commonly known as Menelik I.</note>, then David. He was the first who most firmly established the kingdom of Ethiopia, for it is certain, according to the histories of these Ethiopians, that the preceding Ethiopian Kings had no stability or security in their Kingdom until Arue, who first established the seat of his kingdom at Axum for 400 years. Then Agabo his brother for 200; then Ghedur, otherwise called Sabannit, for 100 years, having conquered all of Ethiopia; then Makeda his daughter for 80 years, who was the mother of the said Melich, who reigned 29 years; Audede his son for one year; Auda his brother 11 years; Gegasio 3 years; Zangua 44 years; Gasio 1; Antet 61; Basara 9; Cavada 2; Chauze 10; Endur 9; Guaza 1; Eudrach 1; Chaales 1; Setija 17; Aglaba 3; Auscua 1; Breguas 17; Guaze 17; Beseclugna 17; Baazena 27, under whose reign our Lord Jesus Christ was born. But this is not overly certain nor assured, as Gilbert Génébrard <note>A prominent 16th-century French theologian and Hebraist.</note> demonstrates in his *Cosmography*.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE #

Among modern writers, Don Francisco Álvarez <note>A Portuguese missionary and explorer (c. 1465–1541) who provided one of the first detailed European accounts of Ethiopia.</note>, in his travels through Ethiopia describing the city of Aksum <note>original: "Caxumo"</note>, one of the largest and most spacious cities in all Ethiopia, states that the Ethiopians maintain that this city was once the residence of the Queen of Sheba. She was a native of an Ethiopian city named Sabaim, near the aforementioned Aksum, and she went to visit Solomon, King of Judea, moved by the renown of his great wisdom, as is contained in the Old Testament. The Ethiopian histories—which the aforementioned Álvarez claims to have seen and read in the Abyssinian language <note>Referring to Ge'ez, the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Church.</note>, originally taken from Hebrew and Chaldean—name her Makeda. In this same city, this Queen—named Candace in the 8th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles and by her own name, Judith, who was born two miles from this city—made her ordinary dwelling. She was the first to plant the faith of Jesus Christ in Ethiopia and caused the first church to be built and constructed. This church is still standing and is very beautiful, bearing the title of Saint Mary of Zion, because the sacred table and stone of the altar were brought there from Mount Zion in Jerusalem. This lady was converted to the Christian faith by one of her agents, a Eunuch whom the Deacon Saint Philip instructed in the Gospel doctrine.

The histories of Ethiopia contain that this Queen of Sheba named Makeda, of whom I have spoken before, having arrived from her own country at the city of Jerusalem to see and know the wisdom of the great Solomon, King of the Israelites, was entertained very familiarly by this great King. By him, she had a child who brought to Ethiopia the true knowledge of the God of Israel, as well as the ways of life and ceremonies of the Jews regarding the act of circumcision. Marius Victorinus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian and Christian philosopher.</note> confirms these words, saying that these same histories report that this Queen of Sheba, having visited King Solomon as stated, obtained from him twelve thousand Jews—namely, one thousand from each tribe of Israel—whom she took with her to her country of Ethiopia. These people having greatly increased and multiplied there into families, the nobles of that country have since boasted and bragged of being descended and proceeded from the seed of the Israelites. For this reason, those Ethiopians are still circumcised today—not out of necessity for their salvation, as they assert, but rather to demonstrate and teach the prerogative and grandeur of their bloodline. Or, as written by Ludovicus Carretus <note>A 16th-century Jewish physician who converted to Christianity; his "Epistle to the Jews" was a well-known conversion narrative.</note>, a Jew by nation mentioned above, in his Epistle to the Jews, it is for the sake of the memory and love they bear for our Lord Jesus Christ, who was circumcised. It is true that not all Ethiopians observe such a custom; specifically those who are furthest south, nor those who are close neighbors to the Libyans and the Nigrites <note>A historical term used to describe the peoples of the Niger River region.</note>, because they are for the most part of the superstition of Muhammad. Because they hold that they preserve the articles of the Christian Faith exactly as they were written by the Apostles, they have a sovereign King or Emperor to whom is permitted and given the appointment <note>original: "collation"; the legal right to grant a church benefice or office</note> of all the benefices of the Kingdom—these being his own—as well as other ecclesiastical dignities and prelacies. Although he is neither a priest nor in any way promoted to the sacred order and rank of the clergy, he oversees an infinite number of Archbishops and Metropolitans <note>High-ranking bishops who preside over a provincial capital</note>, each of whom has under him at least twenty Bishops. They have one great and sovereign leader to whom all report, who ordinarily follows the Royal Court and who depends upon the Patriarch of Grand Cairo <note>Historically the Patriarch of Alexandria, who resided in Cairo and oversaw the Ethiopian Church for centuries</note> who formerly resided in Alexandria in Egypt. However, in our own time, they have recognized by letters and by actions the Holy Apostolic See of Rome, not as the appointer or as having the power to establish their Bishops, but only as the head of the Churches and the mother of the flock for the foundation of doctrine, just as Christians have at all times testified concerning this Holy See and the universal Bishop who presides there.

The histories of these Ethiopians recount that this Queen Candace—of whom mention is made in the Acts of the Apostles under the title of Queen of Ethiopia—was named in her own right **Judith**. She was born two miles from **Axum** <note>original: "Caxumo"; the ancient capital of the Aksumite Empire</note>, a city in the Kingdom of Angote in Ethiopia, and she was the first to plant the faith of Jesus Christ our Lord in Ethiopia. She also caused the first church to be built there, which is still standing—very beautiful and magnificent—bearing the title of **Saint Mary of Zion**. This name was given because the Table and sacred stone of the altar were brought there from Mount Zion in Jerusalem; for the Ethiopians have a custom of naming their churches after stones <note>The author refers to the *tabot*, the consecrated wooden or stone slab representing the Ark of the Covenant</note. This Queen was converted to the Christian faith by her agent, **Philip the Eunuch**, whom the Deacon **Saint Philip** (one of the seventy-two disciples) instructed in the Gospel doctrine, as is contained in chapter 8 of the Acts of the Apostles.

This is argued, firstly, because all the ancient Fathers of the Church held it so, and secondly, because all the fragments that **Saint Jerome** cites as being taken from this Gospel are pure Hebrew. The strongest reason is that Saint Matthew did not write only to the Jews and the Syrians, but to all the peoples of the Orient, the furthest of whom used this language as the most learned and grammatical; and even now they use it when celebrating their Masses in that language. In fact, those Ethiopians did not understand Syriac in his time, and even less Greek, but certainly Hebrew, which they learned from childhood in their schools—as they still do today, just as we learn Greek and Latin. In this way, we must interpret the words of Chapter 8 of the Acts of the Apostles, speaking of the Eunuch of the Queen of Ethiopia who, while sitting in his chariot, was reading the Prophet Isaiah. Marius Victorius writes that this Christian religion was spread throughout Ethiopia during the time of Abraham and Azba, brother Kings of Ethiopia, around the year of salvation 460. This Church of Axum <note>original: "Caxumo"</note> is the most revered in Ethiopia due to its antiquity, having 150 Canons named **Debereres** <note>Dabtaras: a unique class of lay clergy in the Ethiopian Church responsible for music and liturgy</note>, and as many Monks; for the religious orders are more privileged than all other ecclesiastics. There are two heads called **Nebreti** <note>The *Nebret* is the traditional title for the administrator of the Cathedral of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum</note>, one over the Canons and the other over the Monks, each having his own court and administering justice to those committed to his care. These men are richly endowed, receiving every day after the Mass—which is sung in the **Tangique** language <note>The author likely refers to Ge'ez, the liturgical language of Ethiopia, which he classifies as an "ancient dialect of the Chaldean language"</note>, an ancient dialect of the Chaldean language, as I noted earlier in the chapter—their bread and wine from their endowment, except on Good Friday when they eat nothing at all. The King, Archbishops, and Bishops, when traveling through the country or walking in public, always have a cross and a vase full of earth carried before them; so that by the one, they may be warned that they are mortal, and by the other, that through the death and passion of Jesus Christ they are saved. Priests marry there, but monks do not, so as to leave a lineage <note>Ethiopian Orthodox tradition allows secular priests to be married, but monks remain celibate</note>; but if their wives die, they are not permitted to enter into a second marriage. There is a great diversity of religious orders who take vows and profession of chastity, obedience, and poverty, living in common and performing great and admirable abstinences under the rule of St. Anthony and St. Macarius, although they have other holy Abbots and Monks who have built many of their monasteries. Of our saints, they recognize only the glorious Virgin Mary Mother of God, St. Michael, the Apostles, and especially St. Thomas and St. Matthew—the latter having converted the inhabitants of Meroë, and the former having traveled from Ethiopia to the Indies to win over the Indians. Among the Martyrs, they greatly revere St. Stephen and St. George, and of the Confessors, the hermits St. Anthony and St. Macarius—whomever unfortunately blasphemes against them is burned alive in the public square. ...if it is a female, these people say that the faith of the parents suffices, and especially that of the mother, and that the holy communion she received while pregnant has sanctified the child in her womb; which child is carried to the Church as is done here <note>The author is likely referring to European customs of his time</note>, and baptized at the door thereof, and not over the fonts, the water being blessed there. The child is sprinkled with this water with the same words that we say, and they use anointing just as in the Roman Church, on the forehead, the shoulders, and the armpits; and the Priest, holding a ewer of water in one hand, performs the pouring with the other, saying: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." In short, they use the same ceremonies as those of our Catholic Church. It is true that they only baptize on Saturday and Sunday, because only on these days do they celebrate the holy Mass, and without it they do not confer the grace of Baptism, because they give the sacred communion to the newly regenerated child. 

In addition to this holy Sacrament of Baptism, all these Ethiopians observe another annual Baptism at the same time as we celebrate the feast of the Epiphany <note>original: "l'apparition de nostre Seigneur," the manifestation of our Lord</note>; during which solemnity they all come to a certain lake, and after some prayers made by a Bishop, they all go down naked into the water and bathe there, being of the opinion that this washing serves to purge those who, having been Christians, had become Moors <note>Used here to mean those who converted to Islam</note>, and then returned through repentance to the Church. Now, throughout all Ethiopia, there are Soldiers and Officers chosen from all parts who are in the King's pay, and who are lightly marked on the skin with a cross using a hot iron; this has been the reason why some have estimated that in Ethiopia this sign was the only thing that served as Baptism. 

What is more, according to the account of Leo Africanus <note>original: "Iean Leon," referring to the 16th-century diplomat and traveler Joannes Leo Africanus</note>, Book 4 of the *Description of Africa*, the inhabitants of the city of Bresk <note>An ancient city in modern-day Algeria</note> in Africa have the custom of painting a black cross on their cheek, and another on their hand—namely in the palm of the hand, under the fingers—this practice being observed by the mountain people of Algiers and Buggie <note>Modern-day Béjaïa, Algeria</note>. This is because, according to African historians, the Goths seized many lands and infinite mountains, by which means a great number were reduced to the Christian faith, for which the Gothic Kings charged their officers to levy no tribute from them. But because at the time of payments they all declared themselves to be Christians, without it being easy to notice and recognize those who were or were not, it was ordained that Christians should be designated and recognized by this cross. Since the lordship was taken from their hands, the whole people returned to the Mohammedan Law <note>Islam</note>. Nevertheless, this manner remained successively from time to time, without many being found who could give a reason for it. The Lords of Mauritania still observe this same custom as well as the nobles, who make a cross on their cheek with a hot iron, and one sees enough of them in Europe thus marked. 

As for the holy communion, they receive it with very great reverence, and honor the bread before it is consecrated in honor of what it is to become, believing firmly in the real presence of the substance of the body of our Lord sacramentally in the Eucharist. Only one Mass is said each day in each Church, and it is not celebrated without incensing, saying...

...[it is believed by] these Ethiopians that it is a sin to do otherwise, and that it shows little respect for such a high and divine mystery. Furthermore, there must be more than one Priest present when the Mass is said, and all those in attendance must receive communion. They are required to observe great fasts, especially the Monks, who fast for more than half the year; during this time, they only say and celebrate Mass at night, and everyone takes communion before going to have their meal. As for which days are designated for these fasts, Francisco Alvarez in his *History of Ethiopia*, chapter 3, and Joseph Scaliger in his *Commentaries on the Abyssinian Calendar* in book 7 of *The Correction of Time*, describe them at great length. The order of the Social Classes is such that the Clergy holds the highest place after the King; then come the <term>Tenquates</term> <note>Likely referring to learned scribes or scholars</note> and <term>Balsamates</term>, which is to say Doctors, and those who make a profession of teaching letters and acting as judges; after them, the Nobility is respected, and finally the Soldiers. 

When someone happens to die, they incense the body and wash it, and afterwards they shroud it and sew it into a linen cloth. The Priests, coming to carry the body to the earth, say several very short prayers, then lift the body and carry it to the Church, the cross always walking before it with the censer and holy water. Being near the Church, they do not carry the body inside it, but rather place it immediately into its grave, having incensed it and thrown holy water inside, without saying any obsequies or vigils <note>Traditional Catholic prayers and watches for the dead</note> except for several chapters of the Gospel of Saint John. They do not sing any Masses for the deceased, just as they do not celebrate any for the private devotion of any living person, since they only sing one single Mass per day in each Church. They mourn their dead for the space of forty days, and as long as their mourning lasts, they are dressed in entirely black garments, which they set aside after this time to resume their ordinary and previous clothing. 

In short, all Christian Ethiopians are uniform in their Religion, without there being any schisms, heresies, or divisions among them regarding their doctrine, because only the Clergy involve themselves in treating and discussing Holy Scripture. Marriage ceremonies are commonly performed there in the same form and manner as in the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church. These Ethiopians, under the authority of Zerah Jacob <note>Emperor of Ethiopia, 1434–1468</note> their Emperor, first pledged obedience to Pope Eugene the Third <note>original: "Eugene troiſieſme"; likely a chronological error by the author referring to Pope Eugene IV (1431–1447), who presided over the Council of Florence</note> residing in Rome, who thereafter sent them a certain rather thick book to serve as instruction for their ceremonies. According to the travels of modern authors, this book is still held and found in Ethiopia today, as stated in the letter inserted at the end of the travels of Alvarez, and as confirmed by Damião de Góis in his book *On the Faith, Religion, and Customs of the Ethiopians*. See what is written at length regarding their customs and religion by Andrea Corsali in his *Epistle and Travels* addressed to Duke Lorenzo de' Medici; Dom Francisco Alvarez in his *Travels in Ethiopia*; Jerónimo Osório in book 9 of the *Deeds of Alfonso* and book 17 of his *History of Portugal*, chapters 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24; Duarte Barbosa in his books of travels; the author of the *Summary of the Kingdoms, Cities, and Peoples of the East*; Sabellicus in his *Rhapsodies* or *Enneads* 10, book 8; André Thevet in book 2, chapter 14 of his *Cosmography*; and François de Belleforest, volume 2.

### Of the Ethiopian, Indian, or Nubian language.

Raphael Volaterran, as reported by Theodore Bibliander in his commentary on the common reasoning of all languages and letters, wrote that the Ethiopians use and employ, up to the present day, the letters and characters of the Babylonians. This author had learned this from those ignorant of the truth of this matter, who, by a common and vulgar persuasion, held that these Ethiopians had learned and received their language, religion, and origin from Abraham the Chaldean. This is not true, given that it is a very certain thing (as we have clearly verified above) that these Ethiopians are descended from none other than Cush, son of Ham, and not from any of the children of Shem. And even though the form and order of writing the letters and characters of the Ethiopian language—which are written from the left hand toward the right—is entirely different from those of the Hebrew language, nevertheless the phonetic power of said letters and characters, the origin of their words, and the forms of declining and conjugating their nouns and verbs approach very closely those of the said Hebrew language. Regarding this, we cite the authority of that great and learned personage Guillaume Postel <note>A 16th-century French polymath and linguist</note>, who, in his treatise on the *Alphabet of the Twelve Languages*, in the chapter on the Indian or Ethiopian language, said the following:

Johann Potken <note>A German priest who published the first printed book in Ge'ez (Ethiopic) in 1513</note>, administrator of the Church of Cologne, was the first who, having had the Psalms of David and the Song of Solomon printed in this our Europe some years ago in the Ethiopian, Indian, and Nubian language, and in its characters, dared—through an ignorance of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syriac languages—to assert along with the common crowd, though without much reason, that this language was the same as and similar to Chaldean. This is despite it being very certain that the Chaldean and Syriac languages are nothing other than the two languages which in ancient times issued and proceeded from the purity of the sole Hebrew language; namely, one being Assyrian or Babylonian, and the other Jerusalemite, which in the time of

These *Ethiopians*, *Indians*, or *Nubians* commonly place two dots at the end of each word, one above the other in the manner of a colon <note>original: "coma"</note>; and at the end of a clause, four dots in a square. Characters of this alphabet [were described by] Sebastian Münster in his *Chaldaic Grammar* <note>original: "Grammaire Chaldaique." In the 16th century, "Chaldaic" was often used as a general term for Semitic languages, including Ethiopic or Syriac</note>, Guillaume Postel in his treatise on the twelve different alphabets and languages in characters <note>Postel was a famous French polyglot and mystic</note>, Giovanni Battista Palatino in his discourse on the teaching of writing in all sorts of ancient and modern letters, and Joseph Scaliger in Book 7 of his *On the Emendation of Time*, and others cited by us in the preceding chapter. As for the alphabet of the letters of the Indians of Calicut <note>Referring to the scripts of Kerala, India</note>, we will not speak of it for the present, but rather we will content ourselves only with referring curious readers to what André Thevet has written in Book 11, Chapter 11 of his *Universal Cosmography*. Regarding the books that are found composed and written in this language for today, we are assured by the voyages and navigations of the moderns that in Ethiopia the Old and New Testament are found written and composed in that language, together with the works of Enoch <note>The Book of Enoch was preserved in its entirety only in the Ethiopic Ge'ez language</note> treating of holy things, along with the "Book of the Battles of the Lord" mentioned in Chapter 21 of Numbers, and books of histories and infinite others. In this regard, Marco Polo the Venetian in Chapter 81 of his travels, Dom Francisco Álvares in his voyage to Ethiopia in Chapter 81, and Damião de Góis—alleged above—mention that the Ethiopians have in their language the books of the Apostolic Constitutions, which they hold so dear that they title them **Manda Abethilis**, **Doctrine of the Apostles** <note>original: "Doctrina Apostolorum"</note>, from which they seem to have taken this title from an Epistle of St. Athanasius, in which, after the books of the Old and New Testament, he recommends others, not as canonical, but as holy and authentic, among which is that which is called *The Doctrine of the Apostles and the Shepherd* <note>original: "doctrina Apostolorum & pastor," referring to the Didache and the Shepherd of Hermas</note>: a copy of which is found in Arabia in the Vatican Library. A certain Ethiopian personage named Brother Christopher Licanate—to whom was given the name Zagazabo at his baptism, which is to say in the Abyssinian tongue "Grace of the Father"—Ambassador of the Emperor called Prester John <note>original: "Prestegiani," the legendary Christian monarch of the East</note>, says: *We have eight books of the laws of the Holy Church which we call Manda Abethilis, which all the Apostles gathered in Jerusalem wrote* <note>original Latin: "Sunt nobis sanctæ Ecclesiæ legum libri octo Manda Abethilis vocamus, quos omnes Apostoli Hierosolymis cõgregati scripserunt"</note>: on this subject Gilbert Génébrard in Book 2, folio 374 of his *Chronology*, and Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie in his introductory Epistle to the reader on the Syriac New Testament [write]: *In truth, not only in Asia among the Syrians, but also in Africa among the Abyssinians and Ethiopians, such ceremonies flourish which they claim were prescribed by the Apostles themselves; they possess eight volumes of the Synods of the Apostles (which they call in their native tongue <term>מנדא</term>, mandea, that is, knowledge <term>κατ' ἐξοχὴν</term> [par excellence]), as can easily be understood from that booklet which Damião de Góis, a Portuguese knight, wrote on the faith, religion, and customs of the Ethiopians.* <note>original Latin: "Nec verò in Asia tm̃ apud Syros, sed etiam in Africa apud Abyssinos, & Æthyopes, tales ceremoniæ vigent..."</note> Dom Francisco Álvares, alleged above in Chapter 147 of his said voyages in Ethiopia, writes that all the books of the Ethiopians, the number of which is very great, are of parchment, because there is no paper in Ethiopia, and are written in the Tangic language <note>Perhaps referring to the language of the Tigray region or a variant of Ge'ez</note>, which is Abyssinian, the first land that received the Evangelical doctrine. In addition to these books, these Ethiopians still have a book in their language on the Papal order, power, and blessing, as it is contained in the letters written by David, Prester John, inserted toward the end of the books of the voyages in Ethiopia by Francisco Álvares; and the prophecies of a Saint Ficatoire and Saint Synode, both hermits.

->*Of Prester John, Prest-Ian, Prestian, or Prestegian, great Emperor, or King of the Ethiopians, Indians, Nubians, & Abyssins.*<-

### CHAP. LII.

Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and orientalist</note>, in Book 2 of his *Chronology*, making mention of the three Kings who came to adore our Lord Jesus Christ, has reported these words worthy of great consideration and remark.

In the 35th year of Herod <note>original: "Herodis 35. tempore"</note>, the Magi, about to adore Christ, came from Persia, which is in the East of the land of Israel (Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 51). Two years later, Herod died of a horrific disease at the age of 71 (Book 2 on the Kings of Israel). He was buried in Herodium, which city was a journey of two and a half days from Jerusalem (ibid.).

More probable is the view of Ammonius of Alexandria <note>A 3rd-century Christian philosopher</note>: that on the 13th day after the birth of Christ, the Magi arrived in Jerusalem, coming under the lead of a certain new star, and proclaimed the King of the Jews born (*In the Harmony*). From this, the Church celebrates the Epiphany on that day. Namely, that they came from Persia or rather another place in the East (of which more soon); in the 33rd year of his [Herod's] reign, the star appeared to the Kings four years before his death (words of Saint Cyprian at the very beginning of his sermon on Baptism). For it is an ancient tradition of the Church that the Magi were Kings and Toparchs <note>original: "Toparchas" — local governors or petty kings of a specific district</note>. Tertullian in his book *Against the Jews*, and Book 3 of *Against Marcion*; Jerome on Psalm 71; Augustine in Book 3 of *The Miracles of Scripture*, chapter four, and in the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert*, sermon 43; Hilary in Book 4 *On the Trinity*; Idacius Clarius to Varimund the Arian—not to mention the Greeks—Athanasius in question 2 of *Various Questions to Prince Antiochus*, which Reclinus translated differently from those commonly extant in his volumes. He says: "We call the Feast of the Epiphany the Day of the Three Kings." [See also] Cantacuzenus, *Apology* 1, etc.

Nor indeed were they only Kings, but they also laid the foundation of that very vast Christian Kingdom in India (for they had come from there, from its province which was called Tarsis, and today Tartestan <note>A reference to Tartary or Central Asia</note> according to Hayto), which he who held for twelve hundred years was called **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles from the 12th to the 17th centuries</note>, being powerful in both Ecclesiastical and secular authority, until around the year 1200 it succumbed to the arms of the Tartars. And from there the Mohammedan empire of the Great Khan arose. (Marco Polo the Venetian in his *Travels*). With the title of Prester John being transferred to 그hat great Christian Emperor of the Abyssinians or Ethiopians (Osório in *The Deeds of Emmanuel, King of Portugal* <note>original: "Osorius in rebus Emmanuelis Reges Lusitaniæ"</note>). Nor is it necessary that they were "great" kings, since God often chooses the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame. But they were all called Kings according to the custom of the East, who could use the scepter and diadem with dignity, whether they were independent or under the law of another: and thus they were distinguished from Dukes, as Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and biblical commentator</note> often notes. This is observed today by the Tartars, Persians, Ethiopians, and other Orientals; for they are not so anxious and concerned in distinguishing between a King and a Prince. Thus Catherine of Alexandria was the daughter of King Costus, that is, a Prince; thus in the Gospel the Lord heals the son of a certain "little king" <note>original: "Reguli"</note>; thus in the Old Testament 30 Kings of the land of Canaan...

<note>original: "naam, quæ alioquin est perexigua, nec iustum Regnum conficit vna acie peremit Iosue."</note> ...for Joshua destroyed in a single engagement that [land] which is otherwise very small and does not constitute a proper Kingdom.

The same Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French scholar and Benedictine archbishop</note> in Book 4 of his said *Chronology* writes: In India there was a certain great Christian King; the Land of Caghat <note>likely referring to the territories of the Khanate or Cathay</note>, from which the three Kings came to Bethlehem, was still entirely Christian, but under the Lord Cham <note>The Great Khan</note>, in the year of Salvation 1253. The Constable of Armenia <note>Sempad the Constable</note>, writing to the King of Cyprus, as found in Vincent [of Beauvais], Book 31, chapter 92. The voyages and navigations of the Portuguese and Spanish report that Pêro da Covilhã and Afonso de Paiva were the first European Ambassadors sent on behalf of Manuel, King of Portugal, to Ethiopia to this great Emperor around the year 1496 or 1497.

Dom Francisco Álvares, a Portuguese by nation, in his travels in Ethiopia writes that the Ethiopian Annals—composed in the Ethiopian, Indian, Nubian, and Abyssinian languages, formerly taken from Hebrew and Chaldean <note>In this period, Ge'ez (Ethiopic) was often associated with Chaldean/Syriac</note>, which he saw in Axum <note>Caxumo</note>, the principal city of Ethiopia—state that the Queen of Sheba, who came from Meroë <note>Meroc</note> to see this great King Solomon in the city of Jerusalem, was named Makeda in her own name (others say Nicaula), and that she had a son by the said Solomon named Meilech, and later David. She established and instituted him as her heir to Ethiopia, from whom is descended the race of Kings of the great Ethiopian Empire. This is confirmed by Marinus Victorinus in his discourse on the Kings of Ethiopia, Andrea Corsali in his letter to Duke Lorenzo de' Medici, and Guillaume Postel in his *Alphabet of the Twelve Languages* and in his work on the noble nations who took their names and appellations from Noah and his children. Because of this, all the Ethiopian Kings hold the memory of Solomon in very great reverence, sending offerings every year to the temple in Jerusalem, as children of the house of David and instructed in the law of Moses; this they also take from the New Testament, speaking of the Eunuch <note>The Ethiopian official described in Acts 8</note> sent to Judea in the time of the Apostles, who was baptized by Philip, one of the seven deacons, and who first planted the Christian Religion in Ethiopia.

As for this word "Prester John," "Prestian," "Prestan," or "Prestegian," a name common and familiar to all the Kings of Ethiopia, Paolo Giovio <note>Paul Ioue</note> in Book 1 of his *Eulogies* maintains that it is corrupted among us, and that the true name of the Kings of this Province is *Belulgiam*, which was common to all the Kings of this country, meaning "Pearl of great price and incomparable excellence." This is confirmed by Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie in his preface to the Syriac New Testament, noting that the Ethiopians call this King and Lord *Ian Belul*, or *Ian* in the Chaldaic language—that is to say, "precious" or "high"—or else as Jean Bodin writes in his *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History*, chapter 5, *Iochan Belul*, "Very precious stone." Some modern authors maintain that Saint Thomas the Apostle, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles, went to preach in Greater India, that he died there, and left such a great multitude of people converted to the faith of Jesus Christ that, as they had elected a Lord to govern them, they gave him this name of Prester John—both because all the Lords were clerics, and because they had this name of John in common since the first one who was elected, who was so named. ...who reigned were chosen by the hand of Saint Thomas, in which was placed a dry vine branch. They would carry this in procession, and when it happened that the one who was to be elected passed by, this hand would sprout leaves, branches, and clusters of grapes, which would then ripen. From these grapes, the wine was pressed for the Mass he said that day, and so on. Juan de Torquemada <note>A Spanish cardinal and theologian, 1388–1468</note> in his *Hexameron*, Day 2, leaves 176 and 177. Damião de Góis <note>A Portuguese humanist and historian</note> in his *History of the Ethiopian Religion* writes that the term *Prester John* <note>original: "Preste Ian"</note> signifies as much as "Powerful, Excellent, and Precious King." Others say that *Ian* or *Gian* means precious or excellent. The same Dom Francisco Álvares cited above maintains that this Emperor has two principal names: *Acegué*, which means Emperor, and *Negus*, meaning King. Sebastian Münster, the German, in his *Chaldean Grammar*, in the chapter on Chaldean letters, asserts that the term *Prester John* is corrupted from the word *Priest Cohen* <note>original: "Prestre Cohan"</note>, which signifies—in both the Hebrew and Chaldean languages—a Priest or Pontiff. Concerning this, one should see what Guillaume Postel <note>A French linguist and polymath</note> writes in his treatise on the *Alphabets of the 12 Languages*, and his treatise on the *Renowned Regions Named After the Children of Noah*. Julius Caesar Scaliger, in his 117th exercise against Girolamo Cardano on *Subtlety*, held (in agreement with Álvares cited above) that the Ethiopians call their Emperor *Negus* or *Acegué*, which is to say King and Emperor.

Some other Ethiopians living near Cape Guardafui call him in their language *Thamnat-Hares*, "Image of the Great God"; the people of Calicut call him *Zobeleth*, "Inexpugnable Mountain"; the Javanese, the people of Taprobana <note>likely Sri Lanka</note>, and those of Borneo call him *Cappach Elisua*, "Son of the Great David"; the Persians call him *Cochouet*; the Ethiopians call him *Gerich*; the Moors call him *Soltan Abyssin*, "Sovereign of the Abyssinians," or *Aticlabaffi*, according to the report of Andrea Corsali cited above in his letter to Duke Lorenzo de' Medici. The great Pico della Mirandola, having read it somewhere in his *Apology* (fifth question on Magic and Kabbalah), calls him by a corrupted word, *Prestam*; and Jean Bodin, in his commentaries on the third book of the hunt by the Greek poet Oppian, calls him *Preste*.

But without lingering on all these preceding opinions, we shall hold it as quite certain that this word *Prester John* or *Prestegian* signifies in the Persian language (which is widely current throughout all of Asia, just as Latin is in the West) as much as if one said "Apostolic." In fact, in this Persian language, the word *Prestegian* <note>original Hebrew-script Persian: פֿרסתגאן</note> in the plural number is the same as the Greek word <term lang="grc">Apostoloi</term> (Apostles); and *Prestegiani* <note>original: פֿרסתגאני</note> is the same as the Greek <term lang="grc">Apostolikos</term> (Apostolic).

-> *Padescha Prestegiani* <note>original Hebrew script: פֿרשט פֿרסתגאני</note> <-

Apostolic King, which is to say, Christian. The Arabs call him in their language *Melich Ressuli* <note>original Hebrew script: מליך רסולי</note>, and his subjects call him *Negus Chauuarauui* <note>original Hebrew script: נגוש חררויי</note>, "Apostolic King," or *Gerichauauraich*. On this matter, one should see Marco Polo the Venetian, book 2, chapter 27 of his travels, who was greatly mistaken in his explanation of this word *Chauuarauui*, as it is a very certain thing that it does not signify "holy man," as that author says, but rather "Apostolic," as I have already stated above. André Thevet, in book 2, chapter 13 of his *Cosmography*, reports that this Emperor is called by some Easterners *Gideroth*, "Lord of the Hot Country." This Emperor or King of Ethiopia—who, through the aforementioned Dom Francisco Álvares, wrote letters both to Manuel, King of Portugal, in the year of salvation 1521, and to Pope Clement VII in the years 1533 and 1548—titled his qualities thus: "I, the King..."

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

<meta>catchword: in In.</meta>

Joseph, Patriarch of Constantinople <note>Joseph II (c. 1360–1439), who attended the Council of Florence to attempt a reconciliation between the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches</note>, accompanied by a great number of Archbishops, Bishops, and Prelates of all sorts—among whom also appeared the representatives of the Patriarchs of Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem, all in agreement in the love of the holy faith and Christian religion—by whose means, with the grace of the Lord, the unity of the Church was confirmed and all the difficulties of the past, which seemed contrary and repugnant to religion, were removed: and these things being confirmed and established in good order, the Pope wished for each and every person to rejoice in them.

These letters subsequently carry these words:

"Now we send you this book from Pope Eugene <note>Pope Eugene IV (r. 1431–1447), who presided over the Council of Florence</note>, which we have always kept without corruption. We would have also sent you the treatise on the order and power of the Pontifical blessing, had the volume not been too large, for in truth it is bigger than the book of Saint Paul to the Gentiles <note>The collected Epistles of St. Paul</note>. And to declare to you the personages who brought these things from the Pope: they were Theodore, Peter, Didymus, and George, servants of Jesus Christ; assuring you, Most Holy Father, that you will do very well if you have the registers of your Chancery searched, in which I believe you will easily find some memory of the things I am writing back to you. Therefore, your Holiness may firmly believe that whatever you write back to me will be immediately recorded in our books, so that a memory of it remains for posterity. Certainly, he seems very happy to me whose memory is kept by letters in the holy City of Rome, and at the See of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, Lords of the kingdom of heaven and Judges of all the world."

Sir John Mandeville, a knight living in the year of Grace 1322, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>The vernacular "Romance" or "Romanesque" language here refers to an early dialect, possibly Catalan or an Occitan-influenced French, used in the manuscript he is citing</note>, in the chapter regarding why the Emperor is called *Prester John*, writes what follows: *“It has been a long time since an Emperor, who was a very valiant prince and had in his company many other Lords and sons, set out to see the manner of the Christian Church... he took in his company only one knight... and they traversed all Turkey, Syria, and Tartary... Arabia, Aleppo, and all the land of Egypt and India... they came to a church, etc. folio 88.”* <note>original: "Elle ha louch temps que vn Emperador qui era molt valent princep... é vndiſapte eſde vngueren a vna Eſgleia"</note> By these words, this personage asserts that this Emperor first took this surname of Prester John because of a Priest named John whom he saw promoted to holy orders during his pilgrimage. The author of the *Bundle of Time* <note>The *Fasciculus Temporum*, a famous 15th-century world chronicle by Werner Rolevinck</note>, in the description of the Sixth Age, spoke of Prester John in this fashion:

> In the year of Salvation 784, Oger the Dane <note>Ogier the Dane, a legendary paladin of Charlemagne</note>, a most Christian Prince, flourished. In the time of Charlemagne, he secured for Christianity almost all parts beyond the sea, from Jerusalem even unto the trees of the sun <note>The "Trees of the Sun and Moon" were legendary oracular trees from the Alexander the Great legends, often placed in deep India</note>, by God's favor, with great miracles comforting the army. And in Upper India he established an empire, over which he placed John, son of the King of the Frisians, called Prester John because of the devout and holy life that he led; and he subjected fourteen Barons of his own lineage to him, because they held other dominions round about, and where the Christian religion might remain. <note>original Latin: "Anno Salutis 784. Ogerus Dux de Danamarchia... ubi Christiana religio permaneret."</note>

Gilbert Genebrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and physician</note>, in Book 3 of his *Chronography*, citing this passage, says: *“Whether this be true, I know not. For I do not see by what path the Danes, through so many spaces of lands and seas...”* <note>original Latin: "an id verum nescio. But in the Year of Salvation 1162, both this Emperor and King and his successors after him were entirely dispossessed of the better part of this kingdom by Genghis Khan <note>Cingis Cam</note>, calling himself the first Emperor of the Tartars, who, upon the annihilation of that dominion, established his Tartar power and rule there, as is particularly deduced by Marco Polo the Venetian in Books 1, Chapters 51, 52, 53, 54, and 64 of his travels; Marcin Kromer in Book 7 of his *History*; André Thevet in Book 12, Chapter 17 of his *Cosmography*; and Gilbert Génébrard in Book 4 of his *Chronography*. # HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE #

...of the Red Sea in the land neighboring Ethiopia, as confirmed by **Paolo Giovio** <note>An Italian physician and historian (1483–1552) famous for his work on contemporary history and geography</note> in Book 18 of his histories. All the subjects of this great Emperor or King constantly affirm that never has any Emperor, King, nor Prince of any other Province in the world overcome or subjugated their country, nor even the Saracens, Arabs, Turks & other Mahometans <note>Followers of Islam; the text emphasizes the empire's survival against surrounding Islamic powers</note> who have ravaged & destroyed the largest part of Asia & Africa, without ever daring to address themselves to the said country. Several other noteworthy and remarkable particularities regarding this great Emperor or King **Prester John** are treated in the book of **Mandeville** in his travels (chapter on Prester John and his state); **Alvise Cadamosto** <note>A Venetian slave trader and explorer who explored the Atlantic coast of Africa for Portugal</note> in part 2 of his *Navigations*, chapter 60; **Marco Polo the Venetian**, Book 3, chapter 38 of his travels; **Francisco Álvares** in his travels in Ethiopia; **Damião de Góis**, a Portuguese, in his treatise on the faith, Religion & customs of the Ethiopians under the Empire of this Prester John; **André Thevet**, Book 2, chapters 13 & 14 of his *Cosmography*; **Joseph Scaliger**, Book 7 of the *Emendation of Time*, in the chapter of annotations on the Calendar of the Ethiopians; **Antoine du Verdier**, Book 2, chapter 1 of his *Diverse Lessons*; **Juan de Torquemada**, a Spaniard, on the 2nd day of his *Hexameron*; **François de Belleforest**, Book 1, chapter 4 of his *Universal History*, & Book 6, chapters 22 & 23 of the 2nd volume of his *Cosmography*; **Abraham Ortelius**, tables 4 & 47 of his *Theater of the World* <note>The first modern atlas, published in 1570</note>; **Louis Le Roy**, Book 9 of the *Vicissitude of Things*; the author of the *Treasury of Politics*, Book 2, the chapter on the great King of Ethiopia; & **Blaise de Vigenère** in his *Treatise on Ciphers*.

The dominion of this great Emperor or King extends in Africa from one Tropic to the other, reaching an extent of 50 or 52 degrees of latitude, which makes more than a thousand leagues of travel. Its length is from the East to the West, namely from the Red Sea, where **Suakin** and **Massawa** are located, to the Atlantic Ocean; that is to say, Egypt lies to his North, and neighbors him toward **Nubia**, so named in the Hebrew language *Nubiah* <note>original: "Nubiah"</note>, meaning "Sprout of God," because the faith was sprouted in the person of the **Ethiopian Eunuch**, and later of **Candace**, Queen of Ethiopia <note>Referring to the story in the biblical Acts of the Apostles where an Ethiopian official is converted, which the author uses to explain the name "Nubia"</note>, according to G. le Fèvre de la Boderie, folio 24. To the east of him is the Red Sea and part of the Indian Sea, and the Gulf named **Barbarian** <note>The *Sinus Barbaricus*, a historical name for the coast of East Africa</note>, as far as the country of **Malindi** and **Benamate**, unknown to ancient authors. To the south, it looks toward the **Mountains of the Moon** which serve as a closure and wall on that side, or rather the Cape of Good Hope. To the West, it has for boundaries and limits the River **Niger** or **Senegal**, and the kingdoms of Nubia and **Manicongo** <note>The Kingdom of Kongo</note>, as confirmed by **Abraham Ortelius**, table 4 of his *Theater of the Universe*.

Regarding the Kingdoms & Provinces that are under the said dominion of this great Emperor or King, the titles and styles of his patent letters sent to Popes Leo X and Clement VII, and to the King of Portugal—included in the travels of **Álvares** mentioned above, and translated into Latin by **Damião de Góis**, a Portuguese knight, in his discourse on the faith, Religion & customs of the Ethiopians—provide ample proof and demonstration. They state that this Emperor or King is Emperor of Great and High Ethiopia, and of very great kingdoms, jurisdictions, & lands: King of **Goa**, **Cafattes**, **Fatigar**, **Angote**, **Baru**, **Balignanzar**, **Adee**, **Vanga**, **Gojjam** <note>original: "Goyame"</note> (where the sources and fountains of the Nile are found), **Amara**, **Begemder** <note>original: "Baguamedre"</note>, **Ambee**, **Vangussi**, **Tigray** <note>original: "Tigremahon"</note>, **Sabaim**, **Saba**, **Barnagas**, and Lord as far as Nubia, which extends all the way to the land of Egypt.

### Of the several kinds of Christians who are spread and scattered throughout the whole extent of the earth.

Joachim the Abbot <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), a mystic and theologian who organized history into three ages</note>, in his *Appendix of Christian Nations*, has written the following concerning Christians:

The Christian peoples are divided into ten nations, namely the Latins, Greeks, Indians, Jacobites, Nestorians, Maronites, Armenians, Georgians, Syrians, and Mozarabs <note>original: "Gentes Christianorum diuiduntur in decem nationes..."</note>.

The first nation is that of the Latins, who have the Emperor of Germany and many Kings, namely the Kings of Castile, Aragon, Spain, Portugal, Navarre, etc. In the French nation, there is one King of the Franks, and many Dukes, Counts, and Barons. In the nation of Italy, there is the Pope, the King of Sicily and Naples, many Dukes, Counts, Marquises, and great Communes, namely those of Venice, Lucca, Siena, and others. In the Germanic nation, besides the Emperor, who must be Christian, there are many Kings, namely the King of England, Scotland, Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, Denmark <note>original: "Daciæ"</note>, Frisia, Sweden, Norway, Dalmatia, and many Marquises, Landgraves, Dukes, and Counts; likewise the King of Cyprus, and the inhabitants of the island of Malta <note>original: "insulæ Meltidis"</note>, and of other islands obedient to the Roman Church.

The second nation is that of the Greeks, who formerly had the Patriarch of Constantinople, Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, etc., in spiritual matters, and in temporal matters an Emperor, Dukes, and Counts, etc. However, they are now few in number, because the Agarenes <note>A medieval term for Muslims, referring to descendants of Hagar</note> and Turks have occupied and invaded the greatest part of Greece; and these do not obey the Roman Church, and hold many errors which are condemned by the Church, because they say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, but from the Father alone, and they also say that there is no Purgatory.

The third nation is that of the Indians, whose Prince is Prester John <note>A legendary Christian monarch said to rule a vast empire in the East or Africa</note>, whose power exceeds all Christians: for he has seventy-two Kings under him, and when the said King and Lord Prester John rides, he always has a wooden cross carried before him. When he goes to war, he has twelve crosses made of gold and precious stones carried as banners: in his land is the body of the blessed Apostle Thomas in greatest veneration, though others say on the contrary that the body of this Saint is in East India.

The fourth nation is that of the Jacobites <note>Members of the Syriac Orthodox Church</note>; so called after Jacob the Heretic <note>Jacob Baradaeus, who reorganized the Monophysite church in the 6th century</note>, a disciple of the Patriarch of Alexandria. These occupy a great part of Asia in the regions of the East, the land of Mamre which is near Egypt, and the land of Ethiopia as far as India, comprising more than 40 Kingdoms: these are circumcised and baptized with a hot iron <note>A reference to the practice of branding a cross on the skin</note>, printing the mark of the cross on their foreheads and other parts of the body, such as on the chest or arms; these confess to God alone and not to Priests, nor to Jews or Agarenes, and they say that in Christ there is only a divine nature <note>The doctrine of Monophysitism, which held that Christ had a single divine nature rather than distinct human and divine natures</note>. Some of them speak the Chaldean language <note>Syriac or Aramaic</note>, some the Arabic language, and others in other languages according to the diversity of their nations; and these were condemned in the Council of Chalcedon <note>original: "concilio Cedensi"</note>.

The fifth nation is that of the Nestorians, named after the heretic Nestorius, who was the Bishop of Constantinople <note>Nestorius (c. 386–450 AD) was deposed for his views on the nature of Christ</note>. They alone posit two distinct persons in Christ: one divine and the other human. They deny that the Blessed Virgin Mary is the Mother of God, asserting instead that she is the mother of the man Jesus. They use the Chaldean language <note>original: "lingua Chaldaica," referring here to Classical Syriac</note> in their scriptures and consecrate the body of Christ using leavened bread. They inhabit Tartary <note>a historical term for North and Central Asia, including the Mongol Empire</note> and Greater India, and they are many in number. Their land is as vast as Germany and Italy combined; these are the same heretics who were condemned in the third Synod of Ephesus [431 AD], and having been divided from the Roman Church, they have remained obstinate in their views.

The sixth nation is that of the Maronites, named after a certain heretic called Maro. They posit only one intellect and one will in Christ <note>a doctrine known as Monothelitism, which suggests Christ had two natures but only one governing will</note>. They live near Lebanon <note>original: "Lybiam," likely a transcription error for "Libanum"</note> in the province of Phoenicia in great numbers. They are warrior-men, well-taught and experienced in battle, making special use of bows and arrows. Following the custom of the Latins, they use bells; their Bishops use rings, mitres, and pastoral staffs. In their writings, they use the Chaldean script, but in common speech, they use the Arabic language. At one time, they were under the obedience of the Roman Church—for their Patriarch was present at the General Lateran Council held in Rome under Innocent III [1215 AD]—but they later withdrew from the Roman Church. They were first condemned in the Synod of Constantinople, later returned to the obedience of the Roman Church, and have since returned again to their own opinion, in which they persevere to this day.

The seventh nation is that of the Armenians, who live in the kingdom of Armenia near Antioch. They have their own idiom and a language common to all; they sing the Holy Scriptures and the office of the Church and speak in the vernacular tongue so that they may be understood by all laypeople, both men and women. They have their own Primate, whom they call the Catholicos <note>original: "Catholicum"</note>, whom they obey with great devotion and reverence, just as we obey the Pope. They fast during Lent with great devotion, during which they neither eat fish nor drink wine. However, on Fridays, they eat meat.

The eighth nation is that of the Georgians, named after Saint George, whom they hold as their patron in battle. They live in the Eastern regions; they are a handsome, strong, and refined people, and are greatly feared by the Medes, Persians, and Syrians, on whose borders they dwell. They use the Greek language and perform the sacraments after the Greek custom. The clergy have round tonsures <note>original: "coronas," referring to the shaved circle on a priest's head</note> on their heads, while the laymen have square ones. When they come to the Holy Sepulchre, they do not pay tribute to the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims, particularly those in the Levant</note>, and they enter Jerusalem with banners held high because the Saracens fear them. Their women use arms just as the men do; they also have hair and "beards" <note>likely a reference to heavy veils or perhaps a misunderstanding of local fashions</note> like the men, and they wear tall hats on their heads a cubit in height. When they write to the Sultan, whatever they request is immediately granted to them.

The ninth nation is that of the Syrians, so named after the city of Tyre <note>original: "Sur"</note>, which is the most eminent city in Syria or Assyria. In common speech, they use the Saracen language <note>Arabic</note>, but for the divine scriptures and the office of the Mass, they use the Greek language. They have Bishops and observe the customs of the Greeks, obeying them in all things; they perform the Eucharist with leavened bread and hold the opinions of the Greeks against the Latins. They are followed by certain Christians who are called Samaritans in the Holy Land; these were first converted in the time of the Apostles, but they are not well-grounded in the Catholic faith.

The tenth nation is that of the **Mozarabs**. These Mozarabs were once numerous in parts of Africa and Spain, but now they are few. They are called **Mozarabs** because they followed the customs of the Christians of Arabia in many things. <note>The name "Mozarab" comes from the Arabic *musta'rib*, meaning "Arabicized." It refers to Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule and adopted Arabic language and culture while remaining Christian.</note> They use the **Latin language** in their divine services, and they obey the Roman Church and the Latin Prelates. They celebrate the Eucharist with unleavened bread <note>original: "in azymo"</note> like the Latins, but they differ from the Latins in many other respects. Because the natural day is divided into twenty-four hours of day and night, they have just as many offices—including hours, psalms, and hymns—and they have certain prayers that are excessively long, which they do not recite in the Latin fashion; for what the Latins say at the beginning, they say at the end or in the middle. Some divide the Sacrament of the Eucharist into seven parts, and others into ten. This nation is exceedingly devout; in marriage, however, they only unite with people of their own race or nation. Among them, a woman who has lost her first husband never joins with another, but remains in perpetual chastity. 

The cause of such great diversity or division among Christians was that, in ancient times, Christians were restricted from holding general councils; therefore, when heretics arose in various parts of the world, there was no one to apply a remedy. The second cause was the negligence of the Supreme Pontiffs [the Popes], because they did not take care to send envoys to the Christians living in error; for if they had done so, they would have brought many or all back to the one faith and obedience of the Roman Church.

**Barthélemy de Chasseneuz**, in the twelfth part of his *Catalog of the Glory of the World* <note>original: "cathalogue, gloria mundi," referring to the *Catalogus gloriae mundi* (1529), a famous legal and encyclopedic work</note>, consideration 22, writes the following: Of the Christian sects, there are thirteen nations that hold to it, and there are four that are included under the **Latins**, because the Latins are primarily all Christians. And within the Latin nation, there are four other specific nations: namely, the **French** <note>original: "Gallicana"</note>, **German** <note>original: "Germanica"</note>, **Italian** <note>original: "Italica"</note>, and **Spanish** <note>original: "Hispanica"</note> nations. 

But there is one that has held and continues to hold the faith without monstrosities or any error, and without deviation, because it never withdrew from it or strayed in any way: this is the **French nation**, which has always been free of monstrosities, and has always defended, aided, protected, and increased the Catholic faith, and has fought with all its might against almost all other nations [that opposed it]. In this first French nation, the **King of France** is the principal figure, who is called the **"Most Christian"** <note>original: "Christianissimus," a formal title granted to the Kings of France</note> among all the kings of the world. Under him are many Dukes, Counts, Marquises, and Barons obedient to him, as well as the King of Navarre and the King of Yvetot <note>The "Kingdom of Yvetot" was a small, sovereign-like principality in Normandy</note>, although some say the kingdom of Navarre falls under the Spanish nation. 

The second nation is the **Italian**, in which resides the principal figure of all Christendom, who is the **Pope**. He holds the primacy and leadership over the entire Church and the Christian sect, whom everyone obeys, or is bound to obey. In that nation are the King of Sicily, the King of Naples, the Duchy of Venice, the Dukes of Milan, Ferrara, and Urbino, the Marquises of Mantua and Montferrat, and many other Counts, principalities, and lordships, such as Florence, Siena, and Genoa. 

The third nation is the **Spanish**, in which are the Kings of Castile, Leon, Granada, Aragon, and Portugal, along with many Dukes and Counts; the principal kingdom is called Castile and Spain, whose King is called **"The Catholic"** <note>original: "Catholicus," the traditional title of the Spanish monarch</note>. 

The fourth nation is that of the **Germans**, in which is the **Emperor**. There are also many kings, such as the King of England, Scotland, Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, Denmark <note>original: "Daciæ," a common Latinization for Denmark in this period</note>, Frisia, Sweden, Norway, Dalmatia, and Croatia, as well as many Landgraves, Dukes, and Counts. Likewise, the King of Cyprus on the Island of Cyprus. All the aforementioned are obedient to the Roman Church, although many heresies have emanated from this Germany, which were condemned, and...
