To these nations, in these most recent days, has risen the **Lutheran sect**, which has stained Christianity in many ways. The **fifth nation** is that of the **Greeks**, who have the **Patriarch of Constantinople**, as well as Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and others of that kind in spiritual matters. In temporal <note>Meaning worldly or political, as opposed to spiritual.</note> matters, they have an **Emperor**, and they also have Dukes, Counts, Despots <note>original: "Hisbotum," likely a transcription error for "Despotum," a title for high-ranking lords in the Byzantine Empire.</note>, and so on. However, they are now few in number, because the **Hagarenes** <note>A medieval term for Muslims, based on the biblical Hagar.</note> and the **Turks** have occupied and hold the greater part of Greece. These people do not obey the **Roman Church**, although they were at times subject to the Roman Pontiff himself; nonetheless, they have frequently attempted to tear the "seamless tunic of the Lord" <note>A common biblical metaphor for the unity of the Church, referring to the robe of Jesus that was not divided by the soldiers at the Crucifixion.</note>. For this reason, twelve divisions of the Greeks are usually counted, which are listed by **Johann Eck** <note>A prominent 16th-century German theologian and opponent of Martin Luther.</note> in the third book of his treatise *On the Primacy of Peter*, chapter 16. Truly, they now hold many errors and have been condemned by the Church because they say that the **Holy Spirit** does not proceed from the Son <note>original: "Spiritus sanctus nō procedit à Filio." This refers to the "Filioque" controversy, the central theological disagreement between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.</note> and because they do not believe in **purgatory**. 

The **sixth nation** is that of **India**, in which is **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian king of the East who captivated the medieval European imagination; he was believed to rule a vast, wealthy empire in "India" or Ethiopia.</note>, who presides over that people as a **Patriarch**, and one hundred and twenty-seven Archbishoprics are subject to him, each of which is said to have twenty Bishops. These people are reborn through the fountain of baptism in the Roman manner, in the name of the **Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit**. They perform the sacrament of the **Eucharist** with the same rite, with this sole exception: they chant the *Pater Noster* <note>The "Our Father" prayer.</note> before the elevation of the sacrament. After the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Apostles Peter and Paul, and the Blessed John the Baptist, they especially receive and worship them with honor. They also venerate others with the greatest devotion, particularly **Matthew**, their principal teacher. Furthermore, they follow with the highest devotion the blessed **Paul the First Hermit**, **Anthony the Abbot**, **Macarius**, and two other hermits. Indeed, they say their **Emperor** is most Christian, whom seventy-four Kings and almost infinite Princes obey—excepting only twelve small rulers <note>original: "regulis"</note> who observe the laws of **Muhammad**, yet who nonetheless obey the Emperor's commands in all other things. 

Truly, in the time of **Clement V**, specifically in the year of our salvation 1306, this Emperor is said to have sent thirty legates to the **King of Spain**, offering him aid against the infidels, as a certain Genoese priest, the provost of Saint Mark, declares and wrote in his treatise on the customs of this people, titled *Mappa Mundi* <note>Map of the World.</note>. These legates, approaching the aforementioned Pope Clement V in **Avignon** with reverence, were instructed in many things; with many gifts and Apostolic letters, they came to visit the "thresholds of the Apostles" <note>A traditional term for a pilgrimage to the tombs of Peter and Paul in Rome.</note>, Peter and Paul; and having visited them, they returned to their own lands with joy. However, while waiting in **Genoa** for many days for the time of sailing, they were asked much about their tribes, customs, and regions, and they left a written account, which the same author reported. **Philip of Bergamo** <note>A 15th-century Augustinian friar and chronicler.</note> says these things in the eighth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles*. Whenever the said Prester John rides, he always has a wooden cross carried before him; but when he goes to war, he then has two crosses carried: one of gold and the other of precious stones. In that land, the body of **St. Thomas the Apostle** is held in the greatest veneration. I believe in my heart that these people should be exalted in our Christian faith after the **Latins**—namely the French, Italians, Spanish, and Germans—and should be preferred over all other Christian nations, since they do not differ much from our Christian faith, except that they do not approve of the **Roman Pope** as the Supreme Pontiff of the whole Church and do not approve of his primacy. 3. ...all the Easterners and territories were once subject to the Roman Pope. The **seventh nation** of Christianity is that of the **Jacobites**, named after Jacob, the heretic disciple of the Patriarch of Alexandria. <note>Referring to Jacob Baradaeus, who reorganized the Syriac Orthodox Church in the 6th century.</note> These people occupy a great part of Asia in the Eastern regions, as well as the **Land of Mamre** <note>A biblical location near Hebron, though here used to describe the Levant/Egypt region.</note>, which is near Egypt, and the land of Ethiopia as far as Judea—more than forty kingdoms. They practice circumcision and are baptized with a red-hot iron, branding the sign of the cross on their foreheads and other parts of the body, such as the chest or arms. They confess their sins to God alone and not to priests, unlike the **Indians** and **Hagarenes** <note>A term for Muslims, referring to the descendants of Hagar.</note>. They claim there is only a divine nature in Christ. <note>This is the doctrine of Miaphysitism, which the author labels as heresy.</note> Some of them speak the **Chaldean language** <note>Likely referring to Syriac, a dialect of Aramaic used in liturgy.</note>, others Arabic, and others speak various languages according to the diversity of their nations.

The **eighth nation** of Christianity is those called **Nestorians**, named after the heretic Nestorius, a disciple of that name who was from Constantinople. These people posit two persons in Christ—one divine and the other human—and they deny that the Blessed Mary is the mother of God, but rather the mother of the man Jesus. Likewise, they deny that Christ is one in the Word and in the flesh, but is instead separate: one the son of God, the other the son of man. As **Juan de Torquemada** <note>original: "Ioan. de Turrecremata" - a 15th-century Spanish theologian and defender of papal authority.</note> writes extensively about them in his work on heretics... They use the **Chaldean language** in their scriptures and consecrate the body of Christ using leavened bread. They inhabit **Tartary** <note>Central and North Asia.</note> and **Greater India**, and they are many in number; their land is as large as Germany and Italy combined. These heretics were condemned in the **Council of Ephesus** <note>Held in 431 AD.</note> and were separated from the Roman Church, remaining in their stubbornness. Extensive refutations of their errors are written by the same Juan de Torquemada. **Philip of Bergamo** <note>original: "Philippus Bergomensis" - an Augustinian friar and chronicler.</note> says in the ninth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles* that they hold yet another error preached by Nestorius the heresiarch: namely, that living virtuously is of no benefit to human life, as is found in the passage discussing "certain heretics," because he claimed that **predestination** alone brought about salvation or dominion, which is entirely false. One could here adapt the subject of predestination, which belongs to theologians, but I only refer you to **Bernardino de Bustis** <note>A popular 15th-century Franciscan preacher.</note>... where he refutes this error and speaks at length on the matter of predestination.

The **ninth nation** is those called **Maronites**, after a certain heretic Maron, who posits only one intellect and one will in Christ. <note>This refers to Monothelitism, a 7th-century theological attempt to bridge the gap between Miaphysites and the Chalcedonian church.</note> They inhabit **Libya** <note>Likely a general term for the coast of Africa or the Levant.</note> in the province of **Phoenicia** in great numbers; they are skilled and experienced in battle, specifically using bows and arrows. They use bells in the manner of the Latins, and their bishops use rings, miters, and pastoral staffs. In their divine scriptures, they use the **Chaldean** script, and in common speech, they use **Arabic**. They were at one time under the obedience of the Roman Church; indeed, their Patriarch was present at the **General Lateran Council** held in Rome under Pope Innocent III, but they later withdrew. They were first condemned in the **Synod of Constantinople**, then returned to the obedience of the Roman Church, and have since returned again to their false opinion, in which they persist.

The **tenth nation** is those called **Armenians**, who live in the kingdom of Armenia near Antioch. They have their own idiom and common language, and they sing the Holy Scriptures and the Church office in the common tongue so that they are understood by all secular men and women. They have their own primate whom they call the **Catholicos**, whom they obey as if he were the Pope with great devotion and reverence. They fast during Lent, in which they do not eat...

...they [the Armenians] eat fish, nor do they drink wine; however, on Fridays they eat meat. In the times of Emperor Constantine, they received the faith of Christ along with the Scots or Hibernians <note>The author is likely confusing the 'Iberians' of the Caucasus (modern Georgians) with the 'Hibernians' (the Irish) due to the similarity of the names. The **Eleventh Nation** of Christians is those who are called **Georgians**, after Saint George, whom they have as their patron in battles. They live in the Eastern parts and are a very handsome, strong, and refined people. They are greatly feared by the Medes, Persians, and Assyrians, in whose borders they dwell. They use the Greek language and practice the sacraments according to the Greek custom. The clergy have round tonsures <note>original: "coronas rotundas" — the shaved part of a priest's head.</note> on their heads, while the secular people have square ones. When they come to the Holy Sepulchre, they do not pay tribute to the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval Europeans for Muslims.</note>, and they enter Jerusalem with banners raised high because the Saracens fear them. Their women use weapons just like the men, and they wear tall hats on their heads, a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note> in height. When they write to the Sultan, what they request is immediately granted.

Philip of Bergamo <note>Philippus Bergomensis (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk and author of the 'Supplementum Chronicarum,' a popular historical compendium.</note> says in the ninth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles* that the Scots or Hibernians are today called the Georgian people and worship Christ to this day, although they are far from the Apostolic See <note>The Papacy in Rome.</note>, the teacher of truth. He claims they do not preserve the full truth of the Gospel because they are surrounded by barbarian nations. For these (as he says) are established in the Northern part, and in the year of Christ 338, during the time of Emperor Constantine, they miraculously received the covenants of the Word of God and the faith of Christ. 

A certain Christian captive woman provided the cause for this great good. While she led a modest and holy life in that region and spent days and nights in prayer, she became an object of admiration to those nations. When they asked why she afflicted herself so much, she responded that she thus worshipped her God, who is Christ. The barbarians, wondering at nothing more than this (as we know of such novelties), began to hold the little woman in honor. Now, it was the custom of that nation that when a small child fell ill, it was carried around by its mother to the neighboring houses in search of remedies. It happened that a certain mother, after she had carried her boy around for some time and found no healing, went to the captive woman as if drunk with grief and sought her help. The woman replied that she knew of no human remedy, but that the Lord Jesus Christ whom she worshipped could grant the health that men despaired of. Placing the little boy upon her hairshirt <term>hairshirt (cilice): a garment of rough animal hair worn against the skin as a sign of penance and devotion</term> and pouring out a prayer to God Christ, she immediately returned him to his mother healed. Soon the rumor of the deed filled the whole city and even reached the Queen, who, being afflicted with pain, saw to it that the captive was brought to her. When the captive refused to enter the royal house, she poured out a prayer to God for the Queen; immediately, the Queen herself was restored to health and was thus admonished to believe in Christ and to adore Him who had provided her healing. Moved by these benefits and words, the Queen asked her husband to become a Christian. Although he had promised to do so, and despite being moved by signs and the frequent urging of his wife, he did not see to his baptism—not so much because he was an enemy of the faith, but because he was doubtful. ...once, when he went to hunt in the deepest forests, and having arrived there, a sudden storm arose; darkness covered everything so completely that he could see no one, nor could he be seen by them. Not knowing what ought to be done, he remembered the promise made to his wife and then prayed to Christ, asking that if He were God, He might deliver him from such great perils. Without delay, the clearest daylight was restored to the world. Having been brought back to the city, the King explained what had happened to the Queen as a miracle. The captive woman <note>Saint Nino, a slave woman who is credited with bringing Christianity to Georgia (Iberia) in the 4th century.</note> was summoned, and her counsel was heard. She said that idols must be immediately rejected and Christ must be worshiped; she urged that He be supplicated and that a basilica be constructed. 

The King, having called the people together, preached the Gospel and, though not yet initiated into the sacred rites, became the Apostle to his own nation. The men believed through the King, and the women through the Queen. A temple of great workmanship was constructed, and when the circuit of the walls had been persistently raised, the columns were set in place. But though the first and second were erected, the third could not be raised by any machines or any strength. After they had labored until nightfall, everyone withdrew, and only the captive woman remained at the Church in persevering prayer. On the following day at first light, as the people returned, the column was found suspended in the air above its base by the space of one foot. At the sight of this miracle, everyone magnified God and recognized the true faith of the captive woman. While everyone was stupefied, the column was gradually lowered onto the base without anyone touching it. Soon, the remaining columns were erected with great success. 

Once the Church was perfected and the faith of the people confirmed, at the persuasion of the captive woman, an embassy from the whole nation was sent to the Emperor Constantine in Greece <note>Original: "Constantinum Imperatorem in Græciam." Referring to the Eastern Roman Empire centered in Constantinople.</note>, and the events were explained, and priests were requested to fulfill the service begun among them. The Emperor satisfied these requests with a most joyful countenance; so says Philip of Bergamo <note>original: "Philippus Bergomensis," referring to Jacopo Filippo Foresti (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk and historian from Bergamo.</note> in the place mentioned above.

The **Twelfth Nation** of Christians is that of those called **Syrians**, from the city of Sur <note>Tyre</note>, which is eminent in Syria or Assyria. In their common speech, they use the Saracen language <note>original: "lingua Sarracenica," referring to Arabic.</note>; in the divine scriptures and the office of the Mass, they use the Greek language. They have Bishops and preserve the custom of the Greeks, obeying them in all things. They perform the sacrament of the Eucharist with leavened bread, and they hold the opinions of the Greeks against the Latins. Certain Christians follow these, who in the Holy Land are called **Samaritans**, converted in the first era of the Apostles, but they are not well-grounded in the faith.

The **Thirteenth Nation** is that of those called **Mozarabs**. Formerly, there were many of these in parts of Africa and Spain, but now there are few. They are called Mozarabs because they held the customs of Christians according to the Arabic way in many things <note>The Mozarabs were Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule; the name comes from "musta'rib," meaning "Arabized."</note>. These use the Latin language in divine offices and obey the Roman Church and the Latin prelates; they perform the Eucharist in unleavened bread <note>original: "in Azimo," referring to the host used in the Western Church.</note> just like the Latins, but they differ from them in many things. For in the divine offices, they have very long "hours," because since the natural day is divided into twenty-four hours of day and night, they have as many offices, each with its own hours, psalms, and hymns, as well as certain prayers, and they are excessively long, which they do not say in the manner of the Latins. For that which the Latins say at the beginning, they say at the end or in the middle. Some divide the sacrament of the Eucharist into seven parts, others into ten. It is a nation very devoted to marriage; they do not join themselves except to persons of their own people or nation. Among them, a woman who has lost her first husband never joins with another but remains in perpetual chastity. 

All these aforementioned sects or nations use three languages, namely Hebrew or Arabic, Greek, and Latin, whence—as it is held in Luke 23 and John 19—the title or inscription of the Cross of Jesus Christ was written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin...

...from <term>Gratian's Decree</term> <note>The foundational collection of Canon Law; the text here refers to Distinction 9.</note>, who says this: "Just as the reliability of the Old Testament books is to be examined against the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the New Testament requires the standard of the Greek speech." <note>original: "vt veterum librorum fides de Hebræis voluminibus examinanda est, ita nouorum veritas, Græci sermonis normam desiderat"</note> This is understood to refer to the Old and New Testaments. The text also states in the final chapter of Distinction 20: "Regarding those causes where no authority for loosening or binding <note>A legal and theological term for the power of the Church to forgive sins or make laws.</note> appears in the books of the Old and New Testaments, or in the four Gospels along with all the writings of the Apostles, one should recur to the divine Greek writings." 

However, the <term>Great Gloss</term> <note>The standard 13th-century commentary on legal texts.</note> on the said chapter *Ut veterum* says that Jerome, in his second prologue to the Bible, holds the opposite view. He claims that the Latin copies are more correctly emended than the Greek and Hebrew ones. But Augustine, in the aforementioned chapter *Ut veterum*, was looking back to the primitive Church, when the Greek and Hebrew copies were not yet corrupted. 

As time passed and the Christian population grew significantly, many heresies sprouted among the Greeks. Out of envy for the Christians, both the Jews and the Greeks corrupted their own copies. Thus, it happened that their copies became more corrupted than the Latin ones. Jerome refers to this later period, or perhaps he is referring to Latin copies translated by faithful interpreters. Augustine, on the other hand, was referring to Latin copies translated not by the faithful, but by counterfeiters. In this matter, as the said Gloss states, Jerome is to be believed more than Augustine. 

Among these three—Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory—Augustine is to be believed more in matters of disputation; Jerome in matters of history and translations; and Gregory is preferred in matters of morality. This is because "not everyone is expert in all things, but specific people in specific areas," <note>original: "non omnes in omnibus, sed certi per certa"</note> as is stated in the text of the <term>Digest</term> <note>A massive collection of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> regarding the clarifying of old laws. "Nor can we all do all things." This is the opinion of the said Gloss, which is cited and followed by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> and after him by Felinus in the chapter *Ne initiaris* at the end of the section on constitutions. There, Felinus says that this Gloss was approved by Ludovicus Romanus in his legal commentaries.

However, the <term>Archdeacon</term> <note>Guido de Baysio, a prominent commentator on Canon Law.</note> in the said final chapter of Distinction 20—and after him the Provost and Geminianus—state that when a written text is found to be contradictory or doubtful, one must recur to the Greek language. This is understood according to those times when the integrity of the Catholic faith flourished among the Greeks. But since today they are "headless" <note>original: "acephali"—likely referring here to the Great Schism, meaning they are without the "head" of the Church (the Pope) or lack proper leadership.</note> and their copies are corrupted and full of errors, one should not recur to their volumes. Indeed, it is not likely that those who do not sincerely hold the unity of the Catholic faith would have preserved the integrity of their volumes; rather, they likely corrupted them out of hatred for the Latins (who are the unshakable observers of the faith’s unity). For adversaries and enemies lie easily, as noted in the legal texts where many concordances agree in the commentary on inquiries.

Albericus de Rosate, in his first Constitution and in his dictionary under the word "Language" <note>original: "lingua"</note>, says that among all languages, three are most excellent: namely Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Of these, Greek is said to be the clearest and most resonant. Its variety is discerned in five parts: the first is called "Mixed" or "Common"; the second, "Athenian," which the Greek authors used; the third, that which the Egyptians and Syrians have; the fourth, "Ionic"; and the fifth, "Aeolic." Or otherwise: one is called Attic, another Boeotian, the third Aeolic, the fourth Doric, the fifth...

<note>original: "stini"</note> [Augu]stine, in the ninth <term>Distinction</term> <note>A division within the "Decretum Gratiani," a foundational collection of Canon Law.</note>, who says that just as the reliability of the Old Books must be examined against the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the New [Testament] requires the standard of the Greek language. This should be understood regarding the Old and New Testaments. The text also states at the end of the 20th Distinction that in causes where no authority for binding or loosing appears in the books of the Old and New Testaments and the four Gospels, along with all the writings of the Apostles, one should recur to the divine Greek writings. 

However, the <term>Great Gloss</term> <note>The standard medieval commentary on Canon Law.</note> on the said chapter "As the Ancients" <note>original: "ut veterum"</note> says that **Jerome** <note>Hieronymus, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> holds the contrary in the second prologue of the Bible, saying that the Latin copies are more corrected than the Greek and Hebrew ones. But **Augustine**, in the aforementioned chapter "As the Ancients," is looking back to the Primitive Church, when the Greek and Hebrew copies were not yet corrupted. As time passed and the Christian people grew greatly in number, many heresies sprouted among the Greeks. Out of envy for the Christians, the Jews and Greeks corrupted their own copies; thus it happened that their copies became more corrupted than the Latin ones. This is the time to which Jerome refers, or else he refers to Latin copies translated by faithful interpreters.

**Augustine**, on the other hand, refers to Latin copies translated not by the faithful, but by falsifiers. In this matter, as the said Gloss says, Jerome is to be believed more than Augustine. <header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE [LANGUAGES]</header>

<margin>judicial:</margin> How much the Greek language surpasses the Latin is written by <term>Budé</term> <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist scholar.</note> in his treatise *On the As and its Parts*, book one, folio 7. Indeed, it is said there are four types of the Latin language: first, the **Ancient** <note>original: "prisca"</note>, which is the oldest form used by the people of Italy under Janus and Saturn; second, the **Latin** <note>original: "Latina"</note>, used by the Italians from the time of King Latinus and other kings of Tuscany, in which the <term>Law of the Twelve Tables</term> <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BCE.</note> was written; third, the **Roman** <note>original: "Romana"</note>, which the Roman people used after the expulsion of the Kings; and fourth, the **Mixed** <note>original: "mixta"</note>, which took hold in the city after the Empire had expanded, along with new customs and people, corrupting the integrity of speech through <term>solecisms</term> <note>Grammatical mistakes.</note> and <term>barbarisms</term> <note>The use of non-standard or foreign words.</note>.

All Eastern peoples clash their words in the throat, such as the Hebrews and Syrians. Mediterranean nations produce their speech in the palate, such as the Greeks and Asians. Westerners, however, break their words against the teeth, such as the Italians and Spanish. I would add that the Northerners and Germans form their words in the chest; we French, however, use the throat, palate, and chest. Hence it is commonly said: **the Italians bleat like goats, the Germans howl, the French sing, and the English shout for joy.** <note>original: "Itali caprisant, Alemani ululant, Galli cantant, & Angli iubilant."</note> This is also stated by Albericus in the place cited below, who says he found in the authentic scriptures on Genesis and in the *Inventory of the Entire World* (in the section on the building of the Tower) the reason for the diversity of languages. <term>Isidore</term> <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar and encyclopedist.</note> says the same in his book *Etymologies*, noting that the speech of the Greeks is more elegant than the others, as I mentioned above. <term>William Durand</term> <note>A 13th-century liturgical writer.</note> in his *Rationale of the Divine Offices* says that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages because of the Law. The Greek language is the **Teacher**, and the Latin language is the **Interpreter**, owing to the dominion of the Roman Empire and the Papacy. Therefore, it is said that Hebrew was the mother of all tongues, for before the pride of the Tower of Babylon divided them, there was one language for all nations, as held in Genesis 11: "And the earth was of one tongue and of the same speech." And again the Lord says: "Behold, they are one people, and they all have one tongue." Because of that sin, seventy entirely different languages were introduced (as discussed below in the 69th distinction regarding famous towers). Whence Remigius says regarding the passage in 1 Corinthians 14, "languages shall cease": just as before the Tower of Babel there was one Hebrew tongue, so some doctors believe that after the Judgment, that same one shall remain. Thus, as I said, there is variety in many languages, and where there is variety, there is dissention; but in the kingdom of the saints, there will be no dissention, and therefore no variety of languages. Likewise, Bernard says that although many know many things, there will be one language for all: an unwearied shouting for joy, one affection, eternal love; and there will be a common omnipotence, wisdom, peace, justice, and intelligence for all. In that peace, there will be no diversity of tongues. Yet, it is a gift to use different languages, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 14: "I thank my God that I speak in the tongues of you all," and the Apostles spoke in various tongues in Acts 2. Regarding the praise of this Hebrew language, see more in the *Margarita Philosophica* <note>An early encyclopedia from 1503 by Gregor Reisch.</note> in the section on Hebrew instruction, where he praises it for its antiquity and priority, since it preceded all others in purity, holiness, abundance of meaning, and utility, excelling all others most elegantly. And Isidore says in his first book of *Etymologies* that the Greek letters, along with their names, were taken from the characters of the Hebrews, just as **A** comes from **Aleph**...

...[A]leph, Alpha, a, and so on for several others. It is held as an indubitable truth, and certain among nearly all, that the Latin language gushed forth from Greek sources. Whether this is entirely true, I have discussed above in this part, in the 17th consideration, where Gaul is praised for its tradition of letters.

Brother Brochard <note>Burchard of Mount Sion, a German Dominican friar and traveler.</note>, a monk living in the year of salvation 1283, wrote in his description of the places of the Holy Land that in his time, the following peoples and nations were found in Jerusalem and in the Holy Land:

> In the Land of Promise, there are men from every nation under heaven, and each people lives according to their own way of life. And, to speak the truth to our great shame, none in that land are found to be worse or more corrupt in their morals than the Christians. I believe the reason for this is as follows: When someone in Spain, France, Germany, Italy, or other Christian nations has been caught as a criminal—be it a murderer, bandit, thief, incestuous person, adulterer, fornicator, or traitor—and fears that the judge will impose a punishment worthy of his crime, he flees and moves to the Holy Land. It is as if he intends to wipe away the evil he committed; but when he arrives there, he has changed his location, not his soul. Thus, what is written has happened to him: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin?* <note>A reference to Jeremiah 13:23, implying that a change of scenery does not change a person's inherent nature.</note> There are not a few such men in the Holy Land today, who rob pilgrims and their own countrymen who turn to them in good faith, suspecting no evil from them. These detestable fathers leave behind even more detestable sons, who trample the holy places with polluted feet, and by their wicked lives, they cause the holy things of God to fall into great contempt.
>
> Besides the Christians in the Land of Promise, there are also various other peoples, especially the **Saracens** <note>original: "Saraceni"; a term used by medieval Europeans for Muslims.</note>, who preach Muhammad and observe his law. They also recognize Christ as a great Prophet, conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, but they deny that he suffered and died; rather, they say that when it pleased him, he ascended into heaven. They say he sits at the right hand of the Father as a Son. But they say Muhammad sits at the left hand of God, and that he was sent only to them as God's messenger. These followers of Muhammad are greatly addicted to impurity, and they take as many wives as they can feed, in addition to being defiled by the vice of Gomorrah <note>original: "Gomorrhaico fœdati sunt vitio"; a historical euphemism for sodomy or homosexual acts.</note>. Yet they are hospitable and sufficiently humane, a fact I have experienced for myself more than once. For a small service shown to them, they return a generous reward.
> 
> Furthermore, in this land there are **Syrians**, who are indeed Christians, but they keep no faith with the **Latins** <note>original: "Latinis"; here referring to the Roman Catholic Church and Western Europeans.</note>. They live miserably and poorly; devoted to greed, they grant alms to no one. The wealthiest among them lives no more delicately than the poorest. They live among the Saracens and for the most part are bound to their service. In their dress, they differ almost not at all from the Saracens, except that they distinguish themselves by a woolen belt.
> 
> The **Greeks** are likewise Christians, but they are schismatics and estranged from obedience to the Roman Church. They are also entangled in many other errors—may God grant that many follies have not also crept in among the Latins. Among the Greeks, almost all the prelates are monks and practice great abstinence; they are held in great reverence and honor by the common people.
>
> There are also in this land Armenians, Georgians, Nestorians, and Nubians...

<note>original: "labeani"</note> Jabeans, Chaldeans, Maronites, Ethiopians, Egyptians, and many other nations, all of whom indeed confess Christ and have their own Patriarchs. Some are heretics <note>In the medieval Catholic view, "heretic" applied to any group that disagreed with Roman dogma, such as the nature of Christ's divinity.</note> and have taken their names from the founders of their sects, such as the Nestorians, Jacobites, and the like. Yet there are many among these sects who are quite simple, knowing nothing of these heresies; they are devoted to Christ, mortifying their flesh with fasts and wearing the simplest of garments, so that they even far surpass the religious orders of the Roman Church in their devotion.

The Nubians and Jabeans say that they, or rather their ancestors, received the faith from Saint Matthew and were baptized by him. They claim to have received their manner of baptism from him, which they strive to keep inviolable today, relying on this authority: *He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire* <note>original: "Ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu sancto & igne," a reference to Matthew 3:11.</note>. For when they are baptized, they brand a cross onto their face or another part of the body with a hot iron, and these are considered the most devout among the Eastern peoples.

There is also the nation of the Midianites, who are now called Bedouins and Turonians, who have filled a large part of the Holy Land. These people devote themselves solely to raising livestock and camels, of which they have an exceeding abundance. They have no fixed dwelling place, but where they find good pastures, they stay there with their tents for as long as it takes for the grass to be grazed, until they are forced to seek another place for their flocks. They are a very warlike people and have filled all of Syria; they have particularly occupied the banks of the Jordan from Lebanon all the way to the desert of <term>Pharan</term> <note>The Wilderness of Paran, a location mentioned in the Bible as a place where the Israelites spent time during the Exodus.</note>. The mountains beyond the Jordan provide the best fodder for sheep, goats, and other cattle. They have rams and wethers so thick and fat that a single tail is enough for three or four men to eat.

The Nestorians live around Beirut and Byblos in the plains of Lebanon toward Iturea.

The Maronites, however, have occupied the region around the "fountain of the gardens" <note>A poetic or local name for a spring near Tripoli.</note> descending from Lebanon toward Tripoli, and they are said to have forty thousand fighting men.

Furthermore, around the fortress of Arcas <note>A Crusader-era castle near Tripoli.</note> past Tripoli live the Saracens who are called Vanni. Associated with them are the Saracens whom they call the <term>Assassins</term> <note>The OCR text uses "Asininos," likely a corruption or pejorative variation of "Hashshashin."</note>, living in the mountains as far as the fortress of Antaradus, possessing many castles and towns and occupying very fertile land. These are said to have originated from Persia, and they have increased so much in number that they are claimed to be able to produce forty thousand armed men. A few years ago, they wished to submit themselves to Roman obedience <note>That is, to convert to Roman Catholicism.</note>, but they were hindered by the Templars and withdrew from their purpose. No Sultan has yet been able to bring these Assassins to order, but they establish their own laws and rights for themselves, using them as they please; they are a terror to all neighboring nations because of their ferocity.

And since I have touched upon these Eastern nations here, it did not seem useless to make more extensive mention of them. For today there are many who, while knowing nothing, wish to know everything, asserting that no Christians are found in these vast regions all the way to India, but that the treacherous Muhammad has defiled all places. This is not true; rather, Christ has his worshippers everywhere in the world, except in Arabia and Egypt, where Christians are rarely found, but almost everyone there has given their name to Muhammad. It is indeed true that all Christians across the sea—namely the Armenians, Cappadocians, Greeks, Chaldeans, Medes, Parthians, Indians, Nubians, Jabeans, Asians, Georgians, and the rest of the Eastern peoples—are not men accustomed to war. Rather, when they are attacked in war by Saracens, Turks, or Tartars <note>The author uses "Tartars" to refer to the Mongols, who dominated much of Asia during this period.</note>, they become their tributaries and allow them every dominion, enduring the tax collectors, provided that they can preserve peace and harmony as far as it lies within them. From this, it happens that those regions which Christians inhabit are thought to belong to the Saracens and to be subject to their treachery, even though almost everyone there is Christian. I experienced this myself in Cilicia <note>original: "Cicilia," a common medieval misspelling of Cilicia in Southern Turkey.</note> and Lesser Armenia, which are subject to the prince of the Tartars; nevertheless, they are purely Christian. They inhabit those regions, frequenting churches, hearing Masses, kneeling, and praying devoutly. They also show great honor to religious persons, which I experienced myself when I stayed there for some time. Furthermore, those whom we judge to be condemned heretics—such as the Nestorians, Jacobites, Maronites, Georgians, and the like—I found for the most part to be good and simple men, living sincerely toward God and men. They practice great abstinence, and during Lent they eat neither fish nor oil. They listen attentively to the word of God, as I saw on the evening of Palm Sunday, when they flocked to the sermon in great crowds. Moreover, they have their own Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and other prelates, except for the Nestorians, who in place of the Pope have a prelate whom they call the *Iacelichum* <note>original: "Iacelichum," a Latinization of the Syriac "Qatoliqa" or Catholicos, the title for the head of the Church of the East.</note>, whom a great part of the East obeys.

->Truly the Armenians and Georgians have prelates whom they call Catholicos,<-
who have under them Archbishops, Bishops, and other prelates. These men lead the people by their excellent way of life, teaching them equally by word and example. And although they inhabit very well-fortified castles and possess great wealth, they nonetheless dress in cheap and dirty clothes with very wide sleeves. Their outer garment is a coarse and red sheepskin, and beneath it they wear a gray and worn tunic. Their topmost garment is a black scapular, cheap and rough like haircloth. I also attended their sacred rites once on the Day of the Annunciation, and I noticed that they use almost the same ceremonies and prayers as we do in the Mass, except that they use their own language and not the Roman one. Note also that the Catholicos himself and all other prelates are Monks, and no one except Monks is admitted to these ecclesiastical offices. The secular clergy and priests, however, have almost no authority and do nothing else except celebrate the divine offices. At all hours they give the signal with a wooden board <note>A "semantron," a wooden or metal plank struck with a mallet, used in Eastern Christianity instead of bells.</note>, for they do not have bells; and then they rise at night for morning prayers, waking one another so that all may gather. Nor do they go back to sleep after those short prayers are finished, but they sit in the church teaching the people until dawn. All priests are married, and no one is permitted to perform the office of a priest unless he has a legitimate wife. They celebrate Masses only on Saturday and the Lord's Day; on the remaining days of the week, they devote themselves to their wives <note>original: "amplexibus vacant," literally "they are free for embraces."</note>. However, if his wife dies, the priest shall remain continent and cannot marry another wife. If he commits fornication or adultery, he loses his office and his church without any hope of recovery. ...if one commits adultery <note>original Latin: "ad adulterium"</note>, the priest who is her husband must either practice continence or lose his office and his Church. But a wife committing adultery shall lose her nose, and the man who lies with her shall be castrated, even if he has a lawful wife. I saw this done once with my own eyes. When a priest dies, his widow must remain continent, and if she presumes to enter into another marriage, she shall be burned; however, if she chooses to live as a prostitute, she suffers no harm, and this often happens among them. This seems to me the primary reason why so many prostitutes are found in those lands; for the wives of such priests, being unwilling to remain continent, become prostitutes. Thieves committing a theft that is not very harmful, and other malefactors who have not deserved death, are castrated, so that they do not father sons who might imitate their father's character. I know that when I was with the King of Armenia, the Queen had more than sixty Eunuchs. The King, along with all his Princes and nobles, gladly hears the word of God, which is also devoutly presented to them from the sacred books every day at the third hour by the Monks—a practice they call *Vstraphete* <note>Likely a corruption of the Armenian word 'Vardapet,' referring to a doctor or teacher of the church.</note>—using the commentaries of John Chrysostom, Gregory Nazianzen, and Cyril (whom they call *Kyrill*). They are devout and well-behaved in Church; you would not easily see anyone there who is dissolute or undisciplined. When the Bishop performs the service, he has his ministers standing by him—such as the deacon, subdeacon, and acolyte—and he celebrates the accustomed ceremonies with great gravity.

A certain ancient Spanish author has written the following regarding this matter.

Even assuming that the greatest and truest Christendom is in Europe, under our mother the Holy Roman Church, one does not fail to find Christians in all parts of the world, or in the greater part of it. For besides those whom we commonly frequent and of whom we have particular knowledge here, there is on the side of Germany, Hungary, and Poland within our Europe, a significant Christendom consisting of those of Russia, Prussia, Lithuania, Muscovy, Prasody, and a great part of Tartary <note>A historical name for the vast region of North and Central Asia.</note>, and other Provinces which follow the Greek Church—though not entirely, because in several things they hold different opinions and are separate from it. Besides this, there are the Kingdoms of Scotland, Norway, Sweden, Gothland, and Westrogothia, and a large part of the Coast toward the North, as we shall speak of more specifically another time. And leaving Europe, because it is so well known, if we pass into Libya or Africa, which is the second part of the earth, we will find that besides the lands the Portuguese have won and converted to our Christian Religion on the southern coast, there are no fewer Christians in the interior than in our Europe. ->*On Greek Christians.*<-

The Greek Christians of today occupy a greater extent of territory than the Christians of the Latin and Roman Church. These Greeks, being separated and divided from those of the Roman Church, have chosen another way of life quite different from the Latin one. ### Of the Patriarchs of the Greeks.

There are four Patriarchs among the Greeks of the Eastern Church: the first and principal is he of Constantinople, the second he of Jerusalem, the third he of Cairo <note>Though titled "of Alexandria," the Patriarch often resided in Cairo during this period</note>, and the fourth he of Antioch. These four Patriarchs have great power over the Greeks, even though they are not very wealthy: for the total income each has for annual living amounts to only two hundred crowns <note>original: "efcus"; the Ecu was a gold coin</note>. Each of them has a certain territory under his rule and Ecclesiastical government: he of Constantinople has the land of Candia <note>Crete</note>, Chios, and all the Greeks of the Empire of Constantinople as far as Philippopolis, and all the land of Athens and of Anatolia <note>original: "Natolie"</note>. He of Jerusalem has all the land of Cyprus and Judea, with the greater part of Galilee. He of Cairo has the land of Egypt, Alexandria, Africa, and other surrounding lands. He of Antioch has the land of Syria, Greater and Lesser Armenia as far as Persia. These aforementioned Patriarchs are elected and elevated to this office of leadership as very elderly men bearing great white beards; furthermore, they possess such honorable gravity and such sweetness of face that they move men to honor them. You will perhaps ask me why the said Patriarch and the common people hate us Christians of the Latin Church so much and do not wish to follow our law? We answer you that they claim to be the first converted to the faith and are totally convinced that we others have added to the Gospel. They err in several points: for in the first place they perform the Supper <note>The Eucharist</note> and communicate under the form of leavened bread, and give the bread separately. Likewise at Easter, both great and small receive under two species <note>Both bread and wine</note>: which Pope Julius, writing to the Bishops of Egypt, reproved, along with several other ceremonies observed by them in various parts. They take no account of the Sacraments of the Catholic Church and pay them no reverence; indeed, if some priest celebrates the Mass upon their altars in the Latin fashion, once the Mass is said, they wash the said altars as if they were polluted and unclean, and as if we Latins were excommunicated. # LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

...schismatics <note>A term used by the author for those who separated from the Roman Catholic Church</note> hating us so much that they prefer to associate with the Turks, Arabs, Jews, and other infidels than with us who are in obedience to the Pope of Rome. These four Greek Patriarchs mentioned above are not the heads of the entire Greek order, but they have a superintendent, namely the Archbishop of Ohrid, a country in Bulgaria or Serbia, commonly called Valona, who is like a Pope over all the Patriarchs. According to the ancient Councils and Synods, he has the power to wear miters—which the aforementioned four Patriarchs, Bishops, and Archbishops never wear—and even less so, croziers <note>A hooked staff carried by a bishop as a symbol of pastoral office</note>. See André Thevet in his *Cosmography of the Levant*, chapter 29, and book 18, chapters 13 and 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*; Gilbert Génébrard, book 4 of his *Chronography*, pages 753 and 758, speaking of the Greek Patriarchs who believe what the Pope of Rome and the Latin Church decide regarding the Sacraments of the Church, according to the testimony of Orechouius Roxolan <note>Stanisław Orzechowski, a Polish-Ruthenian thinker</note> in his epistle to Hosius concerning the Patriarchate of Constantinople, and the position and authority of the Roman Pontiff.

The Muscovites <note>A common term for Russians at this time</note> maintain in their histories that they were first instructed in the Christian religion by Saint Thomas the Apostle; but whether that be true or not, they are currently so large, wealthy, and strong in war that they compel the Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> to allow their primary Patriarch of the Greeks—to whom they are subject in religious matters—to reside in complete safety with his monks in the city of Constantinople, a privilege he has not been willing to grant to any other Patriarchs of the Eastern Churches. Now, these Muscovites obey this Patriarch of Constantinople, and notwithstanding this, they have a Metropolitan <note>A high-ranking bishop in Eastern churches</note> whom they recognize as sovereign, and who rarely leaves the company of their Duke <note>The Tsar</note>, just as the Mufti <note>An Islamic legal authority</note> remains in the company of the Grand Turk. The clergy have income from certain farms and some other extraordinary things, but not from the cities or villages where they rule; for these depend solely on the will of the Prince. They do, however, have justice and jurisdiction for the regulation of the Clergy, though criminal offenses fall under the sole justice of the Prince. Some members of the Clergy are so reformed that they will not consume meat unless they are prone to illness; likewise, some monks live austerely according to their rule, especially those of the order of Saint Basil. They hold all their revenue in common for the benefit and support of the monastery, and they are so reformed that they have very little contact with the Laity; for this reason, they are not married like their secular priests—indeed, they cannot be—and they are entirely subject to their Prince. The Levantines <note>People of the Eastern Mediterranean</note> commonly call them Christians of Saint Paul. They perform their divine service in a corrupted Greek language <note>The author likely refers to Church Slavonic</note>, and this is why they have always been ill-disposed toward the Roman and Latin Church. They have as their ecclesiastical doctors Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Neocaesarea, and Saint John Chrysostom, whom they call in their language *Stalausta*, which is to say "Golden-mouthed" <note>original: "Stalausta," a French corruption of the Slavic "Zlatoust"</note>. They have few preachers, contenting themselves only with the readings performed by their priests every Sunday, who read them the Gospel, the Epistles of the Apostles, and the books of the Doctors in their own language understood by all. ### *Of the East Indian Christians.*

Ancient histories, according to the testimony of Saint Gregory Nazianzen in his *Oration against the Arians* <note>original: "Oraison contre les Arrians"</note> and Saint Gregory the Great in his 17th *Homily on the Gospel*, record that although the Indians had Saint Thomas as their Apostle—and though he is currently the patron of the Christians in the Orient—apostolic history nevertheless confirms (according to the words of Abdias of Babylon in book 8 of the *Apostolic History*) that Saint Bartholomew also carried the Gospel to the Indies. It is held that he arrived there before Saint Thomas and suffered martyrdom there. However, since the aforementioned Abdias describes three distinct regions of India <note>Medieval geographers often divided the vast East into "Three Indias": India Major, India Minor, and Middle India (sometimes including parts of Ethiopia or Arabia)</note> in the passage cited above, it is not impossible that two Apostles were employed there, as the commission was great and important, requiring two great leaders to accomplish it well. Furthermore, after the Apostles, there were also other figures who carried the word of God to the Indians, who had strayed from the true doctrine learned from the Apostles. Thus, in the time of the Emperor Commodus, there was a holy person named Pantenus <note>Pantenus was a Stoic philosopher who became the head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria</note> who, having withdrawn from the Stoic sect to Christianity and being the principal regent of the school of Alexandria in Egypt, was ordained to announce the word of God to the Eastern regions. This is testified by Saint Jerome in his book *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "des hommes illustres"</note> and Eusebius in book 5, chapter 10 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. They assert that in these Indies, this holy person found the Gospel of Saint Matthew (which had been received there before he arrived) in the hands of some who made profession of Christianity in those countries. It appears that this Gospel was announced to those Indians by the aforementioned Saint Bartholomew, who left it written in Hebrew letters and language, and it was preserved until the time mentioned above when Pantenus was in India. This truth was once again preached there by Frumentius <note>Saint Frumentius, the first Bishop of Axum, credited with bringing Christianity to the Aksumite Kingdom in Ethiopia</note> during the time of Constantine the Great, according to the testimony of Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian historian</note> in book 1, chapter 15 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. He freely admits that Saint Thomas converted the Parthians, Saint Matthew converted Ethiopia, and Saint Bartholomew converted the "First India," but that none of our Lord's disciples had ever entered "Inner India"—where there are many different barbarian nations, each with different languages—until the time of Constantine the Great. This is described in detail by Sozomen <note>Salaminus Hermias Sozomenus, another 5th-century historian</note> in book 2, chapter 25 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and by Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, known for his Latin translations of Greek ecclesiastical works</note> in book 1, chapter 9 of his history, both of whom mention this Frumentius and his companion Aedesius. Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville</note>, speaking of this Saint Thomas, says that he died from a spear thrust, and his body, according to what is written in his *Life*, was carried to the province of Syria, to the city of Edessa <note>original: "Ædife"</note>. This is confirmed by Antonio de Torquemada on the second day of his *Hexameron*. Now, while Saint Matthew was the one who preached in Ethiopia and Saint Thomas in India, the rule of Prester John <note>original: "Preftegiani"; the legendary Christian patriarch and king of the East</note> later succeeded this Christian community. His principality was great and powerful, but a long time later it was lost, and the Great Khan, Emperor of the Tartars, became its master in the year of salvation 1162, having entirely chased away and expelled the aforementioned Prester John, whom he drove back completely into Ethiopia.

In order not to leave anything noteworthy in this place concerning the Apostle Saint Thomas—the patron of the Eastern Indian Christians mentioned above—we shall say that Marco Polo the Venetian <note>original: "M. Paule Venitien"</note>, in book 3, chapter 24 of his travels in Tartary, writes that this Apostle was slain in the Kingdom of Var, located in the East Indies, and that his body was preserved in his time in a certain church of that kingdom. In the following chapter 27, he seems to contradict himself, saying that in the province of Maabar (or Malabar), located in Greater India, lay the body of this Blessed Apostle who endured martyrdom for the name of Jesus Christ in that very province. He notes that many Christians lived there and that the Indians held this Apostle to be a great Prophet, calling him *Avariiam* <note>original: "Auariiam"</note>, which means "holy man" in the Indian language. Joseph the Indian <note>a 15th-century Indian Christian priest who traveled to Europe</note>, in book 2, chapter 142 of his voyages, confirms these last words of Marco Polo, saying further that the temple where the body of this Blessed Apostle lies is similar to that of Saint John and Saint Paul in the city of Venice. John Mandeville, in his travels, speaks of this quite extensively. Duarte Barbosa <note>original: "Odouard Barboffe"</note>, a Portuguese writer, in his work on India, writes these words regarding this fact: "Moving a little away from the city of Quilon <note>original: "Coulan"; modern-day Kollam in Kerala, India</note> in the East Indies, one sees a point of land extending into the sea, upon which sits a beautiful and large church in honor of Saint Thomas. It was built because of a miracle he performed there before dying, which the Christians of the country told me they had described in their books, which they keep and honor with great reverence. And the miracle is this: That the Holy Apostle, finding himself in the city of Quilon very poorly dressed among the crowd of citizens who were heathens and idolaters, sought to win over the people and draw them to the faith of Jesus Christ, having with him some natives of the country whom he had converted and baptized..."

One morning, then, as he was preaching, a large piece of wood was seen appearing at sea, which came to rest against the shore. The King wanted to have it and commanded that by the strength of men and elephants it be brought to land, but it was impossible to move it. The King, annoyed by this, came himself in person, thinking that his presence would further encourage the people, but they gained nothing by it. Seeing this, the holy Apostle, and noting that the King was distressed at being unable to have this wood, said to him: "Sire, will you grant me this favor, if I bring this wood onto the land, that you give me as much land as I shall need to build a temple in honor of my Lord the true God, who made heaven and earth, by whose command I have set out?" The King, looking at this poor man, said to him: "And how could you provide for this, since all my forces could not suffice?" "With the help of the great God whom I announce, I am confident I can pull it to shore, for He is stronger than you and all other men." The King had the land he requested measured and delivered to him, and Saint Thomas, approaching the floating wood, tied it with a cord and belt <note>This refers to the traditional legend where Saint Thomas moves a massive log—intended for a royal palace—using only his priest’s girdle, proving his divine mission.</note>, and pulled it easily toward the place designated for the building of the Church. The King was greatly astonished by this, but nevertheless did not wish to become a Christian. The Apostle used this wood for the construction of the Church, and it sufficed for everything that was necessary there, not without the wonder of everyone. Once the Church was completed, the King gave him a certain income from the pepper produced in the country of Coulan <note>Modern-day Kollam (Quilon) in Kerala, a major center of the ancient spice trade.</note>, which the Christians of Saint Thomas enjoy to this day in memory of such a miracle.

In the end, this King persecuted the Apostle, who, following the command of God, retired elsewhere and went to the Region of Choromandel <note>The Coromandel Coast, the southeastern coast of the Indian subcontinent.</note>, and to the city of Malabar, or Maliapur <note>Mylapore, now a neighborhood in Chennai, traditionally held as the site of Saint Thomas’s death.</note>, where he was killed and martyred, and where his tomb is shown to this day. Thus, they returned loaded with great riches, and sending others in their place, they went to sow seeds to reap a harvest for their own profit rather than for the salvation of the Indians. This is what the aforementioned Armenians still do today, according to the testimony of Manuel Acosta <note>Manuel da Costa (1541–1604), a Jesuit who wrote about the missions in the East.</note>, a Jesuit, in his *Commentaries on the Indies*. Therefore, according to the aforementioned Barbosa <note>Duarte Barbosa (c. 1480–1521), a Portuguese explorer whose writings provided early European accounts of India.</note>, it was in the city of Malabar or Maliapur that this Saint Thomas was martyred. After those of Coulan had (as we have said) persecuted him, he retired to the said Malabar or Maliapur, where, beginning to preach, he made a singular profit, drawing many to the knowledge of the Gospel. ...[he] is no longer in the Indies, inasmuch as his disciples, stealing him away, carried him to the city of Edessa in Mesopotamia; though it is well said, he says, that the tomb remains there, and that from its earth, King Mazdai <note>original: "Mesdee"; a king in Indian tradition associated with the martyrdom of St. Thomas</note>—who had put the Apostle to death—took a small amount and placed it around the neck of his son, who was possessed by a devil, and he immediately received healing.

Osorius <note>Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), a Portuguese historian known as the "Portuguese Cicero"</note> in book 4 of the *History of Portugal*, and several other modern travelers and navigators, have left in writing that the sepulcher of this holy personage was searched for near the city of Coromandel, by the command of King Manuel of Portugal given to Duarte de Meneses <note>original: "Eduard de Meneses"</note>, his Viceroy in the Indies. In executing this, the aforementioned Duarte commanded Emanuel Frias, Governor of the said city, to carry out this search. Complying with this, he traveled with Priests and Architects toward Mylapore <note>original: "Maliapur"</note>, to a place filled with the ruins of many beautiful and ancient buildings. Among these was found a rather ruined temple, in which, within a very old and ancient stone tomb, were seen the bones of this holy personage, and the iron tip of a lance with a piece of a walking staff, and an earthen vessel. These bones were placed in a silver shrine within the aforementioned temple, which was then repaired by the Portuguese, and later transported with great pomp and magnificence to the city of Goa, as Father Pierre du Jarric of Toulouse <note>A Jesuit historian (1566–1617) who wrote about missions in the East Indies</note> deduces at length in book 2.

He states that if one opposes this history with the authority of the ecclesiastical histories of Rufinus (book 2, ch. 5), Socrates (book 4, ch. 14), and Sozomen <note>Three major historians of the early Christian Church</note> (book six, chapter eighteen), as well as the Martyrologies—specifically the Roman one, which places on the 3rd of July the translation of the body of this holy personage from the city of Calamine in India to Edessa in Mesopotamia, and from there to the city of Ortona <note>original: "Orthone"</note>, which is in the Apulia <note>original: "Appouille"</note> region of Italy—one must first say what Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>original: "D. Halicarnasse"; an ancient Greek historian</note> replied to those who marveled at seeing several sepulchers for the same souls <note>original: "Ames"; likely a reference to the many "tombs of Aeneas" discussed by Dionysius</note>. Being certain that his body was in only one of them, he said that this is a common and vulgar doubt, especially regarding those who were illustrious personages and who traveled through many countries. This is because empty monuments <note>The author is referring to cenotaphs—monuments erected to honor someone whose remains are elsewhere</note> were erected in several places, either in recognition of some good deed received from them in those lands, or because some relics of their lineage remained, or because they stayed there for a long time and showed themselves to be humane and kind toward their hosts.

The same can be answered if one did not know that these monuments or sepulchers were not entirely empty of the relics of this Holy Personage; rather, since the translation of these relics is celebrated, it is necessary to confess that some were there. Thus, it is better to say, along with the learned Baronius <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a giant of Catholic ecclesiastical history</note> in his *Roman Martyrology* for July 3rd, that the transport of a portion of the relics—not only of the said Apostle, but also of several other Saints—has given occasion for some to think that their bodies were in several places. This is not because, in fact, all the relics of the same Saint are in different places, but because one part is in one, and another in another. Very often, a part is taken for the whole by a very frequent figure of speech called <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a part represents the whole, or vice versa; here, a single bone might be called "the body of the Saint"</note>.

<summary>This page addresses the conflicting historical accounts regarding the location of Saint Thomas the Apostle's remains, explaining that while his body was reportedly found by the Portuguese in India, various traditions and "empty monuments" (cenotaphs) led to claims of his burial in Mesopotamia and Italy.</summary>

Now, that the relics of Saint Thomas have been dispersed in several places is testified by Saint Chrysostom <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> in a Homily that he gave in praise of the said Apostle. This was brought to light by Father Fronton du Duc, a Jesuit and great researcher of Church antiquities—especially the works of Saint Chrysostom which had gone astray—along with sixteen other Panegyrics written in praise of various Saints. In that of Saint Thomas, which is the 14th, Saint Chrysostom speaks these words: "The relics of the righteous man (speaking of this Saint) have surpassed the earth; he has shown himself more ample, and has extended further than any other created thing; grace has spread him throughout the whole world. There is no corner that does not have some small portion of Saint Thomas. He has filled the whole world, and yet remains whole in every place." Many other things worthy of note in this history are treated in *Osorius* <note>Jerónimo Osório, a 16th-century Portuguese historian.</note>, book 3 of his histories; *João de Barros* in his 3rd decade of *Asia*; *Pietro Maffei* in the 12th book of his history of the *Indies*; the author of the *History of China*, part 2, book three; *André Thevet*, book eleven, chapter eighteen of his *Universal Cosmography*; and in *Father Gaspar Zelandois* in his *Indian Epistle of the year 1553*.

To be brief, the Indian and Oriental Christians are as follows: Their temples are built like ours, except that there is no image or figure in them, save only for the cross, which is placed everywhere very large and high. All the Indian Christians hold this in honor and reverence. Those who wish to be appointed to the dignity of Bishop must go as far as their <term>Catholicos</term> <note>The title of the patriarch or head of the Church of the East.</note> who is in Armenia <note>The author likely refers to the Patriarch in Mesopotamia, though "Armenia" was often used broadly in this period for the region.</note>. This leader attributes to himself the power to consecrate Bishops, against the authority of the Holy Apostolic See, calling himself—falsely—the substitute of Saint Peter, and holding the place of the Patriarch of Antioch, wearing a crown in the shape of a cross. These Indian Christians do not baptize their children until forty days after their birth, unless they see in them an extreme necessity due to the threat of death. They confess as we do and receive the holy sacrament, which they consecrate if possible with unleavened bread, just as the Catholics do here. Having no wine because their country does not produce it, they use <term>currants</term> <note>original: "raisins de Corinthe"</note>, which they soak in water to extract a substance that they use in place of wine. They do not use holy unction for the sick, but instead pray over the patient and give them a blessing. They use holy water as we do and pray for the deceased. They have the four Evangelists with their Gospels, observe Lent and Advent by fasting and praying during them, and perform and keep many other fine and great Christian ceremonies concerning the service of God and His Church. They make use of both the Old and New Testaments, according to the interpretation of their doctors, both ancient and modern, as described more particularly by *Marco Polo the Venetian* in book three, chapters twenty-eight and twenty-nine of his travels; *Joseph the Indian* in book two, chapters 132, 133, and 134 of his navigations; *Alvise Cadamosto* in book two of his navigations, chapters fifty-six, 57, and fifty-eight; and *Ludovico di Varthema*, book 6, chapter...

One of their Bishops, from the "Island of Pepper" <note>likely referring to the Malabar Coast of India, famous for pepper production</note> located in the East Indies, came on their behalf to Rome to Pope Gregory XIII to offer obedience to the Holy See on November 24, 1584, and to learn from His Holiness if he would wish and intend for them to continue receiving the Bishops sent by their aforementioned Patriarch, as is confirmed by the *History of China*, parts 2 and 3. On this subject, Gilbert Génébrard <note>A French Benedictine exegete and orientalist.</note> writes in book 4 of his *Cosmography* for the year 1584: 

The Archbishop of Angamaly <note>original: "Angulianensis." Angamaly was the seat of the Saint Thomas Christians in Kerala, India.</note> in that part of India where the Christians of Saint Thomas are, requested from the Supreme Pontiff through the Jesuits the characters of the Chaldean or Syriac language, so that they might not only print their own books (for they celebrate the Mass and canonical prayers in that language or even in Hebrew <note>original: "vel etiam Hebraica." Early modern scholars often grouped Syriac/Aramaic and Hebrew together.</note>) but also translate our own works into that language. This is also noted by Emmanuel Teixeira in his *Epistles*.

Modern travelers assure us that the East Indians recognize that the first Christians among them were the inhabitants of the Island of Socotra, where the aforementioned Saint Thomas first preached and announced the Christian religion. They have had, and still have, temples and altars like ours from ancient times, which are decorated with nothing but crosses and have no images. On fasting days, which they observe very strictly, they abstain from eating anything; they marry only one wife; they observe the same feasts, and on the same days, as we Europeans do—even those of the saints—and they pay the full tithes of grains and fruits to their priests. However, they are still so ignorant, despite professing Christianity, that they do not understand a single word of the Christian religion, according to Osório in book 5 of his *History of Portugal* and Father Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian.</note> in book 3 of his *History of the Indies*. In short, anyone wishing to report everything recorded about these East Indian Christians here would never be finished. Whoever wishes to see more should read André Thevet, book 11, chapter 18 of his *Cosmography*; then Escalante, chapter 16 of his *Narratives*; I. ### CHAPTER 53.

Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264), author of the massive encyclopedia *Speculum Maius*.</note> in books 29 and 30 and Nauclerus <note>Johannes Nauclerus (1425–1510), a German historian.</note> in Volume 2, Generation 42, write that Pope Innocent IV, in the year of Salvation 1245, sent as an ambassador one Ascelin, a monk of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, along with three others, to the Tatars <note>A historical term used here to describe the Mongol Empire.</note> and their King Baitho <note>likely referring to the Mongol commander Baiju or Batu Khan</note>, to induce them to embrace Christianity; however, they achieved nothing, and this pilgrimage lasted three years and seven months. It is certainly true that they reported having seen many Christians in Tartary, commanded by a Prince named Cuine <note>Güyük Khan, the third Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.</note>, who supported priests and clerics who celebrated and administered sacred and divine things, singing and performing psalms in the manner of the Greeks at certain hours prescribed for this purpose.

Around the year of Salvation 1245, the third Cham <note>Khan</note> or Emperor of the aforementioned Tatars, at the prayer and supplication of the King of the Armenians, was converted to the faith of Jesus Christ and was baptized, according to the report of Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a medieval chronicler and member of the Armenian royalty.</note> in his histories of the Tatars. This Khan afterwards undertook the defense of the Christians against the Saracens, having sent forces commanded by Hielon <note>Hulagu Khan, founder of the Ilkhanate.</note>, his brother, who subjugated Persia and a great part of Syria and Mesopotamia. In the year of Salvation 1258, this same man defeated and captured Muftacene <note>Al-Musta'sim Billah, the last Abbasid Caliph of Baghdad.</note>, the Caliph of Babylon <note>Baghdad was often called Babylon in medieval European texts.</note>, who had greatly afflicted and tormented the Christians, proposing various punishments for them under these insulting words from the Gospel: "Say to this mountain and it shall be moved" <note>original: "Dicite monti huic & transfertur". A reference to Matthew 17:20; the legend says the Caliph challenged the Christians to prove their faith by moving a mountain.</note>. Having shut him in a tower with all his treasures, he caused him to die of hunger among them. From that Caliph until the Sophy <note>The Safavid dynasty of Persia.</note>, the people of Persia had no sovereign Doctor of their law. For this reason, in the year of Salvation 1500, these people easily admitted the Sophy as the sovereign Doctor of their said law, tracing his origin and doctrine to Haly <note>Ali ibn Abi Talib</note>, the son-in-law of Mahomet <note>Muhammad</note>; this is confirmed by James Nauarchus in his *Asiatic Epistles*. At that time, while the Christians were in contention with the Egyptians over the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the aforementioned Hielon and Abfaga <note>Abaqa Khan</note>—in the same manner that Tamerlane <note>Timur the Lame</note> did a hundred years later—descended from Tartary into Syria, declaring themselves neither friends nor enemies. Following Pagan superstition, they made profession of neither Christianity nor Islam. Although they were summoned with gifts and presents from Baldwin <note>Baldwin II of Constantinople or perhaps a regional Latin ruler.</note> to embrace Christianity, they nevertheless preferred to follow Islam, according to Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian.</note> in book 2 of *Illustrious Men*, in the chapter on Tamerlane. Saint Louis, King of France, arriving at the Island of Cyprus with his army to go on the conquest of the Holy Land in the year 1249, received Tatar Ambassadors sent to him by a Prince Erchaltans <note>Eljigidei, a Mongol commander.</note>, with letters by which he learned that three years previously the Tatars had made profession of the faith of Jesus Christ and had been baptized, as Gaguin <note>Robert Gaguin (1433–1501).</note> writes in book 7. A copy of the letters mentioned above is inserted in Vincent, book 13, chapter 91.
