...a singular art all the deeds and miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ, and others concerning the Christian Religion, as confirmed by the aforementioned Gaguin <note>Robert Gaguin (c. 1425–1501), a French Renaissance humanist and diplomat.</note> book 7, and Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais.</note> book 3, chapters 92 and 94.

Several Tatars came to the Council of Lyon to see Pope Innocent IV; having returned to their country, they made profession of Christianity and were baptized, as held by Biondo <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), an Italian Renaissance humanist historian.</note> and Martin <note>Martin of Troppau (d. 1278), author of the *Chronicon Pontificum et Imperatorum*.</note> in his Chronicle; though it is true that some relate this to the time of Pope Gregory X, according to book 5, chapter 1 of the *Sacred History Continued*.

We read in the travels of Mr. Marco Polo, living in the year of Salvation 1275, that Niccolo, Marco, and Maffeo, Venetians, were sent with Khutughtu <note>originally: "Chotogalus"</note>, a great Tatar Lord, on behalf of Khubilai <note>originally: "Cabyla"</note>, 6th Khan or Emperor of the Tatars, to Pope Clement, to beseech him to send priests or doctors to teach him and his people the faith of Jesus Christ.

In the year 1290, Möngke Khan <note>originally: "Mangu Cam"</note>, 5th Emperor of the Tatars, was miraculously converted to Christianity by his wife, the daughter of Hethum <note>originally: "Haiton"</note>, King of Armenia, and was baptized with his brother Hulagu <note>originally: "Allan" or "Hielon"</note> and all his family. Shortly afterward, Hulagu descended with a great army into Palestine, causing a crucifix to be carried on his banners and standards like the Melkite Catholics <note>originally: "Cathes Melechinees"</note> in order to recover Jerusalem (Guillaume de Nangis). A short time later, these same Tatars returned to their former impiety; and since that time they have been Mahometans, or rather *Sagomorbates* <note>A corruption of "Shakyamuni," referring to Buddhism, which medieval writers sometimes confused with a sect of Islam or a distinct paganism.</note> because of *Sagomor-bar* their Prophet whom they worship, as the Saracens and Turks do Mahomet; this *Sagomor-bar* taught them many things concerning God, governance, and good morals, and among these an edict that the Great Khans of the Tatars, successors of Genghis Khan <note>originally: "Cingis Cham"</note>, swear at the beginning of their reign: not to afflict the Christians, nor to constrain them to pay a larger or more excessive tribute than their other subjects. The aforementioned Hulagu having defeated the Saracens in this same year of Salvation 1290, made himself the peaceful ruler of the kingdom of Syria and Jerusalem: but 3 years later the Sultan of Babylon reconquered it from him, as is contained in the continuation of Nangis and Sabellico <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), an Italian historian.</note> Ennead 9, book 7.

In the year 1302, Ghazan <note>originally: "Cabagade"</note>, the Tatar King of Persia, having renounced the Christian faith, embraced Mahometism and made his subjects Alcoranists <note>Followers of the Quran.</note>; and from that time the Christian Religion was banished from among the Tatars. The Turks, having defeated the aforementioned Tatars under the leadership and power of Osman <note>originally: "Ottomā"</note> their first great lord, and the Parthians having defeated the successors of this same Ghazan, occupied Persia in the year 1350 under the leadership of Gepsar their Sultan. The rest of these Tatars divided into Hordes across Europe and Asia, each of which established a Prince for itself. For some settled in the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimean Peninsula.</note>, now called Gazaria, and those are called Perekopians <note>originally: "Precopites"</note>, whose Prince gave his daughter in marriage to Selim, father of the late Suleiman; others are called Nogais <note>originally: "Mogaues"</note>, who do not obey a single Prince but govern themselves in the form of a Republic, and from those proceeded the Horde of the Jagatais <note>originally: "Hagutaues"</note> or Zavolhenses, whose metropolitan city is Samarkand <note>originally: "Sinarcand"</note>, of which the great Tamerlane was a native.

Brother Antoine Geuffroy, knight of St. John of Jerusalem, in his treatise on the origin of the Turks, speaks otherwise of all the above, detailing at length the lives and conquests of the Great Khans of Tartary.

Marco Polo the Venetian, in Book 1, chapters 47, 49, 62, and 63 of his travels in Tartary <note>A historical name used by Europeans for the vast region of North and Central Asia, from the Caspian Sea to the Pacific Ocean, dominated by the Mongol Empire.</note>, asserts that in his time, Christians were found in many and various provinces and cities under the rule of the Great Khan of Tartary in Asia. These Christians were Nestorians <note>Members of the Church of the East, a branch of Christianity that spread widely across Asia along the Silk Road.</note>; he speaks of them further in the subsequent Book 2, chapter 61, and in the following Book 3, chapter 50, where he mentions certain other Tatar Christians whom he calls Nestorian Ruchenes <note>likely referring to the Rus' or Russians living under the Golden Horde.</note>.

Ludovico di Varthema <note>original: "Louys Vuactoman"</note>, a Roman Patrician, writes in Book 6, chapter 14 of his navigations that there are several Christians in Tartary who are subjects of the Great Khan of the Tatars. They are baptized (as we other Christians are), believe in the twelve Apostles and the four Evangelists, write in the manner of the Armenians, celebrate the Nativity, death, and passion of Jesus Christ, observe Lent and certain feasts of the Saints. This author says he spoke and conferred with these Christians who had arrived in the East Indies; they assured him that in their Tartary, there were several Christian kings near the borders of the Turkish Empire, called by some the Rumes <note>A term derived from "Rome," used in the East to refer to Christians or the Byzantine (Roman) Empire.</note>.

The histories of the Tatars according to Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a monk and historian from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia who recorded the history of the Mongols.</note>, in Book 1 of his history of the Tatars, state that Möngke Khan <note>original: "Mangu Cham," the fourth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.</note>, the Great Emperor of the Tatars, was the one who so greatly respected the Christian name. Solicited by Hayton, King of Armenia, in the year 1253, he willed that total liberty be granted to Christians throughout all his lands, and that none be so bold as to hinder them in the exercise of their religion. He received Baptism, though his successors cared little for it. He made a law for Christians stating that in all the lands the Tatars had conquered, and those they would conquer hereafter, they would swear to leave Christian Churches intact, and that both clergy and laypeople should live in total liberty, exempt from servitude, and without paying any tribute whatsoever, except according to the taxes imposed by the Kings upon the native inhabitants of Tartary. This law has benefited Christians so greatly that it is a marvel.

The Lord of Joinville <note>Jean de Joinville, the biographer and companion of King Louis IX of France.</note>, in chapter 19 of the life of Saint Louis, recounts this history differently, as reported by Nicolas Vignier in part 3 of his *Historical Library*, citing the book of John of Plano Carpini <note>original: "Iean Capin"</note> of the Order of the Cordeliers <note>The Franciscans.</note>, who was sent by Pope Innocent to this Khan; the book is titled *On the Origin, Manners, Ceremonies, Religion, and Manner of Warfare of the Tatars*.

Formerly, the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians.</note> were those who once held the Indies under the Empire of their Prester John <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles from the 12th to the 17th centuries.</note>, whom Genghis Khan <note>original: "Cingis Cham"</note> and his successors entirely drove out from there. By this means, the religion of the Indians—which was the superstition of the Gentiles, worshipping a plurality of gods—was lost, replaced by that of the Tatar who worshipped a single God and honored a certain Prophet of his nation named Sagomonbar <note>Likely a corruption of Shakyamuni (the Buddha), whom some early Western writers confused for a local Tatar prophet.</note>. However, the Christian race was not removed, except for those who were native Ethiopians. This is the reason why the Nestorians, Georgians, and Armenians still worship Jesus Christ there and celebrate the mysteries of our Religion. These Christians know nothing of the Councils celebrated in the Greek and Latin Churches; nevertheless, they hold to most of the ceremonies of the early Church, which was planted in those quarters by some Apostles or their disciples. The Tatar Kings and Princes still support more than ten million Christians today in those countries, who live according to the simplicity of the doctrine

Apostolic <note>Likely referring to the papal legates or missionaries sent from Rome.</note> envoys, who, when one confers with them, say and maintain that since the Easterners began to be divided on the matter of religion, and one believed one thing and another something else, there appeared soon after a Muhammad among the Arabs, a Sagomonbar <note>A corruption of Shakyamuni Burkan, referring to the Buddha.</note> among the Tartars, a Xaqua <note>Shaka, another name for the Buddha.</note> among the more Eastern Indians, a Xaholan among the Bengalis, an Ali <note>Haly</note> among the Persians, a Sharif <note>Cheriph</note> among the Africans, an Azelcon among the Asians, Comassan and Alxamath among the Cephaliens, and Kalmorath among the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note>. These men, under the pretext of preaching the purity of doctrine and speaking of a single God, won over the whole Levant and gained the advantage over the divided Christians. It is held that one of the ancestors of the Great Khan of these Tartars, being asked why he did not become a Christian, since he was so fully informed of the excellence of our religion, replied: "How do you want me to do so, being surrounded as I am by subjects of diverse religions? If I became a Christian, and my ministers did not perform miracles and things as marvelous as those done by the priests and enchanters who serve our idols, I would be spinning the rope that would cause the end of my life." In short, this Tartar acts somewhat like a Christian when with Christians, and follows the Law of Moses or Judaizes with the Jews, and becomes an idolater with his own people; for he celebrates Christmas and Easter with the Christians, as well as other feasts common to them, and carries himself likewise with all the Muhammadans.

->See A. Theuet book 12, ch. 19 of his Universal Cosmography.<-

Hayton the Armenian, in Book 1, Chapter 2, of the Tartars, describing the kingdom of Tarsis <note>Likely referring to the Uighur Kingdom of Qocho.</note> toward Tartary, says that in this kingdom there are people called Iogours <note>Uighurs</note> who since ancient times have worshipped idols, except for ten generations or lineages of those three Kings who came, led by the celestial star, to worship our Lord Jesus Christ in the city of Bethlehem; and that in his time, there were still among the Tartars several great and noble personages of this race who held firmly to the faith of Jesus Christ. This same author in the subsequent Chapter 4 maintains that in his time, part of the inhabitants of the kingdom of Chorasmia <note>Khwarazm, in modern Uzbekistan/Turkmenistan.</note> toward the country of Turkestan were Christians living in the manner, fashion, and religion of the Greeks, and that they were called *Soldini*.

Sigismund Herberstein <note>original: "Sigismond Liber," referring to the author of Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii.</note>, in his history of the affairs of Muscovy, describing at length the Tartars and their countries and regions, says that moving from the East toward the South near the Meotide Marshes <note>The Sea of Azov.</note> and the Pontus <note>The Black Sea.</note>, toward the river Cupa which empties into the aforementioned marshes, are the Aphgases <note>Abkhazians</note>. Beyond them are found great mountains reaching to the river Merule, which discharges into the said Pontus; these mountains are inhabited by the Circassians <note>original: "Circasses ou Cikz"</note>, who obey neither the Turk nor the Tartars because their mountains are inaccessible. Rather, they are Christians living according to their own laws and according to the Greek religion, using the Slavonic language in their common speech and in the celebration of their divine service, as the *Ruthenians* <note>Ancestors of modern Ukrainians, Belarusians, and Russians.</note> assert.

Today, in the kingdom of Mangi <note>Southern China.</note>, currently subject to the Great Khan of Tartary, there is a city named Cinghianfu <note>Zhenjiang.</note>, inhabited by people who worship idols, in which there are two Christian churches, though they belong to the *Nestorians*. These were founded in the year 1274 by a man named Marfachis <note>Mar Sarghis, a Nestorian Christian official mentioned in the travels of Marco Polo.</note>, whom the Great Khan of Tartary had placed there as governor.

### Of the Jacobite Christians.

John Mandeville, an English Knight living in the year of salvation 1322, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>original: "langue Romaneſque"; referring here to the vernacular French in which his famous (and often fantastical) travels were circulated</note>, in the chapter on the law of the Jacobins—that is to say, the Jacobites cited above—speaks ampy of these Jacobites and of their religion. Hayton the Armenian, in book 1, chapter 54 of his history of the Tartars, makes mention of certain Christians named Rapti <note>Possibly a corruption of "Copts"</note>, who lived in his time according to the manner, fashion, and religion of the Jacobites, and who boasted of being the oldest inhabitants of the land of Egypt. In this regard, one should see Leo Africanus <note>I. Leon</note>, book 8 of his *History of Africa*, speaking of Asyut <note>Aſioth</note>. The same Leo Africanus, in the aforementioned book 8, chapter on Alexandria in his same *History of Africa*, says these words regarding the aforementioned Jacobites: "There are in Alexandria, among its inhabitants, Christians called Jacobites, who have their church where the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist used to be, which the Venetians carried off by stealth <note>original: "d’em-blee"</note>, transporting it to their city of Venice. All these Jacobites make a living by trade or practice the arts, paying a certain tribute to the Lord of Great Cairo; in Elchian <note>Likely Al-Khanka, a city north of Cairo</note>, a city situated on the Nile, there are also some of these Jacobites." The author of the *Summary of Kingdoms, Cities, and Oriental Peoples* writes that near Susa <note>Suz</note> dwell certain Christian Arabs, some of whom are circumcised after the manner and fashion of the Jews, and others not; the circumcised being called Jacobites, and the others Melkites <note>original: "Malaquiti"; the Melkites were Middle Eastern Christians who remained in communion with the Byzantine Emperor</note>, who observe two Lents, one at Christmas and the other at Easter as we do. Most of them are hermits and persons of holy life; the others trade at El-Tor <note>Tor, a port on the Sinai Peninsula</note>, Jeddah <note>Zidem</note>, and Mecca, and are held and reputed by all to be men of good character and conscience. Jacques de Vitry, in his *History of Jerusalem*, chapter 37, writes that in the year of salvation 1171, there were a great number of these Jacobites, who were not only scattered throughout Syria, but also through India and Ethiopia, who still retained circumcision along with baptism, as do the Saracens. They confessed their sins to God alone and imprinted a mark of fire <note>a ritual brand or tattoo</note> on the foreheads of their children. André Thevet <note>A. Theuet</note>, in book 11, chapter 18 of his *Universal Cosmography*, says these words about these Jacobites:

"The Christians who live here and there, scattered through the Indies, and who are at the sepulcher of Saint Thomas, are for the most part Jacobites—a people who differ in belief and ceremonies from all other Levantine Christians, and who have been thus deceived by the most malicious heretic who ever was on earth; and it must be noted here, that before he had embraced Christianity, he had been..."

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF</header>

[He was] Jewish, and the son of a father named Azzas and a mother called Arama from the Island of Carpathos <note>Located in the Aegean Sea</note>, situated between Rhodes and Thasos. It happened that he was taken as a slave at the age of 17 and sold to a Greek priest, who had him baptized and gave him the name James <note>original: "Iaques"; likely referring to Jacob Baradaeus, though the details here are semi-legendary</note>, instructing him so well in languages that he earned the rank of sovereign Legate of the Patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt. After the death of the Patriarch, he achieved the dignity of the Patriarchate himself. He lived for eight years in a fairly Catholic manner, but once they had expired, he became a heretic and infected the people of the Orient with his devilish opinion more than Arius <note>The 4th-century priest whose teachings on the nature of Christ were declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea</note> ever did. It was he who first introduced and admitted this sect of "Judaizers," approving of circumcision, which many of them still observe today.

Others, instead of Baptism, have certain characters branded with a hot iron onto the arms of their small children, or others behind the neck or at the temples. They hold that such incisions are equivalent to a baptism that delivers them from original sin, basing this on what is said in the Gospel of Saint John: *He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.* <note>Though the text attributes this to the Gospel of John, these words were spoken by John the Baptist in Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16.</note> And as these people are entirely unlearned <note>original: "idiot"; meaning uneducated in theology</note>, not understanding the mysteries of Holy Scripture, they were also perverted in their affections and excommunicated from the Greek Church by the authority of Patriarch Dioscorus, who was then under the obedience of the Latin Church.

Secondly, these people never confess their sins to a priest. Their bishops, priests, and other ministers are married. All Christians have always detested these people—thus named after the author of such a heresy—and have also held them as schismatics. However, they do not for that reason enter into conflict or controversy through arms or popular sedition, for trade is free and open to them just as it is to others who consider themselves more Catholic.

I do not wish to forget to remind you here that while traveling through the land of Asia Minor, three leagues from the city of Seleucia in a ruined place that the local shepherds call Mellothi, I was shown the tomb of the aforementioned Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heretical movement</note>. Having been banished from Egypt and relegated to the Island of Grabusa <note>original: "Crabusé"</note>—distant from the mainland of Pamphylia by about five leagues—he found a way, with the help of some pirates, to escape to Asia, where he again committed many evils. Having lived in this madness until the age of 74, he was killed in an ambush by an Armenian lord.

Those of this persuasion have a beautiful chapel in Jerusalem, within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where I have often seen them celebrate Mass and other services according to their tradition and custom. I have seen four others: one in Egypt, and the three others in the cities of Suez <note>original: "Zidem"</note>, Tor, and Bubutor, which border the Red Sea. They have a particular language <note>Syriac</note>, which is hardly understood by anyone but themselves, and they have thirty-two letters in their alphabet, which are quite strange.

And as it happened that these people had no support, they turned in the year 1552 toward the Roman Bishop, who was Julius III, sending the Legate of the Patriarch of Antioch, named Moses of Mardin <note>original: "Moses Mardenus"</note>—a learned man born in the land of Syria—to make a profession of their faith. He protested that they held what their churches formerly held in the time of Isaac Comnenus, Emperor of Constantinople, who lived in the year of the world 5020, and in the year of our Lord 1058; this monarch punished them so well that he ran...

### On the Nestorian Christians.

Marco Polo the Venetian, in book 1 of his travels in Tartary, writes that in his time, in several and various provinces and cities under the rule of the Great Khan of Tartary in Asia, there were Christians who were named Nestorians <note>A Christian sect named after Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, whose views on the nature of Christ were condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431 AD</note>. Niccolò de' Conti, the Venetian, in his travels to the Indies, and the author of the summary of the Kingdoms, cities, and peoples of the Orient, maintain that in their time there were many Nestorian Christians spread throughout all of Asia, just as the Jews are in Europe. Giovanni Empoli, a factor <note>A commercial agent or representative</note> for the King of Portugal in his navigations to the East Indies, recounts that these Nestorian Christians are otherwise named Nazarenes. Ludovico di Varthema, in book 3, chapter 2 of his navigations of India, says that these Nestorian Christians are surnamed by four other names, namely: of Saint John, of Saint James, of Saint Matthew, and of Saint Thomas.

André Thevet, in book 10, chapter 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*, maintains that on the Island of Gisire or Giferte <note>Likely Gezira, referring to Upper Mesopotamia/Al-Jazira</note>, located in the Euphrates River in Asia, there are many Armenian, Jacobite, and Nestorian Christians, and that there resides the Great Patriarch of the aforementioned Nestorians, whom some Levantine peoples call *Sid*, and others *Sulaca* <note>Likely referring to Yohannan Sulaqa, the first Patriarch of the Chaldean Catholic Church, who was consecrated in Rome in 1553</note>: whom they hold as head and sovereign Bishop, and who is in such reputation among them as the Pope is among Catholics. He maintains three Bishops in the principal cities of the Persian country, namely one in the noble city which was first founded by Darius son of Hystaspes, 521 years before our Lord, named Arbela <note>Modern-day Erbil</note>, and the others Salmas and Ador Beigani <note>Azerbaijan</note>, situated eight leagues away, where in former times was built, stretching toward the East, the great city of Nineveh mentioned in Holy Scripture, named at present by those of the country Ninimich, otherwise Nisroch. I know well that some have in the past broken their heads <note>A colorful idiom for "struggled greatly" or "worried themselves"</note> trying to know where this city of Nineveh had been—a Hebrew word which signifies nothing other than "beauty"—and have wished to say that it was on the edge of the Mediterranean Sea at a...

André Thevet, aforementioned, in the sixth book, twelfth chapter of his *Universal Cosmography*, writes that the Maronites are monks who were formerly heretics, otherwise called Monothelites <term>Monothelites: from the Greek for "one will," a 7th-century belief that Christ had two natures but only one divine-human will</term>, and they bear the name of a certain Maron who said that in Jesus Christ there was only one will, and consequently one operation: an error into which the Emperor Heraclius fell during the time that Muhammad’s soldiers were performing wonders in Syria, pillaging the entire territory of Damascus as far as Aleppo. This Maron was not the inventor of the sect, but rather it was a fellow native of Antioch named Macarius, who was condemned along with him by the Sixth Council of Constantinople, as some Greek Bishops of the country related to me, and have also written in their histories. Others say, which is more likely, that this Council was celebrated in Rome around the year of our Lord 647 under Pope Martin I <note>The author refers to the Lateran Council of 649, which condemned Monothelitism</note>, where two hundred Bishops condemned the error of several Patriarchs of Constantinople who had troubled the faith received in the Church, and above all, they condemned these Maronites and their accomplices. Since the Emperor was infected by this heresy, and the Pope resisted him—using censures appropriate for such an effect, and not for his own private profit—Constans <note>Constans II, reigned 641–668</note>, grandson of Heraclius, had him seized and put in prison, where he died in great misery in the year 652, the seventh year of his Pontificate; but a short time later, while he himself was making war on the Catholic Bishops, he was defeated by the Saracens, and fled like one who did not wish to enjoy the prayers of those who were good people, whom the false prophets who deceived him had ruined with their heresies. Finally, these Maronites, having been separated from the true faith of the Church for a space of nearly five hundred years, recognized their state, and detesting their error by the grace of God, they embraced union and returned to the same faith, opinion, and belief as us, submitting themselves to the legitimate Pastors of the Church of God. As proof of this, and of the obedience they bore to it, their Patriarch came to the General Council celebrated in Rome in the year 1515 <note>The author likely means the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 under Innocent III, or is confusing it with the Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517)</note> under Pope Innocent III, where he abjured the ancient errors on behalf of his people, and protested to live under the obedience of the Roman See. However, being currently scattered as they are, and living more in the mountains than elsewhere—as I have seen while conversing with them, except for those who go as pilgrims to Jerusalem—they know no one to recognize but their own Pastors and ministers. These men celebrate the divine office in Hebrew <note>original: "Hebrieu" — The author likely means Syriac, the liturgical language of the Maronites, which was often confused with Hebrew or called "Chaldean" by Westerners at the time</note>, although in their common speech they speak Arabic for the most part, and follow the customs of the Roman Church in very few ceremonies; they live for the most part at present on Mount Lebanon and the surrounding lands. The same Thevet speaks again of these Maronites in book 11, chapter 18, of his same *Universal Cosmography*. So does Gilbert Génébrard in book 4 of his *Chronography*, speaking of Acurius Joseph <note>Likely Joseph el-Ruzzi, a Maronite Patriarch</note> sent by his Patriarch and the Maronites from the monastery of Saint Mary of Kanubin on Mount Lebanon in the year 1515 to Rome to recognize the Pope as the sovereign head of the Church; and of Siud the Syrian <note>Referring to Shimun VIII Sulaqa</note>, also Patriarch of the aforementioned Nestorians, who in the year 1552 did the same.

> The Maronites, so named after Maron the Heresiarch <term>Heresiarch: the founder of a heretical sect</term>, are a warlike nation, very skilled in arms, archery, and the arquebus <note>an early type of long gun supported on a tripod or forked rest</note>. And though they are in the midst of Turks and Arabs, they fear neither, and valiantly defend themselves from their assaults. They were heretics for a very long time, and moreover inconstant and fickle in their belief: for at the time of the Lateran Council celebrated in Rome under Innocent III, their Patriarch swore obedience to the Holy See and assisted at this Council; but they lasted little in their holy opinion, rather they returned to their former vomit <note>a biblical idiom referring to a return to one's previous errors or sins</note>, so that they and their error were condemned at the Council of Constance. Since then, they returned for a second time to the bosom of the Roman Church, but they hardly stayed there; instead, they persevered long enough in their error until our own time when, abjuring their error for the third time into the hands of their Patriarch named Emeris, they call themselves Roman Catholics today. Throughout all time they used bells in their churches, and their Bishops wore miters, rings, and croziers like ours, contrary to the custom of the Eastern Church, as they still do now that they are reunited with our Church, using all our ceremonies, and so forth.

### On the Armenian Christians.

Pierre Belon, in book 3, chapter 13 of his *Observations of the Levant*, writes that at the very beginning of the Turkish conquest, the Armenians were the first to be assailed when those Turks came out of Scythia <note>a vast region of central Eurasia</note>: for the Armenians, who were then Christians, found themselves the weaker party and lost their Kingdom. But notwithstanding this, they have always remained constant in the Christian faith: as it appears that even today they hold the name throughout all of Turkey; for to name an "Armenian" in that country is understood to mean a "Christian." If an Armenian becomes a Turk <note>converts to Islam</note>, he loses his name. One finds them inhabiting towns and villages as far as beyond Armenia, and in Asamie, and in Adiabene <note>an ancient kingdom in northern Mesopotamia</note>, given that the King of Persia allows them to live in his country. They are also a peaceful and humane people, and are commonly poor farmers, good gardeners, and those who dress the vines well. The Priests of these Armenians are married like those of the Greeks, and celebrate the Mass with a chalice like the Latins, and are dressed in the same ornaments of copes and chasubles; they do not consecrate using large bread like the Greeks, but in a small host <note>unleavened wafer</note> like the Latins, and all those assisting respond to the Priests.

## Of the Colchian Christians.

The Colchians <note>an ancient kingdom on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, in what is now Georgia</note>, a people descended from the Egyptians, were formerly circumcised, just like the aforementioned Egyptians according to the report of Diodorus Siculus in book 2, chapter 1 of his *Antiquities*; as I have remarked here before. They presently inhabit the region of ancient Colchis in Asia, which is now divided and split into two provinces: the first bearing the name of Lazia or Laxia <note>home of the Laz people</note> which extends as far as Trebizond and is further inland, and the other named Mingrelia, which is almost entirely coastal. Procopius, in book 1 of the *Persian Wars*, holds that these Colchians were Christians long before his age. But M. Michou <note>Maciej Miechowita, a Polish scholar and author of "Tractatus de duabus Sarmatiis"</note> in book 1, chapter 7 of his *Sarmatia*, writes that the history of Moravia records that the Mingrelians were converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by Cyril and Methodius, sent there by the Emperor of the Greeks, Michael III of that name, in the year of our Lord 861. Consequently, to this very day, these people follow the faith and Religion of the Greeks <note>Eastern Orthodox Christianity</note>, having previously been called Gazares and currently, by the Greeks, Abgazares and Abgazeles <note>referring to the Abkhazian people</note>. And one must carefully consider these authorities, given that between the Empire of Justinian, in whose time the said Procopius lived, and this Emperor Michael cited by the aforementioned Michou, there is a span of about 321 years. This leads some to believe that the Persians, reconquering this country, returned it to Paganism, and it persisted in this impiety while the disciples of Muhammad poisoned the Persian Empire with their Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>, until the aforementioned holy Figures went there to sow the Christian faith. Since that time, as is probable, these Mingrelians have strayed from the union of the Apostolic Church of Rome. Ambroise Contaren <note>Ambrogio Contarini, a Venetian diplomat who traveled to Persia</note> in chapter 2 of his *Voyage to Persia*, holds that these Mingrelians do not occupy more than three days' travel of land; and even that is all mountainous and full of thickets, where the men are beast-like, wearing their heads shaved. They are Christians, but steeped in various heresies, celebrating divine service in the Greek manner. They are under the domination of the Turk, who is Lord of the Empire of Trebizond, to which they were previously subjects after the crown of Constantinople was fragmented and divided into two different empires. At present, they are often constrained and forced to sell their own children for lack of money to pay the taxes <term>daces: royal or feudal duties</term> and impositions they owe to the Grand Seigneur <note>the Ottoman Sultan</note>.

See A. Thevet, book 8, chapter 12 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and F. de Belleforest, volume 2, book 3, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

# THE SYRIAN CHRISTIANS

## CHAP. LIV.

We have previously, in the chapter on the Syrians and the Syriac language, treated these Syrian Christians or Syrians at length. The city of Toledo, among others, had the favor of obtaining seven Temples <note>churches</note> for the exercise of the Christian Religion: namely, Saint Just, Saint Luke, Saint Torquatus, Saint Mark, Saint Eulalia, Saint Sebastian, and Saint Mary. These **Mus'Arabes**, otherwise named **Moz Arabes** Christians, celebrated their divine offices according to the manner used in the time of the Gothic Kings, and following the institution of an **Isidore, Bishop of Seville**, or of **Leander**, as was the custom in all the said Spains to serve God at that time. And this continued until the service called **Gregorian** or **Roman** was introduced at the time mentioned hereafter. And this **Mus'Arabe** office is still maintained today as a mark of antiquity in the Chapel of the Company of the Body of God <note>original: "du corps de Dieu"; likely the Mozarabic Chapel of Corpus Christi</note> in the great Church of Toledo, and other places in that city. From this year of Salvation 714 until the year of salvation 950, these Mozarabic Christians lived in great tranquility and rest, not being forced or searched regarding their Religion in any way whatsoever, and justice was administered to them, in exchange for the tributes and pensions imposed upon them; but when **Haly Hatan** came to the kingship, he was such a zealot of his Mohammedan religion, and held such great hatred for that of the Christians, that he had an edict published by which it was commanded that all Christian inhabitants in the lands and cities subject to him leave the Christian Religion and, by being circumcised, take that of **Mohammed**, on pain of death. But notwithstanding this wretched edict, the **Mus'Arabes** or **MozArabes** Christians did not cease to celebrate this office among themselves, both in Toledo and in Castile and Leon, until the time of King **Don Alfonso VI**, in the year of salvation 1121 <note>historical dates for this transition vary; Alfonso VI captured Toledo in 1085</note>. This King, desiring in everything and everywhere to show himself an affectionate son of the holy see of Rome, wanted the rite to be changed, and in its place the office called **Gregorian** (after its author) was received—that is to say, from **Gregory VII**. For this reason, he sent for the Pope's Bull, which commanded that the said Roman office be celebrated from then on in all the Churches of the Spains, just as was done in France; and for this reason, it is called by some Spaniards the **Gallican office**. To ordain this, a legate had been sent to Spain a few years earlier by the said Pope **Gregory VII** (predecessor of **Urban II**): one **Richard, Abbot of Saint Victor of Marseille**, who took great pains for the introduction of the new Gregorian or Roman office and the abolition of the said **Mozarabic** office.

...or Musarabic: For which reason, and to put into effect what had been ordained in this matter, upon the return from Rome of Don Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo, a general council was created and assembled in Spain in the city of Toledo. There, the Clergy, Knights, and people of Toledo, Castile, León, Asturias, Galicia, and Portugal were present, or their deputies in great numbers. With Don Bernard presiding and the King being present, great debates, seditions, and disputes were brought forward, as the Spaniards did not wish to abandon their ancient ways to receive a new <term>office</term> <note>The "office" refers to the liturgy or the specific set of prayers and ceremonies used in the Mass.</note>. So much so that, as the arguments and reasons of neither side were sufficient, they came to the furious and beastly manner of trial by duel, which was quite common at that time. Two Knights were placed on the field of battle: one for the King and those who desired the change of the rite, and the other for the Knights and the people who refused it and wished to retain the Musarabic or Mozarabic rite. Jean Ruis took up arms for the latter and defeated the one who fought for the Roman rite, whose name is unknown. Nonetheless, such was the persistent urging of the King, the Queen, the Archbishop of Toledo, Don Bertrand <note>likely referring to Bernard of Sedirac</note>, and others of that party, that this matter was referred to another kind of judgment and test, namely, by fire. Therefore, having brought two books—one containing the rite and usage of Rome, the other ancient and Musarabic—they threw them both into a very hot fire. From this fire, the Roman book leaped out immediately, so it is said, and the other remained there without being in any way damaged or spoiled. Because of this, it was conjectured that both were agreeable to God; for this reason, it was ordered that they would retain the ancient manner of the rite in the six parishes of the city of Toledo, and that in the great Cathedral Church and others within it, the Gregorian or Roman rite would be introduced and put into use, as well as throughout the remainder of the Kingdom of Don Alfonso. This was settled and agreed upon more by force, and to please the King and obey the Pope (who confirmed and approved it), than out of good will. However, in several monasteries of Spain, the Musarabic rite remained for a long time afterward. Even in the same great Church of Toledo, since that time, a Mass is still sung in Musarabic every day in a chapel called the Body of the Lord <note>original: "Corpus Domini"</note>. The six parishes of this city, in which this rite was held, had been held by the Musarabic or Mozarabic Christians throughout the time that the Moors ruled there; these parishes are: Saint Luke, Saint Just, Saint Torquatus, Saint Mark, Saint Eulalia, and Saint Sebastian. Now, whether the Musarabic rite used in ancient times was the same as that held today, or whether it has been reformed and corrected, is not something that can be doubted: for it is certain that in religion all things have been adapted to the times, inclinations, and affections of those who have lived from age to age, especially concerning ecclesiastical order and discipline. A certain author I have with me named J. Yafee has described at length in Latin the form and manner of this Musarabic rite, and of its Masses and ceremonies. G. In the year of Christ 714, Christians permitted to live in Spain as taxpayers were called Mozarabs <note>original: "Mozarabes"</note>, because they were mixed with the Arabs. P. Maffei, in book 1 of his history of the Indies, makes mention of certain nations of Africa who are commonly called Moses, who in many things follow Christian institutions, and even in the giving of names, which they most often borrow from the holy Apostles.

->*Of several other Christians.*<-

Pierre Belon, in book 2, chapter 85, of his observations of several singularities and memorable things of the Levant, writes that Christian nations most often send men, more or fewer depending on the region, to inhabit the city of Jerusalem and to stay at the Holy Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ. From this, it happens that one counts twelve languages of the Christian religion, different from one another, and it is reckoned that there are twelve principal ones; however, this author says he finds only eight. Among these, the Latin nation, which they call <term>Frank</term> <note>From "Frank," the general term used in the Levant for Western Europeans</note>, is placed before all the others and includes all those obedient to the Roman Church. The second is the Greek nation, which is called in their language <term>Romæos</term> <note>referring to the Eastern Roman or Byzantine identity</note>, whose obedience is not to the command of the Pope, but they have their own Patriarchs. The third nation is the Armenian, which is closer to our ceremonies than the Greek. Consequently, the other nations include the Jacobites, who are from the region converted to the faith by Saint James the Greater; others are Georgians, which is a nation governed by its own laws, and which is adjacent to the Persians, having their borders at East India, and who have been subjugated by no one; thus they are absolute masters of themselves. Others are named Christians of the Belt <note>A term often applied to Copts or Melkites, referencing the "zunnar" belt they were sometimes required to wear</note>, who have taken the surname of Copts, who were brought to the faith by Saint Thomas. Others are Indians, who are sent there from the country ruled by Prester John <note>A legendary Christian king; here identifying his kingdom with Ethiopia</note>, and are very black, called Abyssinians. And because they are baptized in fire, they wear three branding marks <note>original: "brusleures"</note>: one between the two eyes above the nose, and the other two near the temples; they are not as black as the Ethiopians. Others are Nestorians, and others are called Maronites, who are the same as the Arabs <note>likely referring to their use of the Arabic language</note>. Each of these nations has a chapel of its own, because they all differ in some points, and they are maintained by money sent to them by the princes of their provinces. The Greeks hold the Choir and have custody of the site of Calvary, and the Latins have custody of the Sepulchre.

The religious men of all the aforementioned Christian nations enter there and exit when they please without paying anything. The Church of this Holy Sepulchre of our Lord encloses the entire circuit of Calvary, which is on flat ground and not on a mountain, as many have believed. It is high and round in shape, with an opening for light. And in the middle of this circle, the Holy Sepulchre is below, in the middle of the nave, inside the enclosure of a small chapel covered with a round vault, all of fine marble. The Guardian of the Franciscans <note>original: "Cordeliers," a name for the Order of Friars Minor in France</note> of Mount Sion is accustomed to giving a certification to pilgrims who have been sent by someone, so that it may be a testimony for them that they have been there; it contains all other things that I have not specified in detail here for the sake of brevity. The Lord of Villamont, in his modern travels, speaks extensively of all these particulars.

In the year 1580, a certain *David Chytraeus* <note>original: "Dauid Chythreus," a Lutheran theologian</note>, a Lutheran, had a speech of his printed in Frankfurt entitled, *On the State of the Churches at this time in Greece, Asia, Africa, Ethiopia, Armenia, Persia, etc.* <note>original Latin: "De statu Ecclesiarum hoc tempore in Græcia, Asia, Africa, Æthiopia, Armenia, Perside, &c."</note>, in which he demonstrates that all these provinces and regions, which comprise the greater part of this universe, attend to the Mass, *attend to the Masses* <note>original Latin: "Missis operam dare"</note>, that is to say, to the celebration of Masses. His companions—*Martin Crusius*, a teacher <note>original: "pedant"</note> of Tübingen, in his *Turcogrecia* and *Germanogrecia*; *Gerlachius*, a Protestant Minister; and *Wenceslaus von Ludovitz*, Agent of the Emperor in Turkey—in their epistles, give similar testimony. And even if they wished to deny or conceal it, they would be refuted by the travel books of the Catholics who have been to those countries, according to the report of *André Thevet*, book 6, chapter 9, of his *Universal Cosmography*, which confesses to having often seen, and still seeing today in the city of Jerusalem, on the same day, the celebration of Masses by fourteen Oriental and overseas Christian nations, all diverse and separated by long stretches of land and different languages from one another. This is confirmed by *G. Genebrard* in book 4 of his *Chronography*, and book 1, chapter 4, of his *Apostolic Liturgy*, following *André Thevet*, book 11, chapter 18, of his *Universal Cosmography*, and book 19, chapter 12, following.

At the last Jubilee celebrated in Rome in the year 1600, besides the infinite number of Christians from our Europe, several other Christians from the East—inhabitants of China, the Mughal Empire <note>original: "Mogor"</note>, and Japan <note>original: "Giapan"</note>, and from the ends of the Indies—were found there and attended in devotion, via express embassies from their Emperors, Kings, Sophis <note>The Safavid rulers of Persia</note>, Kwambaku <note>original: "Quabacondons," referring to the Japanese title "Kampaku" or regent</note>, Chins, and other titles they have among themselves, according to their languages and nations. So many from Egypt, and from a great part of the adjacent Libya, also presented themselves there—an infinite number of other Christians—tending toward their conversion, or rather their reversion to the ancient faith of their Fathers, from which they had strayed for a time. This clearly demonstrates that in the end, the Catholic Church will remain victorious over all the upheavals that have come upon it. Even the Grand Duke of Muscovy and the Great Khan of the Tartars sent some of their people there, from which there is great likelihood that God will keep them in His mercy and bring them back with the remnants of Israel, as He knows they are faithful. In the aforementioned country of **Mogor** <note>The Mughal Empire in northern India</note>, which is between the Indus River and the Ganges River, the Jesuits have worked so diligently for the spiritual well-being of the souls of the inhabitants there that the King, named **Mahomet Zelabdin Echebar** <note>Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar (r. 1556–1605)</note>, descended from the lineage of the great **Tamerlam** <note>Tamerlane</note>, now freely allows his children to be raised in Christianity, and attends the divine service celebrated daily by the aforementioned Jesuits with great reverence; this is despite the **Mullas** <note>Mullahs</note>, who are their priests, the **Gioges** <note>Yogis or Jogis, Hindu ascetics</note>, who are their monks, and the **Brachmans** <note>Brahmins</note>, who are their ministers.

Regarding the great and ample kingdom of **China**, situated in the easternmost part of Asia on the continent of the East Indies, modern accounts report that Christianity was first known and heard of there in the Year of Salvation 1575, through the ministry of a certain Father **Martin Herrade** <note>Martín de Rada</note>, Provincial of the Augustinians and native of Pamplona, and one **Hierosme Marin** <note>Jerónimo Marín</note>, a native of the city of Mexico, sent from the Philippine Islands (otherwise called the Islands of the West), which are distant from that kingdom by two hundred leagues. They first entered that kingdom led by a particular captain of the King named **Omoncon**, accompanied by **Synsay**, a merchant of the said kingdom, who unexpectedly arrived at the aforementioned islands, as is fully recounted in the *History of China*. Shortly thereafter—namely, in the year 1579—a certain Father **Pedre d'Alfare** <note>Pedro de Alfaro</note>, a native of Seville and guardian of the aforementioned Philippine Islands, of the Order of Saint Francis of the Province of Saint Joseph; a Father **Juan Baptiste of Pesare** from Italy; Brother **Sebastian of Saint Francis** of Baeza in Spain; and a religious Father **Augustin of Tordesillas**, all priests, made a voyage to this great kingdom by the command of the late King of Spain and his Great Council of the Indies. They remained on this journey for seven months, as is recounted in the second part, book 3, of the *History of China*. Since then, in the year 1583, certain Augustinian monks, and also those of the Observance of Saint Francis, along with Jesuits (called there "Fathers of Saint Paul"), went to take up their residence in the city of **Xauquin** <note>Zhaoqing, then the seat of the Viceroy of Liangguang</note>, where the Viceroy of China resides, where they had a convent and church built, in which they began to celebrate Mass regularly. In the year 1584, a certain Father **Martin Ignace** <note>Martín Ignacio de Loyola</note>, Guardian of the Order of Saint Francis, made the same journey from Spain to this kingdom, where he baptized several inhabitants whom he instructed in Christianity; from that kingdom, he returned to Spain via the East Indies after having made a circuit of the earth, as is recounted in the second part of the third book titled *Itinerary of the New World*. Following these good Fathers, some fifteen or twenty years ago, a good number of **Jacobin** <note>Dominican</note> monks from Spain went to the aforementioned kingdom of China by the command of the aforementioned King of Spain and the Lords of his Royal Council of the Indies, in order to assist in the enterprise of the aforementioned religious men. Serving not a little in the conversion of these Chinese people is the great desire they have to do so because of their books, in which it is written that from the side of the West, the "true law" must come to them, which will raise them to heaven to be angels there. Currently, several Chinese merchants who have become Christians have settled in the aforementioned Philippine Islands to live freely in their religion, being housed in a town called **Mauilles** <note>Manila</note>, having among them many artisans, such as shoemakers, tailors, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, and...

As for **Japan**, a Kingdom 600 leagues long and 30 wide, divided and shared among many Lords, distant from China by about 300 leagues, it was instructed in the Christian Religion by Father **Francis Xavier**. It was first discovered by **Antonio Mota**, **Francisco Zeimoto**, and **Antonio Peixoto** in the Year of Salvation 1542, when [Martim Afonso de] Sousa took the government of the Indies, according to Antonio Galvão’s book on the discoverers of the New World. Despite the rigors of **Taicosama** <note>Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), the regent who first issued edicts against Christians</note>, the wars in **Korea**, and the troubles of the five Regents against **Daisusama** <note>Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616), the first Shogun of the Tokugawa Shogunate</note>, the current Emperor of **Teuse** <note>Possibly a corruption of 'Tenshi' (Emperor) or a reference to the Shogunate's seat</note>, the principal seat of the Empire of Japan; and even despite the regrettable death of **Lord Augustin** <note>Konishi Yukinaga (1555–1600), a prominent Christian daimyo executed after the Battle of Sekigahara</note>, a great pillar of Christianity in the said Japan, nevertheless the aforementioned Jesuits have not tired of doing good in **Meaco** <note>The old name for Kyoto</note>, **Amakusa**, and among other peoples where they have their residences. Notwithstanding all the oppressions that have been inflicted upon them there, they have sometimes baptized more than twenty-five thousand people from one of these nations alone. The **Tono** <note>from the Japanese *Tono*, meaning 'Lord'</note>, who is the high provost of the said Japan and who persecuted them, was himself converted by them. What caused and served as an argument for the conversion of these peoples was that **Taicosama** was made a **Kami** <note>original: "Came"</note>, that is to say, a God in their language, and his statue was erected like that of Nebuchadnezzar to be adored. On this subject, the aforementioned Jesuits took the opportunity to tell these people that the *Taicosamas* had been nothing but men and could not be *Kami*; this the people recognized through the vivid reasons preached to them. A vision also occurred of a cross, which moved those people to want to be baptized and to renounce the **Kami** and **Hotoke** <note>original: "Cames, & Fotoques"</note>, who are their gods and their saints. And things have progressed so far in the Christian Religion that at present there are seven or eight Christian Churches: namely at **Bungo**, a city situated toward the North at some 33 and a half degrees from the equator; the second at **Kuchinotsu** <note>original: "Cutamé"</note>; the third at **Hirado** <note>original: "Firande"</note>, which is a neighboring island subject to Japan and very rich, where the number of Christians is more than two thousand; the fourth at **Hakata** <note>original: "Facata"</note>; the fifth in the great city of **Kagoshima** <note>original: "Cangoxima"</note>, which is the southernmost of the island and placed at some 31 degrees <note>The OCR reads 21, but Kagoshima is located at roughly 31 degrees North</note> and some hundred leagues distant from Bungo; the sixth is at **Yamaguchi** <note>original: "Almangut"</note>, and this Church and that of Kagoshima are the first that were established on this island around the year of our Lord 1548. The seventh is that of **Meaco**, the capital city of all the Japanese, and where the preachers have also had the most difficulty because of the university and monasteries of the idolaters <note>Refers to Buddhist monks and centers of learning</note> who resisted them; nevertheless, the King supporting our fathers, they preached there freely and converted a great number of people to holy baptism. The last is that of **Sakai** <note>original: "Sacaïa"</note>, a city situated near Meaco, but which lives under its own laws without being subject to any King whatsoever. Throughout all these Churches, one sees the newly converted Japanese so ardent in the Christian faith that it is impossible that any fear of death or torments could turn them away from it. See Father **Torres**, Jesuit, in his letters from Japan; Father **Xavier** in his letters from the said Japan; Father **Frois** in his letters; and Father **du Jarric of Toulouse** in his books on the history of the East Indies.

# ON THE ORIGIN OR INVENTION OF LETTERS, OR
*Characters of languages.*

## CHAPTER LVI.

**M**arcus Tullius Cicero, in the first of his *Tusculan Disputations*, concluded from the invention of letters the divinity of the soul and spirit of man, and argued that human nature was too excellent to be thought of as born and proceeding from corporeal existence alone, saying: <margin>“</margin>What is that power—what is it, indeed—which investigates hidden things? <note>original Latin: "Quid illa vis, quę tandem est, quę inuestigat occulta?"</note> <margin>“</margin>That which is called invention and discovery—does it seem to you to be composed of this earthly, mortal, and <margin>“</margin>decaying nature? <note>original Latin: "quæ inuentio atque excogitatio dicitur ex hac ne tibi terrena mortali que natura & caduca concreta ea videtur?"</note> Or who was the first—as it seemed to Pythagoras, a man of supreme wisdom—to <margin>“</margin>give names to all things? <note>original Latin: "aut qui primus... omnibus rebus imposuit nomina"</note> Or who gathered together scattered men and called them to the society <margin>“</margin>of life? Or who limited the sounds of the voice, which seemed infinite, with a few <margin>“</margin>marks of letters? <note>original Latin: "aut qui sonos vocis, qui infiniti videbantur paucis literarũ notis terminarunt?"</note> This gift, handed down from God to mortals, all <margin>“</margin>wise men endowed with judgment and virtue have pursued with admiration and the highest gratitude <margin>“</margin>of soul. Cælius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus (1469–1525) was an Italian scholar famous for his "Antiquarum Lectionum" (Ancient Readings), a massive encyclopedia of classical knowledge.</note> in book 4 of his *Ancient Readings*: <margin>“</margin>For what of that majesty of writing which acquires for us the knowledge of such great things, <margin>“</margin>prolongs it through antiquity, and lets nothing perish? And that time, which consumes all <margin>“</margin>things, it compels to succumb to our hands? <note>original Latin: "Quid enim illa scribendi Maiestas... & quod omnia conterit tépus, nostris cogit manibus succumbere?"</note> What is more magnificent than this? What <margin>“</margin>is equally wonderful: that this was given to man, over which even the greedy <margin>“</margin>rapacity of death has no right? <note>original Latin: "id esse homini datum, in quod ne mortis quidem auida rapacitas ius vllũ habeat"</note> What of those volumes woven from so <margin>“</margin>many and such great laws, which finally display the excellence of a more <margin>“</margin>civilized life? What of the faith of words and agreements <margin>“</margin>preserved in public tablets against the depravity of minds? I would <margin>“</margin>dare to say that if our hands were separated [from the use of letters], we would not only be unarmed, but even <margin>“</margin>unhappier than the beasts. ...their Hebrew letters, expressed and engraved in the Heavens according to the position of the fixed stars, just as I have amply described earlier in chapter 9 of this discourse. The Greeks do the same regarding their Δ <note>The Greek letter Delta.</note>, or *deltaton*. Palamedes <note>A legendary Greek hero from the time of the Trojan War, often credited with inventing various letters of the alphabet, weights, and measures.</note> attributed the invention of the four Greek letters Θ, Ξ, Φ, χ <note>Theta, Xi, Phi, and Chi.</note>, which he first brought to light, to the immortal Gods. For when it was one day objected to him that these four letters had been taught to him by the Greeks and were not his own invention, he replied, according to Philostratus:

> I did not find the letters, but I was found by them; for they had long been lying in the house of the Muses and were in need of such a man, etc. <note>original Greek: "ἐγὼ γράμματα οὐχ εὗρον ἀλλ᾽ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν εὑρέθην· πάλαι γὰρ ταῦτα ἐν μουσῶν οἴκῳ κείμενα ἐδεῖτο ἀνδρὸς τοιούτου"</note> That is to say, I did not invent the letters, but I was invented by them, because having been long hidden in the houses of the Muses, they had need of such a person. For the Gods are accustomed to bringing such inventions to light through wise men; as for the cranes <note>Ancient authors often claimed the flight patterns of cranes inspired the shapes of certain letters.</note>, they do not know these said letters, but only seem to approve of their order when they travel to Libya to fight the Pygmies.

Plutarch in book 9 of his *Symposiacs* <note>A collection of dinner-table discussions on various philosophical and historical topics.</note> and Cicero in book 3 of *The Nature of the Gods*, have written on this subject that the God Mercury was the first who taught the Egyptians the letters he had invented. Then, speaking of Cadmus <note>A Phoenician prince in Greek mythology credited with bringing the alphabet to the Greeks.</note>, who was held to have been the first to bring these letters to the Greeks, they attribute the invention of them to the Phoenicians, as several other authors, both ancient and modern, have done. The same Plutarch takes the Phoenicians to be the Hebrews; for when the question was raised as to why Alpha held the first rank and order among the Greek letters, Ammonius <note>A philosopher and teacher of Plutarch.</note> is introduced, provoking Plutarch of Chaeronea to the debate with these following words, saying:

> Do you then, as a Boeotian, offer no help to Cadmus, who they say placed Alpha before all others because the Phoenicians call the ox by this name? <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν οὖν τῷ Κάδμῳ βοηθεῖς ὁ Βοιώτιος ᾗ φασὶ τὸ ἄλφα πάντων προτάξαι διὰ τὸ Φοίνικας οὕτω καλεῖν τὸν βοῦν."</note>
> Do you bring any help or aid to Cadmus, you who are a Boeotian? It is said he placed Alpha in the first rank and order of the letters because the Phoenicians call an ox by that name; which he did not wish to place in the second or third rank among necessary things, as Hesiod did, but rather in the first place—the Hebrews calling the ox *Aluph* <note>The Hebrew word "Eleph" or "Aluph" refers to an ox or a leader; the letter Aleph is anciently derived from a pictogram of an ox head.</note> in their language?

Cyprian Martyr <note>Likely referring to the early Christian writer Cyprian of Carthage, or a text attributed to him.</note> in the 4th treatise on *The Vanity of Idols*: In Crete, one sees the cave of Jupiter and also his sepulcher, and it is held as quite certain in that place that Saturn was driven out by him, and from there Latinus <note>In mythology, the king of the Latins; the author here links his name to the word for "hiding."</note> took his name from *latebra* <note>Latin: a hiding place or retreat.</note>, who first instituted the art of printing letters and of minting money, because of which the term *Aerarium Saturni* <note>Latin: "The Treasury of Saturn," the public treasury in ancient Rome.</note> originated in Italy in former times. Several ancient writers, exalting the invention of these letters as more than human, have reported these words: Diodorus Siculus, book 1, chapter 1: The Egyptians assert that it is they who invented letters, the course of the Stars, Geometry, and several other arts and sciences. And in book 6, chapter 13, following the time when Attin, son of the Sun, having gone into Egypt, had taught Astrology to the Egyptians: finally, Greece having been devastated by the deluge, many thousands of men perished, and the memories of letters fell into oblivion. This provided an argument, after several centuries had passed, for the estimation that Cadmus, son of Agenor, was the one who first introduced letters into Greece; so that the Greeks, led by a common error and ignorance, feel themselves his debtors in that they attribute this invention to him. ...inventions, disciplines, and whatever else is useful and necessary for life and community. Josephus <note>original: "Iosephe"; referring to Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, in the first book of his *Antiquities*, maintains that Seth, son of Adam, and their children were the first to record astronomy in writing, which they had learned from their first father, Adam. This led the Arabs to attribute Theology and all other sciences to this Seth, son of the aforementioned Adam—which is most true and certain, as we have discussed extensively in the preceding chapters 2, 3, 5, and 9 of this present work. Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss orientalist and linguist.</note> says in his commentary *On the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, in the chapter concerning the origin of letters:

It is consistent with reason that Adam—who had fallen into sin through the seduction of Satan but was soon after restored by divine grace—depicted his thoughts and the memory of past deeds through letters. This is fitting for the excellence and dignity of the first man. For whom else should we consider that God, or that "divine man" (as Plato says), who first discovered letters? Or to whom should we rather attribute that "divine mind" (as it seemed to Cicero and Pythagoras), who reduced so many distinct voices to certain laws and marked the elements of human speech with suitable signs, than to Adam himself? According to the testimony of Holy Scripture, he gave the most appropriate names to all things, which God also approved. Indeed, since the power of reason is most vast, and puts itself forward and comes under the senses both in words and in works, no work of human reason appears more excellent to me than that which, by the marks and signs of letters, depicts speech—through which reason presents itself—and even depicts itself. It deposits this in books, as if in chests to be preserved, and transfers itself into other minds whose bodies are separated by the greatest intervals of both place and time. And so the mind found an instrument suited to its nature, by which it might grasp with a tool divine and human things, things embodied and things without bodies, and—to put it simply—whatever man can comprehend with his mind, and propose them to others for perception and judgment. Furthermore, it sufficiently refutes the opinions of those who attribute the receipt of letters to Pagan authors, or to Moses, or to Abraham, or to a single writing of the Prophet Enoch <note>A biblical figure often associated with the invention of writing and ancient wisdom in mystical traditions.</note>, who flourished about 800 years before the Flood. It is also pleasing to transcribe here some ancient verses concerning the inventors of letters, which Petrus Crinitus <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), an Italian humanist scholar.</note> testifies to have found in an ancient manuscript in the Library of Septimana, in book 17 of *On Honest Discipline*, chapter 1:

> Moses was the first to carve out the Hebrew letters,
> The Phoenicians with sagacious minds founded the Attic.
> Abraham found the Syrian and the Chaldean as well,
> Those which we Latins write, Nicostrata published.
> Isis, with no less skill, produced the Egyptian,
> Ulfilas <note>original: "Gulfila"; the 4th-century bishop who translated the Bible into Gothic and created the Gothic alphabet.</note> brought forth the Gothic, which we see as the last.

Pliny and Solinus <note>Roman authors Gaius Plinius Secundus and Gaius Julius Solinus.</note> say that the Pelasgians <note>An ancient people who inhabited the Aegean region before the Greeks.</note> were the first who carried letters to the lands of the Latins. Some maintain that Nicostrata, mother of the Arcadian Evander, was the one who first gave letters to the Latins. Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric.</note> relates in book 1 that the Arcadians under Evander—who came to Italy after the Pelasgians—brought letters there. Titus Livius <note>Livy, the famous Roman historian.</note> in the first book of his *Decades* calls this Evander the author of them, writing in this manner: "Evander then, having fled from the Peloponnese, came to these places where he ruled more by authority and majesty..."

As for **K**, taken from the Greeks, there is no good author who advises that it be used in any way: the letter **Q** was received because it has a softer sound than **C**. The letter **X** was taken from the Greeks, but we can do without it, as **Quintilian** <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 AD), a Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> remarks, by using these letters **C** and **S**, or **G** and **S**, as in these Latin words *Apex* <note>original: "Apecs"</note> and *Grex* <note>original: "Grecs"</note> which mean **summit** and **flock**. **Y** and **Z** also have their source in the fountains of Greece, but are so adopted by us that we only use them in words that are naturally Greek. **Theodore Bibliander** <note>A 16th-century Swiss scholar and linguist who studied the relationships between languages.</note> says:

> Furthermore, since the **Hebrew letters** are the primary ones from which the letters of other nations and peoples were born and propagated—and this is not obscure if one attentively inspects the forms themselves—I will also add some things regarding at what time such a great benefit was transferred from the family of **Heber** <note>The traditional ancestor of the Hebrews, from whom the name is derived.</note> to other nations, and through which men. For when the entire race of **Adam** used one speech, there was also one common form of letters. But with the introduction of a plurality of languages, diverse writing also followed. And among the children of **Ham** <note>original: "Cham"</note>, **Canaan** prevailed, from whom the **Phoenicians** descend. Their language and letter forms approach the Hebrew most closely in name, form, and order. For among good authors, such as **Serapion** and others, the order of letters is the same as that observed by the Hebrews themselves. Among the sons of **Japheth**, **Javan** <note>In the biblical "Table of Nations," Javan is associated with the Greeks.</note> prevailed, from whom the **Greeks** lead their origin: whose letters likewise agree for the most part with the Hebrew in number, order, names, and power. From them flowed the letters of other nations which are worn by public use, such as those of the **Latins** from the Greeks, and likewise of the **Sarmatians** <note>An ancient people of Iranian origin who lived in what is now Ukraine and southern Russia.</note> and **Teutons** <note>Germanic peoples.</note>. However, the use of writing increased later among some barbarian nations, as **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote in Greek.</note> says in Book 8 of his *Various History*, where he cites **Androtion** writing about the ignorance of letters and disciplines among the **Thracians** and other barbarians, noting that none of the ancient Thracians knew letters. Indeed, he would have said it was a disgrace for all barbarians in **Europe** to use letters, yet the **Asians**, as it is told, used them more; whence some dare to say that **Orpheus** was not a wise man, but others fabricated his fables. **Herodotus**, writing about **Cadmus** <note>The legendary Phoenician prince who founded Thebes and brought the alphabet to Greece.</note>—who they say brought letters to the Greeks—writes thus in his book *Terpsichore*: "As I have found by inquiry, there were Phoenicians among those who came with Cadmus to the land now called **Boeotia**, and they inhabited it, having been allotted the **Tanagric** district. Whence the **Cadmeans** were first driven out by the **Argives**, and again by the **Boeotians**; if the **Zephyrians** <note>Likely referring to a specific subgroup or location mentioned in the classical text.</note> were expelled, they turned toward **Athens**. They were received by the Athenians under conditions that they would be citizens among them, many things worthy of memory being imposed upon them. These Phoenicians who arrived with Cadmus, of whom the Zephyrians were part, while they inhabited this region, introduced many other doctrines into **Greece**, and especially letters, which in my opinion did not exist among the Greeks before; and those were first of the kind which all Phoenicians use. Then, with the progress of time, along with the sound, they changed the ancient shape <note>original: "modulum pristinum"</note>, and since at that time their neighbors in most of the surrounding places were **Ionians**, who had received letters by learning them from the Phoenicians, they used them, arranging them with a few of their own; and in using them, they confessed, as reason suggested, that they were called 'Phoenician' because they had been brought into Greece by the Phoenicians. And by an ancient custom they called skins *biblos* <note>A term usually associated with papyrus, but here used to describe writing on animal skins.</note>, because at one time, due to a shortage of books—that is, papyrus—they used goat and sheep skins. Even to my own memory, many of the barbarians write on such skins; indeed, even men themselves in **Boeotian Thebes**, in the temple of **Ismenian Apollo**, saw the Cadmean letters..."

> **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC Greek historian.</note> in his 6th book says it is an error of Greece to attribute the invention of letters to **Cadmus**, son of Agenor; he says Cadmus was merely the first to bring letters to Greece after the great flood, an event which had destroyed previous records of writing. Regarding the time when letters were brought to Italy, judgment was previously rendered using the words of **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author.</note>, to which I will add these few points from the first book of the *Roman Antiquities* of **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**: roughly sixty years before the Trojan War, certain Arcadians led by **Evander** <note>A culture hero from Arcadia who brought Greek pantheon and laws to Italy.</note> arrived in Italy and founded the Palatine settlement. Some say that **Carmenta** <note>Evander’s mother, a prophetess said to have adapted the Greek alphabet into the Latin one.</note> only changed the forms of the letters. Others say that **Hercules** brought letters to Italy from the Falisci <note>An ancient Italic people.</note>. As **Victorinus** <note>Marius Victorinus, a 4th-century grammarian.</note> testifies, **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note> writes in his 6th book: "The deeds of the Romans from the founding of the city to its capture [by the Gauls], I have set forth in five books; these matters are obscure due to their great antiquity, like objects seen from a vast distance, and also because in those times writing was extremely rare, though it is the only faithful guardian of the memory of past deeds." **Cornelius Tacitus**, writing about the Germans, says they celebrate **Tuisto** and his son **Mannus** <note>The mythical ancestors of the Germanic peoples.</note> as the origin of their race in ancient songs, which is their only form of memory and annals. Regarding the Goths and Franks, we have already spoken in our list of languages. Furthermore, six hundred years ago, the **Turks** embraced **Arabic letters** along with the religion of the Saracens, and long after them, the **Tartars** <note>A general term used here for Central Asian nomadic groups, including the Mongols.</note> did the same. In our own age, the **Hungarian language** has finally begun to be recorded in writing. **Otto Heurnius** <note>A Dutch physician and philosopher (1577–1652).</note> conforms to the above in his work on the Chaldean language.

Those who wish to see many other fine discourses on the invention of letters and grammar—which **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> attributes to **Prometheus**, who lived in the time of the Hebrew Judges—should read **Julius Pollux** in his *Onomasticon*, book 4; **Quintilian**, books 4 and 7; **P. Crinitus**, book 16, chapter 8 of *On Honest Discipline*; **Gregor Reisch**, the Carthusian, in book 1, treatise 1 of his *Philosophical Pearl* <note>original: "Marguerite philosophique," a famous 16th-century encyclopedia.</note>; **Polydore Vergil**, book 1, chapter 6 of *On the Inventors of Things*; **Theodor Zwinger**, volume 2, book 1 of his *Great Theater of Human Life*; **Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa**, chapters 2 and 3 of his treatise *On the Vanity of the Sciences*; **Theodor Bibliander** in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*; **Petrus Ramus**, book 1 of *Grammar Schools*; and **Pierre Grégoire**, book 16 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. As for the parts of this grammar, **Raffaele Volaterranus**, book 32 of his *Philology*—in the chapter on the cyclic sciences, and primarily on grammar, letters, syllables, and feet—has written amply and learnedly on everything one might desire. After him, **Caelius Secundus Curio** in his book divided into three parts entitled *The School, or on the Perfect Grammarian*; and more excellently and profoundly, **Luis de Figueiredo**, the Portuguese, in his preface to his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*.
