# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE. On the Region of the Greeks.

**Ortelius** <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous Flemish cartographer and geographer who created the first modern atlas.</note> in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasure* says: "Greece, the most noble region of Europe, and the source and mother of all learning." <note>original Latin: "Græcia, Europæ nobilissima regio, totiúsque eruditionis fons & mater."</note> It was called **Hellas** <gloss>Hellas</gloss> by its inhabitants. We have observed that its dwellers were most frequently called by these names among the most ancient writers: the **Achaeans** <gloss>Achaioi</gloss>, **Achivi**, **Argives** <gloss>Argeioi</gloss>, **Danaans** <gloss>Danaoi</gloss>, **Dolopes** <gloss>Dolopes</gloss>, **Dorians** <gloss>Dorieis</gloss>, **Dryopes** <gloss>Dryopes</gloss>, **Graians**, **Gratugena**, **Hellenes** <gloss>Hellenes</gloss>, **Ionians** <gloss>Iones</gloss>, **Myrmidons** <gloss>Myrmidones</gloss>, and **Pelasgians** <gloss>Pelasgoi</gloss>. But **Nicolaus Gerbelius** <note>A 16th-century German scholar who wrote extensively on Greek geography.</note> noted the same even before us. I understand that those who inhabit it today call it **Romechi**, and the Turks call it **Horomeli**. To **Leunclavius** <note>Johannes Leunclavius, a 16th-century historian known for his studies of the Ottoman Empire.</note> it is **Rumelia**. It is called **Phobel** by the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in Isaiah 61, and **Javan** among the same (where **Saint Jerome** <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> reads "Greece") in Ezekiel 27 and Zechariah 9.

True Greece is **Achaia**: thus **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman author and administrator.</note> says in his 8th book of letters to Maximus. This same area is called Hellas by **Polyhistor**. On this subject, see **Petrus Fabri**, *Agonisticon*, book 3, chapter 15. In **Xenophon's** *Cyropaedia*, book 1, there are also "Asiatic Greeks." Either he is mistaken, or they are on the coast of the Aegean Sea in Asia Minor, where there were many Greek colonies, or in the region of Galatia where the **Gallo-Greeks** lived: whom **Plutarch** calls "Asian Greeks" in his *Sayings*. According to **Suidas** <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>, "Greece" was also the name of a village from which the region took its name; see the entry for Achaia.

**Greater Greece**, or *Magna Graecia*, is a region of Italy according to **Ptolemy**. Between the Bruttii and the Salentini, **Pliny** calls Italy "Greece" in book 36, chapter 5, and the "coast of Greece" in book 3, chapter 5. To distinguish it from this, **Livy** in his 7th book calls the area that is true Greece (that is, Hellas) "Further Greece."

**Achaia** <gloss>Achaia</gloss> is a region of Greece which **Ptolemy** also names Hellas. **Pliny Caecilius** calls it "Pure Greece" <note>original Latin: "meram græciam"</note> in his 8th book of letters to his friend Romanus. Today it seems to be called **Livadia**. There is another Achaia in the Peloponnese which is renamed by the same Ptolemy; it is called **Ionia**, **Ias**, and **Olenus** by **Diodorus**. It is called **Aegialos** by **Pausanias** and Pliny. **Herodotus** writes in his book *Polymnia* that the inhabitants were called <term>Pelasgians</term> <note>The Pelasgians were the indigenous people who inhabited the Aegean region before the arrival of the Greeks.</note> Aegiales, which means "people of the coast." **Giacomo Gastaldi** <note>A prominent 16th-century Venetian cartographer.</note> reports that it is now called "High Romania." **Apuleius** calls the entire Peloponnese "Achaia," on which see the entry for Lacedaemon. For **Thucydides**, it is also the name of a city in the Peloponnese. There is an Achaia region, an Achaia village, and an Achaean people in Asiatic Sarmatia near the Black Sea, according to Ptolemy, Strabo, Pomponius, Dionysius, Appian, and the *Circumnavigation* of Arrian.

Some write **Achaea** <gloss>Achaia</gloss> with three syllables; there is also a city of that name on the island of Rhodes, as witnessed by Diodorus and **Athenaeus** in his 8th book. According to **Appian** in his *Syrian Wars*, it is in Parthiene. It is also in Macedonia and even in Crete, unless **Gesner** is mistaken in his entry on the "Achaean Deer." There is also a spring called Achaia in Messenia near the city of Dorium, according to Pausanias. **Aelian** mentions an "Achaean Gulf" in the 1st book of *On Animals*, chapter 12.

**Nicolaus Gerbelius**, in his *Commentaries on the Description of Greece by Sophianos*, in the chapter on the names of Greece, wrote the following:

"Before the Trojan War, which is recorded among the most ancient events by historians, I find that the Greeks achieved nothing worthy of memory under a common name. This lasted until Alexander, son of Priam, also called **Paris**, under the most unlucky omens, seized **Helen**, the wife of Menelaus, as we also said above. For then, in the city of Aulis in Boeotia, a conspiracy was formed by the leaders of the Greeks..."

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE. Concerning the Region of the Greeks.
<sig>Nnnn 2</sig>

**Abraham Ortelius**, in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasury*, writes: **Greece** is "the most noble region of Europe, and the source and mother of all learning." <note>original Latin: "Græcia, Europæ nobilissima regio, totiusque eruditionis fons & mater." Ortelius was a famous 16th-century Flemish cartographer.</note> It was called **Hellas** <gloss>Hellas</gloss> by its inhabitants. We have observed that its inhabitants are frequently called by these names among the most ancient writers: **Achaians** <gloss>Akhaioi</gloss>, **Argives** <gloss>Argeioi</gloss>, **Danaans** <gloss>Danaoi</gloss>, **Dolopes** <gloss>Dolopes</gloss>, **Dorians** <gloss>Dorieis</gloss>, **Dryopes** <gloss>Dryopes</gloss>, **Graians** <gloss>Graioi</gloss>, **Greek-born**, **Hellenes** <gloss>Hellenes</gloss>, **Ionians** <gloss>Iones</gloss>, **Myrmidons** <gloss>Myrmidones</gloss>, and **Pelasgians** <gloss>Pelasgoi</gloss>. But **Nicolaus Gerbel** also noted the same before us. I understand that those who live there today call it **Romechi** <note>A reference to "Romaioi," the term used by Greeks in the Byzantine and Ottoman periods to identify themselves as Romans.</note>, and the Turks call it **Horomeli**. It is **Rumelia** according to **Leunclavius**. It is called **Phobel** by the seventy interpreters <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in Isaiah 61, and **Javan** by the same (where **St. Jerome** reads "Greece") in Ezekiel 27 and Zechariah 9.

True **Greece** is **Achaia**: so says **Pliny** in his 8th letter to Maximus. This same region is **Hellas** to **Polyhistor**. Add to this **Petrus Faber** in his *Agonisticon*, book 3, chapter 15. In **Xenophon's** *Cyropaedia*, book 1, there are also "Asiatic Greeks." Either I am mistaken, or they are on the coast of the Aegean Sea in Asia Minor, where there are many Greek colonies, or in the region of **Galatia** where the **Gallo-Greeks** are: whom **Plutarch** calls "Asian Greeks" in his *Sayings*. According to **Suidas**, there is also a village called **Greece** from which the region takes its name; see the entry for **Achaia**.

**Greater Greece** (or *Magna Graecia*) is a region of Italy according to **Ptolemy**. **Pliny** calls the area between the Brutii and the Salentini "Grecian Italy" in book 36, chapter 5, and the "Grecian coast" in book 3, chapter 5. To distinguish it, **Livy** in his 7th book calls that which is true Greece (that is, Hellas) "**Further Greece**."

**Achaia** <gloss>Akhaia</gloss> is a region of Greece which **Ptolemy** also names Hellas. **Pliny Caecilius** calls it "Pure Greece" in his 8th book of letters to his friend Romanus. Today it seems to be called **Livadia**. There is another **Achaia** in the **Peloponnese** which is specifically named by the same Ptolemy; it is called **Ionia**, **Ias**, and **Olenus** by **Diodorus**. It is called **Aegialos** by **Pausanias** and **Pliny**. **Herodotus** writes in his *Polymnia* that the inhabitants were called **Pelasgian Aegialeans**, which means "coastal people." **Giacomo Gastaldi** reports that it is now called **High Romania**. **Apuleius** calls the entire Peloponnesus "Achaia"; on this, see the entry for **Lacedaemon**. For **Thucydides** in book 1, it is also the name of a city in the Peloponnese. There is an Achaia region, an Achaia village, and the Achaian people in **Asiatic Sarmatia** <note>An ancient region covering parts of present-day Russia and Ukraine.</note> near the Black Sea, according to Ptolemy, Strabo, Pomponius, Dionysius, Appian, and the *Periplus* of Arrian.

Some write **Achaea** <gloss>Akhaia</gloss> as three syllables. Achaia is also a city on the island of **Rhodes**, as witnessed by Diodorus; and according to **Athenaeus** in book 8, it is in **Parthienae**. According to **Appian** in his *Syriaca*, it is in Macedonia and also in **Crete**, unless **Gesner** is mistaken regarding the "Achaian Deer." There is also an Achaian spring in **Messenia** near the city of Dorium, according to Pausanias. **Aelian** mentions an **Achaian Gulf** in book 1 of *On Animals*, chapter 12.

**Nicolaus Gerbel**, in his *Commentaries on the Description of Greece* by **Sophianos**, in the chapter on the names of Greece, wrote what follows:

> Before the Trojan War, which is remembered among historians as being among the most ancient events, I find that the Greeks achieved nothing of common note at home or abroad. This remained so until Alexander, son of Priam, also known as Paris, under the most unhappy omens, abducted Helen, the wife of Menelaus, as we have already said above. For then, at the city of Aulis in Boeotia, a conspiracy was formed by the leaders of the Greeks...

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE [GREEKS]</header>

...and by the common consent of all Greece, war was waged against Priam <note>King Priam of Troy, referring to the Trojan War.</note>. For this reason, Thucydides records that before the time of Hellen—whom the same author identifies as the son of Deucalion, while the commentator on Pindar calls him the son of Prometheus and Clymene, and others the son of Ion—the Greeks were not called by a single name. Instead, he relates that individual tribes, most notably the Pelasgians, each took their own names for themselves. However, once Hellen and his sons gained power in Phthiotis, they allied themselves with neighboring cities for the purpose of commerce. From this shared interaction, they became accustomed to a single language and eventually adopted one name, being called **Hellenes** after Hellen. Yet, this name did not immediately spread to the entire nation; at first, it applied only to the people of Phthiotis who served as soldiers under Achilles in the Trojan expedition.

Therefore, Pliny, with his usual great learning, asserts that Greece frequently changed its name and was most often named after its kings. Because a King **Graecus** was born there, it was called **Graecia** (Greece). Because **Hellen** (as we have said) held the kingdom there, the Greeks were called **Hellenes**. Homer named these same people, though not all in one place, **Myrmidons**, **Hellenes**, and **Achaians**. However, the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator</note> of Homer affirms that only Thessaly is called "true Greece" by Homer. We shall briefly explain the names that are more common and well-known among authors, which are primarily: **Achaians, Argives, Danaans, Pelopes, Hellenes, Ionians, Myrmidons,** and **Pelasgians.**

### A C H A I A N S.

Xuthus, the son of Aeolus, having taken Creusa, the daughter of Erechtheus, in marriage, fathered two sons by her: Ion and Achaeus. One of them, Ion, took possession of Athens and called the region of Attica **Ionia** after himself, and the Athenians **Ionians**. Achaeus, when he had stained himself with the blood of his own kin, fled to Thessaly; becoming the Lord of that region, he called the Thessalians **Achaians** after himself. Thus, Homer often uses the name through <term>metonymy</term> <note>A figure of speech where a related term or a part is used to represent the whole; here, using one tribe's name for all Greeks.</note> to refer to Greece as **Achaia** and the Greeks as **Achaians**, as in Book 3 of the *Iliad*:

> To horse-breeding Argos and Achaia, land of beautiful women.
<note>original Greek: "Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ Ἀχαιΐδα καλλιγύναικα."</note>

And in Book 11 of the *Iliad*:

> But come, let us see if we might somehow arm the sons of the Achaians.
<note>original Greek: "Ἀλλ᾽ ἄγετ᾽ αἴκεν πῶς θωρήξοmen υἷας ἀχαιῶν."</note>

The remaining matters pertaining to the Achaians in Thessaly we shall save for when we discuss that region.

### A R G I V E S.

The **Argives** were named after Argus, the son of Apis and Niobe, as the Scholiasts of Homer prefer. There are some who think the Argives and the region of Argia received their name from the "clarity" or fame <note>A play on the Latin and Greek roots implying "bright" or "shining."</note> of the city itself. We will discuss this more copiously a little later in the section on Regions. But if you have looked closely at the map—which, as I have often advised, you should do—you will see the city of Argos and the region of Argia beautifully and diligently marked in capital letters. Didymus, in Book 18 of the *Odyssey* (if the title is correct), records that all of Greece is called **Argos** because that city is situated in the middle of Greece. Strabo, however, in Book 8, mentions from Euripides that Danaus lived in the citadel of the Argives. Since he far surpassed the previous kings in the greatness of his deeds, he decreed throughout all of Greece that the people previously called **Pelasgiotas** should be named **Danaans** after himself, so that this name might be used publicly thereafter. Virgil used both names in these two verses:

<note>original: "Ferus omnia Iuppiter Argos / Transtulit, incensa Danai dominantur in urbe." These lines from Virgil’s Aeneid describe the moment the Greeks (Danai) finally seized control of Troy as it burned.</note>

### DANAI.

We have already mentioned that the **Danai** <note>One of the primary names used by Homer to refer to the Greeks, specifically those from the region of Argos.</note> took their name from **Danaus**. However, the commentator on Homer has explained this matter a bit more clearly. **Belus** (he says)—the son of Neptune and Libya (after whom the land of Libya was named) and brother of Agenor—married Anthinoë, the daughter of the Nile, while he was reigning in Egypt. With her, he fathered the twins **Aegyptus** and **Danaus**. Belus placed Danaus in charge of Libya and Aegyptus in charge of Arabia; after Aegyptus conquered the **Melampodes** <note>Literally "Black-feet," an ancient name for the people of the Nile region.</note>, the region of Egypt gained its name from him. Aegyptus had fifty sons by various wives, and Danaus had just as many daughters. 

But when the brothers Aegyptus and Danaus disputed over the kingdom (as often happens), and Danaus was warned by an oracle that he would be killed by one of his grandsons, he had his daughters kill his brother's sons, though one or two were spared. Having committed this crime, and on the advice of **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena, who was said to have helped Danaus escape.</note>, he was the first to build a ship. He called it a **pentekontoros** <note>original: πεντηκόντορον; a ship with fifty oars, named after the number of his daughters.</note> because of the number of his daughters (for there were fifty, as we said). Fleeing from Libya in this ship with his daughters, he arrived at **Rhodes**. There, after erecting a statue to **Lindian Minerva**, he moved on to **Argos**. **Elenor**, who was then reigning there, surrendered the administration of the kingdom to Danaus, who then called the people of Argos "Danai" after himself.

### DOLOPES.

The **Dolopes** lived in **Thessaly**; from them, the region of Thessaly itself and the city of **Clymene** were called "Dolopian," as noted by Apollonius of Rhodes. **Peleus** <note>The father of the famous hero Achilles.</note> once held this land, and he granted Dolopia to **Phoenix** when he came to Oeus as a kinsman; he also entrusted his young son **Achilles**, still a boy, to Phoenix to be educated. **Homer** mentions the Dolopes in this verse from the 9th book of the *Iliad*:

> *I dwelt on the frontier of Phthia, ruling over the Dolopes.*
<note>original: Ναῖον δ' ἐσχατιήω Φθίης Δολόπεσσιν ἀνάσσων.</note>

In this passage, Phoenix recounts this entire history in several verses. Therefore, since the **Myrmidons** (whom we shall discuss later) served under Achilles, and the Dolopes served under Phoenix, **Virgil** joined them in these verses from the second book of the *Aeneid*:

> — *Who, in telling such things,*
> *whether of the Myrmidons, or the Dolopes, or a soldier of harsh Ulysses,*
> *could refrain from tears?*
<note>original: "Quis talia fando / Myrmidonum, Dolopumue, aut duri miles Vlyssi / Temperet à lacrymis?"</note>

**Didymus** writes in the 11th book of the *Odyssey* that **Scyros** was a city of Dolopia. And the commentator on **Pindar** has left it on record that the Dolopes were the best **slingers** <note>Light infantry specialized in using slings to hurl stones or lead bullets with high velocity and precision.</note>.

### HELLENES.

We have previously recounted from **Thucydides** the occasion on which the Greeks were named **Hellenes**. However, **Eustathius**, in his commentary on the second book of the *Iliad*, reports that **Hellas** was a city in Thessaly that took its name from a king, and that name was later applied to all Greeks. Homer uses the names **Phthia** and **Hellas** interchangeably...

He [Homer] is accustomed to name them Myrmidons, Hellenes, and Achaeans, as in these verses from the aforementioned Book 2:
> Those who ruled Phthia and Hellas of the beautiful women, 
> and were called Myrmidons and Hellenes and Achaeans.
<note>original: "Οἵ τ’ ἄρχον Φθίην ἠδ’ Ἑλλάδα καλλιγύναικα / Μυρμιδόνες δὲ καλεῦντο καὶ Ἕλληνες καὶ Ἀχαιοί." These lines are from the "Catalogue of Ships" in Homer's Iliad.</note>

### I O N I A N S.

We stated above regarding the Achaeans that **Ion** was the son of **Xuthus**; after Ion had occupied Athens, he called the whole of Attica "Ionia" and the people of Attica "Ionians." This we have explained diligently in our description of the geography of Greece. The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on a classical text.</note> on Homer’s Book 13 names him **Xanthus**, whom he had called Xuthus in Book 1. This passage must therefore be corrected based on **Eustathius** <note>A 12th-century scholar and Archbishop of Thessalonica known for his extensive commentaries on Homer.</note>, who writes that **Hellen** was the son of **Deucalion** <note>The "Noah" figure of Greek mythology who survived the great flood.</note>, and that Hellen fathered Xuthus, and Xuthus fathered Ion and Achaeus. From these figures, as we have said, the Greeks are named Hellenes, Ionians, and Achaeans.

### M Y R M I D O N S.

The **Myrmidons** are Greeks who, as we touched upon regarding the Dolopes, served as soldiers under **Achilles**, specifically being from the region of **Phthiotis**. Homer is accustomed to join them with the rest of the Greeks, as appeared in the verses we cited above. Regarding the origin of the Myrmidons, the following story is recounted among the ancients: Between Attica and the Peloponnese, in the mouth of the Saronic Gulf, lies the island of **Aegina**, facing Attica and Athens. While **Aeacus** reigned there, **Juno** <note>The Roman name for Hera, queen of the gods.</note> corrupted the whole island with a plague. As the blight spread further and further, the island was stripped of its people. Aeacus, taking this solitude and the lack of citizens poorly, prayed to his father **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> to repair this loss in some way. Jupiter took a huge swarm of ants, which he had caught sight of in a nearby oak tree, and gave them to his son transformed into humans. From this they were named Myrmidons, since <term>myrmex</term> <note>original: "μύρμηξ"</note> is the Greek word for "ant." **Strabo** <note>An ancient Greek geographer and historian.</note>, however, records in Book 8 that the Aeginetans were not born from ants, but received this name because they lived in caves and dug-out hollows after the manner of ants. Eustathius, in his commentary on Book 11 of the *Iliad*, thinks they were named after the hero **Myrmidon**. In that passage, he mentions both the mythological story and Strabo’s opinion.

### P E L A S G I A N S.

**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note> has recorded in his *Description of Arcadia* that first in Arcadia, **Pelasgus** was appointed to the supreme command because he excelled others in the beauty and strength of his body, as well as the excellence of his mind. For Pelasgus was the first to devise little huts so that men might be safe from cold and heat; next, he invented tunics made from animal skins, which were still used in Euboea and Phocis even in Pausanias's time. Because of these extraordinary virtues, the region itself was named **Pelasgia** and the people **Pelasgians**. Eustathius writes that Pelasgus was the son of Eumon and Larissa, and that his brothers were Phthius and Achaeus; from Pelasgus came Pelasgia, and Pelasgian Argos, and so forth.

beginning, was unknown in the time of the Patriarch Abraham and the first monarch of Assyria; and yet **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church known for his *Chronicon* or "Book of Times."</note> in his *Book of Times* puts forward that under the reign of **Ninus**, son of Belus, there was one **Europs** who commanded the **Sicyonians** <note>Inhabitants of Sicyon, an ancient city-state in the Peloponnese.</note>, who was the son of **Aegialeus**; and at that time the Sicyonians held dominion over all of Greece. And if the history of **Troy** has any truth to it, according to what **Herodotus**, **Thucydides**, and several other ancient authors believe, one finds no historian whatsoever who, before this Trojan War, makes much account of the Greeks, or who relates that this nation made itself known in general under the title of **Greeks** <note>original: "Gregeois"</note>; rather, each nation tried to advance itself and carry its own name, and to hold actual sovereignty over its neighbors. For although the poet **Homer** makes **Agamemnon** the Colonel and chief of the Greeks, yet each city, country, and Prince held their own place and prepared their own equipment for the common cause and defense, and to avenge the injury done to the King of Sparta, **Menelaus**. This is amply verified by Thucydides in the preface to Book 1 of his *Greek Histories*, reporting that before the Trojan War, **Hellas** <note>The native name for Greece.</note> did nothing as a whole, and that the entire country had not yet been graced with this name: seeing as before **Hellen**, son of **Deucalion**, this name was unknown, and each people had their own name, and the Greeks even called themselves **Pelasgians**. So it was that those who were true Greeks bore the name of **Hellenes**, and the others had their particular appellations, without being placed or numbered among the **Barbarians** for that reason. As for this word "Greece" given to the whole region, it came—as **Pliny** says in Book 4, chapter 7—from the King of the country named **Grecus**, just as from Hellen the country had been called Hellas. But I do not know from where Pliny fished this up, given that **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note>, a very diligent researcher of the antiquities of all Greece, does not speak of this King at all, and **Suidas** <note>Refers to the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> testifies that the Greek land took the name of Greece from a village bearing that title. From wherever the name may have taken its origin, it has nonetheless had such an extent that whatever misfortune followed this nation, and whatever alterations it felt, its name has remained with it.

Now these **Hellenes** were called **Achaeans** and **Myrmidons** by the aforementioned poet Homer, although some have since held that only **Thessaly** bore the name of Greece. Be that as it may, here are the names most known and formerly used among the Greeks to recognize one another in their divisions, leagues, and factions: namely, **Achaeans**, **Dorians**, **Argives**, **Danaans**, **Dolopes**, **Hellenes**, **Ionians**, **Myrmidons**, and **Pelasgians**. The Achaeans had this origin: **Xuthus**, son of **Aeolus**, took **Creusa**, daughter of **Erechtheus**, in marriage, by whom he had two children, **Ion** and **Achaeus**. The elder, Ion, was Lord of **Athens** and the **Attic** country; but Achaeus, stained by the blood of his subjects, was constrained to flee to Thessaly, and making himself master of the country, he called the inhabitants by his name. From this it later happened that **Corinth** being in **Achaia**, and being the richest city in Greece, the rest of the Greeks were named Achaeans, and Greece bore the name of Achaia; although, as Pausanias says in Book 7, only the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> and **Argives** among all the **Peloponnesians** bore the name of Achaia as a special privilege. The **Dorians** were so named by **Dorus**, son of Hellen, who having gone out...

But it is likely that the **Argives** were named after the capital city of the country, called **Argos**, regardless of the claim that they bear this title from **Argus**, son of **Apis** <note>original: "l'Apride"; likely referring to the lineage of Apis, a mythological king of Argos.</note> and **Niobe**. However, **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note> in Book 2 gives him another source, saying that **Argos** and the Argive Region took the name from **Argus**, grandson of **Phoroneus** and born of one of his daughters; he provides a long discourse on this history, which can be read in his *Corinthiaca* <note>The section of Pausanias's *Description of Greece* covering Corinth and Argos.</note>.

Now, because the Argive Princes once held almost the Empire of all Greece, it also happened that—either because the city of Argos was in the middle of Greece or because of the power of its Princes—the whole country bore the name **Argolis** <note>original: "Argie"</note>, and the inhabitants were called **Argives**. After this, **Danaus**, King of Argos, having more strength than the Kings his predecessors, desired that his subjects—who previously called themselves **Pelasgians** <note>original: "Pelagiotes"; the Pelasgians were the indigenous people of Greece before the arrival of the Hellenes.</note>—should bear the title of **Danaans** <note>original: "Danaes"</note> in remembrance of him, and for the perpetual memory of his glory and greatness. An edict for this was published throughout Greece, so much so that both the Greeks and the Latins have adopted this name of Danaans when wishing to mention the Greeks in general.

Now this Danaus had come from **Libya**, being the son of **Belus** and **Antinoe**, and having a brother named **Aegyptus**, from whom the Egyptian country takes its name. But a dissension having arisen between the brothers over the sovereignty, Danaus, having put his brother's children to death, fled to Greece. Arriving at Argos, **Gelanor** <note>original: "Helenor"</note>, who commanded there, gave Danaus a share in his Lordship, who (as has been said) desired that his subjects bear his name. This is why the poet **Virgil**, in nearly all his verses where he mentions the Greeks, gives them no other name than Danaans—whether he is referring to the antiquity of the name or wishes to blame them for the betrayals of this prince.

The **Dolopes** were in **Thessaly**, from whom both the Thessalian country was named **Dolopia**, and the City of **Clymene**, **Dolopis**. Over this country once reigned **Peleus**, who left the region to **Phoenix**, his kinsman, who had come to visit him, placing his son **Achilles** in his hands to be instructed. Thus, in the **Trojan War**, the Dolopes were under the charge of Phoenix, and the **Myrmidons** under the leadership of Achilles, according to the report of **Homer** in Book 9 of the *Iliad*.

As for the **Myrmidons**, according to **Strabo** in Book 8, they are **Phthiotes** and **Aeginetans**, who were so called not because they were descended from ants <note>original: "formis"</note> emerging in squadrons from a tree and changed into men, as the Greek fables claim, but rather because they lived in grottoes and underground places, just as do the ants, which the Greeks call in their language **myrmex** <note>original: μύρμηξ</note>. Others hold that they were so called by an ancient Lord and Hero named **Myrmidon**, which is quite likely, since other nations have also partly taken the name of those who first commanded them; regarding which one should see what **Eustathius** <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop of Thessalonica known for his commentaries on Homer.</note> writes on Book 2 of Homer’s *Iliad*.

Previously, we have cited ancient authors mentioning the **Hellenes** <note>original: "helleniens"</note> and why they were so called; but having since researched other reasons for this name, we have found that there was in Thessaly a city named **Hellas** <note>original: "Hellade"</note>, having taken this name from a King who commanded there, and from which all the Greek country was later named. Others hold that the Greeks received this title from a certain giant named **Hellech**, who was descended from the race of **Japheth**, son of **Noah**, and who had been present at the undertaking...

**Pausanias**, in Book 8, or *Description of Arcadia*, writes that a certain person of the Arcadian nation named **Pelasgus** (whose race this Author does not declare, much less who his father and mother were, though some make him the son of **Jupiter** and **Niobe**), being a most excellent man, handsome, noble, and industrious above all others of his time, was elected and chosen to command his country of **Arcadia**. The Greeks were induced to do this because they had neither the wit to clothe themselves, nor the skill to build houses to inhabit and defend themselves from the severity of the weather and the fury of wild beasts, nor did they have the wit to use letters. This man was the first who taught them to erect small dwellings and rustic huts crudely built; he also taught them to make clothing and robes from the skins of swine <note>original: "peaux de pourceaux"</note> sewn clumsily together, and showed them how to sustain themselves—in place of herbs and roots, which were sometimes unpleasant to their taste and harmful because of their venom—with acorns proceeding from oaks, and he made them practice the use of letters. Then, a long time after, Pelasgia and the Pelasgians were named Arcadia and Arcadians, after a King of that region named Arcas, son of Callisto, daughter of Lycaon. It is even certain that before Hellen, son of Deucalion, the Greeks themselves called themselves Pelasgians, according to the report of Herodotus <note>The "Father of History" (5th century BC).</note> in Book 1 of his *Histories*, and Thucydides in the preface of Book 1 of his *Histories*. Indeed, both Gaul and Italy saw Greek colonies in their lands; as for Spain <note>original: "Heſpagne"</note>, it is a certain thing that various waves of Greeks populated it in the past, as can be gathered from the ancient chroniclers of Spain. And so that even the Scythian barbarians would not be without a taste of Greek sweetness, one finds in Arrian's work on the Euxine <note>The Black Sea.</note> and Xenophon's Book 4 of the *Expedition of Cyrus* <note>The *Anabasis*, describing the journey of Greek mercenaries.</note>, that the Greeks built cities among the Scythians, just as they also did in the very deserts of the Trebizond country <note>original: "Trapeſontin"; the region around the city of Trapezus on the Black Sea.</note> according to the report of the poet Ovid in Book 3 of the *Tristia*. And since the Athenians were among the most daring in making such journeys, they also built more beautiful cities than all the rest of the Greeks, and were the fathers of the Ionians in Asia. > <note>original: "Et antiqua quidem illa diuifio inter Atticos atque Afianos fuit..." This is a famous passage from Quintilian’s *Institutio Oratoria*, discussing the "Attic" (plain and refined) versus the "Asian" (ornate and boastful) styles of rhetoric.</note> And indeed, that ancient division was between the Attics and the Asians, when the former were held to be concise and sound, whereas the latter were considered inflated and empty. In the former, nothing was superfluous; in the latter, judgment and moderation were mostly lacking. Some, whose school of thought this is, believe this happened because, as the Greek language gradually flowed into the nearby cities of Asia, those not yet sufficiently skilled in speaking lusted after eloquence. Therefore, they began to express in a roundabout way those things which could have been designated directly, and then they persisted in that. To me, however, it seems the difference in speech was made by the nature of both the speakers and the listeners: because the Attics, being refined and sharp, would tolerate nothing empty or redundant. The Asian people, otherwise more tumid and boastful, were inflated by a vainer glory of speaking. Soon, those who divided these styles added a third, the Rhodian type, which they want to be a sort of middle ground and a mixture of both. For they are neither as concise as the Attics nor as abundant as the Asians, so that they seem to have something of the nation and something of the founder; for Aeschines <note>An Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes.</note>, who had chosen this place for his exile, brought there the studies of Athens, which, like seeds sown in a different climate and soil, degenerated and mixed that Attic flavor with a foreign one. Some are therefore considered slow and relaxed, yet not without weight, resembling neither pure springs nor turbulent torrents, but gentle pools. Again, nothing is more famous than Laconic <note>The style of the Spartans (from Laconia), known for being very brief.</note> brevity in speaking and writing. See on this subject what T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1509–1564), a Swiss Orientalist and linguist.</note> writes in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*.

> Divine History in Genesis 11 <note>The "Table of Nations" is actually found in Genesis 10; the author or his source likely conflated the genealogy with the Tower of Babel story in chapter 11.</note> makes it certain that the sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Meshech, and Tiras. By these the islands of the nations were divided in their regions, each according to his own language and families in their nations. These are enumerated more extensively by Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his works on geography and heresy.</note> in his exposition of the Catholic faith, which he titled *The Discourse Secured by an Anchor* <note>Original: "orationem anchora firmatam," referring to the *Ancoratus*.</note>, and by Procopius in his commentaries on the book of Genesis.

These points are laid out by the aforementioned author to demonstrate, first, the great antiquity of both the Greek language and the people who spoke it in ancient times, as well as the status and extent of the regions where it was once the common and familiar tongue.

But it is a very difficult thing to know if the first and most ancient Greeks used the same and similar letter characters, twenty-four in number, which we use at present in Greek books written by hand and printed in various places—such as France, Italy, Spain, and Germany, as well as other regions of this World. For the Greek characters we have at present are quite different and unlike the old and ancient Greek characters. These exist in three distinct styles found engraved and in relief here and there on old medals, cameos, ancient marbles, and bronzes, which we shall represent in illustrations hereafter.

” The Greeks, who try to establish the antiquity of their race with myths when they cannot do so with reason, possessed letters before the Deucalion flood <note>In Greek mythology, a great flood similar to the biblical Deluge; Deucalion was the son of Prometheus.</note>, according to the testimony of Diodorus, who writes that Actis, son of the Sun, set out from Greece for Egypt and passed on the principles of astrology; but when Greece was overwhelmed by the flood, the records of these letters were destroyed. Many centuries later, Cadmus, son of Agenor, bringing letters back from Phoenicia to Greece, was considered their inventor. To these, during the Trojan War, Palamedes added four based on the flight of cranes: θ, ξ, φ, χ <note>theta, xi, phi, chi</note>. An equal number were added by Simonides Melicus: ζ, η, ψ, ω <note>zeta, eta, psi, omega</note>. Aristotle, however, thinks there were eighteen ancient letters, with two added later by Epicharmus: θ and χ. Hence, they are called the 'daughters of Cadmus' by Ausonius. Herodotus in Book 5 of his *Histories* writes that Cadmus shared letters with the Greeks along with many other sciences, which the neighboring Ionians mixed with their own and called by the common name 'Phoenician.' He testifies that he saw examples of these in Boeotian Thebes in the temple of Ismenian Apollo, engraved on tripods, which were similar to Ionian letters. For the Ionians certainly call goat and sheep skins *bibloi*, which they used to write upon in the past due to a shortage of books—that is, *diphtherai* <note>original: "Græci, qui generis antiquitatem... dyphtherarum, inscribebant." Diphtherai refers to prepared animal skins used as parchment.</note>.

Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist who wrote *De Inventoribus Rerum*, a history of discoveries and "firsts."</note>, in book 1, chapter 16, of *On the Invention of Things*, seems to have written as much on the subject when he says the following, following the grammarian Lactantius [in his commentary on] the 4th book of the *Thebaid*.

Where the same Diodorus, a little later, speaking of letters (concerning the first inventor of which I see there is great debate among good authors), seems to wish to attribute the invention to the Egyptians, speaking in this manner: The Egyptians affirm that it is they who invented letters, the course of the stars, geometry, and several arts and sciences. Some say it was a certain man named Menon who was the inventor in the land of Egypt. But it must not be forgotten that among the Egyptians, instead of letters, they used certain characters containing the images of animals, with which they expressed the concepts of their souls <note>A reference to Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, just as I shall declare when speaking of obelisks. Pliny, in book seven, chapter 56, says that he has always judged that letters were found by the Assyrians, and that Cadmus, son of Agenor, was the one who first brought these sixteen letters from Phoenicia into Greece: A, B, C, D, E, Z, I, L, N, O, P, R, S, T, V. To these, during the Trojan War, Palamedes added these four, shaped thus: θ ξ φ χ. After him, Simonides Melicus invented an equal number in this form: ψ ζ η ω, the power of which is recognized among our own. Aristotle says that the ancient letters were eighteen in number, namely: A B Γ Δ E Z I K Λ M N O Π P Σ T Υ Φ. And he says that Epicharmus, and not Palamedes, added two to them, as Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A 15th-century Italian diplomat and scholar.</note> testifies. Some say it was not Cadmus, but the Phoenicians who first carried letters into Greece, having arrived with the said Cadmus; or that it was not him at all, but that this happened many centuries later. ...came into Greece in the company of Cadmus <note>In Greek mythology, the Phoenician prince who founded Thebes and introduced the alphabet.</note>, among whom were the Gephyreans <note original="Zephirees">A clan of Phoenician origin who settled in Boeotia with Cadmus.</note> while they stayed in that region; besides several arts and sciences that they introduced into Greece, they also brought there the letters which are now used by the Greeks. Previously, it seems to me, the Greeks had no knowledge of them; and these were the first letters, which all the Phoenicians still use now. The same is confirmed by Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian.</note> in his sixth book, saying: "For those who say that the Phoenicians, having learned the letters from the Muses, gave them thereafter to the Greeks, mean that it was those who crossed with Cadmus into Europe, from which it happened that the Greeks called these 'Phoenician letters'." This is why the poet Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD), author of the epic *Pharsalia*.</note> says in his third book,

> *If common renown must be believed,*
> *The Phoenicians were the first to dare invent,*
> *And mark figures for the still-rough voice,*
> *So that our concepts endure for all hours,*
> *And for all time.*

The same Diodorus clearly shows in book 6, chapter 13, that it was not Cadmus who was the first to give letters to the Greeks, who had them long before, when he says: "At the time when Actis <note original="Attin">Duret likely refers to Actis, one of the Heliadae (sons of the Sun/Helios), who according to Diodorus fled to Egypt after a murder and founded Heliopolis.</note>, son of the Sun, having passed into Egypt, had taught astrology to the Egyptians, eventually Greece was devastated by the deluge <note>The Great Flood, often associated in Greek myth with Deucalion.</note>; many thousands of men perished, and the records of letters fell into oblivion. This provided an argument, after many centuries had passed, for people to estimate that Cadmus, son of Agenor, was the one who first introduced letters into Greece; so the Greeks, led by a common error and ignorance, feel themselves his debtors in that they attribute this invention to him." Furthermore, Josephus <note>The Jewish-Roman historian Flavius Josephus.</note> in the first book of *Against Apion*, asserts that before Homer, the Greeks had no letters whatsoever, saying thus: "After this there arose a great question and debate as to whether they had used letters in all antiquity, etc."

This has moved some personages to say that it is not improbable that at the beginning of the establishment of Greek letters, the ancient Greeks used these first characters, and that thereafter others proceeded or emanated from the pattern and model of these, given that we see how our own handwriting has changed and shifted over the last three or four hundred years, and the characters of printing also for the last hundred or hundred and twenty years. The most ancient authors who have wished to concern themselves with treating antiquity assure us, as I have already noted in the chapter above, that the first and ancient Greeks took and drew the majority of their Greek letter characters from the Assyrian or Phoenician letters. The Phoenicians were, according to the common saying of the said Greeks, the first who invented the characters of the Greek letters and the vermilion <note>A bright red pigment, here referring to the ink used for ancient inscriptions or manuscripts.</note> for writing, according to the testimony of the poet Lucan:

> *The Phoenicians were the first, if fame is believed, who dared*
> *To mark the voice that will remain with rough figures.*

The historian Herodotus, in the fifth book of his *Histories*, seems to confirm this antiquity of Greek letters as proceeding from Cadmus <note>According to Greek legend, Cadmus was a Phoenician prince who introduced the alphabet to the Greeks.</note>, when he says that the Phoenicians brought several sciences to Greece, and principally letters, which before them were unknown to the Greeks. These first letters were the very ones used by the Phoenicians. The Greek author Xenophon seems to agree with this in his *Equivocals*, mentioning five different men named Cadmus, as does Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon.</note> in his works under the entry "Cadmus." However, Diodorus Siculus, in Book 6, Chapter 13, speaks of it differently, saying that Cadmus did nothing more than renew them, as the Greeks had lost the use of them due to the flood that occurred in their country. Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and writer of the 6th century.</note>, in Book 8, Chapter 12, speaking of these letters, writes the following:

> And so that we may appear to offer something carefully researched, the more common opinion holds that Mercury, the restorer of many arts, is said to have first gathered these [letters] from the flight of Strymonian birds <note>Strymonian birds refers to cranes from the Strymon River.</note>; for even today, cranes that fly in formation describe the shapes of the alphabet by nature's teaching, in which order etc. <note original="Et vt aliquid studiosè exquisitum decere videamur has primum vt frequentior tradit opinio, mercurius reparator artium multarum, volatu strymoniarum auium collegisse memoratur:nam & hodie grues qui classem consociant, Aphabeti formas natura imbuente describunt, quem in ordinem &c.">This passage reflects the ancient belief that the formation of migrating cranes inspired the shapes of certain letters.</note>

Archilochus in his works, Xenophon in his *Equivocals*, Myrsilus of Methymna, Berossus the Elder, and Annius of Viterbo <note>A 15th-century Dominican friar known for his "Antiquities," which contained many forged historical documents.</note> write that the ancient Greeks derived their letter characters from the Celts and Gallo-Greeks. This is confirmed by Guillaume Postel <note>A famous 16th-century French polymath and linguist.</note> in his treatise on Phoenician letters, asserting that several centuries before Cadmus, the Gauls had the use of letters, and that Sarron, King of the Celts, was the first who opened schools in Gaul to teach these letters. Josephus, in his book against Apion the Grammarian, maintains that the Greeks used no letters before the time of the poet Homer. Marcus Tullius Cicero in his *Brutus*, and Eusebius of Caesarea in the tenth book of his *Preparation*, deny this for many reasons too long to detail; among others, they argue that we read in antiquity of several books having been composed in Greek characters and the Greek language long before the poet Homer, such as those by Linus, Philammon, Thamyris, Amphion, Orpheus, Musaeus, and others whom I mention hereafter when speaking of Homer and his writings. André Thevet <note>Thevet was a 16th-century Franciscan explorer and writer.</note>, in Book 14, Chapter 5 of his *Cosmography*, reports according to the histories of the Levant that the last man to bear the name of Homer—a native of the island of Negroponte <note>Modern Euboea, Greece.</note> living 450 years after the Great Homer—was the one who reformed the Greek letters and reduced them to more beautiful and pleasing shapes. And afterwards, in the following Book 18, Chapter 8, he continues that a certain person native to Samos named Pyrach Caleb invented Greek letters, according to the modern Asiatic Greeks. But without wandering too far afield, we can assert that just as the prophet Moses had (as I noted previously) two kinds of characters—one for sacred things, namely Hebrew, which is what we have, and the other for profane things like justice, policy, commerce, and similar worldly affairs, and therefore vulgar and used by all the Jewish people—this is held to be the Samaritan script, used by the ancient Chaldeans, which was later communicated to the Phoenicians. From Hebrew came Syriac and Arabic, and from Phoenician, Greek was born and fashioned—

...quently the Latin [alphabet], which consists entirely, or nearly so, of Greek capitals, as one can see and as Pliny testifies in Book 7, Chapter 58. There, he mentions an ancient bronze tablet brought from Delphi to Rome bearing this inscription here:

->Nausikrates the Athenian dedicated me.<-
<note>original: "ΝΑΥΣΙΚΡΑ ΤΗΣ Ο ΜΕΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΜΕ ΤΕΘΕΙKΕΝ."</note>

By this, he strives to prove that the ancient Greek letters were almost the same as the Roman or Latin ones. In the preceding Chapter 56, he states these letters were Assyrian, or according to others, Syriac. However, they are undoubtedly Samaritan—which, except for <term>Aleph</term> and <term>Yod</term> (two mysterious characters), are so similar to the Greek and Latin ones if one considers and takes them in reverse <note>The author refers to the transition from the right-to-left direction of Semitic scripts to the left-to-right direction of Greek and Latin.</note>, that they are almost the same thing. This is further confirmed by Eusebius through the very naming of the Greek letters; following the imitation of <term>Chaldaism</term> <note>Referring to Aramaic linguistic influence where nouns often end in an "a" sound.</note>, an "A" was added to most as their ending, along with some transpositions in others: such as *Alpha* instead of *Aleph*, *Betha* for *Beth*, *Gamma* for *Gamel* or *Gimel*, and *Delta* for *Daleth*, etc.

Therefore, it is certain that these Greek letters proceeded from the Samaritan ones we represented in a figure above in the chapter on the Samaritan language. If one considers and takes them in reverse, they are both almost the same thing. The reason for this inversion was, according to some authors, that Noah—or Janus <note>Renaissance scholars often identified the biblical Noah with the Roman god Janus, the god of transitions and beginnings.</note>—and his children, having set out from the East to go to the West, did so because the movement of the West (that is, of the planets) is carried from the left to the right. Since the <term>primum mobile</term> <note>In the geocentric model, the outermost sphere that moves the entire heavens from East to West.</note> was contrary to this, they endeavored—in conformity with the Western movement of the heavens—to invert the use of the letters they had brought from Phoenicia. This seems to be recognized by Suidas, a Greek author describing the life of Abraham, and by Eusebius through the naming of the Greek letters, which, in imitation of Chaldaism, had an "A" added to the end of most, with some transpositions, such as *Alpha* instead of *Aleph*, *Betha* for *Beth*, *Gamma* for *Gimel*, *Delta* for *Daleth*, and so on. Regarding what is deduced above, one may consult Raphael Volaterranus in Book 33 of his *Commentaries*; Polydore Vergil in Book 1, Chapter 6 of *On the Discovery of Things*; Alessandro Sardi in Book 1, Chapter 1 of *On the Discovery of Things*; and Guillaume Postel in his treatise on Phoenician letters or ancient characters of the Greek and Latin languages. Furthermore, the Greeks at their arrival were very coarse, crude, and barbaric, as related by Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle. The first among them were the Athenians, who became civilized and polished both themselves and their language, which they brought to perfection in the time of Plato, Aristotle, Isocrates, Demosthenes, Aeschines, and other learned Greek personages. These are mentioned by Cicero in his *Brutus*, all the Greeks having been so copious and abundant in words that they came to produce, through their inventions and traditions, four languages: the Attic, Doric, Aeolic, and Ionic. From each of these, the Greek poets—choosing and electing various words and figures as it best suited their fancy—gave birth to another called "Common"...

### LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE. 667

...after all, a single name refers to all five <note>The author refers to the five principal dialects: Attic, Ionic, Doric, Aeolic, and the Common (Koine) dialect.</note>, the Greek language, with everyone always considering the Athenian or Attic dialect to be more elegant, fluent, and eloquent than the others.

This Greek language gained credit, reputation, and esteem through its elegance, sweetness, eloquence, and richness; through the philosophy which was treated therein alongside all manner of arts, sciences, and disciplines—as stated by St. Chrysostom and C. Heresbachius <note>Conrad Heresbach (1496–1576), a German humanist and advisor to the Duke of Cleves.</note> in their orations in praise of Greek literature. It spread through the voyages and colonies of the Athenians and through the arms of the Macedonians <note>Referring to the conquests of Alexander the Great.</note>, who, ruling far into Asia—specifically in Syria and Egypt—made their language understood in many diverse regions of this universe. So much so that, according to Cicero in his *Oration for Archias*, it was in his time known, read, and recognized by almost all the nations of the world. What is more, the old and ancient Hebrew Testament, translated into the Greek language by the Seventy Greek Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, and the New Testament, first written and composed in Greek by the Evangelists, have made this language known in infinite places across this universe. See Louis le Roy, book five of *The Vicissitude of Things* <note>Loys Le Roy (1510–1577), a French humanist professor known for his work on the cyclical nature of history.</note>, regarding the comparison of Greek knowledge to that of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Persians, Indians, and others; and the comparison of the philosophers of Greece with the Chaldeans of Babylon and the priests of Egypt; and the comparison of the Greeks with the Persians, Indians, and the Nomads of Syria and Arabia, concerning Greek eloquence, poetry, and history.

T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1509–1564), a Swiss Orientalist and linguist.</note>, in his *Commentary on the common character of all languages and letters*, made such a judgment regarding the Greek and Latin languages:

> If one adds the Greek language to the Latin, he will receive from both the seeds of many other arts. Thus, moving from those languages, he will not come to any art as a raw or new student. Indeed, he will draw speech from those authors in whom there are not only words—nor could there be. For it is necessary that many things from other disciplines be sprinkled throughout. By the same effort, he will learn both the Greek and Latin languages. Add to this that Greek is extremely learned and rich. And just as the Latin language can instruct and assist others with its abundance, so Greek increases and adorns both Latin itself and others; it is as necessary for the perfection of Latinity as Latin is for Italian or Spanish. Nor was anyone ever absolutely skilled in the Latin tongue unless he was also imbued with Greek: for from the Greek language flowed the Latin, and from the Latin flowed the Italian, Spanish, and French—nations for whom the Latin language was once the vernacular. Thus, we find by experience that the Latin language becomes more fertile and eloquent through the Greek, and from Latin come the rest of the languages of Europe, but especially those three I just named. It would be most advantageous for people to become accustomed to the Latin language, both so they might rightly understand it and all arts through it, and so they might return their own native speech from it—like more abundant water derived from a fountain—purer and wealthier. Furthermore, many things are committed to memory in Greek letters concerning history, the nature of things, private and public customs, medicine, and piety, which are drawn more easily and more purely from the original sources themselves. <note>original: "Si quis Latinæ linguæ Græcam adiūxerit... hauriuntur & purius."</note>

In the Greek language, there are great depths and vast labyrinths...

It is a very certain thing that peoples and nations, in passing from country to country, alter and change their customs, languages, religions, kingdoms, and domains: the victors seize everything beautiful they find in the lands of the vanquished, erasing their titles or destroying out of envy what they cannot carry away, in order to abolish their honor and virtue, so that only their own might be celebrated. Thus do the Turks act today as they rule over Christians; in the same way did the Goths, Alans, Huns, Vandals, Suebi <note>original: "Sueniens"</note>, Heruli, Lombards, and other peoples of old. These conquerors, at many different times, took over countries and regions whose languages they disdained; neither understanding nor knowing how to read them, they altered and corrupted them, creating new ones through the commixtion and mixing of their own languages with those they found. This happened because the poor people remaining after such migrations learned the language of the cruel and inhuman usurpers to use with them, making themselves more agreeable subjects.

Furthermore, these barbarians, relating everything to war and thereby despising the sciences and disciplines, burned the libraries and books that had been preserved, in which the learned and scholarly had recorded their names and memories. Thus, with the loss of languages followed the loss of the sciences and disciplines written in them. From this has come a great ignorance in this universe, which has lasted a long time. And from there has come—namely, from grammatical Greek—the vernacular Greek of today; from Latin came Italian, Spanish, and French (where one finds, at least in Spanish, several Arabic words because the Arabs and Saracens held the Spains for a long time); from grammatical Arabic came the vernacular and Moorish language used from Syria to the Strait of Morocco, which is as close to its source as Italian is to Latin. From German and French came English; from Arabic came Moorish; from Tartar came Turkish (related to each other like Italian and Spanish). And thus, from those which are in use today, others are being made and will be made in the future.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF

...that in one and the same country and language, differences in speaking and pronunciation appear in a short space of time, it is nonetheless true that there are everywhere those who are more elegant and eloquent: such were the Athenians in Greece, the Romans in Italy, and today the Tuscans [in Italy], the Castilians in Spain, the Saxons in Germany, the Persians in Asia, and the noble courtiers and the learned and scholarly in France.

Synonyms, <term>Συνωνυμία</term> <note>original: "Synonyma"</note>, the commonality of names and verbs as interpreted by Aristotle in Book 3, Chapter 2 of his *Rhetoric to Theodectes*, and Romanus Aquila in his works, who say that the Greeks used these figures in their Greek tongue when they saw and recognized—in order to speak more eloquently and more articulately in their said language, the most beautiful and excellent in the world among all others—that the dignity and excellence of a description could not be distinctly and properly signified and expressed by a single word or verb. In place of which, they made it a custom to use several nouns and verbs, in order to express it and give it to be understood more easily. Hermogenian <note>Likely referring to Hermogenes of Tarsus, a 2nd-century rhetorician</note> calls these figures <term>ποικιλίας ἢ ὀνομάτων</term> <note>original Greek: "poikilias ē onomatōn"</note>, varieties or rather diversities of names. The Greek grammarians, in this regard, call names and verbs that are dissimilar in letters and vowels, yet possess the same energy and meaning, <term>Συνώνυμα</term> <note>Synonyms</note>; these are what the Latins call "Univocal" <note>original: "Vniuoca"</note>. Among the Greek poets, Aeschylus used these the most, as Aristophanes remarked. I can boldly say that there is no language in the world so full and abundant in synonyms as Greek, as Julius Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian and sophist</note>, a Greek author, demonstrates to all those eager for the Greek language in his book of *Onomastics* (a dictionary of Greek synonyms), and as Joachim Camerarius does in his *Commentary on the Ornament of Synonyms*. I shall not linger to take the trouble of citing any Greek passages in this regard. Beyond these synonyms, we find in the Greek language <term>ὁμώνυμα</term> <note>Homonyms</note>, which the Latins call "equivocal"; <term>πολυώνυμα</term> <note>Polyonyms</note>; <term>ἑτερώνυμα</term> <note>Heteronyms</note>; <term>ὁμογενέα</term> <note>Homogeneous words</note>; <term>ἑτερογενέα</term> <note>Heterogeneous words</note>; <term>ὁμοιοειδέα</term> <note>Words of similar form</note>; <term>ἑτεροειδέα</term> <note>Words of different form</note>; and others explained by Greek grammarians and philosophers in several places, and after them by Fabius Quintilianus <note>The Roman rhetorician Quintilian</note> in his works. See Julius Pollux, Book 8 of the *Onomasticon*; Martin Rullandus the German in his book of *Greek Synonyms*; Henri Estienne <note>The famous Renaissance scholar and printer</note> in his great *Greek Treasury* under the word <term>συνώνυμα</term> <note>synonyms</note>; and Pierre Grégoire, Book 2, Chapter 5 of his *Syntax of the Miraculous Art*. Furthermore, synonyms are called *Nirdafim* in Hebrew, meaning "of consequence" <note>original: "de consequentia"</note>. Father Louis in his *Globe*, Book 2, Chapter 2, says in this regard that we have a certain Hebrew author who composed a book titled *Ohel Moed* <note>The "Tent of Meeting," a work on Hebrew synonyms by Solomon ben Abraham Urbino, 1480</note> concerning Hebrew synonyms.

Epithets, <term>ἐπίθετα</term> <note>Epitheta</note>, according to the opinion of Aristotle in the third book of the *Rhetoric to Theodectes*, chapters 2 and 3, and Hermogenian, are adjectives placed beside substantive nouns, as if one were to say <term>παρὰ τὸ ἐπιτίθεσθαι τῷ ὀνοματικῷ</term> <note>meaning: "placed beside or added to the noun"</note>, added to substantives for the ornament and embellishment of a speech. Macrobius in Book 1, Chapter 2 of the *Saturnalia* says: "An adjective, which the Greeks call an <term>epitheton</term>..." <note>original Latin: "Adiectiuum quod Græci ἐπίθετον vocant"</note>. Quintilian, in his eighth book, sixth chapter, says: "For the epithet—which we correctly call an appositive <note>original: "appositum"</note>, and which is called 'the follower' by some—provides ornament; poets use them more frequently and more freely, for it is enough for them that the epithet agree..." <note>original Latin: "ornat enim ἐπίθετον quod recté dicimus appositum, à nonnullis sequens dicitur, eo Poetæ & frequentius & liberius vtuntur, namque illis satis est conuenire"</note>

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

...to come from the word to which it is attached: Theodore Gaza <note>A 15th-century Byzantine humanist and translator</note>, instead of the term **Epithets** <note>original: "Epitheta"</note>, uses **Adjectives** <note>original: "Adiectitia"</note>. Therefore, **Epithets** are rhetorical figures or adjective ornaments, which are placed and set before substantive nouns with wonderful grace and beauty for three reasons and considerations. The first is to discern and know the name of a thing that is found in two places, or which signifies two meanings. The second is to demonstrate the property of the thing. The last is for the ornament and embellishment of the thing. Epithets differ from <term>Antonomasia</term> <note>original Greek: "$\alpha\upsilon\tau\omega\nu\upsilon\mu\alpha\sigma\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$" (autonomasias), a figure of speech where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name</note> in that Epithets are always placed and arranged in conjunction with a substantive noun, as I have already said. Antonomasias are placed and arranged on their own in place of a proper and particular name, as Fabius Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman educator and rhetorician</note> explains more amply in several places in his works. If there is a language in the world abundant in Epithets, it is Greek, as those who set themselves to read Greek authors can judge, and principally Homer and Pindar, who hardly use substantives in their works without immediately accompanying them with admirable and excellent adjectives, which we may otherwise call Epithets. I will not recite the passages from them at present, because I have not decided in this place to cite all the elegances and refinements of the Greeks, which can be seen by reading their books. See Varinus Phavorinus <note>Guarino Favorino, author of a major Greek dictionary in 1523</note> in his Greek dictionary and commentary on the entire Greek language, and Henri Estienne <note>A renowned 16th-century French scholar and printer</note> in his great *Thesaurus of the Greek Language* under the words **epitheton** and **epithetos** <note>original Greek: "$\epsilon\pi\acute{\iota}\theta\epsilon\tau\omicron\nu$" and "$\epsilon\pi\acute{\iota}\theta\epsilon\tau\omicron\varsigma$"</note>.

**Metaphors** <note>original Greek: "$M\epsilon\tau\alpha\phi\omicron\rho\alpha\acute{\iota}$", Latin: "metaphoræ"</note>, metaphors or "translations" <note>In the classical sense of "carrying across" a meaning from one word to another</note>, as Aristotle explains amply in Book 3, Chapters 2, 3, 10, and 11 of his *Rhetoric* and in his *Poetics* (and also Theodectes <note>A 4th-century BC Greek rhetorician and tragic poet</note>), are figures or tropes by which we mention one thing through a similarity, not by its own proper word or name, but by a dissimilar one. We can otherwise say these metaphors occur when nouns or verbs are transported and transferred from their own proper place to another, where their particular word is lacking, and where the transposed word is more eloquent and natural than the proper one itself.

> ->Cicero in Book 4 of the *Rhetoric to Herennius* <note>A fundamental Roman textbook on rhetoric, long attributed to Cicero but now thought to be anonymous</note>: "A metaphor [translation] occurs when a word is transferred to some thing from another thing, because it seems it can be rightly transferred due to a similarity," <note>original Latin: "Translatio est cùm verbum in quandam rem transfertur ex alia re, quod propter similitudinem rectè videtur posse transferri"</note> etc.<- This form or figure of speech is of great force and efficacy, and is very much practiced in several forms and manners in Greek poems and orations, as the aforementioned Cicero explains amply in the place cited above, and in the third book of his work *On the Orator* <note>original Latin: "de Oratore"</note>.

Verrius Flaccus <note>A Roman grammarian of the 1st century BC</note> says: "A metaphor is what the Greeks call it; we [call it] translation <note>original: "translationem"</note>, that is, a word borrowed from home <note>original: "domo mutuatum verbum"</note> which we use." These metaphors ravish and carry away the readers or listeners silently where they desire, and stir them with strange movements with great delectation and pleasure, as Cicero remarks in his *The Perfect Orator* <note>original Latin title: "Orator"</note>: "From every kind [of figure], metaphors will be the most frequent, because through similarity they transfer minds and bring them back and move them here and there; which movement of thought, being quickly agitated, delights of its own accord; and other things from the arrangement of words which are taken as lights bring great ornament to the oration." <note>original Latin: "Ex omni genere frequentissimæ translationes erunt... qui motus cogitationis celeriter agitatus per se ipse delectat..."</note> This same author in the treatise *On the Orator* has written many beautiful things about these figures, which bring a great enrichment, in

Quintilian, after having premised in chapter 6 of his 3rd book that Hermagoras <note>A Greek rhetorician of the 2nd century BC</note> was the first to teach metaphors and translations <note>The author uses "translation" in the archaic sense of "transferred meaning"</note>, says the following in chapter 6 of his eighth book: *Let us begin with that which is both the most frequent and by far the most beautiful; I speak of "translation" [metaphor], which is called "metaphora" in Greek, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Incipiamus ab eo qui cum frequentißimus est, tum longè pulcherrimus, translationem dico, quæ metaphora Græcè dicitur, &c."</note>. In short, we find no forms or properties of speech more sublime, excellent, and admirable—according to the report of Cicero in the third book of *The Orator* cited above—than metaphors. These are otherwise named by the Greeks <gloss>naming figures</gloss> <note>original Greek: "σχήματ' ὀνοματώδη" (schemat' onomatode); figures that give names to things lacking them</note>, which are figures of speech difficult to handle and express, and with which Demosthenes is greatly filled (having been criticized for this by Aeschines). The same is true of Plato, Thucydides, Homer, Pindar, and other Greek authors, who have left almost no comparison or metaphor of anything in the world worthy of note that they have not used to embellish and illustrate their writings. This can be seen more particularly by reading them, although we find that Hebrew authors also use them in their works regularly, along with allegories, parables, various and obscure enigmas, as well as epitaphs, emphases, hyperboles, amplifications, and other types of figures and ornaments. This is evident from reading Hebrew and Chaldean <note>Aramaic texts, often associated with biblical commentary</note> writings, as is amply verified by several Hebrew examples drawn from the Hebrew scriptures by *B. Arias Montanus* <note>Benito Arias Montano, a famous 16th-century Spanish scholar and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> in his treatise *On the division of things from which secret speech is established and symbols are sought* <note>original Latin: "diuisione rerum ex quibus Arcanus instituitur sermo ac symbola petuntur"</note>, along with Latin authors, though not as often as the Greeks.

Cicero and Fabius <note>Quintilian's middle name was Fabius</note> in the places cited above, Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*, and Henri Estienne in his treatise on the *Conformity of the French and Greek Languages* all agree on this. Concluding this curious research here, I will only remark that metaphors engender and produce other figures that the Greeks call <term>catachresis</term> <note>original Greek: "κατάχρησιν" (katachresin); the use of a word in a way that departs from its strict meaning</note>, abuses, allegories, similes, and others mentioned by Marcus Tullius Cicero in his *The Orator*, Fabius Quintilian in book 8, chapter 6 cited above, and in several other places in his works; Varinus Phavorinus <note>Guarino Favorino, a Renaissance lexicographer</note> cited above, and Henri Estienne in his great *Thesaurus of the Greek Language* under the words *catachresis* and *metaphor*.

**Various Tenses.** Those who have tasted even a few elements of the Greek language are not unaware that it surpasses and excels over other languages in that it is adorned and illustrated by various tenses and numbers in its verbs. # LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

...actions of two persons only <note>The "Dual" number, used when referring specifically to a pair, distinct from singular (one) or plural (three or more).</note>, while the singular and plural indicate those of one or many: all of which ornaments and embellishments are not seen in the verbs of the Hebrew language, as those who wish to make the attempt may perceive by comparing the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin grammars that are found today. It is true that the Greek language recognizes no gerunds or supines <note>Latin grammatical forms used to turn verbs into nouns or express purpose.</note>, but in their place it uses infinitives, to which it adds neuter articles. It has this unique and fitting quality: it very often uses one of the aforementioned tenses for another, as Guillaume Budé <note>A famous 16th-century French humanist and scholar.</note> proves in his commentaries on the Greek language—a thing we see practiced in Hebrew within the Hebrew Prophets quite often, as confirmed by Elia Levita <note>A renowned Renaissance Hebrew teacher and scholar.</note> in his *Chosen Book*, and Michael Neander <note>A German scholar and philologist.</note> in his *Questions on the Hebrew Language*.

The Hebrews have three parts of speech: the noun, the verb, and <term>milah</term> <note>Hebrew: מלה</note>, that is, a co-significative word, under which the indeclinable parts and the pronouns are included. The Arabs also have three parts of speech: <term>Phael</term> <note>Arabic: Fi’l</note> the verb, <term>Ismi</term> <note>Arabic: Ism</note> the noun, and <term>Herph</term> <note>Arabic: Harf</note> the particle, which three parts of speech are found in the Oriental languages. The Rabbi who disputes against Khosrow <note>Likely a reference to Judah Halevi’s *Kuzari*, though the author identifies the king as Persian rather than Khazar.</note>, King of Persia, asserts—in the passage where he proves that all the languages of this Universe proceeded from Hebrew—that the Greek and Latin languages, in their first beginnings, had only these three parts of speech. See on this subject Quintilian <note>A famous Roman educator and rhetorician.</note>, book 1, chapter 6.

### Its Cases. 
The Greek language has a certain number of cases beyond the singular and plural, more than Latin: namely, the Dual Numbers, which it names in its own language <gloss>dual numbers</gloss> <note>original Greek: αριθμοὺς δυϊκούς</note>. In this, it agrees somewhat with Hebrew, which also has certain nouns adorned with Dual numbers besides the singular and plural. And although some have remarked that the Latins are not destitute of them (as Marcus Fabius Quintilian refers at some length in book 1, chapter 5 of his *Institutes*), we must nevertheless learn that the Duals of the Latins are found only in verbs, and even then are uncertain at every turn. This is contrary to those of the Greeks, which are regularly encountered in all Greek verbs and nouns, unless they are imperfect. Diomedes <note>A 4th-century Latin grammarian.</note> writes in his first book that the most ancient Greeks had no Duals, but rather that they are an invention of the moderns, because the ancient Greek authors most often used the plural for the Dual in their works, as demonstrated by the verses of Homer cited by this author. All Duals in the Greek language signify only two persons and no more; and these Duals, when placed within nouns, have only two forms proper to them: their nominative, accusative, and vocative share one, while their genitive and dative share the other. It is true that this language recognizes no ablatives, but in their place it uses its genitives and datives as eloquently and elegantly as Hebrew and Latin can use their ablatives.

And a thousand other beauties: the virtue of the Greek language depends on several sorts of accents or "spirits" named the acute accent, the grave accent, the accent...
