...circumflex, aspirated <note>The "rough breathing" mark (spiritus asper)</note>, smooth <note>original: "tenue"; the "smooth breathing" mark (spiritus lenis)</note>, apostrophe, hyphen, and hypodiastole <note>A mark used to distinguish words that might otherwise be read as one</note>, which are shaped in various ways as those well-versed in this language know very well. Their power and beauty are particularly declared by the Greek author Demetrius Chalcondyle <note>A major Greek scholar of the Renaissance who taught in Italy</note> in his Grammar, by Theodore of Gaza in his books on the Institutions of Grammar, by Clenard <note>Nicolaes Cleynaerts, a Flemish grammarian</note> in his Greek Grammar, and by René Guillon in his *Enchiridion of Greek Accents*, in his annotations on Clenard’s grammar, and in his *Isagoges* <note>Introductory manuals</note> on the Greek language, as well as by Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*. 

Meanwhile, Hebrew also has its own accents, thirty-four in number, variously named and shaped as I have stated above and will say more fully hereafter. This language and Greek surpass Latin in this regard, as in others; Latin has sought in some places to claim accents for itself, but with very poor grace, as can be seen in Quintilian, Book 1, Chapter 5 of his *Oratorical Institutions*, Diomedes in Book 2, and Isidore in his *Etymologies*. 

It is a miraculous thing, the beauty and enrichment provided by accents in this Greek language, which would have no grace or excellence if it were stripped and destitute of them. Furthermore, its perfection depends on the articles—masculine, feminine, and neuter—which are placed and arranged before each noun, whether masculine, feminine, or neuter, as well as before the infinitives of verbs. This is done with much more grace than in Hebrew, which uses four letters—<term>bekalam</term> <note>בכלם: The letters Bet, Kaph, Lamed, and Mem, used as prefixes to indicate prepositions or relationships</note>—very elegantly and with an admirable brevity, placed at the front or head of their infinitives to express what other languages do through their gerunds, supines, and subjunctives <note>Latin grammatical forms used to describe verb-based nouns or secondary actions</note>. As Michael Neander teaches in the fourth part of his *Questions on the Hebrew Language*, this said Hebrew language, in place of those Greek articles, uses before its indeclinable nouns—masculine, feminine, and common—its letters <term>mem, aleph, lamed, he, het</term> <note>מ, א, ל, ה, ח</note>, enriched and illustrated with various points underneath. 

Both of these languages surpass Latin in this, which recognizes none, although it seems that *hic, haec, hoc* <note>Latin: "this" (masculine, feminine, neuter)</note> have such power and virtue. Indeed, it is known that the Greek language is adorned in most of its nouns by inclined forms, enclitics, syneuclitices <note>Grammatical terms referring to how accents shift or merge when words are used together</note>, synaereses <note>The blending of two vowel sounds</note>, and crases <note>The contraction of two vowels into one</note>, along with ligatures, joins, and abbreviations of letters in its writing that are very agreeable and fine. It possesses something rare and marvelous among all other languages: namely, the five Dialects or properties of speech—Attic, Doric, Aeolic, Ionic, and Common. The Attic was so named, according to the report of John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator</note>, after Attis, daughter of Cranaus; the Aeolic from Aeolus, son of Hellen; the Doric from Dorus, son of Hellen; and the Ionic from Ion, son of Xuthus. The Common dialect participates in all four together. 

The properties of these Dialects are fully described by John the Grammarian Philoponus, John Tryphon the Grammarian, and Corinthus in their grammars, and by Plutarch in the treatise on the Dialects found in Homer. Of these Dialects, the "passions" <note>Linguistic transformations or alterations of words</note> found in their diction are divided into quantity and quality. The types of quantity are divided into <term>endeia</term> <note>Greek: "deficiency" or the omission of a sound</note> and pleonasm <note>The use of more words or sounds than necessary for clarity</note>; those of quality are divided into metathesis <note>The transposition of letters or sounds</note> and metalepsis <note>A complex form of substitution</note>. These make five passions in total: pleonasm, <term>endeia</term>, metathesis, metalepsis, and tmesis <note>The separation of parts of a compound word by an intervening word</note>. Pleonasm is a superabundance or superfluity of time and elements; <term>en-</term>

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE
<header>LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.</header>

...[En]deia <note>original: "Endeie"; from the Greek *endeia*, meaning a deficiency or omission of a letter or syllable</note>, a defect or reduction of time or of an element. Metathesis, a transposition or change of an element from its proper place to another, which is otherwise called <note>original Greek: ἐνάλλαξις & ὑπέρθεσις</note> enallage and hyperthesis—meaning "exchange" or "substitution." Metalepsis, a "transsumption" <note>a change in the meaning of a word or the substitution of a term</note> or change of an element. Tmesis, a section or resolution of a compound word into two separate terms. 

The types of Endeia are nine in number: Apheresis, Arsis, Systole, Syncope, Synalepha, Ellipsis, Parellipsis, Ecthlipsis, and Apocope. 

**Arsis** is a removal <note>original Latin: "sublatio"</note> or rejection at the beginning of a doubled syllable. **Systole** is a shortening <note>original: "correption"</note> when long syllables are made short and short ones long. **Syncope** is a trimming or a rejection of a syllable in the middle of a word. **Synalepha** is a contraction or a union of two syllables into one vowel through the delivery of a tone in seven different ways. **Ellipsis** is a defect or rejection of a vowel in the middle that does not form a full syllable. **Parellipsis** is an omission of doubled consonants. **Ecthlipsis** is an elision or rejection of a consonant between two syllables. **Apocope** is a trimming of a syllable at the end of a word. 

The types of Pleonasm <note>the use of more words or parts of words than are necessary for clear expression, often for rhetorical effect</note> are also nine in number: Prothesis, Anadiplosis, Ectasis, Epentasis, Diaeresis, Parenthesis, Diplasiasmus, Parempitosis, and Proschematismus. 

**Prothesis** is the opposite of Apheresis; **Anadiplosis** is the opposite of Arsis; **Systole** is the opposite of Ectasis; **Syncope** is the opposite of Epentasis; **Synalepha** is the opposite of Diaeresis; **Parenthesis** is the opposite of Ellipsis; **Diplasiasmus** <note>original: "Diaplasme"</note> is the opposite of Parellipsis; **Parempitosis** <note>original: "Peremptose"</note> is the opposite of Ecthlipsis; and **Proschematismus** is the opposite of Apocope. 

**Prothesis** is an addition or joining of an element at the beginning of a syllable. **Anadiplosis** is a doubling or a second pronunciation of the first and second syllables by using the same consonants. **Ectasis** is a lengthening <note>original: "production"</note> of short syllables into long ones, or the shortening of long ones into short. **Epentasis** <note>original: "Epectase"</note> is a superabundance of a syllable in the middle of its accent. **Diaeresis** is a division, resolution, or separation of one syllable into two. **Parenthesis** is an interposition or addition of a vowel that does not form its own syllable. **Diplasiasmus** <note>original: "Diaplasme"</note> is a doubling or addition of a consonant in the middle of a word that does not make a new syllable. **Parempitosis** <note>original: "Peremptose"</note> is an equal division or addition of consonants in the middle that do not complete the syllable. **Proschematismus** is an addition of a syllable at the end.

There are still infinite other beautiful details and singularities of ornament in this language, which are shown more specifically (following the Greek authors previously mentioned) by Quintilian in his works; Constantine Lascaris in his *Erotemata* <note>original: "Droictemates"; one of the first Greek grammars printed in the West</note>; Brother Urbain in his *Institutions of Greek Grammar* <note>Urbanus Bellunensis, a tutor to Erasmus</note>; Manuel Moschopulus in his books on *Attic Dialects* <note>original: "voix Attiques"</note>; Linacre in his book on *Greek Grammar*; Georg Fabricius in his *Grammatical Divisions*; Raffaele Volaterrano in book 34 of his *Commentaries*; Julius Caesar Scaliger in his books on *Poetics*; and Valentinus Erythraeus in his *Grammatical Figures*, and infinite others treating this subject; Urbanus Bellunensis in his *Greek Institutions*; and P. Grégoire in book 16 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. 

In most of these details and singularities of ornament, the Hebrews are not trained at all, as Benedictus Arias Montanus <note>a Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> teaches in his *Common and Familiar Idioms of the Hebrew Language*. From the above, it follows that we know that Plato in his *Cratylus* <note>a dialogue on the philosophy of language and the naming of things</note> strives (but in vain) to derive the character of Greek names from an imitation of Hebrew ones, as Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Italian Neoplatonist philosopher</note> also does in his Com—

In the first decade, these Pythagoreans included simple numbers <note>1 through 9</note>; in the second, the tens; and in the third, the hundreds. When wishing to divine something, they took the name they wished to test, and after dividing it, they calculated and converted it into numbers and values. > *That some are of greater numbers, and others small,*
> *Whenever they face the doubtful perils of battle,*
> *Whichever side stands with the greater number, victory favors,*
> *The smallest numbers are omens of death, the highest [omens of life],*
> *Thus they say Patroclus perished by Hector’s hand,*
> *Thus they say Hector soon fell to Achilles.*

This is demonstrated at length in book 2, chapter 20 of the *Occult Philosophy* by the aforementioned Agrippa, and in the book by Caspar Peucer on the *Principal Types of Divinations* in the section on Lots. They perverted all the mysteries of the Christian faith under the shadow of their transpositions of Greek letters, constructing and assimilating a number and body which they called "Truth." They persuaded themselves that without this mystery, one could not find the sense of the celestial word in the Gospels, as reported by Irenaeus in book 1 *Against Heresies*, chapters 9 and 10, and Epiphanius in *Heresies* 34 and 35. But we Christians will utterly reject these damnable curiosities, which are entirely contrary to Religion, seeing as it is very certain that if this Science had been of such great recommendation, our Lord Jesus Christ would not have failed to teach it to us in His Church. ->Concerning the poet Homer and his writings composed in the Greek language.<-

Many ancient authors hold that the Greek poet Homer is the first and most ancient writer to have ever existed among the Greeks. However, this is denied by Aristotle in his *Poetics*, Aelian in his *Various History*, Pausanias in his *Description of Boeotia*, Josephus in book 1 *Against Apion*, Eusebius in book 10, chapter 3 of his *Preparation*, Justin Martyr in his book *Against the Greeks*, Theodoret in book 2 of *On the Healing of Greek Affections*, and Athenagoras the Christian philosopher in his works. They maintain that before this poet flourished in Greece, there were Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Demodocus, Phemius, the Sibyls, Epimenides of Crete, Aristeas of Proconnesus, Asbolus the Centaur, Isatis, Drimon, Horus of Samos, Protenidas of Athens, Philammon, Thamyris, Olenus, Amphion, Olympus, Orebantius of Troezen, Syagrus, Dares the Phrygian, and others. These figures had composed and published works in the Greek language before him, dealing with divine, celestial, natural, moral, political, and military matters, as well as music and the secret doctrine of numbers. 

Tatian and Suidas, Greek authors, seem to agree with this, writing that Homer drew all the subject matter for his poetry from the Greek works of one Eveclus and a Corinnus; the latter was an Iliensian heroic poet and a disciple of Palamedes, who was the first to write an *Iliad* during the Trojan War, which greatly served this same Homer. Indeed, it is a well-established fact, according to the report of Solinus, that this poet inserted into his poems several verses from those of Daphne, priestess of Delphi—as confirmed by Diodorus Siculus in book 5, chapter 7—and from those of the Sibyls, as has been well and curiously noted by Gilbert Génébrard in his writings on Perionius’s book on the *Lives of Holy Women*, and in books 1 and 2 of his *Chronography*. 

Saint Clement and Justin Martyr go much further when they assert in their works that this poet was aided by the Hebrew writings of the Prophet Moses, which he had seen in Egypt, where he had traveled for that purpose. This poet was first named Melesigenes, and later <term>Homeros</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμηρος</note> for two reasons (according to the report of Suidas): one because, during the war between the Smyrneans and Colophonians, he was given as a hostage <note>The Greek word "homeros" means hostage</note> between them; or because he spoke divinely to the Smyrneans as they deliberated on a matter, giving them good counsel to wage war. Others say it was because he was blind <note>Another Greek dialectal meaning for the word</note>, but the best reason is that he was so named Homer because he was never conquered or overcome by greed <note>or worldly desire</note>, which proceeds principally from the eyes. His parents are uncertain, though many strive to write of them, including Aristotle in the third book of the *Art of Poetry*, and Plutarch in the...

This uncertainty moved the grammarian Didymus <note>Didymus Chalcenterus, a scholar in Alexandria known for his prolific writing</note> to compose 4,000 books on the contradictions among Greek authors regarding this question, as Seneca writes in book 13 of his *Letters*, Letter 89 <note>Seneca's Moral Letters to Lucilius, typically cited today as Letter 88</note>, recounting many peculiarities of this poet. The time in which he flourished is also uncertain: for some write that he lived in the year 3150 from the creation of the world; others say 3560. Some say 120 years after the destruction of Troy; according to Herodotus, 168 years after the said destruction; according to Crates, 80 years after; and according to Archilochus, 500 years after. Aulus Gellius in book 17, chapter 21, and Plutarch in his works say it was 140 years after the aforementioned destruction. Cornelius Nepos says 160; Solinus 272. Following Suidas and several other ancient authors—among whose number are Saint Cyril in book 1 *Against Julian*, and Philochorus in book 1 of the *Stromata* <note>a "miscellany" or "tapestry" of various topics</note>—they speak of it quite differently, as Matthew Beroalde <note>a 16th-century French chronologist</note> notes very well in book 4, chapter 5 of his *Chronicle*.

His poems or poetic works are the *Iliad*, the *Odyssey*, the *Hymns*, and the *Battle of the Frogs and Mice*. The *Iliad* was not composed by him all at once, but at several and diverse times, leaving now one book here and now another there. Being thus scattered, they were gathered and put in order, along with the books of the *Odyssey*, by Pisistratus, the Tyrant of Athens (according to Cicero in book 3 of *On the Orator*), or by his son Hipparchus, as reported by Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* and Aelian in book 8 of his *Various History*. Some other authors attribute this to Aristarchus, who, by the command of the aforementioned Pisistratus, corrected the <term>rhapsody</term> <note>the collection of epic songs</note> of this poet and was the first to divide it into 24 parts, corresponding to the number of letters in the Greek alphabet. After all these, Zenodotus of Ephesus—a grammarian, poet, and disciple of Philitas, and tutor to the children of King Ptolemy I—corrected them and put them back in order, according to the aforementioned Suidas.

These poems and poetic works are filled with many Greek words and phrases from every Greek dialect, as Plutarch discusses in his treatise on the dialects found in Homer. We read in this same author, in the *Life of Lycurgus*, as well as in Heraclides’ treatise *On States* and Aelian in the 13th book of his *Various History*, that the first person to bring these poems from Ionia to the Peloponnese—where they were in the hands of the successors of Creophylus—was Lycurgus. Solon, having collected them all, placed them in a public location with an ordinance that each book should be read and recited in order at every Greek festival, as affirmed by Julius Caesar Scaliger in book 1, chapter 41 of his *Poetics*, and Caelius <note>Lodovico Ricchieri, also known as Caelius Rhodiginus</note> in book 7, chapter 29 of his works. As for the other Greek poems or writings by Suidas and Gyraldus...

### On the Philosopher Plato and his writings composed in the Greek language.

Julius Firmicus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman senator and astrologer</note>, having taken the trouble to calculate and draw up the horoscope of the Philosopher Plato, wrote that he found through its computation that this personage was born by nature to be most eloquent, and endowed with a celestial spirit and understanding for comprehending all the secrets of the supreme divinity. To this point, the Greeks have asserted that while he was still in his cradle, a swarm of bees was found to have placed its honey within his mouth; this presaged the future eloquence of this great figure, as recounted by Aelian in book 10 of his *Various History*, Pliny in book eleven, chapter 17, and Valerius Maximus in book 1. It is even said that Socrates saw in a dream a small swan in his lap, which began to clothe itself in feathers, with the help of which, soaring into the air, it came to sing most sweetly and melodiously; and that the following day, when Plato was brought to him to be instructed, he said that this was the fulfillment of his previous dream.

This Plato was first called Aristocles, but because of his broad shoulders, high forehead, and large body—or perhaps for the breadth of his speech—he was surnamed <term>Platōn</term> <note>original: "Πλάτων"; the name derives from the Greek word "platýs," meaning broad or wide</note> Plato, as Suidas and Laertius write. He was called the "Attic honey-bee," because of which Cicero, following the Greeks, said in his *Brutus*:

> Who was more abundant in speaking than Plato? For if Jupiter were to speak Greek, as the Philosophers say, he would speak just so. <note>original: "Quis uberior in dicendo Platone? Iouem sic, ut aiunt Philosophi, si Græcè loquatur, loqui"</note>

The same author in his *Tusculan Disputations* names him the God of Philosophy. Some call him the imitator of Moses, or the "Attic Moses," as he drew many beautiful things from that Hebrew Prophet; as noted (following Numenius the Pythagorean) by Josephus in his rebuttal against Apion <note>The text incorrectly cites "Apollonie Molon," referring to the grammarian Apollonius Molon whom Josephus refutes in "Against Apion"</note>, Suidas in his dictionary, Justin Martyr in his *Exhortation*, Eusebius in his *Preparation*, Theodoret in his book *On Greek Affections*, Ficino in his *Commentaries on Plato*, and Juan Luis Vives in his commentaries on book 8, chapter 11 of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*. 

This Philosopher lived and flourished in the year of the created world 3770 <note>The author uses a chronology dating from the biblical creation, placing Plato in the 4th century BCE</note>, some time after the Peloponnesian War, and lived eighty-one years, dying around the 108th Olympiad. He was so highly prized by the Greeks that Aristocles of Messene composed ten books comparing him and Homer, according to Suidas; for this reason, Cicero calls him the "Homer of Philosophers," and Quintilian says he is filled with divine and Homeric eloquence. His Greek style, according to Aristotle, holds the middle ground between prose and verse or poetry, with such sweetness and eloquence that nothing more divine or miraculous can be imagined. This moved the Father of Latin eloquence <note>Cicero</note> to say that he would rather err with Plato than hold the correct opinion with all the other Philosophers. It is no wonder if a Cleombrotus, or another listener of Hegesias, having heard certain of his discourses concerning the immortality of the soul, killed and took their own lives in order to enjoy—

St. Augustine prized him so much that in his book *Against the Academics* he wrote that if, in the doctrine of Jesus Christ, he had to use reasons and deductions, he would seek them nowhere else but in the writings of this personage: which is more than verified by St. Dionysius the Areopagite, Eusebius, and St. Cyril, saying the Platonists were true Christians, except in a few points. This is confirmed by Symphorien Champier <note>original: "Symphorien Camperius"; a French physician and humanist who sought to harmonize ancient philosophy with Christianity</note> in his book *On the Theology of Orpheus*, supported by the authority of St. Basil, St. Augustine, and others, maintaining that in some writings of this Philosopher, the Gospel of St. John was found transcribed almost in its entirety: indeed, some ancient authors write that inside his tomb was found a plate inscribed with these words, translated into English <note>original: "tournez en François" (translated into French)</note>, *I believe in Jesus Christ who will be born of a Virgin, who will suffer for the human race, and who will rise on the third day.* Many beautiful and excellent discourses of this Philosopher are detailed after Labeo, Varro, Apuleius, and other ancients by the same St. Augustine in book 7 of his *Confessions*, and in his *City of God* book 8, reporting that this Labeo numbered Plato among the demigods, that Varro assured that Plato had felt better of divine and human things than other Philosophers, and that Apuleius had estimated Plato to be not only superior to the Heroes, but equal to the gods themselves, because he alone had entered into the inner chamber <note>original: "cabinet"</note> of the supreme divinity. His Greek writings, almost all divided and split into dialogues in which his master Socrates is always introduced speaking, treating many diverse matters, have been translated from Greek into several languages and dispersed among infinite nations, which teach us the true divine Philosophy. The great Giovanni Pico della Mirandola proposed in his life to accord and reconcile the writings of this personage with those of Aristotle, as Boethius had previously undertaken: but both remained under the burden <note>meaning they died or failed before the difficult task was completed</note> before accomplishing their promise: whoever wishes to see several other things on this matter should read Pausanias in his *Attica*, Plutarch in the *Life of Dion*, Aelian book 13 of his *Various History*, Diogenes Laertius book 3 of the *Life of the Philosophers*, Aulus Gellius book 3 chapter 17 of his *Attic Nights*, Suidas in what he collected of Plato in his Greek works, Valerius Maximus book 8 chapter 7, St. Augustine book 8 chapter 4 of the *City of God*, Cardinal Bessarion in his commentaries in praise of Plato against George of Trebizond, St. Jerome volume 3 in the *Epistle to Paulinus*, Pietro Crinito book 12 chapter 1 and book 24 chapter 1 of *On Honest Discipline*, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente et vno"</note>, Marsilio Ficino in his *Commentaries on Plato*, Caelius Rhodiginus in infinite places of his *Various Readings*, Gessner and Josias Simmler in their *Historical Libraries*, Raffaele Volterrano book 18 of his *Commentaries*, André Thevet book 2 chapter 29 of *Illustrious Men*, and Louis Le Roy book 5 of the *Vicissitude of Things*.

->Concerning the historian Herodotus and his writings composed in the Greek language.<-

Herodotus, a Greek historian born of illustrious parents and a native of the city of Halicarnassus—now called Messy <note>Halicarnassus is the modern-day city of Bodrum, Turkey. In the 16th century, it was sometimes referred to as Mesy or Mausi.</note>, located at 57 degrees 50 minutes longitude and 36 degrees 10 minutes latitude, in the country and region of Caria in Asia Minor—flourished around the year 3699 since the creation of the world. <note>This "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) system, common in Renaissance scholarship, places Herodotus in the 5th century BCE.</note> Cicero, in the third book of *The Orator* and the first of his *Laws*, calls him the **Prince and Father of History** <note>original: "Principem & Patrem historiæ"</note>, because he is among the most eloquent and one of the most ancient historians among the Greeks. Strabo, in his final book, held the opinion that he wrote a false and fabulous history rather than a true and certain one, partly drawn and extracted from the Greek histories of one Xanthus the Lydian <note>A 5th-century BCE historian who wrote a history of Lydia (Lydiaca) and preceded Herodotus.</note>, who was older than he. This work is contained in nine books under the name of the **nine Muses**: which history he began to compose in the Ionic Greek language while living on the island of Samos, where he had been exiled by Lygdamis, the tyrant of Halicarnassus. Besides this history, he wrote a compendium or brief discourse in the Greek language on the **life of Homer**. These works have been translated from Greek into Latin by several and various authors, as taught by Conrad Gesner and Josias Simler in their historical bibliographies. Lucian, a Greek author, in his dialogue titled *Herodotus, or Aetion*, strove to recount how he became known in a short time to all the Greeks. Quintilian, in book 9, chapter 14 of his *Institutes*, following Aristotle’s discourse in his *Poetics*, wrote these words in praise of the Greek Histories of this personage:

> In Herodotus, while everything—as I feel it—flows smoothly, the dialect itself possesses such a charm that it seems to embrace even hidden musical rhythms. <note>original Latin: "In Herodoto cum omnia vt sentio leuiter fluant, tum ipsa dialectos habet eam iucunditatem, vt latentes etiam numeros complexa videatur."</note>

And in book 10, chapter one:

> Many have written history excellently: Thucydides is dense, brief, and always driving himself forward; Herodotus is sweet, clear, and expansive. The former is better at portraying stirred emotions, the latter at relaxed ones; the former is superior in formal speeches, the latter in conversational ones; the former in force, the latter in pleasure. <note>original Latin: "Historiam multi scripsere præclarè, densus & breuis & semper instans sibi Thucidides, dulcis & candidus & effusus Herodotus, Ille concitatis hic remissis affectibus melior; ille concionibus, hic sermonibus, ille vi, hic voluptate."</note>

This personage died having gone into exile at Thurii, one of the colonies of the Athenians, and was buried there. Some hold that it was in the city of Pella or Ieuize in Macedonia. See Cicero in his *Orator*; Strabo, book 14; Plutarch, *On the Malice of Herodotus*; Suidas in his works; Pliny, book 12, chapter 14; Athenaeus, book 12, chapter 14 of his *Deipnosophists* <note>Literally "The Banquet of the Learned," an ancient Greek work detailing a series of dinner table conversations.</note>; Aulus Gellius, book 15, chapter 23; Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*, citing Hermogenes; Jean Pontanus in one of his epistles on this author; Henri Estienne in his *Apology for Herodotus*; Victorius, book 28, chapter 21 of his *Variae*; Gilbert Génébrard, book 2 of his *Chronography*; Jean Bodin, chapter four of his *Method of History*; François de Belleforest, volume two, chapter seven of his *Universal Cosmography*; and Antoine du Verdier, book 2 of his *Prosopography*.

### On the Orator Demosthenes and his writings composed
### in the Greek language.

Those who wish to be fully informed of the parents, country, and Greek city from which this great Greek orator Demosthenes was born, should read Plutarch in the *Life of Demosthenes*, and in his treatise on the *Lives of the Ten Orators*, as well as Suidas in his works. <note>Demosthenes (384–322 BCE) is widely considered the greatest of the ancient Greek orators. "Suidas" refers to the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> This figure, a native of Athens, was aided and served in his life by the Greek orations of a certain Zoilus, or Zethus of Amphipolis, and of a Polycrates and Alcidamas, who were disciples of Gorgias and Isocrates. <note>These men were famous rhetoricians and teachers of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE who shaped the art of persuasion.</note> With these orations, he progressed so far in the oratorical art that he acquired in his time such a reputation as an eloquent man in the Greek tongue that no one before or since has been able to match him. He was a disciple of Plato, whom he heard for some time, and was a friend of Aristotle; he was so accomplished in Greek eloquence that he was esteemed to be the rule and the law of speaking well and orating well in that language. There is such force in his words, and they are so well arranged and ordered, that one could add nothing to them nor take anything away. For in the legal cases he handled and the orations he wrote, one could find no subtlety or cleverness that is not included there, nor anything more lofty, grave, eloquent, or better adorned and set down in writing that is not encountered at every turn, as Cicero maintains in his *Brutus*. <note>Cicero’s *Brutus* is a history of Roman oratory that frequently uses Greek orators as the gold standard.</note> Moreover, there are no principles for governing a Republic that cannot be found within them. These works tend not only toward utility, but toward honor and integrity, so much so that Plato and Aristotle are not found to have philosophized better in their schools than he did in the public assemblies of Athens around the year 3780 from the creation of the world. <note>This "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) date is a Renaissance calculation placing him in the 4th century BCE.</note> This we can easily see in his beautiful arguments and Greek orations printed in several places, which comprise a large, entire volume remaining from his other writings. This is why a certain person, greatly admiring the orations proceeding from the admirable torrent of eloquence from this man's mind, one day asked Cicero—the most articulate and eloquent man of his century—which of Demosthenes' orations seemed to him the best. He replied that the longest and the greatest was the one most to be prized. Saint Jerome said this brief word about him in Latin: *Demosthenes is said to have spent more oil than wine, and to have always preceded all craftsmen with his nocturnal vigils.* <note>original: "Plus olei quàm vini expendisse dicitur Demosthenes, & omnes opifices nocturnis semper vigiliis præuenisse." This refers to the anecdote that Demosthenes' speeches "smelled of the lamp," meaning they were the product of intense late-night study rather than drunken inspiration.</note> Cicero, cited above, although a great and perfect Latin orator himself, held him in such high regard and esteem that he judged him to have possessed within himself all the arts of speaking well and excellently—which all those who attentively contemplate his writings in the Greek language will confess. See what is written of this Orator by Lucian in his *Praise of Demosthenes*; Libanius the Sophist in the *Life of Demosthenes*; Ulpian the Rhetorician in his prefaces to the *Orations of Demosthenes*; Caecilius Siculus in his comparison of Demosthenes and Cicero; Pausanias in his *Description of Greece*; Quintilian in Book 10, Chapter 1; Cicero in his discourses titled *Brutus* and *On the Orator*; Aulus Gellius in Book 3, Chapter 13 and the last chapter of Book 17; Plutarch in his comparison of Cicero with Demosthenes; Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*; and Caelius. <note>Guillaume Budé was a 16th-century French humanist; Caelius likely refers to the scholar Lodovico Ricchieri.</note>

Polydore Vergil, in book 1, chapter 16, regarding the origin of philosophy and its two principles, and who it was that invented ethics and dialectics, and introduced debates through dialogues, writes of the Greek philosophers as follows: <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555) was an Italian humanist famous for his work *On Discovery* (*De Inventoribus Rerum*).</note>

Philosophy—which Cicero in book 1 of *On Duties* and the *Tusculan Disputations* calls the "Love of wisdom" <note>original: "Amour de sapience," translating the Latin *philosophia*.</note> and the desire for it, and that which seeks virtue and drives away vice—was brought to Greece, as they say, by the Greeks who learned it from barbarian and foreign nations. For it is held that among the Persians there were first the Magi (which means "Wise Men"), who flourished in that province; the Chaldeans were renowned among the Assyrians and the region of ancient Babylon. The Indians had their Brahmins and Gymnosophists, <note>Gymnosophists, or "naked philosophers," was the Greek name for certain Indian ascetics.</note> the prince and head of whose sect was a certain Buddha, <note>original: "Budde." The Egyptians hold the opinion that Vulcan was the son of the Nile and that he declared the principles of philosophy. 

Diogenes Laertius affirms that philosophy had its beginning in Greece, because the Greeks hold that Musaeus and Linus were the first wise men raised among them and on Greek soil. But Eusebius, with better reason, says in the second book of his *Preparation for the Gospel* that philosophy, as well as the rest of the arts and sciences, took its source from the Hebrew nation. From this he concludes that the Greek philosophers received their wisdom from the Jews, seeing as they lived more than a thousand years after Moses, as Porphyry testifies. <note>The argument that Greek wisdom was "stolen" or borrowed from Hebrew scripture was a common theme among early Christian apologists like Eusebius.</note> He also notes that among the Greeks the name "Philosopher" was not yet found; rather, Pythagoras was the first who named Philosophy—that is to say, the love of wisdom—and called himself a Philosopher—that is to say, a lover of wisdom. He also said that the name and effect of wisdom should be attributed to God alone, according to Lactantius in book 3, chapter 2 of his *Divine Institutes*. 

For previously, that which is now called Philosophy was called "Sophia" <note>original: "Sophie," from the Greek word for wisdom.</note>, and those who are now called Philosophers were called "Sophoi" <note>original: "Sophes," from the Greek word for wise men.</note>. Now, this philosophy had two beginnings based on the places where it was celebrated: one called Ionian by Anaximander, because Thales of Miletus was from the land of Ionia, and it was he who instructed Anaximander; the other principle was surnamed Italic, having its source in Pythagoras, who spent a long time in the study of philosophy in that part of Italy which was later named Magna Graecia [Great Greece], and is now a part of Calabria. But one must not think that there was ever a man so devoted to his particular tongue that he did not mix some words and dialects of other languages among his works. Indeed, the more learned a man was, the more he scattered diverse words, chosen from the most learned of each nation, throughout his writings. Plutarch, in a book on the life of Homer, shows this at length when he gives an ample discourse on the verses of this excellent Greek Poet, whom he praises for the variety of dialects and Greek language recognized in his poetry; so much so that the Ionians, Dorians, Aeolians, and Attics can see therein how excellent this personage was, who, like a honeybee, <note>A classic metaphor for a scholar who gathers the best "nectar" from many sources to create a unified work.</note> had gathered the flowers of all their languages together. Now, if this Greek language was once held in such high regard, this can teach us: that all the most excellent men of whatever foreign nation under Heaven have striven to possess knowledge of it. Regarding this, Herodotus in Book 2 writes that Psammetichus, King of the Egyptians, brought Greeks to Egypt to teach the children of his subjects Greek letters and the Greek language. Among the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people from the Eurasian Steppes.</note> (according to Herodotus in Book 4), Anacharsis <note>The OCR reads "Anaxarchis," but refers to the famous Scythian philosopher.</note> the great Philosopher and Prince of a great house, brought the Greek language, knowledge, and the "computations"—or rather superstitions—of Greece to the Scythians. From this, it has happened that the Gallic language has retained several phrases, filled with Greek words and idioms.

The Carthaginians also loved and cherished it, as descendants of the Phoenicians and allies of the Greeks against the Romans, as Livy assures in the third decade, Book 9.

Philostratus, the Greek Sophist, in the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, writes that when this great personage went to visit the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>From the Greek for "naked wise men," these were ancient Indian philosophers who lived as ascetics.</note> or "Naked Sages" of India, he spoke to King Phraotes, whom he found so well-versed in Greek letters and sciences that he was amazed that a man considered a <term>Barbarian</term> <note>In the classical world, "Barbarian" simply referred to anyone who was not Greek or did not speak Greek.</note> had such perfect knowledge of them. He was even more astonished when he heard the philosopher Iarchas <note>The OCR reads "Iaebas."</note> discourse in the Greek language as correctly as those who were native to the land of Greece and most learned in that tongue. Roman histories assure us that Augustus Caesar devoted himself greatly to the study of Greek letters and language, and that he stayed in Greece for a long time to gain a complete and perfect knowledge of it. He succeeded to such an extent that he composed fine and beautiful verses in this Greek language and took great pleasure in speaking Greek when conversing privately with his friends, as Suetonius Tranquillus relates in the life of this Emperor Augustus. The learned Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607) was an influential Italian historian and cardinal.</note> in the first volume of his *Ecclesiastical Annals* confirms this very well, providing sure proof that the Greek language was in common use and spoken in Rome during the time of this Emperor.

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]</header>

And who does not well know that the Romans in general sent their children to study in Athens out of the desire they had for them to learn the Greek language? Titus, son of the Emperor Vespasian, was well-versed in both Greek and Latin letters; the Emperor Alexander Severus, while at rest after hearing petitions and doing justice for his subjects, had no occupation more agreeable than reading Greek books. According to Lampridius <note>Aelius Lampridius, one of the traditional authors of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> in his biography, while dining, if something was read to him, he preferred it to be in Greek rather than in his mother tongue. The Emperor Hadrian was devoted to it more than was reasonable; Antoninus and Aurelian, as they were very learned, also had a perfect knowledge of Greek letters. 

And what is most marvelous is what Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note> recounts: that Romulus, Father of the Romans and the first King of the proud city of Rome, wrote his own deeds and the victories obtained against his adversaries in Greek. In this, one should note the desire that all have had to understand and embrace this language, the most polished and eloquent of all others. What is more, the first and most ancient Romans drew their laws to civilize their Republic from the wisdom of the Greeks; for instance, Spurius Postumius, Aulus Manlius, and Publius Sulpicius <note>These three men were part of the embassy sent to Athens around 454 BCE to study the laws of Solon before the creation of the Law of the Twelve Tables.</note> were sent to Athens to bring back its laws, as well as the ways of life, rights, and customs observed by the rest of the cities of Greece. There were also various legislators, such as the ancient King Cecrops, Draco, and Solon in Athens—one of the Seven Sages, whose laws were sought after by the Romans; Lycurgus in Lacedaemon <note>Another name for Sparta.</note>; Nicodorus in Mantinea; Zaleucus at Locri; and Minos, who gave laws and civil order to the Candiots <note>An archaic term for the inhabitants of Crete.</note>. 

But what use is it for me to say that so many great personages in olden times studied the Greek language, since the Evangelists and Apostles themselves—though Hebrews and Jews by nation, using their own Hebrew or Syriac tongue as their native and common speech—wrote the sacred books containing Christian doctrine and religion for the most part in the Greek language? This was done as much for the sweetness of the language as for the fact that almost everywhere in the world there were men instructed in it, who by this means could very easily embrace and follow the Christian religion. Furthermore, those two great Hebrew personages, Josephus and Philo—Jews by nation and learned in their Hebrew tongue above all others—nevertheless did not hesitate to write their books in Greek rather than in Hebrew, due to the perfection of that language which was so widely embraced and cherished by men of all nations. This is as Saint Jerome assures us in the preface to the second book of his *Commentaries on Galatians*. G. Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and champion of the Hebrew language.</note>, on this subject in Book 1, Chapter 5, page 25 of his *Liturgy*, reported these words:

> Durandus, in the *Rationale of the Divine Offices* <note>original: "Durant. in ration. diuinor. officior." — Referring to Guillaume Durand's 13th-century liturgical manual.</note>: In the primitive Church, the mysteries <note>original: "mysteria" — Referring to the liturgical rites or the Eucharist.</note> were celebrated in Hebrew, but in the time of the Emperor Hadrian, they began to be celebrated in Greek in the Eastern Church, etc.

This same author, in his *Chronography* on page 192, explaining how and when the Greek language was first taught in Jerusalem, says what follows: "Antiochus Epiphanes drove Onias from the priesthood and supported his brother Jason <note>Jason was a Hellenizing High Priest of Israel who encouraged Greek customs.</note>, who pledged three [thousand] talents each year..."

For they produced their aforementioned Translation according to the sense rather than according to the exact words of Holy Scripture, by the testimony of Saint Jerome.

Chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography* <note>original: "Cosmograph. vniuerselle"</note>.

See what I write regarding these aforementioned peoples and the Jacobites <note>A historical name for the Syriac Orthodox Church, following the teachings of Jacob Baradaeus</note> later on, following the opinion of Mandeville <note>Sir John Mandeville, the supposed author of a famous 14th-century book of travels</note> in his *Travels*, in the chapter on the law of the Jacobites, and other authors cited hereafter.

Pierre Belon <note>A French explorer and naturalist (1517–1564) who traveled extensively in the Levant</note>, book 1, chapter 3 of his *Observations*, speaking of the common tongue of the Greeks of today, reports these words: "The authors of all good sciences and disciplines that we revere today were for the most part born in Greece; but as fortune permits things to change suddenly, from the rich and opulent land it was anciently—well-furnished with people learned in all disciplines, and ruling by its virtue over a great part of the world—it is now reduced to such a state that there remains not a single foot of land that has not been made tributary under the yoke of the Turks, or under the servitude of the Venetians. The Turk holds the greatest part, both on the mainland and at sea. The Greeks who are under the Venetians have a somewhat better lot regarding religion than those who are tributaries of the Turk; and making a comparison of one to the other, I find that just as those who are under the subjection of the Turks govern themselves according to the Turkish way of doing things, so too those who are under the yoke of the Venetians govern themselves in the Venetian manner. All the Greeks, on both sides, live today in such a marvelous reign of ignorance that there is no city in their country where there is a University, and they take no pleasure in learning letters and sciences. All indifferently speak a language corrupted from the ancient one; nevertheless, their words approach closer to good Greek than the words of the Italians approach Latin. Those in the cities under the Venetians speak Italian as well as Greek, but the villagers speak only pure Greek; it is the same for the Greeks of the country where the Turk dominates, for those in the large cities speak Turkish and Greek, but in the villages they speak only Greek." This is confirmed by G. Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French polyglot and diplomat</note> in his book on the alphabet of the twelve languages, and by recent travelers to the Levant. In short, the Greeks of today, to whomever they are subjects, are so stupefied and hold letters in such little account that there is not a single University in the whole country of Greece; and what is worse, they do not care for their children to be instructed to know anything—indeed, among the Greek priests, you will hardly find one who knows anything more than how to read. They all speak corrupted Greek, entirely different from the ancient language. It is true that (as in times past) some speak more properly and eloquently than others: those who stay in the Venetian cities, such as in Candia <note>Modern-day Crete</note>, Corfu, and Zante <note>Zakynthos</note> or Cephalonia, speak Greek and Italian; but the peasants know only the Greek tongue, and those who are in the Turkish cities speak Greek, Slavonic <note>original: "Esclauon"</note>, and the Turkish language. Nonetheless, there are those who mock those who do not speak as properly as they do; even the inhabitants of Constantinople believe that those of the Islands could not approach their eloquence and fine speech. Although languages shift and change incessantly like all things in this Universe, and though in the same country and language a great difference in speaking and pronouncing appears in a short space of time, it is nonetheless true that there have always been some more elegant and eloquent than others; such as were the Athenians in Greece, and the Romans in Italy. ...that of the common people was less elegant than that of men of state and more refined citizens: as one can see in the Latin of Vitruvius, who was a master mason, and of Cicero, a man of Consular rank. This author, in the third book of *The Orator* <note>Original: "De Oratore". Cicero was a Roman statesman and philosopher renowned for his rhetoric.</note>, writes that in his time, the learning of the Athenians was lost in Athens, the city remaining only as a residence for studies, which the citizens themselves did not care for, but which foreigners enjoyed, drawn there somewhat by the name and authority of the city. He notes, however, that an unlearned Athenian still surpassed the most learned men of Asia—not in his words, but in the sound of his voice—and not so much for speaking well, but for speaking sweetly. Similarly (he says), there is a certain voice proper to the Roman people and to the city, in which nothing offends or displeases, and which lacks any hint of foreignness; so much so that the Romans, though studying less than the Latins <note>The "Latins" here refers to the other peoples of the Italian peninsula who spoke Latin but were not original inhabitants of the city of Rome.</note>, surpassed the most scholarly among them through the sweetness of their voices.

The Greeks living in true Greece, Asia, Italy, Sicily, and other islands had four languages <note>The author uses "languages" where we would now say "dialects".</note> as I have said before: Attic, Doric, Aeolic, and Ionic. From these, the Greeks selected words and figures from each as they saw fit, and gave birth to one called "the Common" <note>The *Koine* Greek, which became the lingua franca of the Mediterranean after Alexander the Great.</note>. Afterward, under a single name, they called all five the Greek language.

And although the Athenian dialect was more elegant and fertile than the others, scholars who were not Athenian by birth wrote only in their natural style, fearing perhaps that they could never achieve Attic purity, which was rarely and only belatedly achieved by those born elsewhere. For Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>, who had resided for a long time in Athens and was reputed to be highly articulate and eloquent, was recognized as a foreigner in his speech by an old Athenian woman. Pollio <note>Asinius Pollio, a Roman orator and historian.</note> likewise charged Livy <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note> with "Patavinity" <term>Patavinity: A perceived provincialism in Livy's Latin, attributed to his upbringing in Padua (Patavium).</term>. And Virgil, who was from Mantua, was reproached because he did not speak "Roman."

Furthermore, the further any language wanders from its natural source, the less pure and clean it becomes. Just as in ancient times the Syrians and Egyptians speaking Greek did not speak it as purely as the Athenians, neither did the Gauls, Spaniards, or Africans speak Latin as well as the Romans. But even if their words were Greek or Latin, they retained the phrasing of their own country. Thus, when speaking Greek or Latin, they were always recognized as foreigners, just as we see today with the English, Scots, Germans, Flemings, Italians, and Spaniards speaking French, unless they learned it while very young.

Now these languages, like all human things, have a beginning, progress, perfection, corruption, and an end. They are first crude, then they become polished alongside the civility of manners and knowledge; and after having lasted some time in purity and eloquence, they are altered and corrupted, and finally they perish, until through the passage of time no trace of their writing remains. In short, the Greeks were at the beginning very coarse, as Plato, Aristotle, and Thucydides say; the first among them to become civilized were the Athenians, who polished their language and brought it to perfection. It did not remain there long, but was corrupted and lost along with the liberty of the country, supplanted by the Macedonians, Syrians, Romans, and other foreigners who ruled there. Consequently, the native character and true elegance and eloquence of Greek, such as was spoken...

The strange and cruel ravages of the Arabs, Saracens, and Turks, in both Asia and Europe, drove out good letters, sciences, and disciplines from Greece, from where they withdrew to Italy and France under the guidance of several excellent individuals. Through the toil, labor, and study of these men, the sciences and doctrines—illuminated by means of the Greek language—returned to prominence and began, so to speak, to live again, having been buried and entombed in profound ignorance since the first destruction the Goths had wrought in Italy. For he translated from Greek into Latin Aristotle’s *History of Animals* and Theophrastus’s *History of Plants* in such a way that, by first softening the harshness of the Latin words, he joined them properly and then assembled or coupled them together, following the example of the composition of the aforementioned Greek language, expressing the force and virtue of the Greek words through new Latin words very skillfully, and with such a bold and successful translation that he greatly enriched the Latin language.

He composed grammatical institutions in his language which are still seen today, as well as several other books on rhetoric and other subjects.

Argyropoulos asked him what country he was from and if he understood the Greek language; to which he replied that Germany was his country and that he had learned something of the Greek language. ...it is known that the great wisdom and providence of God ensured that the Greek language had been planted throughout the extent of this great Roman Empire shortly before the time of Emperor Julius Caesar. This occurred for no other reason or occasion than that the Evangelists and Apostles, who were to write, preach, and announce His Gospel in this language, might be more easily understood by the peoples and nations destined to receive them. For this same cause, we must believe that the same wisdom and providence of God allowed the Turks to occupy Greece in the time of our fathers, so that by means of the Greeks exiled and banished from that land—refugees who retreated to Italy, France, and Germany—the Italians, French, and Germans might recognize the most beautiful and excellent discourses and secrets of this Gospel, which was first written and composed in the Greek language. This language they then taught and learned in the form and manner that has been more particularly detailed above in this chapter.

Polydore Vergil <note>Polydorus Vergilius (c. 1470–1555), an Italian humanist scholar and historian.</note> in book 4 of the *History of England*, following Werner <note>Werner Rolevinck (1425–1502), author of the *Fasciculus Temporum*, a popular universal history.</note> in the *Bundle of Times* <note>original: "Faisceau des temps"</note>, holds that Charlemagne was the first to transport the Academy to Paris. Long before, this Academy had come from the city of Athens to that of Rome; it was moved through the ministry of four disciples of the monk Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an influential English scholar and monk.</note>, named Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus, a Frankish Benedictine theologian.</note>, Albinus <note>Alcuin of York, the primary scholar of Charlemagne's court.</note>, Claudius, and Johannes Scotus <note>John Scotus Erigena, an Irish Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>. This is confirmed by Erphordiensis in chapter 69 and Cardinal Francesco Zabarella <note>An Italian canonist and cardinal (1360–1417).</note> regarding the *Clementines* <note>A collection of decrees in Canon Law.</note> in the section on Masters, question 5. Gilbert Génébrard <note>A French Benedictine exegete and historian (1535–1597).</note> speaks of it amply in book 3 of his *Chronography* on leaf 519.

Our History of France records that the late King Francis I, at the persuasion of Guillaume Budé and Jean du Bellay, first established public professors of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages in the University of Paris. Specifically, for the Hebrew language, François Vatable; for Greek, Pierre Danés of Paris. To these he added others, namely Agathius Guidacerius, a doctor of the Hebrew language, and Jacques Toussain <note>Jacques Toussain (d. 1547), a renowned French scholar of Greek.</note>, a doctor of the Greek language. Later, upon the promotion of Pierre Castillan <note>Pierre Duchâtel (c. 1480–1552), a humanist who served as the king's librarian and reader.</note>, his <term>Anagnoste</term> <note>A royal reader or librarian who read aloud to the monarch.</note>, he likewise established public professors in the Latin language, according to the confirmation of Carion in book 3 and Jean du Tillet in his *Chronicle*.

### *Hebrew language.*

Those who know and recognize the beauties, perfections, and excellences of ancient languages, and who wish to take close notice of what we have deduced and discussed above regarding these learned tongues, cannot be in any way ignorant of the fact that the Hebrew language is the least elegant, least copious, and least filled with words, nouns, phrases, and verbs of any language there is. But in place of this, that language can boast of the existence of its unadorned, unaffected, and non-variegated phrasing, which is instead pressed, tight...

-># LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.<-

...and constrained, but nevertheless diversified—or rather, to speak properly and correctly, entirely significant or mysterious—being able easily, properly, simply, and clearly to express and explain all human and divine descriptions and conceptions, just as the aforementioned Greek language does. This language consists of the beauties, perfections, eloquence, and elegances we have deduced above, principally in that it is easy and effortless to speak and pronounce, greatly satisfying the ear. It is, by the same means, copious and abundant in synonyms and all kinds of words, nouns, dictions, and verbs, with infinite other figures and phrases of eloquence and of speaking well and perfectly. For it is a most certain thing that its pronunciation is incomparably easier and simpler than that of the aforementioned Hebrew language, or any other language whatsoever, greatly delighting and ravishing the hearing with its sweetness and eloquence, and filling it also with its strength and vehemence, far better than any other language. Furthermore, it is so rich and opulent in all kinds of words, nouns, dictions, and verbs—even regarding all the arts, both liberal and mechanical—that it lends to all other languages and borrows from none. What is even more marvelous is that whenever some new thing arises that does not yet have a name, it has the means on the spot to provide and furnish it with one, without waiting for help from any other language whatsoever. This is amply confirmed by many ancient Greek authors, as well as Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist</note> in his *Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary arranged by subject matter</note>, Guillaume Budé <note>A leading French humanist (1467–1540)</note> in the first book of *On the As* <note>original: "De Asse"; a famous treatise on ancient coins and measures</note> and in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*, Henri Estienne <note>A famous French printer and classical scholar</note> throughout his *Treasury of the Greek Language* <note>original: "Theatre de la langue Grecque"; likely referring to his monumental "Thesaurus Graecae Linguae"</note>, Angelo Canini in his *Greek Grammar* printed by Morel, and Aldus Manutius <note>The famous Venetian printer and humanist (c. 1449–1515)</note> in his *Institutions of Greek Grammar*.

Theodor Bibliander <note>A Swiss Orientalist and linguist (1505–1564)</note>, in his commentary on the *Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, making a comparison of this Greek language with Latin, used these words:

> <note>original Latin: "Lingua Græca est erudita admodum & locuplex..."</note> The Greek language is extremely learned and rich; and just as the Latin language can instruct and help others with its own abundance, so Greek augments and adorns both Latin itself and others as well, and is as necessary for the perfection of Latinity as Latin is for Italian or Spanish. Nor has anyone ever been absolutely skilled in Latin speech unless he was imbued with Greek. For from the Greek tongue flowed Latin, and from Latin flowed Italian, Spanish, and French—nations for whom the Latin language was once the vernacular. And we find through usage that the Latin language becomes more fertile and eloquent through Greek, and from Latin the remaining languages of Europe, but especially those three I just listed. It would be most advantageous for these to grow accustomed to Latin speech, both so they might properly understand it (and through it, all the arts), and so they might render their own native speech purer and more opulent from it, like more abundant water derived from a fountain. Furthermore, many things are committed to memory in Greek literature—in history, the nature of things, private and public customs, medicine, and piety—which are drawn from these very sources both more easily and more purely. ❧

> Having done this beforehand, we will say that Saint John, at the end of his Gospel, made solemn mention of Traditions when he said, "There are enough other things that Jesus did, that if they were written down in detail, I do not believe the world itself could contain the books that would have to be made." <note>A reference to John 21:25</note> On this subject, the great Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> writes in a certain part of his works that Jesus Christ, the Master of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they did not want to write down lest they become common knowledge among the general public. This is confirmed by the very learned Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>An Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494) known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man"</note> in his *Oration on the Dignity of Man*. Then Rabbi Johanan, assisted by some others in the year 300, expanded it into the <term>Jerusalem Talmud</term>, which around the year 436 had its entire and perfect completion in that which is called the <term>Babylonian Talmud</term> by Rabbi Ashi <note>original: "Rabbi Assé"</note>, which the Jews have always used since, as can be seen. Nevertheless, we do not know for certain the true nature of this state <note>original: "accez" (access/fit), referring to the prophetic state or ecstasy</note>, but he who obtained it knew it well, having intervened as one who records in writing what is dictated softly into his ear, and who sets down everything that was recounted to him. Rather, they were given to establish an unvarying foundation upon which we can seat and plant a firm and assured bulwark for our belief against all the batteries and assaults of sects, heresies, fantastic inventions, and curious novelties, with which the evil spirit incessantly strives to disturb the peace of our souls and consciences. ...the infallible promise of our Savior in Saint Matthew 28: *Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age.* Therefore, it was very wisely ordained at the sixth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople in the year 681—where the Emperor was present and a certain reconciliation and agreement was made between the Greek Church and the Latin Church—that if any dispute should arise regarding the understanding of the Scriptures, no one should presume to interpret them otherwise than the lights of the Church have understood from the explanations given in their writings. We should seek the praise of adhering to them rather than anything that might come from our own workshops and inventions; for fear that in giving ourselves free rein, we might fail to achieve what we intend in our projects.

This conforms to what is expressly ordained in Deuteronomy 17: *If you perceive any difficulty and doubt in the judgment you are to pronounce, go to the place the Lord your God has ordained for you to find the Priests and Levites. Once you have been informed by them, you shall follow their opinion. And whoever is so arrogant and presumptuous as to refuse to obey what the Priest, appointed then to the ministry of the Lord your God, has decided, that man shall be put to death, and this evil shall be removed from Israel.* 

Because the malice of the enemy and the instability of our own brains cast us down at every hour without us knowing where, making us grope against the double-edged blade of the scriptures, we need a sure and faithful escort in this to lead us through this darkness toward the understanding of divine things. In regard to the human spirit, this works much like sight does for the body: if you try to strain it too much to penetrate further, or to reach something smaller and finer than the capacity of your eye allows, not only will it fail to grasp its target, but it will weaken its own strength and remain more sluggish in the future. 

In the same way, those who wish to excessively stretch their thoughts and meditation to reach the knowledge of something will debilitate their understanding; they will even make themselves less capable than they used to be. It is just as if one tried to look directly at the sun with a steady eye, without anything interposed between the two—such as a veil <note>original: "crespe," a thin silken fabric</note> or a cloth sieve <note>original: "estamine," a loosely woven fabric used for filtering</note>—to soften the overly vivid penetration of its rays. Those rays, being incomparably more powerful, would extinguish the light of the eyes. Therefore, we must soberly keep within the barriers of modesty limited for us in the understanding of the scriptures, where each person, according to their capacity and vocation, must seek a middle path. This can be no surer than what the universal consent of the Church prescribes for us, without straying from the obedience we owe it. 

Nor should we be curious to know more than we ought, as says Ecclesiastes 7, and the Apostle in Romans 11: *Do not be high-minded, but fear.* <note>original Latin: "Noli altum sapere, sed time." This is a famous warning against intellectual pride.</note> For once that boundary is broken, a terrible opening is made for infinite erroneous opinions, which then crowd into our souls and consciences—just as enemies would in large groups through the breach of a fortress, or the fury of a torrent across the fields if the dike or sluice holding it back should break, however slightly.

->Concerning the Armenians.<-

### CHAP. LXIII.

Strabo, in book 11 of his *Geography*, left a written record stating that Armenia formerly took its name from a Thessalian named Armen, a native of a city in Thessaly called Armenia. This city was situated between Pherae and Larissa. This Armen followed Jason on his voyage; after returning from Greece, he went back to the Levant <note>A historical term for the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East.</note> and conquered the Provinces of Mingrelia, Georgia, and Albania <note>This refers to Caucasian Albania, an ancient kingdom in the eastern Caucasus, not the modern Balkan country.</note>, which he populated and instructed in the superstitions of the Greeks. After Jason died, this Armen gathered the troupe of Greeks and caused the settlement of this province. From this, it happened that in ancient times the Armenians dressed, armed themselves, and spurred their horses in the manner of the Thessalians, as Justin seems to confirm in book 42 of his *Histories*. Some authors hold that Armenia was so named after the Arameans or Syrians, of whom we have previously spoken at length; they were the first to settle there, according to Guillaume Postel in his discourse on the distinguished regions that took their names from the children of Noah, and André Thevet in book 8, chapter 13 of his *Cosmography*. Others say it was named from these Hebrew words ארם מן יה <term>Aram Min Iah <note>original: "Aram Min Iah"; translating to 'Highland from God' or 'Height of God'.</note></term>, and by contraction *Armenia*, meaning the height of God. At present, this province is still called Armenia, or *Aremnoe*, without having lost its ancient name. It is true that the learned Abraham Ortelius, in his *Geographical Synonyms*, wrote the following words about it:

> Greater Armenia <gloss>original: "Ἀρμενία"; Armenia</gloss> according to Ptolemy and others; Strabo writes it with an aspiration <gloss>original: "Ἁρμενία"; Harmenia</gloss>, a region of Asia. In later centuries it was nicknamed "the Second," as is clear from the book of *Notitiae* <note>original: "libro Notitiarum"; referring to the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire's administrative organization.</note>. Arias [Montanus] in his Biblical Appendix testifies that it is called *Arias* in Hebrew. It is called Turcomania by Mercator and Girava. Thevet writes that it is called *Thoura Aremnoe*—that is, the mountains of Armenia—by the Mesopotamians and Persians, and is called *Zelbiodibes* by the Nestorians—that is, mountains inhabited by wolves. I would believe that it retains its ancient name among the Christian inhabitants. Lesser Armenia is nicknamed "the First" in the book of *Notitiae*. It is also called White Syria <gloss>original: "λευκοσυρία"; Leucosyria</gloss> by Procopius in book 1 of the *Persian War*. In the Holy Scriptures it is called Ararat. Likewise, it is called Uz, according to the testimony of Arias Montanus. Today, if Girava is correct, it is called Anaduole; if Castaldo says so, Pegian. Eustathius writes that Armenia was divided into four parts by King Justinian: the first called the Seven-cities <gloss>original: "ἑπταπολις"; Heptapolis</gloss>; the second, the Five-cities <gloss>original: "πεντάπολις"; Pentapolis</gloss>; the third, the Six-cities <gloss>original: "ἑξάπολις"; Hexapolis</gloss>; the fourth called Tzopharis <gloss>original: "τζοφαρνη"</gloss> and Balbitena <gloss>original: "βαλβιτηνὴ"</gloss>.

This Province is situated in Asia, and thus limited by Ptolemy in book 5, chapter 13, table 3 of Asia. To the North of it lies a part of Mingrelia, Iberia <note>Ancient Caucasian Iberia, modern Georgia.</note>, and Albania along the river Cur, otherwise called the Cyrus; to the West it...

[Armenia] looks toward Cappadocia along the Moschian mountains <note>A range in the Caucasus, often associated with the biblical Meshech.</note> which are part of Mount Taurus, and a portion of the Euphrates river; to the South, it borders Mesopotamia according to the said Mount Taurus, called Kurdistan <note>original: "Corthestan"</note> where it joins the Euphrates and the Tigris; it also looks toward Assyria near Mount Niphates. To the East, its limit is partly the Caspian Sea, from the place where the River Kur enters it—otherwise called the Cyrus, and formerly bearing the name Corax and Mede—up to the mouth of the Araxes near the roots of Mount Caspian. This same mountain also borders it as far as Mount Niphates. Although Appian writes that it is the Araxes river that divides this Province from the land of the Medes, the truth is that it is not the Araxes, but rather Mount Caspian that causes this separation.

Haiton the Armenian, in his *Book of the Tartars*, chapter 9, partitioned and divided this Province into four kingdoms, though almost always a single King held command there. Giosafat Barbaro, in the fourth chapter of the book of his travels in Persia, writes that the Turks first occupied it in the year 1230, taking it from the brothers Roupen and Leo <note>referring to the Rubenid dynasty of Cilician Armenia</note>, which is confirmed by André Thevet in book 8, chapter 15 of his *Cosmography*. Today, these same Turks command the greater part of it, and the Sophy <note>A traditional term for the Safavid Shah of Persia.</note> commands the other part which stretches toward Diyarbakır <note>original: "Diarbeth"</note>. 

However, the Muhammadan religion has not held such credit and reputation there that one does not find many Armenian Christians and Catholics within it. These do not use the exact same ceremonies in their Churches as we Christians do in our Roman Church, but they hold nearly—or very nearly—the same foundation of belief as ours. This can be seen in the travels of Duarte Barbosa, a Portuguese in the Indies; the travels of Brother Nicole le Huen, a Carmelite Doctor of Theology; and those of an anonymous Merchant in Persia. It is also found in the treatise on the twelve different languages and characters by the late Guillaume Postel; in book 8, chapters 13, 14, and 15 of the *Cosmography* by André Thevet; and in volume 2, book 3, chapters 7, 8, and 9 of the *Universal Cosmography* by François de Belleforest.

The Catholicos <note>The primate or head of the Armenian Church.</note> or Primate of these Armenians—named *Roa* by them and by the Turks, and *Ethasept* by the Persians—sent his profession of faith to the Holy General Council of Trent in the name of all the Churches subject to him. He submitted himself to the rule and censure of the Catholic Apostolic Church of Rome, abjuring and condemning all sects, errors, opinions, and beliefs which have been, are, or shall be condemned by this Apostolic Church. His written decree was seen by several honorable persons still living today, held in the hands of a certain Chaldean Deacon who came from Rome to this kingdom to see and note the manner and order that our Ecclesiastics observed in the celebration of divine service. 

These Armenians are the only ones among all the subjects and tributaries of the Turks who are not made or rendered into slaves and serfs by them. This is because, as they say, an Armenian once prophesied that the glory and renown of Muhammad would spread throughout the Universe. In memory of this, no one of that nation is placed into servitude by the Muhammadans, as Leonikos Chalcondyles assures in book 3 of his *History of the Turks*. However, Guillaume Postel, in his treatise on the twelve languages with entirely different characters, speaks of it differently, saying that these Armenians are held in great honor and reverence among the Muhammadans for having formerly received their Prophet Muhammad very well when he returned with his troops from the ex-

## *On the Armenian Language.*

### CHAPTER LXII.

Theodore Bibliander, in his *Commentary on the Common Reasoning of All Languages and Letters*, speaking of the language and letters of the Armenians, says the following, following Haiton the Armenian, who flourished in the year of Salvation 1300:

The Armenians have Armenian letters, and others which are called Haloen <note>Likely referring to the Caucasian Albanian script, often associated with Armenian history</note>. And because there are a thousand bishops joined to their Patriarch, whom they call the <term>Catholicos</term> <note>The title of the head of the Armenian Apostolic Church</note>, all called Christians; and in order to clearly demonstrate in how many places and provinces the use of the Armenian language extends, I will cite here the very words of Haiton the Armenian in his histories, saying that in the land of Armenia there are four kingdoms, possessed throughout time by one single and unique King. This Haiton, in chapter 9, speaking of these Armenians, says: "They have Armenian letters, and others also which are called Haloen" <note>original Latin: "Literas habent Armenicas, & alias etiam quæ dicuntur Haloen."</note>. The longitude of this land begins from the kingdom of Persia and extends toward the West as far as the kingdom of Turkey; its latitude begins from the city of Mirale, called the Iron Gate <note>Likely Derbent, the "Gates of Alexander," a strategic pass between the Caucasus and the Caspian Sea</note> at the foot of Mount Caucasus or Cocas, and reaches as far as the kingdom of Media. That the ancient language of the Armenians agrees closely with the Chaldean and Syriac languages is verified as much by the origin of these Armenians, who are descended from Aram, son of Shem <note>Referring to the biblical table of nations in Genesis</note>, as by the proper names of men, places, and other arguments. Guillaume Postel, a very learned man in this language, speaks thus of this tongue which was in use among these Armenians in the time of the aforementioned Haiton, and which is still used among them today: "Among all the languages of this Universe, Armenian is the most difficult to pronounce, since it has many things in common with the languages of the Orientals, many others with that of the Greeks, and many others still with that of the Gauls <note>Postel was known for attempting to link Armenian phonology to French/Gaulish</note>." This language, in matters concerning religion, is not only in use among these Armenians in both Upper and Lower Armenia, as is commonly believed, but also throughout all the provinces and regions of Muhammad—such as in all of Asia Minor, Syria, Tartary, Persia, and regions situated around the Pontic or Black Sea, and principally

[Frenchmen] and Venetians allied together conquered Constantinople, they performed many good services for Prince Henry, brother of Count Baldwin of Flanders, then elected the first French Emperor of Greece, while he was making war against the Greeks of Anatolia near the city of Landrimiti <note>Modern-day Edremit in Turkey</note>; it may be some 300 years ago.
