The Spaniards boast and brag that they currently possess his works translated from Italian into Spanish, divided into two parts titled *Orlando Enamorado* <note>Roland in Love</note> and *Orlando Furioso* <note>Roland Mad</note>; but I believe that this translation was drawn instead from the Italian works of Ludovico Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*—of whom I discourse amply hereafter—rather than from the works of the aforementioned Petrarch. Within the last few years, a certain person named Philippe de Maldeghen, Lord of Leyschot, had his French translation of the Italian *Sonnets* and *Triumphs* of the said Petrarch printed in Brussels, at the beginning of which he placed the lives of Petrarch and of Lady Laura.

### On Ludovico or Luigi Ariosto, Italian, and of his poems composed in the Italian language.

Ludovico or Luigi Ariosto, a native of the city of Ferrara in Italy, was the son of Niccolò Ariosto and Daria de Malaguzzi. From his tenderest youth, he devoted himself entirely to Italian poetry, preferring to be held and reputed as one of the first among the Italian poets rather than second or third among the Latin poets. In his early years, he composed in the Tuscan language <note>The dialect of Tuscany, which became the standard for literary Italian.</note> the fable of *Thisbe* and other poems—namely, Satires full of sharp and biting rebukes in the manner of the Latin satiric poets Persius and Juvenal, and also Comedies filled with pleasant and joyful discourse, as beautiful and refined as those of Plautus the comic playwright. After the trial of these subjects, having read and leafed through a great quantity of good authors, he set about putting into writing that excellent, divine, flowing, pathetic, and diverse work in Italian titled *Orlando Furioso*, containing 51 Cantos, including the five that were newly added following the others. This work is and shall forever be infinitely recommended by the most learned and scholarly men in every language.

## ON THE ITALIAN TORQUATO TASSO AND HIS POEMS
->composed in the Italian language.<-

Torquato Tasso, or Torquate Tasse, the most modern of the Italian poets, was the son of Bernardo Tasso, who in his lifetime was Secretary to the Prince of Salerno. Bernardo wrote in his time a rather large and thick volume in the Italian language titled *The Works of Bernardo Tasso*, divided and partitioned into five books, which is found in print today in Italy and which I have in my possession. It contains several various Italian poems, very graceful and delicate, such as sonnets, elegies, odes, psalms, and others addressed to several different Lords and Ladies of his time. This Torquato Tasso, son of the aforementioned Bernardo, at the age of 19 or 20, composed a very beautiful Tuscan poem in the style and manner of Ariosto mentioned above, titled *Rinaldo* <note>original: "Riualdo," a likely misspelling of Tasso's early epic "Rinaldo"</note>, containing ten *Canti* or songs, concerning the loves and deeds of arms of the said Rinaldo, which was printed in Italy. Since then, he has shown himself to be very eloquent, highly expressive, and nearly inimitable in his twenty books or songs of Italian heroic verse or poems, so diversified, sharp, subtle, polished, and eloquent, compiled into a poem titled *Jerusalem Delivered by Lord Torquato Tasso* <note>original: "Gerusaléme liberata del Signor Torquato Tasso"</note>, addressed to the Most Serene Lord Don Alfonso II <note>The text reads "XI," but Alfonso II d'Este was the 5th Duke of Ferrara and Tasso's patron.</note>, 5th Duke of Ferrara. It treats the deeds, actions, and prowess of the Christians in the conquest of the Holy Land with Godfrey of Bouillon <note>original: "Godefroy de Billon," a leader of the First Crusade.</note>. This poem, in the judgment of the most learned and skilled in languages, surpasses in grandeur of style and gravity of words—being figurative, concise, sharp, polished, and abundant in all the flowers and riches of Italian eloquence—all other Italian poems composed before it, whether those of Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia, a 14th-century jurist and poet.</note>, Boiardo, Pulci, Dante, Petrarch, Ariosto, Bernardo Tasso his father, and others. Several years ago, he was in the service of the Prince of Piedmont, then joined the household of the Duke of Ferrara, and finally joined the service of the Holy Cardinal Scipione Gonzaga in Rome, where he died some time ago.

This figure, in addition to the writings mentioned above, composed a short play about love in his native Tuscan <note>Italian</note> language titled *Aminta* <note>a highly influential pastoral drama first performed in 1573</note>, which was translated into French verse by a poet from Bordeaux, and into French prose printed in Paris by Abel l'Angelier. This poet died in Italy in the month of April, one thousand five hundred and ninety-five.

### ON THE REGION OF THE SPANIARDS AND PORTUGUESE.

Abraham Ortelius <note>a famous Flemish cartographer</note>, in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasury*, writes that *Hispania* <note>Spain</note> was formerly called *Iberia* <gloss>Iberia</gloss> and *Hesperia* <gloss>the western land</gloss>, according to the authors Strabo, Pliny, and others. Ptolemy and Stephanus write it as *Ispania* <gloss>Ispania</gloss> without the aspiration <note>the 'h' sound</note>; Stephanus also calls the same land *Pannonia* <gloss>Pannonia</gloss> <note>This is likely an error in the source, as Pannonia was a province in Central Europe</note>. The same author distinguishes it into Greater and Lesser Spain. The *Treasury* of Goltzius also mentions Lower Spain based on an ancient inscription. Horace calls it "the furthest Hesperia" to create a distinction, for Italy was also once called Hesperia. Dioscorides, in Book 5, Chapter 102, calls it "Western Iberia" <gloss>Western Iberia</gloss>.

It was formerly called *Celtiberia*, according to Appian of Alexandria. Strabo testifies that its inhabitants changed their name, having been called *Celtiberians* and *Celto-Scythians* in ancient times. He also relates from Myeleanus that they were once called *Igletas* <gloss>Igletes</gloss>. Postel writes that the land is called *Sepharad* by the Hebrews, as does Arias Montanus in his commentaries on Obadiah, where he adds that it is called *Spamia* by the Chaldeans. Josephus reports that the inhabitants are called *Thobelo* <gloss>Thobelites</gloss> <note>descendants of Tubal, son of Japheth</note>. Regarding the name *Spania* once used for this region, I discuss this under the entry for *Iberia*, which you may consult.

Spain was first divided into two provinces: *Citerior* <note>Hither Spain</note> and *Ulterior* <note>Farther Spain</note>. Later, it was divided into three: the Hither part was called *Tarraconensis*, and the Farther part was distinguished into *Baetica* and *Lusitania*, according to Pliny. From this *Iberia*, Valerius Flaccus (Book 5) derives the ethnic term *Iber*. See the entries for *Mauritania*, *Spaniards*, and *Alpini*. See also *Alpini Lusitania* <gloss>Lusitania</gloss>. This is a region of Spain according to Ptolemy and others; today it is called Portugal. Appian of Alexandria writes *Lusitania* with an "i" in the first syllable. Stephanus says its inhabitants are called *Belitani* <gloss>Belintanoi</gloss>, while Pliny calls certain peoples of Hither Spain *Bellitani*. 

But because I see that the etymology of the word *Portugal* is derived by many learned men from *Port of the Gauls* <note>Latin: portu Gallorum</note>, I thought it worthwhile to include the opinion of Osorio here. He says, based on the demonstration of the very learned André de Resende, that it takes its origin from *Caleportu*. This is the name of a small town (which overlooks the mouth of the Douro River) that used to be frequented for the sake of fishing; from there, such a great multitude of men gathered that it turned into a most wealthy city and began to be named *Portogallo*, as if it were *Portus Cale*. From this, it is seen that the whole Kingdom obtained its name. Lusitania, across the Douro River toward the North, is now called *Callaica* <note>Galicia</note>, as Strabo writes. These I [take to be] the *Gallaeci Bracari* <gloss>Gallaicoi Braikarioi</gloss> of Ptolemy and...

### On the Catalan & Spanish Languages.

Some Spanish historians hold that it is recorded in the ancient histories of Spain that certain writers believed the first and most ancient language of the Spaniards was the language of the Basques <note>original: "Biscains"</note> of today. This is primarily because this language has been kept and preserved for so long in its own purity among the said Basques, without any evidence that it has taken or received any terms from other older languages, nor from the languages of the peoples who currently inhabit the areas surrounding the land of Biscay, with whom they have formerly conversed and traded, and continue to converse and trade today. One must certainly believe that there is something very significant in this Basque language in this regard, which is why the aforementioned authors have concluded that it is one of those first languages introduced during the confusion of Babel <note>referring to the biblical account of the origin of different languages</note>, it having pleased God to keep this mark of the first inhabitants within Spain. This discourse is very amply detailed in the *New History of Spain*, Book 1, folio 4. 

Others maintain that during the time of the flourishing Roman Empire, the Latins and Romans mixed with the Spaniards and became so accustomed to the Latin and Roman tongue that it has not left the Spanish lands since that time. Indeed, the Castilian language of today is almost nothing but a corrupted Latin; consequently, from time to time, the Spaniards became such that many among them equaled the renown of the most prized and recommended among the aforementioned Latins and Romans, such as the two Senecas, Siluius <note>likely Silius Italicus, a Roman poet born in Spain</note>, Martial, Lucan, Mela <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer</note>, P. Latto <note>likely Marcus Porcius Latro, a famous teacher of rhetoric</note>, Quintilian, Columella, and others. 

There are other Spanish historians who report that in the time of Charlemagne, King of our French, who came with his people to Spain to aid the Spaniards against the Arabs and Saracens who held the said Spain, the Catalans (an ancient people of that land) came to mix regularly with the French. Because of this, the Latin and Roman language—which these Catalans and all other Spaniards previously used, employed, and spoke—became altered and corrupted among them to such an extent that from it was made and formed a language entirely different from the one then in use among the aforementioned Catalans and Spaniards. This language is hardly different from that of the peoples living beyond the Pyrenees mountains in Gaul: in Aquitaine and Languedoc <note>southern regions of modern-day France</note>. 

The majority of Spanish authors hold that their Spanish language is for the most part corrupted from both the Latin and Roman languages, as well as from several other languages of various peoples and nations who have possessed the Spanish lands at many different times over the last thousand or so years. The Basque language has been preserved in Biscay and parts of Navarre and other surrounding places, but in Granada, Andalusia, Murcia, and Valencia, especially among the peasants, the Moorish and Arabic languages <note>original: "Moresque & Arabesque"</note> prevail.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

...[is] corrupted <note>meaning a language that has evolved or mixed from its original form</note> is in great use, and has been for almost all time, that the peoples of the Spains <note>the author uses the plural "Spains" to reflect the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula</note> have used various languages very different from one another, as Turquet reports in his *New History of Spain*, Book 1, leaf 45.

A certain figure of this century, highly learned in languages, has held that the common language of Spain is hardly different from the Italian language, which the Spaniards took from them when they were subjected to the Italians. And it is not known for certain what language the Spaniards had before, although some say it was the language of the Phoenicians, as will be said hereafter. Some maintain that the Germanic language was once common to both the Gauls and the Spaniards, just as it is today to all the nations toward the North. And just as the Sarmatian language <note>an early term used here to describe the Slavic language family</note> is common to the Slavs, Bohemians, Poles, Muscovites, Russians, Bulgarians, Wallachians, Dalmatians, Illyrians, Lithuanians, and many other neighboring peoples of these nations—except insofar as it is today altered and corrupted by the invasion of the Great Turk, and was formerly confused by the arrival of the Hungarians—so one must believe that the other nations of Western Europe used one and the same language before the Roman Empire was so widely spread: namely, the Germanic tongue. This language would also have been moved and changed into the Roman tongue <note>Latin/Romance</note> if the Romans had been able to overcome that nation as easily as they did Spain and Gaul, and send back colonies and new inhabitants of their own. And one must confess that the language of the Scots, the Danes, or rather the Irish, is very different from the German or Swiss, but these agree in their foundations: which is well proven by many words that are common to both nations. Gaul also still has some traces of its [original] language, which Glarean <note>Heinrich Glarean, a Swiss music theorist and humanist</note> shows through many words and names in a book of his on this matter, as confirmed by Sebastian Münster in Book 1, in the chapter on Spain in his *Universal Cosmography*.

Besides the above, I remember having read formerly that Polybius, Titus Livy, and Appian of Alexandria demonstrate in their works that before the Germans had made their power known, and before they had any reputation, the Carthaginians had already made themselves masters of the Spains, which they possessed for a very long time. Strabo, speaking on this subject regarding the Phoenicians and Greeks, said the following:

"As the Phoenicians, Libyans, and Greeks had in the early ages stayed for a very long time in the Spains, it is also likely that their language took root and origin there, and that the Spaniards received it into their familiar and common usage; and some time later, when the Romans came and conquered the country, there was also a change from this language and the Greek language, from which point the Spaniards became accustomed to using the Latin language, without any history or memory yet proving to us that the Germans had planted their language there." ...[They] of the Spains, who planted their language in them, but here it must be confessed that the Germans were formerly in the aforementioned Spains—the Suebi <note>a large group of Germanic peoples who established a kingdom in Gallaecia (modern Portugal and Galicia)</note>, to be precise—and that they held for some time that part of the said country which now bears the name of Portugal. Being conquered by the Goths, what remained was mixed with the Romans and Goths, and thus their language was composed of a diverse mixture and commingling. Regarding this, *Lazius in Book 8 of the Migrations of Nations* <note>original: "Lazie liur. 8. des migrations des Gents"; Wolfgang Lazius was a 16th-century Austrian historian</note> says that when the Moors and Saracens arrived in the aforementioned Spains, the language of the Spaniards was further corrupted, having within it words and terms from Latin, Gothic, and Syrian languages, and from the Barbary of the Alarbes or Algarbes <note>referring to Arabic influences from North Africa and the Algarve region</note>, the memory of which is still imprinted there. And on this whole subject, one may consult *Jean Bodin* in *his Method of History, last chapter*, and *F. de Belleforest, Book Three, Chapter 28 of his Universal History*. The *Histories of the Saracens* maintain that though they conquered the Spains, they could never defeat or overcome the land of the Asturias <note>a region in northern Spain where the Christian resistance began</note>, in which, by this means, the ancient Spanish-Gothic language remained whole and uncorrupted by the language of the aforementioned Saracens, as is confirmed by *Caelius Augustinus Curio in the first book of the History of the Saracens*.

Regarding the laws of the Spains written in their own language, we will say that in the *sixth book of the Histories of Spain* it is recorded that mention is made in certain ancient Privileges—given by the first Kings of Castile to certain towns of this country—of a volume of Castilian laws according to which, in preceding centuries, justice was administered to the Castilians. It was entitled *The Book of the Judges* <note>original: "Le Liure des Iuges", known in Spanish as the *Fuero Juzgo*</note>, which was of very great authority prior to the time of King Alfonso the Wise, son of Don Ferdinand III, during whose reign the laws of the *Seven Parts* <note>original: "Septes Partidas", a celebrated statutory code of Castile</note> were introduced, according to which the Kingdom of Castile was afterwards ruled and governed. To understand what this volume is, one must know that in the time of the aforementioned Alfonso IV of that name <note>the text likely refers to Alfonso X, "The Wise", though the numbering varies in historical accounts</note>, King of Castile, around the year of our Salvation 1266, several learned men worked by his command to compile, complete, and edit into one volume the book of the laws of Castile, called in the Spanish language *Siete Partidas* (the Seven Parts), which King Don Ferdinand had begun. This was since increased by subsequent Kings with many laws, edicts, and ordinances, and was reviewed and reorganized by *Pero Lopez Alcoçer*, Doctor *Escudero*, *Pero Lopez Arrieta*, and finally by *Bartholomæo d’Athiença*, legal experts. These laws constitute the rights by which the inhabitants of the Kingdoms of Castile and Leon are judged and governed. Until the time and reign of this King, all Titles, Instruments, Contracts, and public Writings were written in the Latin language; but he was the first to have them written in the Castilian language, along with all other sorts of writings, having several books of Holy Scripture translated into that same language. For this reason, the language was greatly embellished and illustrated, as is deduced at length in *Book 12 of the Histories of Spain* cited above.

This language, besides being common and familiar throughout all the Spains, is still today understood and spoken in many—

At present, in the Island of Sardinia, there are two kinds of languages. The nobility speaks better than the simple people who live in the mountains; others speak the Spanish, Catalan, and Aragonese languages. The Royal audience <note>The high court or administrative body</note> is held in this language, and there is a Viceroy and a Regent who assists him, both of whom are Spanish, as noted by André Thevet in Book 16, Chapter 25 of his *Universal Cosmography*. Before him, Sebastian Münster, in Book 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, in the chapter on the language of the Sardinians, wrote the following:

The Sardinians once had their own language, but because various peoples have gone there to live, and foreign Princes have usurped its rule—namely the Latins <note>Romans</note>, Pisans, Genoese, Spanish, and Africans—their language has been greatly corrupted. Nevertheless, many words have been left there which are found in no other language. They still retain many words from the Latin language, especially in the mountains of Barbagia <note>original: "Barbarie"; the rugged interior of Sardinia, historically known as the land of the "Barbarians" or Barbagia</note>, where the Emperors of Rome held their garrisons, as it is written in Book 2 of the *Code of the Office of the Praetorian Prefect of Africa*. From this it comes that the Sardinians speak so differently in different places, according to the different Lords they have had, although they all understand one another. Now, there are two principal languages on this island: one used in the cities, and the other used outside the cities. The citizens use almost the Spanish, Tarragonese, or Catalan language, which they learned from the Spaniards who most often exercise the office of Magistrate in the said cities; the others retain their natural language. Here is the difference between both languages in the Lord's Prayer.

### *On Ausiàs March the Spaniard and his poems composed in the Catalan language.*

Ausiàs March, according to Lucio Marineo Siculo <note>A Sicilian humanist and historian who served at the court of Ferdinand and Isabella</note> in his histories of Spain, and Lilio Gregorio Giraldi in his *Dialogue of the Poets*, was Spanish by nationality, a native of the city of Valencia. During his life, he composed various poems in the Catalan language—the ancient language of Spain—which remained for a long time buried in darkness without anyone making much of them. However, since they have come to the knowledge of the learned and scholarly by being printed and brought to light, they have been, and still are to this day, so cherished and prized by the Spanish and those curious about the Spanish language, as the Italian poems of Petrarch, Ariosto, and Tasso <note>original: "Taste"</note> are by all Italians and those who desire to learn the pure Tuscan tongue. These poems, as I have them before me, printed in the said Catalan language, are titled:

*The works of the valiant Knight and most elegant Poet Ausiàs March, now newly revised and ordered with much diligence, and increased by many Songs.* <note>original Catalan: "Les obres del valeros Cauallier y elegantissim Poëta Ausias Marc, ara nouament ab molta diligentia reuistes y ordenades, y de molts Cants aumentades."</note>

These were printed by Claude Bornat in the city of Barcelona in Spain. They contain ninety-three Cantos or songs of love with stanzas of ten or eleven feet, after which there are six scattered and divided couplets with questions and answers titled *Scattered couplets, questions, and responses* <note>original Catalan: "Coblas esparças, demandas y repostas"</note>; fourteen moral Songs; a spiritual Song named *Spiritual Song* <note>original Catalan: "Cant spiritual"</note>; and the works of death in eight Songs called *The Works of Death, 8 Songs* <note>original Catalan: "las obras de Mort Cants. 8."</note>. The most learned and knowledgeable in the Catalan and Spanish languages maintain that were it not for the fact that this author used the aforementioned Catalan language in these poems—which are entirely filled with inventions, comparisons, and dainty and eloquent digressions and deductions—he would carry away the prize, honor, and laurel above all the Spanish writers whom I mention hereafter. This includes Juan de Mena, also a Spanish poet flourishing in the time of John, King of Castile. This poet’s work is filled, in the great Spanish volume he left before his death, with such majesty and sweetness that Juan Luis Vives <note>The famous Spanish humanist</note> did not fear to name him the Spanish poet *par excellence*, because he can be compared, regarding his Spanish language, to Petrarch. This is confirmed by Francisco Tarafa in his History, Lilio Gregorio Giraldi in his *Dialogue of the Poets*, and Josias Simler in his *Historical Library*. Besides these Spanish authors, those of that nation count a certain poet named Jorge Manrique <note>original: "George Mandrice"; famous for his "Coplas por la muerte de su padre"</note>, who has embellished his Spanish writings with gravity of thought, along with a great sweetness and fluidity of the Castilian language.

### *On Don Antonio de Guevara, a religious man, and his writings composed in the Spanish language.*

Don Antonio de Guevara <note>original: "Iean Anthoine de Gueuare." A Franciscan friar and one of the most influential Spanish writers of the 16th century</note>, a monk of the Order of St. Francis <note>original: "Cordelier," a term for Franciscans in France, named for the knotted cord they wore</note> and later Bishop of Mondoñedo <note>original: "Mõdoguette"</note>, was a great theologian and preacher, as well as the confessor and chronicler to the Emperor Charles V <note>original: "Charles le quint"</note>. He was Spanish by nationality, descended from the house and family of that lord so renowned in the histories of Navarre and Aragon, Don Ladrón de Guevara <note>A noble family name in the Basque region; "Ladrón" was an ancestral name rather than a descriptor</note>, who was a Governor or Captain in Álava, and son of Íñigo <note>original: "Ygnez"</note>, head of the House of Guevara in Álava. During his life, he composed several diverse works in the Spanish or Castilian language: namely, a book titled *The Mount of Calvary* <note>original: "le mont de Caluaire"</note> divided into two volumes on the History of the Passion; *The Contempt of the Court and the Praise of the Countryside* <note>original: "le mespris de la cour, & la louange de la vie rustique"</note>; the *Decade of the Emperors* <note>original: "la Decade des Empereurs"</note>, translated into the French language by Antoine Alaigre; four volumes of *Golden Epistles* <note>original: "epistres dorées," a highly popular collection of moral and historical letters</note>, first translated in part from Spanish into French by F. Gutierry, and since then by several others of this Kingdom in recent times; furthermore, *The Court Favorite* translated into French by Jacques de Rochefort; the *Book of Marcus Aurelius* <note>Also known as "The Dial of Princes," a fictionalized biography used for moral instruction</note>; the *Book of the Christian Prince*; and a collection or mass of sermons translated into our French tongue by several French authors. See on this subject André Thevet, book 13, chapter 10 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

### *On Boscán and Garcilaso de la Vega, Poets, and their poems in the Spanish language.*

Juan Boscán <note>original: "Le Boscan"</note>, a Spanish poet worthy of perpetual memory for having been the perfect and complete friend of Garcilaso de la Vega (of whom more will be said hereafter), wrote several love poems in his Spanish tongue: namely, songs, sonnets in the fashion of the Italian poets, epistles, a very large elegy in the form of a lament for the misfortune of Leander and Hero, and several other Spanish rhythms on various subjects. The whole was compiled into a single volume and divided into three books titled *The Works of Boscán* <note>original: "las obras de Boscan"</note>, printed in Barcelona in Spain. By reading these books, those curious about foreign languages may see and understand the sweetness and <term>delicacy</term> <note>original: "mignardise"</note> of Spanish and Castilian poetry. Garcilaso de la Vega was a very eloquent and articulate Spanish poet who wrote poems in his own language divided into sonnets, songs, elegies, and eclogues, which are included today within the fourth book of the poems of the aforementioned Boscán. ### ON FRIAR LUIS DE GRANADA AND HIS WRITINGS
->in the Spanish language.<-

Friar Luis de Granada <note>A famous Spanish Dominican friar and mystic writer (1504–1588) whose works were widely translated throughout Europe</note>, Doctor of Theology of the Order of Saint Dominic, a Spaniard, delivered several beautiful and learned sermons throughout all the Spains and elsewhere during his life, and composed in his Spanish language a great quantity of books on theology, his primary science and profession; namely: *prayers and spiritual exercises, on prayer and meditation, on contemplation, a summary of prayer, a compendium of prayer and meditation, the Memorial of the Christian Life, The Sinner’s Guide to virtue, the path to attaining the glory of God, devout contemplations on the life, death, and passion of our Lord, the tree of life, sermons on the Last Judgment and several others, the mirror of human life, the Catechism or introduction to the Symbol of the Faith, the discourse on prayers to God for men of the three estates or ages <note>The 'Three Estates' refers to the traditional social hierarchy: the clergy, the nobility, and the commoners</note>, and other Spanish books included in his works in Spanish and French, printed both in Spain and in France recently.*

### On the region of the Germans.

Germany <note>Latin original: "Germania γερμανία"</note>, the broadest region of Europe and the glory of the Roman Empire, which Ptolemy <note>An influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer</note> calls "The Great." By the Hebrews, it is named *Ashkenaz* <note>original: "Ascanes; vel Ascenes"</note>, according to the testimony of Josephus, which is why even today the Jews call its inhabitants *Ashkenazim* <note>The Hebrew term for Jews from Central and Eastern Europe</note>, as Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus, a 16th-century physician and linguist</note> teaches in his *Indoscythica*. By the inhabitants themselves it is called *Teutschlandt*, and by foreigners, *Alemagna*. The Slavs call it *Niemiecka*, the Greeks today call it *Elamags*, and the Turks, *Alamâ*. The ancients divided this into Upper and Lower [Germany]; the inhabitants today distinguish between High and Low Germany <note>original: "Hooch & Niderteutschlandt"</note>. Germany [pri-]

->On the German Language.<-

A few years ago, a certain physician from Brabant named J. Goropius <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), a Dutch physician known for his eccentric theory that Antwerpian Dutch was the language spoken in Paradise</note> brought to light a large book titled *The Origins of Antwerp*, in which he attempts to prove that the Cimbrian language—that is to say, Low German—is the first and most ancient language of this Universe. Since his death, a man from Liège has had several other books by this physician printed on this same subject; in one of them, which he titles *Hermathena*, this Cimbrian language, or Low German, is elevated and exalted above Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.

A great and lengthy discourse would be required to respond to his allegations, but for the present, we will content ourselves with saying only that everything he puts forward for the excellence of his language is a fallacy called in the schools *Petitio principij* <note>original: "Petitio principij" (Begging the question); a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises</note>, when a Sophist takes for granted what is expressly denied to him, and which he could never prove. Goropius sets as the foundation of his arguments that the Cimbrian language has borrowed nothing from any other; that Hebrew is issued from it; and even that Hebrew has borrowed from Cimbrian. But we deny this to the said Goropius and his disciples. If they show some Hebrew words or phrases that relate to the words and terms of Low German, and then conclude that Adam, our first father, spoke Low German, and that the language of the Prophet Moses and the Prophets is difficult, ambiguous, poor, and borrowed from Cimbrian (which he supposedly did not know how to follow well), we will answer them that they are mistaken. They ought to say quite the opposite: that Hebrew preceded all others which were born at Babel <note>Referring to the Tower of Babel, where according to the Bible, the single human language was divided into many</note> and has produced infinite others since, such as High and Low German, and similar ones that are still in use in the world. And to defeat this opinion of the said Goropius and his disciples in a single word, we will bring forth the authority of Gaius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD)</note>, who, speaking of the Germans, said: "men and women alike were ignorant of the secrets of letters there." <note>original: "literarū secreta viri & fœminæ pariter illic ignorant"</note> A certain Annius Vetulonius <note>Likely referring to the forger Annius of Viterbo</note>, before the aforementioned Becanus, held the same opinion, against whom Lylius Giraldus has argued at length in his *History of the Poets*, dialogue 1; as has F. Louys the Portuguese in his *Globe of Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, book 1, chapter 1.

Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss linguist and theologian (1509–1564)</note>, in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, cites the authority of the German Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine polymath and cryptographer</note> and several others concerning this German language, saying: "The Teutonic and Germanic language will now be explained, but first concerning the origin of the Germanic peoples..." <note>original: "De lingua Teutonica & germanica iâ explicabitur, prius tamen de gētiū germ. origine"</note>

> "Germany is commonly divided now into the upper and the lower, *High German and the Netherlanders* <note>original: "hoch Teutschen vnd Niderlander"</note>, which differ not a little in dialect. There are also other divisions among writers, who divide Germany into the first and second; 
> "into the old and the more recent; into the great and that which is enclosed within narrower borders. 
> "Most conclude it within the most famous rivers: the Rhine, the Danube, and the Vistula. 
> "Pomponius <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer of the 1st century AD</note> even moves the borders of Germany to the sources of the Rhine. Certainly the Noricans..." <note>original: "Vulgo germania nūc distribuitur in superiorem & inferiorem... pletique intra celeberrimos fluuios cōcludūnt, Rhenū, Danubiū & Istulā. Pomponius etiam ad Rheni fontes Germaniæ fines promouet. Certè Norici..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Germanic languages, shifting from the specific theories of Goropius Becanus (from the previous page) to the broader historical distribution of Germanic tribes and the origins of their written characters, citing authorities like Arrian, Pliny, and Jordanes.</meta>

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.

The Vindelicians <term>Vindelici: an ancient people inhabiting the Roman province of Raetia, now parts of Bavaria and Switzerland</term> and the inhabitants of the Alpine regions used the Germanic tongue, which they still use today. Arrian <note>Arrian of Nicomedia (c. 86–160 AD), a Greek historian and philosopher</note> also testifies in Book 1 of his *History of Alexander's Campaigns* that the Germans living near the Ionian Gulf, when asked ambitiously by Alexander what they feared most, responded boldly: "that perhaps the sky might one day fall upon them." <note>original: "ne fortasse in eos cælum aliquando ruat"</note> Not without reason, nor without authorities, do I believe the Germans are descended from Ashkenaz, the grandson of Japheth and son of Gomer. <note>This refers to the "Table of Nations" in Genesis 10, a common Renaissance method for tracing linguistic origins.</note> Nor is it a trivial matter that Jordanes <note>Jordanes, a 6th-century Roman bureaucrat and historian of the Goths</note> the Alan places their ancestral seats in Scanzia or Scandinavia, which is called the island of Schonlandia. Adjacent to these were the Goths, who were also called the Guthodes, or rather the Goths themselves were a Germanic race, as authors not to be rashly disregarded report; for their common homeland—namely the Gothic islands—their language, and their customs were the same.

There is also another division of Germany, based roughly on the location of the Germanic peoples, which Pliny sets down in Book 4 of his *Natural History*, Chapter 14. However, because the passage has been corrupted by the faults of transcribers, I shall render it without the errors of the copyists as far as I am able. There are five types of Germans: the Vandals <note>original: "Vandili"</note>; a second group, the Vigeuones <note>often identified as the Ingvaeones, the "coastal people"</note> or Vuaguuoner, that is, those who dwell near deep water, specifically the maritime regions. Closest to the Rhine are the Isteuones <note>Istvaeones</note> or Vilerstenuoner. Then the Heruuones <note>Herminones</note> or Herduuones, who are the inlanders. The fifth part are the Peucini and Basternae, who border the Dacians. Furthermore, it is not our purpose here to investigate which specific tribes are contained within these categories of Germans, as we are writing not so much about the geography of Germany as about its language.

This language is today spread very widely. For even if we set aside the remnants of the Goths in the Tauric Chersonese <note>the Crimea</note>, and if we omit the Transylvanian Saxons <note>original: "Septemcastrenses," referring to the Siebenbürgen Germans in modern Romania</note> who use the Germanic tongue; and if nothing is said of the Jews, who use the Germanic speech almost everywhere among the nations <note>A reference to Yiddish, which the author classifies as a Germanic dialect</note>: after the occupation of parts of Gaul by the Germans, the use of the language extends from the Alps neighboring Italy all the way to farthest Norway and the island of Thule, which is today called Iceland. This is to say, it spans over three hundred German miles in length and breadth. Furthermore, when the Germanic and Gothic peoples invaded the Roman provinces—such as the Lombards, the Ostrogoths and Visigoths, the Rugi, Heruli, Marcomanni, and the Vandals in Italy; the Franks, Burgundians, Goths, and Northmen in Gaul; and the Chatti, Suebi, Alani, Vandals, and Goths in Spain—they mixed their Teutonic speech with the provincial languages. However, the Caledonians, Angles, Scots, Picts, and Attacotti, who occupied the island of Albion after driving out the Britons (who then took that part of Gaul called Brittany <note>original: "Britonum"</note>), brought back their native tongue with them, which in turn has been interspersed with French and semi-Latin words. Concerning the speech of those inhabiting Wales <note>original: "Vualliam"</note> and Cornwall, we have previously noted that it seems related to the language of the Greeks to those who are able to judge both languages.

Furthermore, it is not at all obscure what the Germanic and Teutonic language is today, and what it once was is also established by literary monuments. Historians testify that Ulfilas <note>original: "Vulphilam"</note>—whom others call Gulphila—the Bishop, gave letters <note>an alphabet</note> to the Goths during the reign of Valens. Some believe that Jordanes gave letters to the Getae, whom they consider to be the same as the Goths. However, the order of the letters, their names, and their shapes argue that they were borrowed from the Latins. Nonetheless, the ancient Gothic letters, in which some books are still written, have been somewhat transformed.

What Johannes Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot, polymath, and pioneer of cryptography</note> writes concerning the letters and language of the Germans in Book 6 of his *Polygraphia* should, I judge, be added here. A widespread opinion holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and that they also used the Greek language...

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

» especially in their sacred rites, they constantly affirm. For they say that a great harmony exists between the Greek language and ours, although a long interval of time has almost entirely extinguished that agreement. And a little later: Caesar testifies in his *Commentaries* <note>Julius Caesar’s *Gallic War*</note> that the ancient Druids, the high priests of the sacred rites in Gaul, used the Greek language especially in their rituals; but as the Romans devastated the world, they finally and violently imposed the use of their own letters <note>the Latin alphabet</note> along with their lordship upon many nations. Furthermore, Walstald, who described the history of the Franks in his native tongue, used letters—as Hunibald reports—that were very similar to Greek characters, except that the *Epsilon*, *Ypsilon*, and *Gamma* appear to be inverted. Furthermore, although the Franks subdued almost all of Europe after a long struggle with the Gauls and Romans, they did not abolish the Roman letters which the rest of the Germans had accepted. Regarding what the Venerable Bede <note>An English monk and historian (672–735 AD)</note> relates about the literature of the Northmen <note>Nortmanni: refers here to northern Germanic tribes or Vikings</note>—that they mixed Latin and Greek letters together—I believe this was done not out of a common custom of writing, but for a secret reason <note>original: "arcana ratione"</note> which writers use for difficult business when there is a danger that things entrusted to letters might come to the knowledge of those whom it should least reach.

» Regarding the German language itself, anyone who does not begrudge taking the trouble will discover that it obeys the laws of grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric, and does not yield to Roman eloquence in its reasoning and in the things themselves. Indeed, I do not regret the labor and diligence I have spent on knowing my native tongue more precisely; and whatever I seem to have achieved, I will candidly share with others, once I feel that my study is not displeasing to good and sensible men. For the present, I will add a few small things from Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot and polymath</note> from which it will become clear that the German speech conforms to the art of grammar, no differently than Hebrew, Greek, or Latin. That most learned man, formerly my teacher, Johann Camerarius of Dalberg, the most reverend prelate of the Church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which signify the same thing in both the Greek and German languages. Furthermore, what that excellent and wisest Bishop did was also done by Rudolf Agricola <note>A pre-eminent Dutch humanist</note>, the eternal glory of Germany, as well as Sigismund Gelenius, a Bohemian by nation, in a published book. And would that the books of Johannes Aventinus <note>A Bavarian historian (1477–1534)</note> might soon come into the light and public use, for I do not doubt that he wrote many things—as he did regarding other German matters—concerning the language, which are most worthy of being known.

» The same Abbot of Sponheim <note>Trithemius</note> relates these things received from the books of Otfrid, a Monk of Wissembourg: "We read," he says, "that Charles, King of the Franks, surnamed the Great <note>Charlemagne</note>, pitying the barbarism of his nation, attempted to regulate the German language with the assistance of Nanno, Theobald, Albinus <note>Likely Alcuin of York</note>, and Berenger. And as Turpin testifies, although he had begun such an arduous work, he was delayed by the frequent incursions of wars and did not finish it, but, prevented by death, left it incomplete; nor did another rise after him who would recall the care of this matter to his mind." However, the aforementioned Monk Otfrid, formerly a listener and disciple of Rabanus of Fulda, having attained that grammar—however imperfect—under Louis the Pious, the son of the same Charles, wrote many things in our German language, which seem to sound with a wonderful gravity of regular instruction. For he composed many poems according to that same norm in both heroic and elegiac meter. <note>Otfrid’s *Evangelienbuch* (Book of Gospels) is the first substantial literary work in High German, though it used rhyme rather than classical meters.</note> In addition, he composed several things in prose for Louis, King of Germany, the son of Louis the Pious and brother of Lothair.

> No one can quickly estimate how much the unregulated use of speech has varied among the Teutons alone in six hundred years, if they have not frequently re-read the verses in the German language by Otfrid of Weissenburg. The sea flows and ebbs; men, once dead, no longer return to this present life. Manners succeed manners, and the vigor of mortal minds always declines toward softer things. Who today among the Germans—the rivals of the ancient Greeks—maintains an ancient knowledge of the idioms? In the chronicles and ancient histories of the Franks, Hunibald, Doracus, and other writers who preceded us by a thousand years, mixed many things—both in ancient verse and in the prose of the Teutonic speech—into their compositions: things which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the Eastern Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, people of the Rhine, Moselle, Cologne, Saxons, and Thuringians undergoes a notable variation every day? Men change with time, and manners vary; minds change, and garments vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient property of idioms is varied, and nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is a cycle to all things, and variety succeeds the simplicity of minds. Who could bring this perpetual "flowing away," so to speak, back to the harmony of unity? For many times pass, as Scripture says, and knowledge shall be manifold. Beatus Rhenanus <note>A German humanist and historian (1485–1547)</note> places little verses of the Frankish language in the second book of *German Affairs*, which he concludes through no slight conjectures were written in the earliest time when the Franks first gave their name to Christ <note>original: "vt Franci nomen Christo dedere," referring to their conversion to Christianity</note>; these differ not a little from the custom of speech used today. *They are just like the Romans,*
*Even as the Romans [themselves],*
*Now one must also say this,*
*That the Greeks should not oppose it,*
*In swiftness of weapons,*
*So are all the warriors.*

Which today in prose would be expressed in this manner:
*They are altogether like Romans*

These verses differ from present custom in their spelling, words, inflection, structure, and poetic meter. I will illustrate this with a single example: concerning the oath given to the Gibeonites by Joshua and the other Israelites, he sings thus:

> *If any man should break God’s decree* <note>original: "Suuel man den ban Gott breche"</note>
> *Let it be avenged upon him.* <note>original: "Sas man es an im reche."</note>

Instead of this, the language currently in use would say:

> *Whatever man then breaks God’s decree* <note>original: "Vuelcher man denn Gottes ban braech"</note>
> *Let it be avenged upon him.* <note>original: "Sas man es an im raech."</note>

The majority of writers hold that the Germans anciently did not write their German language with any alphabetical characters, but that through the means and benefit of Charlemagne, King of France and Emperor of Germany, they began to set it down in writing in all sorts of discourse, embracing from that time forward the sciences and disciplines. This was well noted by the Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous Benedictine abbot and polymath</note> when speaking of the writers of Germany. Indeed, some historians have asserted that this same Charlemagne was the first to begin composing a grammar in the German language, of which fragments are still found today in Germany, according to their reports. Jean Grachus Pierius worked on this same subject during his life, but being prevented by death, he could not complete his work. One Otfrid of Weissenburg <note>A 9th-century monk and poet</note> composed a treatise on it entitled <term>Grammar of the Teutonic Language</term>, and also after him one Ladislaus Suntheimus in his description of the vulgar tongue in Upper Germany, as well as several other German figures mentioned by Gesner and Simler in their historical libraries.

A certain quite ancient author named Aventinus in the first book of his histories, and Carion in the second book of his *Chronology*, hold that a little after the reign of Frederick II, in the year of salvation 1251 or 1257, this German language first began to be written in Latin letters, having been unable to be written before; although the Germans wish to say that a certain Otfrid, living in the year 874, did this first and gave the first rules to this said language. The reason why these Germans began so late to write their thoughts and discourses in their language using Latin characters is that the said language is very different from Latin, requiring some specific letters and particular diphthongs, such as the double "W" <note>written as "VV"</note>, which is properly a German letter. If the **German** language were today as it was 400 years ago, it could not be written at all; but it is now written so well that there is hardly another in **Europe** that contains as many kinds of books: for in just a few years it has been decorated with the ornament with which we see it clothed today. Now, the names of saints that are given at baptism were introduced, received, and put into use by the **Germans** only since the death of the said Emperor **Frederick II** <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor</note>. Before that time, they used **Pagan** and **Scythian** names, which some families still delight in and use today, seeing that for the most part they were invented in the **Greek** fashion to signify the virtues of ancient **Germany**. And yet, those people do not do well who, encountering such strange and wild names, study how to give them grace through **Latin** declension and endings. For by seeking to find and apply **Euphony** <term>Euphony: the quality of being pleasing to the ear, especially through a harmonious combination of words</term>, or good Latin resonance, they lose and strip away their proper meaning, which the ancient **Germans** observed and wished to be remembered. This is because it appears that in many names, they exercised a singular choice, giving some names suitable to their spirit or character, or to their office; and to others according to their fortune, or perhaps their military strength. In this way, in all their titles, there was always some meaning to incite virtue; but most of these names have since been corrupted. For example, we say **Pharamond** instead of **Waremond**, **Ariovistus** for **Erweste**. For **Herueuan**—which means a man of arms or war—we pronounce and write **Arminius** <note>original: "Ariminie"</note>; **Arnold** for **Ernhold**, **Ferdinand** for **Werdemann**, **Dagobert** for **Deguenerd**. **Degen** means **Hero** or a noble, excellent, and virtuous man; it also means a dagger, as noted by **A. du Verdier, Lord of Vauprivaz** <note>Antoine du Verdier (1544–1600), a French politician and writer</note> in book 5, chapter 25 of his various lessons added to **P. Indeed, at the beginning of said book, the same **Caesar**, describing **Gaul** as being divided into three parts—namely **Belgica**, **Celtica**, and **Aquitania**—says these words: "All these differ from each other in language, laws, and ways of living" <note>original: "Hi omnes lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt."</note>. Thus, as these people have maintained this diversity of language compared to the other **Gauls** until the present, it seems they have preserved their first and ancient language. Being further removed from the conversation and frequent company of the **Romans**, they could not easily alter and corrupt their language. This is clearly seen in the alteration of the languages of **France**, **Spain**, and **Italy**, which are in effect derived, though in a corrupted form, from **Latin**; there is no doubt that in former times they were different from **Latin** and **Roman** tongues. Throughout the country of **Brabant** and others joined to it, they commonly speak **Flemish**, and they even plead their legal cases in this same language, except in that small region where the towns of **Nivelles** and **Genappe** are mainly situated, which is called in **French** the **Roman Country** <note>The "Pays Roman" refers to the Romance-speaking (Walloon) part of the Duchy of Brabant, where dialects derived from Latin—rather than Germanic Flemish—were spoken.</note>. But while in the rest of **Brabant** they ordinarily speak **Flemish**, as has been said, nevertheless there is no man or woman of quality who does not speak **French**, and many speak **German** and **English**, and a good number know **Italian** and **Spanish**—a thing certainly convenient, seemly, and worthy of wonder. I say that in **Brabant** they use the **Flemish** language because, as I have already proposed, all this **Low Country** is included by foreigners under the name of **Flanders**. Consequently, the language—except in places where **French** or **German** is spoken—differs little among them, no more than that of the **Florentines** differs from the rest of the regions of **Tuscany**. Indeed, even now they follow the customs, ways, virtues, and magnanimity of those **Germans**. Some of the high and low **Valaisans**—otherwise the subjects of the **Bishop of Sion**—and other lords who hold the policy of the cities and act as elected magistrates for the handling of affairs, speak **Savoyard** <note>A dialect of Franco-Provençal or Arpitan.</note>, while others speak **German**. ### Of Martin Luther, German, and of his writings composed in the German language.

Martin Luther, a native of Eisleben in the County of Mansfeld in Germany, was born in the year 1483 on the 10th of November around eleven o'clock at night. He was the son of a certain J. Luther <note>Hans Luther, whose name was often Latinized as Johannes.</note> and Margaret, and was named Martin because he was born on the vigil of Saint Martin. He composed various treatises and books in both the Latin and German languages. Most of these are rejected by Catholics for being written against the authority and ceremonies of the Church; however, setting that aside, these works are quite expressive and eloquent regarding the language itself. Specific mention of these treatises and books is made by Sigismund Suevus in his discourse titled *The Catalogue of the Books of the Said Luther*, and by Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler in their historical bibliographies. See also Sleidan in his histories, Carion in Book 3, and Surius in Book 3 of their respective histories. See also Gilbert Génébrard in Book 4 of his *Chronography*, and André Thevet in Book 20, Chapter 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*, all of whom discourse amply on his life, behavior, and his death, which occurred on the 17th day of February, 1546, when he was 63 years old. Father Noël Taillepied, a Franciscan friar, has written a history of the life, character, deeds, doctrine, and death of this individual.

->Of Michel Beuther, German, and of his Writings composed in the German language.<-

Michel Beuther, Doctor of Laws and native of the city of Karlstadt—located in Eastern Franconia on the Main River—composed a history, or rather a discourse on the arrangement of years. He also translated from Latin into the German language the *History* of Johannes Sleidan <note>A famous history of the Reformation by Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556).</note>, which is so well known, seen, and read by the learned men of today. To this, he even added a historical continuation, also composed in the said German language in the form of a brief summary reaching up to the year 1583. These writings are commonly found for sale in Germany, as confirmed by Gesner and J. Simler in their historical bibliographies. They further state that prior to the aforementioned Beuther, a certain German individual named Heinrich Pantaleon, native of the city of Basel, had translated the *History* of the same Johannes Sleidan from Latin into German. I currently have this translation in my hands, sent to me recently from Basel by a friend of mine living there.

### *On the region of the Bohemians.*

Abraham Ortelius <note>A famous Flemish cartographer and geographer (1527–1598) who created the first modern atlas.</note>, in his geographical synonyms and treasury, notes that Tacitus <note>A renowned Roman historian (c. 56 – c. 120 AD).</note> calls it *Boiemum* and Paterculus <note>Velleius Paterculus (c. 19 BC – c. 31 AD), a Roman historian.</note> calls it *Boiohemum* <note>original: "Boiemum Tacito Boiohemum paterculo"</note>; he states this is the name of the region inhabited by Maroboduus <note>A king of the Marcomanni who established a powerful kingdom in Bohemia.</note>. They are called *Baimoi* <note>original: "Βαῖμοι"</note> by Ptolemy. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and philosopher (64 BC – 24 AD).</note>, in the seventh book of his *Geography*, calls them *Colduli* <note>original: "κολοδουλοι"</note>, where he says: in Germany there is the Hercynian Forest; certain people live within the forest itself, such as the *Colduli*, among whom is *Bouiaimum*, the royal residence of Maroboduus. Today this region is called Bohemia. The inhabitants call themselves *Czechos*. In the writings of Aimoin <note>Aimoin of Fleury (c. 960 – c. 1010), a Frankish chronicler.</note>, they are corruptly named *Begamini*.

### *On the language of the Bohemians.*

It is a very certain thing that although the country and Kingdom of Bohemia is entirely surrounded and encircled by German lands, and measures in length and width only a three-day journey, with the Hercynian Forest serving as its walls and enclosure on all sides; nonetheless, the Bohemians do not speak the German language at all. Rather, that language was driven out at the time when the Slavs—or Sclavonians—made themselves lords of this country and Kingdom. For one reads in their annals that there were two brothers who, having departed from Croatia with a large group of people, came to make themselves lords, one of Bohemia and the other of Poland <note>Refers to the legendary brothers Lech (Poland) and Czech (Bohemia).</note>, changing the names of the lands they occupied and teaching their language to the people who lived there, as witnessed by Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar known as Volaterranus.</note> in the second book of his histories. Nevertheless, many are still found who even now use and employ the aforementioned German language, so much so that in the churches and for sermons, this people is taught in the German language; but outside the churches and temples, and even in the cemeteries, they use the Bohemian language. Formerly, among them, it was permitted only to the four Mendicant orders <note>The Dominicans, Franciscans, Carmelites, and Augustinians.</note> to preach and announce the word of God to the people in whatever language seemed best to them. And one recognizes well by this, as Aeneas Sylvius <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, who became Pope Pius II (r. 1458–1464) and wrote a famous history of Bohemia.</note> says, that this region was once Teutonic, and that the Bohemians entered it little by little, of which Wolfgang Lazius <note>A humanist scholar (1514–1565) who wrote on the migration of peoples.</note> gives proof in his *Migrations*. Furthermore, Albert Krantz <note>A German historian (c. 1448–1517) who wrote on the history of Northern Europe.</note> proves by Cornelius Tacitus that the Boians, or Bavarians, were a Gallic nation by origin and held the region between the mountains that is now Bohemia, and that they were later pushed back and driven out by the Marcomanni—that is to say, the Vandals who possess it today. For the Bohemians are these Vandals, and the ancient name has remained in the Province; so that they are called

Bohemians [named] after the Boii <note>The Boii were an ancient Celtic tribe who gave their name to Bohemia (Boihaemum).</note>. The Bohemians are called the "great people" or "great nation" by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), a Greco-Egyptian mathematician and geographer.</note> in book 3, chapter 11, European map 4. And in fact, Germany never had a larger nation than the Vandals <note>In the 16th century, scholars often conflated the ancient Vandals with the Slavic-speaking "Wends."</note> are today, who include the Russians, Poles, Dalmatians, and Bohemians. And of this their language gives good testimony; it is indeed diverse in some ways, but they borrow from one another, and each knows how to speak the language of the other, as Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and scholar (1488–1552) whose *Cosmographia* was one of the most successful books of the 16th century.</note> asserts in book 3 of his *Universal Cosmography*, in the chapter describing the Kingdom of Bohemia. This language is currently spoken by the Moravians.

### *On the region of the Pannonians and Hungarians.*

Abraham Ortelius <note>A Flemish cartographer (1527–1598) recognized as the creator of the first modern atlas.</note>, in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasury*, notes: *Pannonia* <note>original: "παvvoνία"</note>, a region of Europe according to Ptolemy, which he divides into Upper and Lower. Optatus the African <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milevis in North Africa.</note> identifies three Pannonias, contrary to all previous writers and ancient coins. These Pannonias, under the Roman Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and their successors (as is clear from Rufus <note>Sextus Rufus, a 4th-century historian.</note>, Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–397 AD), a Roman soldier and historian.</note>, and the *Book of Notices* <note>The *Notitia Dignitatum*, a unique document of the Roman imperial chancery.</note>), were distinguished by several names: such as Pannonia Prima [the First], perhaps the same as Upper; Pannonia Secunda [the Second], the same as Lower; Savia, or Ripensis [of the riverbank]—the *Book of Notices* has "Ripariensis"—and Valeria Pannonia. Aurelius Victor <note>A Roman historian and politician (c. 320 – c. 390 AD).</note>, in his lives of the Emperors Decius and Didius Julianus, mentions Bubalia and also Sabatia. I believe the former [Savia] is named after the river Savus [Sava], and the latter after the city of Bubalia. The deacon <note>Likely Paul the Deacon (c. 720–799), historian of the Lombards.</note> mentions Pannonia Cibaliensis, named after the city of Cibalae (which Ptolemy places in Lower Pannonia). Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and writer (c. 485 – c. 585 AD).</note>, in the third book of his *Miscellaneous Letters* addressed to Colosseus, mentions Pannonia Sirmiensis, once the seat of the Goths. Amantina Pannonia is also found in Lazius <note>Wolfgang Lazius (1514–1565), an Austrian physician and historian.</note>, cited from Ptolemy and Pliny. Upper Pannonia is occupied today by Austria, Carinthia, and Carniola; Lower Pannonia is entirely under Hungary in our time, which in Slavonic is called *Vergieska* <note>Likely a variation of the Slavic word for "Hungarian" (e.g., Węgierska).</note>. Savia Pannonia is designated as Slavonia by Lazius; Rhenanus <note>Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547), a German humanist historian.</note> calls Valeria *Ktabaten*. A part of Poeonia toward Thrace, where Rhodope is situated, is now called *Clocotinitza* <note>original: "χλοχοτινίξα"</note>, says Eustathius <note>Eustathius of Thessalonica (c. 1115–1195), a Byzantine scholar and archbishop.</note>. See the booklet by Lazius written in the German language regarding the Kingdom of Hungary. The Pannonians were once also called Poeonians by the Greeks especially, but not without error, as Dio [Cassius] <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin (c. 155 – c. 235 AD).</note> teaches in book 49. More than once in Appian’s *Illyrian Wars*, "Paeonians" is incorrectly read for "Pannonians." The same fault occurs in Aristotle's *On Marvelous Things Heard*: where he discusses gold called *apyron* <note>original: "apyro"; meaning gold that has not been through the fire, or pure gold.</note>, see Amanteni, Haginoia, Gepidi, Panoperos, and Paeonia.

"The Yugrians <note>original: "Iuhres aut Iuhri"; an ethnic group from the Ural region considered ancestors of the Hungarians.</note>, from the land of Yugra <note>A region in the northern Ural mountains.</note>, the northernmost and coldest part of Scythia near the Northern Ocean—distant 500 large German miles to the East and North from Moscow, the city of the Muscovites—ascended and came across flat land to the South into the region of the Goths in Scythia, where now the Chagatai <note>original: "Zahadaienses"</note> or Zavolzhye <note>original: "Zauolenses"; literally "those from beyond the Volga".</note> Tatars live. Take note first, that the Yugrians were called such from the Yugra region of Scythia, from which they originated and departed; and even to our times they are called Hugri by the Bohemians, Poles, and Slavs, while by others Hugui, and finally they were called Hungarians. Take note secondly, that the language, speech, and sharp pronunciation of the Yugrians in Hungary are the same as those who live in Yugra in Scythia. However, the Hungarians in Pannonia are worshippers of Christ, and more polished and abundant in all things, while the Yugrians in Scythia remain idolaters and wild to this day.'"

For a clear understanding of the above, see the aforementioned Matthias of Miechów, Book 2, Chapter 5 of *On European Sarmatia*, where he asserts that the Hungarians of today, descended from the ancient Yugrians, use a language similar to that of the aforementioned Yugrians, except that these Hungarians have added to their language some words from the Slavic language concerning things not found in Scythia and Yugra. Sebastian Münster, in Book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, confirms the above. So too does Sigismund von Herberstein <note>A diplomat and writer (1486–1566) whose work provided Western Europe with its first detailed description of Russia and the surrounding regions.</note> in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*. Georg Wernher <note>A 16th-century humanist and scientist known for his work on Hungarian geography and thermal springs.</note> in his *Memorandum on the Admirable Waters of Hungary* dedicated to the said Sigismund von Herberstein.

Although to me, looking at Ptolemy's description, the Carpathian seems to be bounded by the same borders as Dacia <note>An ancient Roman province roughly corresponding to modern Romania.</note>. ,, [Tran]sylvania <note>The Latin text begins midsentence, referring to Transylvania, a historical region now in central Romania.</note> is a province crowded with many inhabitants. For both the Germans, whom they call **Saxons**, and the Hungarians, as well as the most ancient of the Hungarians called **Siculi**—who in their own language are called **Zekheli** and in imitation of this are called **Ceculi** by some—inhabit it. This is not to mention the remnants of the ancient Romans, the **Wallachians** <note>original: "Valachos"; an ethnic group from which modern Romanians descend.</note>, who have many villages and settlements there. However, the Hungarians are in control of affairs, and the power rests with them; thus it happens that the Transylvanians are also considered under the name of Hungarians. Indeed, there is a truly marvelous mixture of diverse peoples and not just one language throughout all of Hungary, as I shall discuss more at length in that commentary in which I attempt to explain the affairs of Hungary, the origins of the peoples therein, their names, laws, customs, and institutions. 

**Sebastian Münster** <note>A German cartographer and cosmographer (1488–1552) whose *Cosmographia* was one of the most influential geographical works of the 16th century.</note> in Book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, in the chapter on Wallachia—a part of Thrace formerly called Gethic, partly subject to the King of Hungary and the other to the Great Turk—writes that in this province, so named because of the **Flacci** <note>Münster refers to a legendary Roman leader, Flaccus, to explain the origin of the name 'Wallachia'.</note> who were descended from the **Quirites** <note>A term for Roman citizens in their civil capacity.</note> who came to live there with a colony of Romans, the Roman language is in use. However, it is so altered and corrupted in every way that it can hardly be understood by a Roman person. Modern historians ensure, however, that in this province, they use **Ruthenian** and **Slavonic** speech. 

**Nicolas Chalcondyle** <note>Laonikos (Nicolas) Chalkokondyles (c. 1430–1490), a Byzantine Greek historian who documented the rise of the Ottoman Empire.</note> in Book 5 of the *History of the Turks*, describing Transylvania, asserts that the language used by the people there is partly Wallachian and partly Hungarian, whose customs and ways of doing things they follow; they are also subjects of the King of Hungary, who sends from his court such a chief and governor as he sees fit. Nevertheless, the cities do not fail to enjoy their ancient liberties and franchises, and each uses its own particular laws and customs, but they all answer to **Hermestat** <note>Hermannstadt, the German name for the city of Sibiu.</note> as the metropolitan city. The same author, in the following chapter on the province of Transylvania in the Kingdom of Hungary, writes that the Transylvanians for the most part speak the **German** language, but that the inhabitants of **Szekely Land** <note>original: "Ceculie"; a specific region in eastern Transylvania inhabited by the Szekler people.</note>, a particular region in the aforementioned Transylvania, have another language than the aforementioned Transylvanians because the said Szeklers speak **Hungarian**. These people have three principal cities, which they call **seats** <note>original: "sieges"; referring to the 'Szék', the administrative territorial units of the Szeklers.</note>, namely **Kysdy**, **Orbay**, and **Schepsy** <note>Modern Kézdiszék, Orbaiszék, and Sepsiszék.</note>, in which the judiciary is exercised, and they assemble there whenever they wish to treat great affairs. The same author, in the following chapter on the fertility of Transylvania, maintains that it is very populous and continues that the people there for the most part use the **Germanic** language, and principally the **Saxon** dialect, which can be especially perceived in **Altandie** <note>Likely referring to the 'Altenland' or 'Altland', the historic administrative center of the Transylvanian Saxons.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, the aforementioned author, in the chapter afterward on the government of the said Transylvania, reports that the Kings of Hungary have long had superintendence over this country and have governed it by a Lieutenant, Provincial, or Bailiff, whom they call in their language a **Voivode** <note>original: "Vuaiuuode"; a title of Slavic origin used for a governor or military commander.</note>. Now this Lieutenant was accustomed to being elected from three peoples of different languages, namely the **Szeklers**, **Wallachians**, and **Teutons** [Germans]. He was like a Vice-Roy, and what is more, some have even reached Royal dignity, as can be seen in **Matthias Hunyadi**, called **Corvinus** <note>Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490), one of the most famous Kings of Hungary.</note>. **Saint Stephen**, King of Hungary, brought the mountainous country of Transylvania under his obedience and constrained its people by force to receive the Christian religion.

->*Of the Region of the Poles.*<-

Abraham Ortelius, in his geographical synonyms and treasury, mentions the *Slaui* <note>Slavs</note> and *Slauonia* <note>Slavonia</note>. I shall describe them in the words of Master Adam <note>Adam of Bremen, a medieval German chronicler.</note>, which are found in book 2 of his ecclesiastical history: <note>original Latin: "Hæc Germaniæ amplissima Prouincia..."</note> "This most vast province of Germany is inhabited by the Vinuli, who were formerly called Vandals. Its width stretches from the South to the North, that is, from the Elbe river all the way to the Scythian Sea. Its length begins from the parish of Hamburg and extends Eastward as far as Bohemia <note>original: "Benguariam"</note>, Hungary, and Greece." The same author names the peoples of this region as the Vagri, Obotrites, Polabingians, Lingones, Warnabi, Chizzini, Circipani, Helvetians <note>likely the Havellians or Hevelli, a Slavic tribe</note>, (the *Heuilli* according to Widukind), Doxani, Lubuszanians, Wilzi, and Stoderani; read Helmold concerning these Slavs. See also the Carniolans.

The Vandals, Venedi, Finns, and Slavs—according to Melanchthon in his commentary on Tacitus, who mentions all of them—are various names for a single nation. Eutropius mentions the Vandals. The *Bandili* <gloss>Bendiloi</gloss> are found in the works of Zosimus and Suidas, and the *Bandali* appear in the Panegyric of Mamertinus. Albert Krantz calls the Bohemians, Poles, Russians, and Dalmatians "Vandals," for he says that the name Vandalia encompasses all these regions. In the vernacular tongue, they are named *Vuenden* and *Vuinden* <note>Wends</note>. P. Niuemontius rejects this opinion in his commentary on Meissen. On these matters, read David Chytraeus in his history of Saxony.

Some modern authors assert that the name of Poland comes from the situation of the Province, because the country is almost a continuous plain and an open countryside. This is called in the Slavic language *Pole*, which also signifies "hunting," because in such level and open ground it is easy to hunt. Indeed, it is well enough known that the Poles are among the greatest hunters in the world. Some call them Polacks, others Lachians or Lechians, as if to say they are the successors and heirs of Lech <note>The legendary founder of Poland.</note>. This can be judged by the fact that the Muscovites and Russians of today call them *Laches*, and the Hungarians <note>original: "Hogres"</note> call them *Lengel* or *Lechel* after the aforementioned name of Lech, as confirmed by André Thevet in book 20, chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, having learned it from [Martin] Kromer’s histories, books 1 and 2.

->*Of the Polish Language.*<-

Laonikos Chalkokondyles <note>A 15th-century Byzantine historian.</note>, in book 1 of the *History of the Turks*, maintains that the Triballians, Mysians, Illyrians, Croats, Poles, and Sarmatians all use the same language among themselves. And if I am permitted to draw a conjecture from this, I would believe that they are all but one and the same race of people, with no difference between them. The same author, in the following book 3, states that the Poles are neighbors of the Sarmatians, whose language is entirely common to them; however, in their manners and ways of doing things, they agree more with the Italians and other Western peoples.

Paolo Giovio, in book 13 of his histories, held that the Poles, Muscovites, Lithuanians, and Roxolans <note>A term then used for inhabitants of present-day Ukraine and Russia.</note> used the Illyrian language, otherwise called Slavic, but somewhat altered and corrupted. He claims all these peoples have perverted it through various inflections and pronunciations of the voice and words. Bulgarians, Serbians, Dalmatians, Croats, Bosnians, Bohemians, Russians, Lithuanians, Muscovites, and other peoples living around them; they hardly differ in language, except that each of these peoples has its own particular way of speaking and pronouncing these words.

The characters <note>The alphabet or script</note> which the Poles use in writing their language are composed partly of Greek and partly of the nature of their own country, just as their ceremonies are also mixed: some holding the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman faith, and others following the schism of the Greeks <note>Eastern Orthodoxy</note> due to being close to the Muscovites. The men and women dress almost all in the fashion of the aforementioned Greeks.

This language of the Poles is in no way similar to the German language, but is as different from it as Basque is from Gascon, or French from Limousin, as I will show hereafter.

André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French Franciscan traveler and cosmographer.</note>, in book 20, chapter 1 of his *Universal Cosmography* <note>original: "Cosmog. vniu."</note>, describing the limits of Poland, writes that the King of Poland rules over all the lands that stretch from the German Sea <note>The Baltic Sea</note> all the way to the Great Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, except for some Tartars who are nearby, and from Western Germany all the way to Muscovy. This is best seen by the titles which the King of Poland uses in his letters and edicts: "Sigismund Augustus <note>Sigismund II Augustus, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (reigned 1548–1572).</note>, by the grace of God, King of Poland, Grand Duke of Lithuania, Russia, Prussia, Masovia, Samogitia, Kyiv, Volhynia, Podlasie, Livonia, and others, etc., Lord and heir, etc." From this it appears in how many nations the Slavonic language is in use, seeing that all of Poland and the aforementioned provinces—Bohemia, Muscovy, and Slavonia—use this language; at least, whoever knows it will be able to be understood without an interpreter in all these regions. Laonikos Chalkokondyles <note>original: "Nicolas Chalcondile," a 15th-century Byzantine historian.</note>, in the thirteenth book of the *History of the Turks*, writes that the Prussians are bordered by the Samogitians, a robust people hardened to labor, having a language and way of life entirely apart, except that in certain things they show some agreement with the ancient Greeks.

The Samogitians <note>Inhabitants of a region in modern-day Lithuania.</note>, neighbors of the Prussians and Lithuanians, use the same language as the Poles, inasmuch as the curates and preachers announce the holy and divine word to them in the Polish language, and they follow the articles of faith of the Church of Rome; although the Russians toward the south and the Muscovites who are to their north are devoted to the way of the Greeks and obey not the Roman Pope but the Primate of Greece and Archbishop of Constantinople, as Maciej Miechowita <note>original: "Matthias Michou," a Polish Renaissance scholar.</note> deduces at length in book 2, chapter 1 of his *European Sarmatia* <note>original: "Sarmatie Europeene"</note>, and Paolo Giovio <note>original: "Paule Ioue"</note> in book 13 of his histories. Furthermore, the aforementioned Polish language has great currency and vogue today, and is understood throughout Russia, Volhynia, Podolia, Masovia, Kuyavia, Livonia, Prussia, Pomerania, Silesia, Moldavia, and Wallachia; the Bible and the laws of Poland are in the common Polish language. And because some have wished to stubbornly maintain that the Polish country, and what is included therein, along with the Swedes <note>original: "Suessiens"</note>, Lapps, and Finns, was contained under the name of Germany and that most of them used one and the same language, I have wished in this place, to demonstrate to the more curious that their speech and pronunciation are as different as Basque is from Gascon, or French from Limousin, to advise
