And it should be noted that after the Kings of Sweden had subjected Finland to their kingdom, they placed several bailiffs and governors there: one resides near Vyborg <note>original: "Vibourg"</note> in a castle built within the lake; another in Porvoo <note>original: "Borge"</note>, on the edge of the Finnish gulf; all of whom are Lieutenants of the King, to exercise justice in his name. There are also other castles and small towns near Vyborg, and principally Lappeenranta <note>original: "Legabour"</note>, Kexholm <note>original: "Kexholin", now Priozersk</note>, and Shlisselburg <note>original: "Netabourg", also known as Nöteborg</note>; but the Grand Duke of Muscovy has taken these from the kingdom of Sweden. There are also fortresses built on this side of the river such as Lappeenranti <note>original: "Lappaenſi"</note>, Kivennapa <note>original: "Kiuineb"</note>, Uusikirkko <note>original: "Neukirk"</note>, and others which are still under the obedience of the King of Sweden.

Modern accounts speaking of these Northern nations state that Henry, King of Sweden <note>Likely referring to Saint Eric (Eric IX) and Bishop Henry of Uppsala, who led a crusade to Finland in the 12th century.</note>, and Henry, Archbishop of Uppsala, have fully devoted themselves to converting the province of Finland to the Christian religion. And in all the surrounding countries, the people are now somewhat converted; for it is certain that on the borders of Norway and the borders of Bothnia and Finland, men and women come from 30 and 40 leagues within the country, when the weather is suitable, to bring to the churches their children—some carrying them in their cradles or in baskets on their shoulders, others putting them atop pack animals—asking for holy Baptism or instruction for living as Christians. And when they can, they bring their tithes and firstfruits; though ignorant of what they are bound to do as Christians, they conform to the law of nature, doing what seems good and praiseworthy to them and fleeing from what seems evil and vicious. Many other things concerning the lives, customs, behaviors, and religions of these Nations are deduced from John and Olaus Magnus <note>Brothers and prominent Swedish historians/cartographers of the 16th century.</note> in their *Northern Histories*, Saxo Grammaticus in his *History of Denmark*, Sidonius Apollinaris in Book 1, Procopius in his *Histories*, Paul the Deacon and Jordanes in their histories, by André Theuet in Book 19, Chapters 15, 16, and following of his *Universal Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest in Book 3, Chapter 6 of his *Universal History*, and in his discourses from the *Cosmography* of Sebastian Münster.

## OF THE REGION OF THE
### *English.*

**O**rtelius <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), the creator of the first modern atlas.</note> in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury*, notes that it is called *Anglia* [England]; *Albion* by Aristotle, Apuleius, and Pliny; *Aluion* <gloss>original: Ἀλουΐων</gloss> by Ptolemy; which is also called *Britannia* [Britain] by others. Avienus calls it the "Island of the Albions." But more truly, as Humphrey Llwyd <note>A Welsh cartographer and antiquary.</note> teaches from the most ancient annals of that island, it is called *Prydania*. This is the island which today contains the kingdoms of England and Scotland.

England, a more southerly part of the island of Albion, derives its name from the Angles, a people of Saxony whom Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD).</note> mentions, who occupied this region.

...they appear, from which even today it is still called **England** <note>original: "Engelandt"</note> (with only the first letter changed). Winfrid <note>original: "Vuunefidus," referring to Saint Boniface, the 8th-century Anglo-Saxon missionary.</note> calls it "Transmarine Saxony," as Beatus Rhenanus <note>A German Renaissance humanist and historian (1485–1547).</note> noted in the first book of his *German Affairs*. More recent Latin writers call the inhabitants **Anglo-Saxons**.

The **British Isles** is the name given by authors to those which today contain the English and Scottish kingdoms along with Ireland and the surrounding islands. Dionysius of Alexandria calls them the *Bretanides* <note>original: βρετανίδες</note>. The largest of these, which today contains the English and Scottish kingdoms, is called **Albion** <note>original: αλουίων</note> by Ptolemy <note>An influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian mathematician and geographer.</note>, and by others it is even called **Britain** by excellence, as if it were the primary one among the British Isles. In Book 60, Dion <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian.</note> reads it as *Brettanica* <note>original: βρεττανική</note>; Appian also uses this in the preface to his history. Stephanus writes it as *Pretanica* <note>original: πρετανίκη</note> with a ‘P’. After the Romans had entirely subjugated this island to their Empire, they divided it into provinces and names. In the *Almagest*, Book 2, the part toward the South is called "Greater" and the part toward the North is called "Lesser." Xiphilinus and Dio divide it into "Upper" and "Lower" Britain. According to Sextus Rufus, who flourished under the Emperor Valentinian, there are **Britannia Prima**, **Britannia Secunda**, **Flavia**, and **Maxima Caesariensis**. The *Book of Notices* <note>referring to the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire's chancery.</note> adds **Valentia**, which Ammianus Marcellinus also mentions.

Humphrey Lhuyd <note>A 16th-century Welsh cartographer and historian famous for his maps and descriptions of Britain.</note> interprets these provinces as follows: he calls **Britannia Prima** that which stretches from the Thames all the way to the Wall. Today this is almost entirely comprised under the name of England (as the Latin common folk call it). He asserts that **Britannia Secunda**, which he writes is also called "the Lesser," is what is commonly named **Scotland**. From **Maxima Caesariensis**, he identifies Kent and the region of the Atrebates. From **Flavia**, he points to the tract of the **West Saxons** along with the Isle of Wight. He indicates that **Valentia** is **Wales** <note>original: "Cambriam"</note>. 

But we must not omit what Humphrey produced from the letters of Sigebert: namely, that before this island was known to the Romans or foreigners, it was divided into three regions, which the language of the natives (which is still in use today in Wales) called **Lhoegria**, **Cambria**, and **Albania**, and they still call them so; see these in their respective places. The same author teaches from the most ancient monuments of that region that this island was called by the general term **Prydain**, from which it is likely the Greeks and Latins derived their "Britain." In the history of Widukind <note>A 10th-century Saxon chronicler.</note>, they are corruptly called *Bracti*, but I read it as *Bretti* in the same manuscript codex. Ponticus Virunius <note>An Italian humanist who summarized the legendary histories of Britain.</note> thinks that Wales <note>original: "Cambriam"</note> was celebrated by Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet.</note> in his 7th Satire with this verse:

->The repeated lesson of Cambre kills the wretched teachers.<-
<note>In Juvenal's original context, "Cambre" refers to a specific rhetorician, but the author here is attempting to link the name to Cambria/Wales.</note>

**Scotland**, the more northern part of the British Isle (which Hegesippus mentions in chapter fifteen), was formerly called **Albania** by Latin writers, and is still called **Albain** by its inhabitants, as Humphrey Lhuyd says. I would argue with Beatus Rhenanus that this Scotland was called **Caledonia** by Tacitus in his *Life of Agricola*.

The **Scots**, whom Orosius, Claudian, and Ammianus mention among Latin writers, are the northern peoples of the British Isle who, originating from Cantabria in Spain and migrating from there into Ireland, finally fixed their seat in Scotland. In the British tongue <note>referring to Welsh or Gaelic</note>, they are called **Guydhyl**, according to Humphrey Lhuyd.

Ireland is called **Hibernia** by Caesar, **Iuverna** by Pomponius Mela, and likewise in the Aldine edition of Solinus. It is **Iuernia** <note>original: Ἰουερνία</note> to Ptolemy, and **Ierna** <note>original: Ἰέρνη</note> to Strabo, Stephanus, and Apuleius.

Aristotle (who is imitated in his little book *On the Universe* <note>original: *libellulo de mundo*</note>) and likewise Claudian <note>A Latin poet of the late 4th century.</note> call it **Vernia** <note>original: $\iota \epsilon \rho \nu \eta$ (*Iernē*)</note>. To Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and commentator on Homer and Dionysius Periegetes.</note>, it is one of the islands called the British Isles. Sextus Avienus <note>A Roman geographer and poet.</note> calls it the **Sacred Island** <note>original: *Sacram*</note>, and likewise calls the inhabitants the **Hierni**. It is called **Western Britain** by Isaac [Tzetzes] in his commentary on Lycophron. This same island is named **Scotland** <note>original: *Scotia*</note> by Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose works were foundational for medieval knowledge.</note> and other writers of the Middle Ages. I believe it is called **Iris** by Diodorus. By its inhabitants, it is called **Erin**. The Britons who live in the region of Albion <note>Great Britain</note>, and who are also called the **Welsh** <note>original: *Vualliquoq*</note>, call it **Yuuerdhon**, and Humphrey Llwyd <note>A famous Welsh cartographer and antiquarian (1527–1568).</note> writes that the inhabitants are called **Enuijdhil**. To the Germans, it is named **Irlandt**, from *Erin* or *Irin* (as all Britons also pronounce the 'E' like the German 'I') and *landt*, which signifies a region. Following them, the Spanish, Italians, and French call it **Ireland**. This island seems to be fabulously described by Plutarch in his short work *On the Face in the Moon* under the name **Ogygia**. Robert Constantin, in his supplement to the Latin language, maintains that it is called **Cerne** by Lycophron. However, I would by no means think that Ireland is described by him under that name, but rather that it refers to the island of the same name which Pliny places in the Ethiopian Sea, opposite the Persian Gulf and facing Ethiopia. For that island lies toward the East, or as Lycophron says, "toward the dawn." Meanwhile, to those like Lycophron who live in Greece or Italy, Ireland lies toward the West. Orpheus also speaks of an island called **Ierne** <note>original: $\iota \epsilon \rho \nu \eta$</note>, but whether it is the same as our Ireland, I leave for others to dispute.

### *Of the English Language.*

All of Great Britain, or the Island of England, is divided into two parts which encompass two Kingdoms. The mountains and the rivers Solway <note>original: *Soluer*</note> and Tweed <note>original: *Tuedo*</note> separate the Kingdom of England from that of Scotland; the Northern part remains to the Scots for a length of four hundred and eighty miles, and the Southern part to the English for 230 miles. That which the English possess is divided into three, and according to some into four principal provinces, distributed into 22 episcopal cities along with two archiepiscopal ones, the names of which, as well as those of the provinces and their characteristics, are described particularly in the histories of this country. And we must say that just as the provinces are different in their customs, so too are they in language, seeing as in the province of **Wales** <note>original: *Vuales ou Galles*</note> they speak differently than in **Cornwall** <note>original: *Cornouialle*</note>, and both of these speak differently than the English. There are also, besides these, two types of languages, seeing as in the farthest part of Scotland, the inhabitants and those who live as savages <note>Referring here to the Highlanders.</note> speak one language similar to that of the English, and another entirely different, which is the **Irish language** <note>Gaelic</note>: a rare and marvelous thing to see various languages in one island.

And to clarify this matter, we shall say that the **English language** is a language composed of the German language and the French language, because of the **Anglo-Saxons** who brought the German language into England, and then the **Normans** <note>original: *Northmans*</note> who occupied this island and also introduced the said French language. The ancient British tongue has remained only in the country of Wales, where the indigenous people retreated when these Anglo-Saxons conquered England: and in fact, the English do not understand

English practitioners and litigants no longer use the French—or rather Norman—language (which they had used since the time of William the Norman <note>William the Conqueror, who introduced Norman French as the language of the English court and law after 1066.</note>), but rather the English language. He <note>Likely referring to King Edward III, who passed the Statute of Pleading in 1362, mandating the use of English in courts.</note> decreed that all acts of causes and trials be written in it; since that time, this English language has always been used throughout all the palaces and courtrooms of justice in England, as confirmed by the aforementioned Polydore Vergil in Book 19 of his *History of England*. Regarding this language in general, very few books are found written and composed in it, except for some books of theology. This has only occurred in the last twenty-five or thirty years, as the Lutherans and Calvinists (whom they call Puritans in England) write against the Catholics, or indeed the Catholics against the Puritans. These two sorts of religions are quite hostile to one another; the Calvinists especially desire greatly to abolish the form of policy <note>The ecclesiastical structure or hierarchy.</note> still observed in England, where the Archbishops, Bishops, Curates, and Chapters have remained intact. The Lutherans and Calvinists do not approve of this, and for this reason, the Archbishops, Bishops, Curates, and Chapters—among whom there are some very learned men—and the aforementioned Lutherans and Calvinists write against one another every day, as confirmed by Sanderus <note>Nicholas Sander (c. 1530–1581), a prominent English Catholic polemicist.</note> in Book 5, Chapter 4 of his *Ecclesiastical Monarchy*.

This English language is so little esteemed by foreigners who go to England that there are few who wish to take the trouble to learn or speak it, unless they are servants or agents <term>facteurs</term> <note>Commercial agents or representatives working abroad.</note> for the sake of useful things and the necessities of life, which depend on the common people who know how to speak no other language.

Whoever wishes to see many beautiful and excellent discourses on the English and England should read Caesar in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, Book 5; Bede, Book 1, Chapter 1; Gildas’s book *On the Ruin of Britain*; William of Newburgh’s *English History*; Albert Krantz’s *Danish History*, Book 1, Chapter 2; Saxo Grammaticus, Book 1 of his *Danish History*; and Polydore Vergil in his books on the *History of England*.

### A. Ortelius in his Geographical Synonyms,
India, *Indike* <note>original: "$\iota\nu\delta\iota\kappa\grave{\eta}$"</note>, the largest and most noble region of Asia. Ptolemy divides this into two, namely India within the Ganges, and India beyond the Ganges. India within the Ganges is called *Indostan* <note>Hindustan</note> by the inhabitants, according to João de Barros, an eyewitness and, so to speak, an "ear-witness"—as one who acted as the viceroy for Portugal in this India for several years. India beyond the Ganges is thought to be called *Heuila*, or, as others write, *Hauilath*, or *Euilath* <note>Biblical Havilah</note>, in the Sacred Scriptures. Niger writes that it is called *Macyn*, or *Magyn* by the inhabitants. He adds that for those sailing from Egypt to India, it is divided into three parts: Lower, Middle, and Upper. The Lower, which is from the Indus river to the Bariam river, is called *Caiferat* <note>Gujarat</note>. The Middle, which extends from there to another river named the Chaberis <note>likely the Kaveri</note>, is called *Minibar* <note>Malabar</note>. The Upper, *Maabar* <note>the Coromandel Coast</note>, which stretches from the Chaberis to the Ganges river. Marco Polo the Venetian relates that in his time it was also divided into many parts, but he calls the larger part *Malabar* and the middle part *Abascia* <note>Abyssinia, which was frequently confused with or grouped under "the Indies" in medieval geography</note>. He does not indicate the smaller part with a specific name. Pliny testifies that India was called the third part of the world by the companions of Alexander who had conquered it. It is certain that today a no smaller part of the world is included under this single name. For the Spaniards commonly call these Indies, together with almost the whole of the recently discovered America, the "Indies."

### The same in his Geographical Treasury,
The Indians were first called Sabaeans, and then also Homerites <note>The Himyarites of ancient Yemen</note>, says Nicephorus Callistus in book 8, chapter 35. He places them in *Arabia Felix* <note>literally "Happy Arabia," the fertile southern part of the Arabian peninsula</note>. There are also Indians properly so-called, people in India beyond the Ganges, according to Ptolemy. But translators read *Sindi* in its place, and more accurately so, as I conjecture. In the Greek codex it is read as *Sindoi* <note>original: "$\sigma\iota\nu\delta\omicron\grave{\iota}$"</note>, and I think Ptolemy wrote *Sindois*. But as I advise in many other places in this Treasury regarding Indian words, the scribe did not notice the doubled "S" from the mouth of the reader. My opinion is confirmed by Hesychius, who holds the *Sindi* to be an Indian race, and records a Sindican port in the same place. Curtius, in book 9, calls those "Maritime Indians" who inhabit the coast of the Red Sea in Gedrosia <note>an ancient region along the coast of the Indian Ocean, in modern Iran and Pakistan</note>, placing them on this side of the Indus river, contrary to Ptolemy and other geographers. Arrian also names Indians on this side of the Indus river in his third book. The same author, in his work on Indian affairs, calls these "Western Indians" (to distinguish them from those beyond, whom he calls "Eastern"). At the Arbis river, Pliny and Arrian extend India toward the West, and add that these people once obeyed the Assyrians. It is likely that this is the India mentioned in the books of Esther and the Maccabees. There are also Indians in Ethiopia according to Procopius in book 6 of *On Buildings*; for he calls them the "Mountains of the Indians," from which the Nile takes its origin. See *Ethiopians*, *Memnones*, and *Rhizophagi* <note>literally "Root-eaters"</note>.

India, *Indike* <note>original: "$\iota\nu\delta\iota\kappa\grave{\eta}$"</note>, the largest and most noble region of Asia; Ptolemy divides this into two, namely India within and beyond the Ganges.

» The author João de Barros—an eyewitness and, so to speak, an "ear-witness," having served as the Portuguese Viceroy in this India for several years—asserts that India within the Ganges is called *Indostan* <note>Hindustan</note> by the inhabitants. India beyond the Ganges is believed to be called *Heuila*, or, as others write, *Hauilath*, or *Euilath* <note>original Latin: "Heuila... Hauilath... Euilath"; referencing the Biblical land of Havilah</note> in the Holy Scriptures. Dominicus Niger writes that it is called *Macyn*, or *Magyn* <note>referring to Mangi, a term for Southern China</note> by the inhabitants. He adds that for those sailing from Egypt to India, it is divided into three parts: Lower, Middle, and Upper. The Lower part, which runs from the Indus River to the Bariam River, is called *Caiferat* <note>Gujarat</note>. The Middle part, extending from there to another river named the Chaberis <note>likely the Kaveri River</note>, is called *Minibar* <note>Malabar</note>. The Upper part, *Maabar* <note>the Coromandel Coast</note>, stretches from the Chaberis to the Ganges River. Marco Polo the Venetian relates that in his time it was also divided into these parts, but here he calls the larger part *Malabar* and the middle part *Abascia* <note>Abyssinia/Ethiopia; early geographers often conflated East Africa with India</note>. It is certain that today no smaller part of the world is encompassed by that name; for the Spaniards commonly call these "Indies" the ancient Indies along with almost the whole of the recently discovered America. Indians are found in Ethiopia, and conversely, Ethiopians in India. See *Ethiopians*, *Atlantis*, *Memnons*, and *Rhizophagi* <note>original: "Rhiſophagi," meaning root-eaters</note>.

Some modern geographers are astonished that those who once divided the earth into three parts <note>Europe, Asia, and Africa</note> did not take heed of the words of Pliny, who, in Book 6, Chapter 7, considering the grandeur of these Indies, uses these words: *The companions of the great King Alexander have left in writing that in this Indian country which was subjugated by their master, there were five thousand cities, and with likely reason showed that, given the innumerable people there and this great expanse of regions, it is the third part of the world, seeing as the Indians never left their country to go conquer other lands.* And yet Alexander the Great did not see a third of the Indies, and never crossed beyond the Ganges toward the south; the glory of this is due to those of our own time, who have done more than he, and more than all the historians, both Greek and Latin, having given us knowledge of what is rarest in this great and very rich Province. 

If then this India is the third part of the earth, by what consideration shall it be so measured? Since Europe makes up one, Asia another, and Africa another, unless we separate it from Asia—just as it never truly had any community with the Asians, and it would be included there improperly insofar as the Kings who held command over Asia never had any power over this great Empire, as we can see in the writings of the ancient Greek and Latin authors. But you will ask me, what is the point of this discussion? For nothing else but to favor the cause of those who call the newly discovered New World the **West Indies**, which I prefer to include under the third part of the earth rather than otherwise, and give the Africans the rank of the fourth part. And this is not without great reason: for those who know the proportions of the terrestrial Globe cannot ignore that by the doubling of the Zones, the East and West face each other in such a way that in our time the Kings of Spain and Portugal have entered into a great dispute over the Molucca Islands.

<meta>catchword: formerly</meta>

Moluccas <note>The Spice Islands in modern-day Indonesia</note>, for this reason alone: that some hold them to be Oriental, others Occidental; and nonetheless all of this is comprised under the name of the Indies. Indian Kings command there, and the people for the most part imitate the customs of the Indians, added to which the same trees and plants grow there, and almost the same animals, except where the Sun already approaches the Poles and the cold causes lions, elephants, tigers, and the like to be unable to live there at all. In short, Religion (such as it is, or an imitation of it) makes them all united, in that it seems the Orientals have given their beliefs to the Occidentals, as is apparent by those of the Island of Zipangu, or Japan <note>original: "Zipangu, ou Giapan"</note>. These are known to be so positioned between the East and West (as we have supposed them) that the Geographers of our time do not rightly know whether they should be named Orientals or otherwise.

This leads us to conclude that the Indies comprise the third part of the earth and are of a different extent than the ancients considered them. Their opinions, however, out of the reverence we owe them, should not be cast aside entirely—not that we wish to dwell on the dreams and ravings of the Greeks, who created a Bacchus subjugating the Indians, and produced a great Hercules as a total conqueror, and an Alexander as Monarch. This is deduced at length by Strabo in Book 15, Diodorus Siculus in Book 3, Pliny in Book 6, Chapter 17, Ptolemy in Book 7, Chapter 1, Table 10 of Asia, Solinus in Chapter 65 of his *Polyhistor*, Philostratus in Book 2, Chapter 15 of the *Life of Apollonius*, Quintus Curtius and Arrian in the *Life of Alexander the Great*, Plutarch in the same life, and several other ancient authors.

Leaving these aside, we shall say—considering the East Indies—that as they are of greater extent than all other Provinces and Regions of this universe, so they are divided into two great parts and Regions, both being known and renowned by the River Ganges. Thus, the part that faces us, and which from our perspective is Western, is called **India within the Ganges** <note>Latin: *India intra Gangem*</note>, because it lies between the aforementioned river and the Indus, which gave its name to the entire land. The part that is further East is named **India beyond the Ganges** <note>Latin: *India extra Gangem*</note> because it lies in that great expanse of country that goes as far as the sea of Cin and Mangi <note>References to China and Southern China</note>, and which spreads toward the Southern parts as far as the Golden Chersonese <note>The Malay Peninsula</note>, now named Malacca. This lies opposite that great Island now called Sumatra, which formerly was known by the name Taprobane <note>While Taprobane usually referred to Sri Lanka/Ceylon in antiquity, many 16th-century writers mistakenly identified it as Sumatra</note>.

These two were named thus according to the words of some Geographers; but in the Holy Scriptures, the Oriental part is denoted by the word *Euilath* <note>Havilah</note>, and the one closer to us *Serian*. The people of the country now call this closer part *Hynd* <note>Hind/Hindustan</note>, and the other which is in the East is now called *Macin* or *Magin* <note>Mangi</note>—so much have things changed, or rather, so little knowledge have we had of foreign history. Some moderns have spoken differently on this matter, holding that the Indies toward the West on this side of the Ganges are called *Euilath* in Holy Scripture and *Indostan* by the Indians, and the Indies beyond the Ganges are called *Seriah* in the aforementioned Holy Scripture and *Macyn* (otherwise China) by the Indians. Moderners who have navigated toward these Indies have divided them for us into three: the High, the Middle, and the Low. The first, which is also the Low, is what is called the country of *Caiserat*, or Gujarat <note>original: "Caiſerat, ou Guzerath"</note>, which in the time...

## ->ON THE LANGUAGE OF THE EAST<-
## ->Indians in general.<-

### CHAPTER LXXVI.

Strabo, in book 15 of his *Geography*, citing the words of a certain very ancient author named Megasthenes, wrote that the Indians of his time had no use for letters, nor any written laws, but that they observed many fine things through memory and the recollection of past events, just as they had learned them from father to son; this is repeated by Caelius Rhodiginus in book 18, chapter 31 of his *Various Lessons*. Diodorus Siculus, regarding this subject in book 3 of his *Histories*, maintains that on a certain island found near the South by Iambulus <note>A Greek writer of a legendary utopian travel narrative</note>, the inhabitants did not write horizontally as we do, but drew the lines of their letters straight, from top to bottom. They had twenty-eight letters in total according to the meanings they assigned to them, though they had only seven characters, each of which was explained in four modes and fashions. The Emperor Augustus <note>Original: "Octaue"</note> seemed to have wanted to imitate this in his Latin writing, according to Suetonius Tranquillus in his *Life of Augustus*, in these words: <margin>cc</margin> "I have noted this especially in his handwriting: he does not divide words, nor does he move letters that exceed <margin>cc</margin> the end of a line to the following one, but instead places them immediately <margin>cc</margin> below and circles them." <note>original: "Notaui & in Chyrographo eius illa præcipuè, non diuidere verba, nec ab extrema parte verſuum abundantes literas in alterum transferre , ſed ibidem ſtatim ſubicit, circumducitque"</note> He argues that the term for a line of poetry, *verse* <note>original: "verſus"</note>, proves this was the custom of the ancients, as the word is derived from *turning* <note>original: "à vertendo factum"</note>.

Regarding this, we will repeat here what we have previously written about the Syriac language and Syriac letters in the chapter on the Syriac language: namely, that the characters of the aforementioned Syriac letters, although they are read from right to left like those of the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs, are nevertheless not formed and written by the Syrians from right to left as the Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs do; rather, they are written from top to bottom toward the chest <note>original: "vers l’estomach"</note>, as this Latin verse denotes:

*From heaven to the stomach, Chaldea rereads the marks.*
<note>original Latin: "E cælo ad stomachum relegit Chaldaea lituras." This refers to the vertical orientation of the script, descending from the sky toward the body.</note>

It seems this is what moved Festus Pompeius <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> to call this kind of writing **downward-turning**, just as we now say **rightward-turning**; specifically as if it were falling and landing from above. For the letters seem to fall and sit upon one another, one carrying the other on its back, as they are applied in the order of the alphabet or in the composition of a word. Thus, it is not without reason that they are believed by that craftsman to have been sent down from heaven—a view confirmed by Teseo Ambrogio in the 9th chapter of his *Introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic languages*; André Theuet in book 18, chapter 14 of his *Cosmography*; and Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie in his epistle on the *New Testament in Syriac*.

> Father Luis of Portugal, in book 1, chapter 1 of his *Globe of Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, confirms this, saying: "Moreover, those first people from whom the Jerusalem Syriac language flowed, holding a middle position between both <note>meaning between those who write left-to-right and right-to-left</note>, write toward the chest—a matter which the legal scholar Andreas Masius and we ourselves discuss at length and with great care in our aforementioned elementary preface. To which is added what Poggio Bracciolini records in book 4 of *On the Vicissitudes of Fortune*: that the Indians write by drawing the pen from the top to the bottom, a practice also observed by the Sinae, or Sinnae, or Chinese."
<note>original Latin: "Primi autem illi, à quibus lingua Syra Hierosolymitana effluxit, medium inter vtrosque tenentes, versus pectus scribunt... Indos à summo ad imum calamum ducentes, scribere, id quod & Sinæ... obseruant."</note>

Modern travelers and navigators assure us that the East Indians, Cathayans <note>People from Northern China</note>, Chinese, and Japanese of today, in following this fashion of forming the characters of the letters of their languages, write from top to bottom. In this, they claim to follow the order of nature, which has given men their heads at the top and their feet at the bottom.

To be brief, these Indians generally write upon the leaves of certain trees growing in their countries, and principally on the trees they call **Tals** <note>The Palmyra palm, *Borassus flabellifer*</note>, from which they make books. These people do not use the method and fashion of forming and writing their letter characters from right to left like the Hebrews and Arabs, nor from left to right like us Christians; rather, they form and write them from top to bottom. However, in the country of **Cambay** <note>A region in Gujarat, India</note>, the inhabitants use paper to form and write their letter characters, which is confirmed—following the aforementioned modern travelers and navigators—by André Theuet in book 11, chapter 23 of his *Cosmography*. Regarding this, Niccolò de' Conti, in his travels in Asia, mentions the inhabitants of the said country of Cambay, maintaining that they do not write like us, nor like the Hebrews and other older peoples descended from them, but indeed like the other East Indians: all along the leaf from the top to the bottom, and that they use three different languages among themselves. Jerónimo Osório, in book 2 of his *History of Portugal*, confirms this, saying that all the reports of the Portuguese sent by them to their King from the Indies stated that these Indians used neither paper nor parchment as we Europeans do, but that they marked their letters with a stylus on the leaves of wild trees they call **palms**, because these trees resemble true palms. He adds that they have very ancient books written on these leaves, made to be of a uniform length, in which they write their annals and memorable histories; then they pierce these leaves through the sides and flatten two wooden covers which they attach quite neatly to these...

This seemed almost impossible to a man who had only just arrived from Europe, but nevertheless, in less than six months, he understood this language very well and knew how to speak it; in short, in a short time he had completed the Grammar, along with a Dictionary of all the words, not without great profit for those who wish to learn it. Indeed, some hold that in this kingdom of Malabar there were, when the Portuguese landed there, eight types of nations, all diverse in ceremonies and **idolatry**, and so distant in affection from one another that they would rather die than approach or ally with one another. That is to say, one is of hieroglyphic <note>original: "Hieroglyphiques"</note> letters, and the other of common letters which, by their assembly, can form all the words one wishes to express; both proceed not across—as with the Hebrews in one way and ourselves in another—but rather from top to bottom.

The first, which they call the writing of China, is generally common to all the regions of the Indies, both of the islands and the mainland, but used only for spiritual matters and non-vulgar doctrines by the **Bonzes** <note>a term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks</note>. These are the younger children of Kings, Princes, and great Lords and other principal figures who are placed into monasteries with great revenues and great respect and authority, to prevent the dismemberment of the state and internal disputes. To these **Bonzes** belongs the administration and conduct of everything depending on the spirituality and religion of their country, according to their ancient idolatrous traditions of infinite kinds, and they themselves are almost infinite in number. ...yet nevertheless there are always some of greater understanding and knowledge than others, not through a doctrine acquired by them in schools, nor by the reading of books: for notwithstanding that paper and printing are not unknown to them, they do not have the same convenience as we do, but rather by an ingrained routine and meditations so constant that there are some who have devoted themselves for 30 or 40 years straight without communication with any person who might challenge their ideas. By this means, these <term>Bonzes</term> <note>A term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks or priests in East Asia.</note> forge strange and very bizarre fantasies in their brains, being restrained in this by no bridle of religion nor reprimand from a magistrate, so that each might abound in his own sense, possessed by a vain and slight inconstancy. But they agree unanimously among themselves concerning the eternity of the world and the perishing of the soul along with the body, persuading themselves that what has come from nothing must also return to nothing; indeed, they have infinite other fantasies entirely contrary to the Christian religion, just as I deduced in the chapter on the Egyptian language cited above. 

These <term>Hieroglyphic</term> <note>Western scholars of this era often characterized Chinese characters as "hieroglyphs" because they viewed them as ideograms representing things rather than sounds.</note> letters of the said China and of the said Cathay <note>Cathay was the medieval name for Northern China; the author treats them as overlapping or related regions.</note> used in the aforementioned East Indies are very difficult to learn to read and to form, because they consist of various figures of beasts, birds, trees, herbs, and in short, everything that nature produces, which serve as their marks. Some are used alone and by themselves, and others are joined and coupled several together to create a character that represents more than one word—much like Centaurs, Chimeras, Sphinxes, and similar monstrosities composed of different natures—so that these Bonzes, however sharp their minds may be, consume the better part of their lives before they can become masters of them. This is according to the modern reports sent from the Indies, which maintain that from the general marks of this entirely hieroglyphic writing, by disguising and coupling them in various ways, entirely new composite characters can be formed, just as in <term>Ciceronian Notes</term> <note>Also known as Tironian notes, a system of shorthand used in ancient Rome.</note> and in our devices and name-ciphers. 

Regarding the matter of religion, they are marvelously attached to their idolatry and superstition, and have so vividly imprinted in their minds many fables told to them of their idols and false gods, that it is very difficult to tear them from their souls. This is principally because all these things are set in verse and in the rhythm of their language, which they value so highly that this alone is enough to persuade them of the greatest falsehoods imaginable; the devil having found this invention to make them believe so many follies that they relate concerning their false gods, even things contrary to their laws and to natural reason. Now they learn these verses or rhythms from their tender youth and sing them with a singular pleasure; for although <note>original: "iaçoit que"</note> their verses are very different from Greek and Latin verses regarding the number of syllables (because each contains 72 syllables), they nevertheless do not lack their own grace and beauty, as confirmed by <term>P. du Jarric</term> <note>Pierre du Jarric (1566–1617), a Jesuit historian who compiled accounts of missionary travels in the East.</note> in book 1, chapter 4 of his history of the East Indies.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF [LANGUAGES]

### CHAP. LXXVII.

->*Of the language of the Chinese in general.*<-

Several modern travelers and navigators, speaking in their voyages and navigations of this very great and ample country of China in the easternmost lands of the Indies, have asserted that Ptolemy, in Book 7, Chapter 3 of his *Geography*, had knowledge of it when he spoke these words:

<note>original Latin: "Sinae..." translated here as Chinese.</note> The Chinese are divided on the North side by a part of the country of the <term>Seres</term> <note>A classical name used by Greeks and Romans for the people of North China, famous for silk production.</note>; on the East and South sides by an unknown land; and on the West side by India, which lies beyond the Ganges according to the line described, as far as the Great Gulf, which likewise bounds them along with the other adjacent regions where the <term>Ichthyophagi Ethiopians</term> <note>Literally "Fish-eating Ethiopians"; a term used by ancient geographers for various coastal populations across Africa and Asia.</note> dwell according to the present description. Then, toward the end, coming to speak of the capital city of the Chinese, he speaks thus: "And the metropolitan city of the aforementioned country is <term>Thinae</term>." <term>Stephanus</term> <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary.</note> mentions it in his *Onomasticon* of cities, saying: "Sina is the metropolitan city of the Sinae, of whom Marcian speaks in his navigations." From this it is presumed that this word *Thinae* in Ptolemy is corrupted—and likewise in the first book of Strabo, where the same name is also read—and that for Θινα <note>Greek: Thina</note> one should read Σινα <note>Greek: Sina</note>, as the aforementioned Stephanus calls it in the previously cited place. 

With him agrees Father Xavier, a Jesuit, in an *Indian Epistle* of the year 1552, where he informs the Father General Loyola that three of his brethren have set out toward the Royal city of China, called Sina or Sinar. After the aforementioned Ptolemy and Stephanus cited above, we find some mention of this Kingdom of China in the Persian and Arabic physicians, who, speaking of the drugs that come from the East Indies, use these names *Seni* and *Sini*. This appears in <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> Book 2, Chapter 124, when he speaks of Cinnamon, which he calls in his language *Darseni* and *Darsini*, which is "Chinese wood." Consistent with him are Serapion, <term>Rhazes</term> <note>Al-Razi (865–925), a Persian physician and chemist.</note> in his *Continent*, <term>Mesue</term> in his *Confection of Alkermes*, and <term>Averroes</term> in his *Colliget*. The same Avicenna, in the aforementioned book Chapter 578, speaking of Rhubarb, calls it in his language *Rauedseni* and *Rauedsini*, which is "Chinese root," thus calling Rhubarb by excellence because it comes from China. 

Upon these passages, Gerard of Cremona, commentator on the said Avicenna, interpreting the word *Seni* or *Sini*, says that it is a place name. And <term>Bellunense</term> <note>Andrea Alpago of Belluno, an Italian physician who translated and commented on Arabic medical works.</note> interpreting the word *Sinir* in Chapter 172, says that it signifies everything coming from the country of Sini. Also, Serapion in his *Simples*, speaking of <term>Zerumbet</term> <note>A type of aromatic ginger (Zingiber zerumbet).</note>, says by the authority of Isaac that it comes from the country named Sini, which is none other than China. Consequently, it results from these authorities that the country of China is situated in the East of Asia in the East Indies, beyond the Ganges, and is named by the name Sina and Sini, as it still is at present throughout the Indies, according to the testimony of moderns. Among others, Father de la Croix in his *Portuguese Voyage* Chapter 1, and Bernardino Escalante in his *Navigation* Chapter 6, note that from there it has come about that the Portuguese and Spaniards frequenting that country, and hearing it called Sini or Sina, have retained the same name, and have

[They] have called it China, by changing the letter *S* to *Ch*, as often happens in their language, as well as in others like Hebrew, where the word *shibboleth* is changed to *schibboleth* in the Book of Judges, chapter 12; in the German and Flemish languages in the word *Visch* or *Vuisch* derived from the Latin *Piscis* <note>meaning "fish"</note>; and similarly in our own language with the word *Chifre* <note>modern French "chiffre" meaning digit or code</note>, taken from the Hebrew word ספרה, *sephira* <note>original Hebrew: ספרה, meaning "counting" or "numbering"</note>. This happens because of the similarity in sound between these two letters, both in Hebrew and Arabic, where there are two "S" sounds, one named ש *Sin*, and the other ס *Schin* <note>The author likely refers to the Hebrew letters *Sin* (שׂ) and *Shin* (שׁ), which share the same character form but differ in sound, though the OCR identifies the character *Samekh* (ס) as well.</note>, as in German and English where *st* and *th* are pronounced like the *Sch* or the *Ch* of our language in words like *Fasten*, *Schall*, and other similar ones; and finally in Spanish, which pronounces the *Ch* with a sound leaning toward that of the letter *S*, which is why they turned the ancient name *Sina* into their modern *China*, as has been said.

This being established, we shall say that Duarte Barbosa <note>original: "Odouard Barboſſe," a Portuguese explorer and writer (c. 1480–1521)</note>, a Portuguese traveler in his voyages to the Indies, divided and partitioned the country and region of the Sinae into two great provinces: one stretching toward the Southeast, and the other toward the Northeast. The first is Cin, Sin, or China; and the other is <term>Mangi</term> <note>A term, famously used by Marco Polo, for Southern China; here the author uses it to describe a northern or eastern region containing several kingdoms.</note>, containing within it the lands and kingdoms of Chequan, Tainfu, Nanqui, Xauton, Quinzi, and Quinzay. Then, speaking of the Chinese, he says that they have their own language, using almost the same accent and manner of speaking and uttering their words as the <term>Tudesques</term> <note>An old term for Germans or people of Germanic tongue.</note> or Germans—not that their words and languages are in any way similar, which André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French explorer and writer.</note> mentions in passing in Book 11, chapter 25 of his *Universal Cosmography*. And speaking of the people of Mangi, he continues by saying that their language is entirely different from that of the Tartars <note>Central Asian peoples, including the Mongols, who had previously ruled China.</note> who rule them, just as the inhabitants are different in their ways of life from the aforementioned Tartars. This country of China, or rather kingdom, consists of fifteen provinces of very great extent, each having its own metropolitan city from which it is named. There are five maritime provinces, namely: Canton, Fujian, Zhejiang, Chequan <note>Possibly a duplicate or variation of Zhejiang</note>, Nanjing, and Beijing; the others are inland, namely: Shaanxi, Sichuan, Shanxi, Henan, Shandong <note>labeled here as Saucium</note>, Yunnan <note>labeled Olamum</note>, Huguang <note>Oquianum</note>, Guangxi, and Anhui.

Some say that there are in this kingdom as many as 240 cities or towns situated on great navigable rivers. Jan Huygen <note>original: "I. Hugo," referring to Jan Huygen van Linschoten, a Dutch traveler.</note> maintains that there are in these provinces large and renowned cities or towns up to the number of 591, and of small ones as many as 1,593, without counting the boroughs, villages, and hamlets.

The Reverend Father Juan González de Mendoza <note>An Augustinian friar whose 1585 book was the primary European source on China for decades.</note>, of the order of Saint Augustine, in his *History of the Great Kingdom of China* situated in the East Indies, divided into two parts—in Book 1, chapter 1 of his first part—speaks of it as follows: "This great kingdom of China, of which we speak here, was discovered and truly well-recognized ten years ago by the Spaniards inhabiting the Philippine Islands, distant from it by two hundred leagues. ...they pronounce with different words. Such is the nature of the character that signifies "City," namely this one: <image-desc>Two hand-drawn characters resembling Chinese ideograms: the first is an X shape over a horizontal line with a hook; the second resembles a capital T with an additional horizontal bar across the vertical stroke.</image-desc>. For everyone understands well that it means "city"; and yet some call it *Leombi*, and others *Fu*, and so on consequently for all the other names and characters. By this means, the Japanese, the Ryukyuans <note>original: "Lechiens," referring to the people of the Ryukyu Islands (modern Okinawa)</note>, the Cochinchinese <note>inhabitants of what is now central Vietnam</note>, those of Sumatra, and other neighboring and adjacent peoples all communicate by writing with the aforementioned Chinese, and yet in speaking to one another they understand each other no more than the Greeks and the Germans do.

As for their schools and studies, the King <note>Referring to the Emperor of the Ming Dynasty</note> maintains them in all the cities at his own cost and expense, as much for learning to read, write, and count, as for teaching moral and natural philosophy, astrology, the laws of the kingdom, and many other singular and curious things. In these schools, the most eminent men they can find in the faculties and sciences teach and hold the chairs; so that there is no one, however poor they may be, who does not learn to read and write: for not to know it at all is held among them as an infamy. To the great studies <note>higher education or universities</note> arrive a great number of scholars, who strive to study well and profit, especially as it is the means by which they most quickly acquire the name of <term>Loytias</term> <note>From the Hokkien "Ló-tia," a term of respect for a magistrate or government official</note>, or knights, and other titles of dignity: as will be said more clearly in the chapter which follows, where it is spoken of the form and manner they maintain in granting the degree of **Loytias**, similar to that of Doctor, which is given among us. To these studies, both small and great, the King sends visitors every year to see and hear how one profits there, and to know who the masters and superiors are, and such other things that concern the conduct of scholastic government. These visitors, in making such visits, honor with words and praises those who study well, exhorting and encouraging them to continue: and on the contrary, they have the others put in prison and punished, whom they see to be unfit for letters and not doing their duty. And as for those who are not suited for it, or who do not want to study, they immediately remove them from the studies, so that they may make room for others who will better benefit. They have a great abundance of paper which they make from the fibers of canes and reeds <note>likely referring to bamboo paper</note> very easily, by which means it is very cheap, and printed books as well: but in the majority of these, one can only write on one side, because it is too thin and delicate. They do not write with such pens as we do, but they are reed pens, the tip of which is made like that of a painter's brush; and notwithstanding this, there is no lack among them of brave and excellent writers, who achieve their status through the pen. When they write to people of distinction, they gild the entire margin of the paper and illuminate it, and once the letter is written, they put it in a pouch and seal it; afterward, because the letter is merely folded. And they use such letters among themselves so much that even if someone goes to visit another person, he always carries a letter that he presents to them himself, by which he says that he comes to kiss their hands, so that it often happens that there are no more than ten characters written on the whole sheet.

The aforementioned author <note>Likely referring to Juan González de Mendoza, whose 1585 history of China was a bestseller</note> in the subsequent 16th chapter asserts that the Art of Printing is much older in this China than it is in our Europe, and that one finds there infinite beautiful and excellent books printed in their own characters and languages. **Father Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), an Italian Jesuit historian</note>, book 6 of his *History of the Indies*:**

> >> To write, the Chinese use very narrow and long small pages of a soft and thin paper. They do not write from the left moving toward the right like the Greeks, nor from the right moving toward the left like the Hebrews; rather, they draw their writing from the top of the page toward the bottom. In this manner, I remember having seen a book printed in that country and sent to Rome to the Vatican, and another in the Laurentian Library of King Philip <note>The library at El Escorial, founded by Philip II of Spain</note>. They use characters like the Egyptians, which the Greeks called Hieroglyphics; each of them serves for a name, and indeed sometimes they serve for an entire meaning. By this means, it happens that although the Chinese use various languages—as they have so many and such separate regions—nevertheless, all that is written is understood equally by everyone. In addition to the specific language of each province or nation, there is a certain common language for the learned which corresponds to the Latin language among us. They commonly name it the Mandarin. This is used by courtiers, secretaries, judges, and magistrates, and they study it very carefully.

They have had their rights and written laws for more than 2,000 years, and as they say, these were never changed (folio 329).

**José de Acosta <note>Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist (1540–1600)</note>, book 6 of his *Natural and Moral History of the Indies, both East and West*, chapter 5:**

> >> There are many who think, and it is indeed the common opinion, that these writings used by the Chinese are letters, like those we use in Europe, and that through them one can write the words of speech, and that they only differ from our letters and writing in the diversity of the characters, just as the Greeks differ from the Latins, and the Hebrews from the Chaldeans. But it is not so; because they have no Alphabet, nor do they write with letters. Instead, all their writing is nothing other than painting and ciphering, and their letters do not signify parts of words <note>original: "parties de dictions," meaning phonetic syllables or letters</note> as ours do, but are figures and representations of things, such as the Sun, fire, a man, the sea, and other things. This is clearly apparent because their writings and *Chapas* <note>original: "Chapas," a term often used by the Portuguese and Spanish for official Chinese decrees or stamped documents</note> are understood by all of them, even though the languages spoken by the Chinese are numerous and very different from one another, in the same way that our numbers or ciphers are [understood] betw—

...understood equally in French, in Spanish, and in Arabic. For this figure "8", wherever it may be, signifies eight, even though the Frenchman calls this number one way, and the Spaniard another. From which it follows that since things themselves are innumerable, the letters or figures used by the Chinese to denote them are almost infinite: so much so that he who must read or write in China, as the Mandarins <note>The term "Mandarin" refers to the scholar-officials of imperial China</note> do, must know and retain at least eighty-five thousand characters or letters, and those who are perfect in this reading know more than one hundred and twenty thousand—a prodigious and strange thing, indeed, which would be unbelievable if it were not attested by people worthy of trust, etc.

The same author in chapter 6 and those following, speaking of the affairs and universities of China, says that all the study of the Chinese is in the Mandarin language, which is very vast and very difficult.

Gotthard Arthus <note>A German historian and translator (1570–1630) known for his work on the *India Orientalis* series</note> in his *History of the East Indies*, chapter fifty-one:

> Paper in China is similar to European paper, though its color is less white; however, it is superior in thinness and purity. Writing pens are made of reeds, into which they place brushes in the manner of our painters. They record everything on these papers, describing the liberal arts, laws, rights, statutes, and their private and public deeds, yielding nothing to the Greeks or Latins. They make the pages narrow and long; and in writing, they do not proceed from left to right like the Greeks and Latins, nor from right to left like the Hebrews, but from the top to the bottom, or from the summit to the base, conducting the lines by a peculiar method. I myself have seen and inspected printed volumes and books of this kind several times with my own eyes. They use letters like those of the Egyptians, which the Greeks called Hieroglyphics. Each of these serves for individual names, and sometimes even for entire meanings. Hence it happens that although the Chinese use various languages—certainly so many in regions so far apart (for there are variations according to the distance of places, and many differences in idioms and dialects)—nevertheless, all equally understand what is recorded in letters. For the alphabet <note>original: "Alphabetum"; the author uses this term loosely to describe the Chinese writing system, which is actually logographic rather than alphabetic</note> is one and the same for all, consisting of more than five thousand <note>There is a significant discrepancy here between the 5,000 characters mentioned by Arthus and the 85,000–120,000 mentioned by the previous author</note> signs for things and words, for the comprehension of which one needs a fortunate memory and long practice. From this, some reason appears why the learned among them are held in such high esteem; for besides the proper speech of each nation and province, there is moreover a certain and common speech of the learned, corresponding to the Latin language among us, which they commonly call Mandarin. This is used by courtiers, scribes, lawyers, judges, and other magistrates, who for that reason commonly obtain the name of Mandarins.

The same author in chapter 53 discourses quite amply on this Chinese language.

> From the concord <note>original: "conspiratione," meaning a "breathing together" or agreement of purpose</note> of Chinese wills and studies, it follows that there is one language common to the Realm which they call Mandarin. This is understood by all, even if not all speak it; this very fact can make the spreading of the Gospel easier, since by knowing one language, someone can suffice to bring the truth to so many and so vast provinces.

> » The language of the Chinese is almost the most difficult of all, and this for three conditions it possesses: the first is that all words are monosyllables, which creates a style of speech that is small, narrow, broken, and interrupted—which indeed causes us offense and distaste; the second cause is that the language is homonymous, and the words... <note>original: "Lingua Chinenfium omnium ferè difficillima eft, idque ob tres quas habet conditiones, quarum prima eft, quod verba omnia monofyllaba funt, quæ genus orationis minutum, anguftum fractum atque interruptum faciunt quod nobis quidem offenfionem & faftidium parit : altera caufa eft, quod lingua Homonyma fit, & vocabula."</note>

Father Diego de Pantoja <note>A Spanish Jesuit missionary (1571–1618) who accompanied Matteo Ricci to Beijing</note> of the Society of Jesus, in his report sent from Beijing <note>original: "Paquin"</note>, a city in China, to the Reverend Father Luis de Guzmán <note>original: "Louys de Gufman"</note> of the same Society, on March 9, 1602, says among other remarks about this country:

> » All the luck and happiness of the Chinese lies in the knowledge of their characters <note>The text uses "lettres" to refer to the written symbols/logograms</note>; they reach as many as forty thousand, even though their words are only monosyllables. Each character signifies [a concept], and not [just] the word, as it is with us. They write not with a pen, but in its place they use a brush <note>original: "pinceau"</note>. Of these forty thousand characters, most are composite; the simple and ordinary ones are no fewer than ten thousand, and yet few people are found in the country who do not know how to read and write. Their study is not done in colleges or public universities (as we were led to believe in Europe); they have none at all. And it is in this that their governance <note>original: "police"</note> is much lacking, among other remarkable defects: everyone provides themselves with a tutor if they have the means; if not, they join with others, paying a certain amount each month. What deceived the first informants in Europe is that every three years the King sends commissioners to the capitals of each Province for the examination, which is held for three degrees, which are like what you would call the Baccalaureate, the Licentiate, and the Doctorate. By the first, one earns the status of being counted among the men of letters from then on, and enjoys several fine privileges and immunities; but it carries the obligation to continue one's studies and to pass through to the second degree. Otherwise, if laziness is observed, and if one does not present themselves at each term for the second attempt, degradation follows with ignominy. One can usually stop at the second degree, which is joined with some office or Mandarinate <note>The rank or office of a "Mandarin" scholar-official</note> that is given when the promotion is made. The third is only granted at the King's court; he who aspires to it goes to present himself to the commissioners and obtains from them travel funds and liberal expenses to the court. When the time for the examination comes, the candidates are locked in prepared booths <note>original: "loges"</note>, all alone for twenty-four hours, having been well and surely searched beforehand; they are left nothing but their brush, their ink, and paper. And it often happens that they enter into such great apprehension, and strain their minds in such a way, that they leave their booths half dead, the rest of their lives ending a few hours later. Upon leaving, their compositions are taken and very correct copies are made of them, the originals with the authors' names being faithfully reserved in the Archives. The copies without names are given to the appointed judges, who examine them like the Areopagites <note>Referring to the judges of the high court of ancient Athens, implying impartial and grave judgment</note>, not knowing whose they are. From this great number of compositions, they select one hundred, two hundred, more or less, according to what the King has been pleased to grant; for in the plurality of Provinces, they place their honor. The composition that is judged the best, and the name of its author recognized, is declared and published with very great applause from all. The others, unnamed, mortified and burdened with shame, return home.

...study until the next examination, and that is the extent of their Academies. Those who reach the <term>doctorate</term>, and particularly the first ones promoted, obtain great favors, privileges, and honors: for to them are committed the most important and high offices of the state. Their compositions are printed and published immediately afterward with the distinguished praise of everyone; in front of their houses, people set up festoons, maypoles, imperial-style beds, escutcheons, books, and banners bearing this inscription: *This is the house of a Doctor.* On the same facade, they place the books of their ancient Philosophers, who they say flourished two thousand five hundred years ago. Yet, the best of all these much-vaunted Philosophers could not manage to equal either Plato or Seneca among our own. All the knowledge of this nation is but a little moral philosophy and rhetoric, or a <term>Topique</term> <note>A system of traditional themes or "commonplaces" used in oratory and argument</note> suited to discoursing on any moral or political subject. Vocal music is also prized there; to welcome us, the King had them sing some motets, which did not seem to me to reach the melody of our own.

The Jesuits who have recently been in this great and vast Kingdom have been so diligent in making themselves more easily understood by its people that they have reduced their languages and speech to the art of Grammar—among others the <term>Aymara</term> language <note>The author is likely conflating reports here; Aymara is an indigenous language of the Andes in South America, though it was indeed codified by Jesuits like Ludovico Bertonio around this time</note>, which is the most noble and excellent. ### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

they eat and drink at all hours. They call the Preachers *Tangins*. Their language is very difficult, consisting of verbs that are all monosyllables, which makes their style of Prayer <note>The French word "Oraison" here can mean both prayer and formal oration or speech</note> very concise, narrow, tight, broken, and interrupted, full of equivocations with Homonyms and Synonyms that they pile one on top of the other, which can only be distinguished by accents, or rather by musical sounds with a diverse prolation or pronunciation. Furthermore, they have no alphabet or index and number of letters, for each thing has its own note and Character, or rather a Hieroglyphic figure, such that throughout one's whole life it is necessary to learn a new alphabet and index of letters.

This creates a very great confusion; nevertheless, a certain modern *Jesuit Father* has reduced it to an art <note>Meaning he systematized the language into a formal grammar</note>, and has made and composed a Dictionary; *Father Martin de Herrada*, Provincial of the Augustinians mentioned above, was the first of the Europeans who learned the Chinese language and reduced it to an art, and made a Grammar of it, along with a Dictionary, as is reported in Part 2, Book 1, Chapter 1 of the *History of China*.

The most difficult part of the aforementioned language is that the Mandarins and the learned use a certain jargon like the <term>Blaisches</term> <note>Likely referring to the inhabitants of Blois, who were famed for their pure French, or perhaps a reference to a specific group known for coded speech</note>, so much so that they do not understand themselves; nevertheless, they remain capable and very eager to understand the doctrine of the faith, and have always honored a Virgin whom they say gave birth, calling her in their language *Schim-mu, ni, an, ni an*, that is to say, Holy Mother and Queen of Queens. Their King entitles himself in his titles and qualities, Lord of the World, and Child of Heaven.

The aforementioned *Father Herrada* and his companions brought several printed books from China in the Chinese language, of which ample mention is made in Part 1, Book 3, Chapter 17 of the *History of China*. In recent days, a certain *Jesuit Father* returned from the Kingdom of the aforementioned China passing through Lyon reported that its King had established two Universities in his Kingdom, where he has placed Jesuits, whom he has created Doctors by his own hand to teach all European languages and sciences and our way of writing; he has forbidden that the ancient letters be taught any longer, and has given ample permission to the said Jesuits to preach the Christian Religion and baptize throughout his Kingdom. <note>This claim about the King of China abolishing traditional Chinese characters in favor of European writing is a historical exaggeration often found in enthusiastic missionary reports of the era</note>

Modern accounts of these countries state that a *Father Matteo Ricci* has, since a few years ago, translated the principal book of China from the Chinese language into the Latin language, and has composed a European and Chinese Lexicon, and other works by means of which it is held that all those who come from Europe to China can, in four years, easily comprehend its languages and doctrines.

Whoever wishes to see several beautiful and excellent discourses on these Indies should read *João de Barros*, Decade 1, Book 6, Chapters 1, 2, and others following in his history of the Indies; *Duarte Barbosa*, Portuguese, Book 1 of his voyages, chapter on the Great Kingdom of China; the author of the summary of the Kingdoms, cities, and peoples of the Orient, chapter on the Kingdom of China; *Pigafetta* in his voyage around the world; *B. Ramusio* in his discourse on the navigation of Arrian; *J. Osorius*, Book 11 of his history of Portugal; *A. Thevet*, Book 11, Chapter 21.

->*Concerning the Great Island of Japan or Giapan.*<-

### CHAP. LXXVI.

Antonio Galvão, in his book on the inventors of the New World, and several Portuguese and Spanish authors report that the three Portuguese figures who follow were the first Europeans who found the Island of Japan in the year of salvation 1542: namely Antonio Mota, Francisco Zeimoto, and Antonio Peixoto, at the time when Martim Afonso de Sousa was Vice-Roy for the King of Portugal in the East Indies in the city of Goa; this is confirmed by Gotthard Arthus in his new history of the East Indies, chapter 56.

Since then, in the year 1549, Francis Xavier, accompanied by Cosme de Torres <note>Original: "Cosme Turrian"</note> and Juan Fernández, Spaniards, a man named Paul <note>Known as Anjirō, the first Japanese convert to Christianity</note> with two of his servants and two Japanese men who had been baptized a short time before, made the voyage to the aforementioned Island and there began to plant the foundations of the Christian Religion.

In the year 1553, several great Lords of this Island came in an Embassy to the Vice-Roy of the Indies to ask him for Doctors and Priests, in order to teach them the Christian Religion, as recorded in the letters from Japan written by the Jesuit Fathers to those of their Congregation in Europe.

The King of Bungo on this Island sent Ambassadors to the late Pope Gregory XIII in Rome to show and render all obedience to His Holiness and to the Holy Apostolic See in the year 1585, as I will note further on in this chapter.

Marco Polo the Venetian, in book 3, chapter 2 of his voyages, makes mention of this great Island under the name of Zipangu, which is situated to the North-East, stretching from Quinsay toward the country of China described by us above, and at the same elevation as Spain, namely from 35 to 40 degrees; it is 600 leagues in length and three hundred in width. The shape of this Island is more round than long, and formed like an oval: having on the southern side the Island of Mazacar with several other small ones near the gulf of the great city of Kagoshima <note>Original: "Cangoxima"</note>, of which mention is made in the letters from Japan; to the North are the Islands of Torsa, Fanfata, and others which are renowned for Meaco <note>Kyoto; original: "Meac"</note>, which is the Royal and Metropolitan city of the whole Island. A certain person named Cosme de Torres in a letter of his inserted in book 3 of the letters from Japan has made an ample description of this Island.

Miguel Vilela <note>Original: "Michel Villette"</note> in his letter to the Jesuit Brothers inserted in the book of letters from Japan writes that the Japanese worship a <term>Bonze</term> <note>A term used by early European explorers for Buddhist monks</note> who died eight hundred years ago (as they say), whom they call Kōbō-Daishi <note>Original: "Combadaxi"</note>, who taught them the...

This Bonze <note>A term used by early travelers for a Buddhist monk</note>, making them believe that he was weary of living in this world, had a large grotto made in the earth, where he shut himself in, saying that at the end of I know not how many thousands of millions of years he would return to the world, and he had this cave sealed, where they believe he remains still. Some modern authors have asserted that Iambulus <note>A Greek merchant and writer known for his tales of a utopian island in the Indian Ocean</note>, a Greek author, during his voyage heard mention of the Japanese and their Island under the name of the "Fortunate Island." He said the inhabitants use and employ twenty-eight characters of letters (as I have already said before) which in their meaning had the virtue and power of twenty-four characters of letters, even though they were only seven in number, each of which moved and changed in four ways; and that these inhabitants formed the lines of their letters and writings from the top toward the bottom. Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss scholar of linguistics and theology</note>, in his *Commentary on the Common Principle of All Languages and Letters*, based on the authority of Suetonius Tranquillus in the *Life of Augustus Caesar*, has reported that this Emperor ordinarily wrote everything in a single sequence, just as the Japanese mentioned above do. Here are the words of the said Suetonius:

> "I have noted this especially in his handwriting: that he does not divide words, nor does he transfer the letters left over at the end of lines to the next, but instead places them immediately below and wraps them around. That this was the custom of the ancients is argued by the word *versus* [a line of writing], derived from *vertendo* [turning]." <note>Original Latin: "Notaui & in Chirographo eius illa præcipuè, non diuidere verba, nec ab extrema parte verſuum abundantes literas in alterum transferre, ſed ibidem ſtatim ſubiicit, circumducitque. Eam veterum conſuetudinem fuiſſe arguit nomen verſus, à vertendo factum."</note>

These matters having been established—so as not to repeat here what we have previously discussed at length in the chapter on the Egyptian language, and the chapter on the language of the East Indians regarding the two kinds of writing in China and Cathay, namely Hieroglyphic letters and common letters, which by their combinations can form all the names one wishes to express, first taught in this Europe by an Embassy from the said Island of Japan <note>The Tenshō Embassy, the first Japanese legation to Europe</note> which, in the year 1585 in the month of March, came from its country to Rome (distant from it by five or six thousand leagues) to offer obedience to the Holy Apostolic See—we will only say that this Embassy, upon leaving Japan, took the route of the Cape of Lago, where there is a gulf of one hundred leagues to cross, and up to China 200, always coasting along its entire Eastern edge until it reached the Kingdom of Mangi <note>A historical name for Southern China</note>. And from there, continuing the navigation on the right hand, they came in sight of the Molucca Islands, from where come Cinnamon, Cloves, and Nutmeg, with other similar aromatics and spices. Then leaving these Islands to the left hand, they drew further out, having on the right the Golden Chersonese, now called Malacca, distant more than 500 leagues from the said Island of Japan; and the Island of Taprobane, commonly called Sumatra <note>While Taprobane was usually Sri Lanka, many early modern maps confused it with Sumatra</note>. From there they pass the mouth of the river Ganges, and the Gulf which takes its name from it, the Gangetic. And leaving to the left the Island of Ceylon, and to the right the point of Malabar, where the Kingdoms of Calicut, Cochin, Cannanore, and other provinces fertile in pepper, ginger, gold, and gemstones are located, they arrived at Goa, another 500 leagues from Malacca, and followed this entire coast to the mouth of the river Indus, and the shores of Gedrosia <note>The coastal region of modern-day Balochistan</note>. The *Relations of Italy* from the year 1585 speak thus of the Embassy:
In the year 1585, Japanese Ambassadors arrived in Rome with letters, first from the King of Bungo <note>original: "Bungensi"; referring to Ōtomo Sōrin, a Christian daimyo</note> with this inscription:
> To the great and most blessed Pope worthy of Adoration, since he is the Vicar of the King of heavens on earth. <note>original: "Ad magnũ & beatissimum Papam Adoratione dignum, cùm ſit ille Vicarius Regis cælorum in terra."</note>

Mention is made of the King of Hyuga <note>original: "Fiungæ"</note>, the brother-in-law and nephew Jerome, as well as Lord Mancio <note>Itō Mancio, the leader of the embassy</note> whom he had sent from himself with these Kingdoms to be devoted to your holiness.
The second letter was from the King of Arima <note>Arima Harunobu</note> with this inscription:
> Let this letter be given to that holy and great Lord, whom I adore as the Vicar of God. <note>original: "Sit data hæc epiſtola illi ſancto & magno Domino, quem ego adoro tanquam Dei Vicarium."</note>

In the same tenor as the first, mentioning Lord Michael <note>Chijiwa Miguel</note>, the King's kinsman sent for that purpose.
The third was from Lord Bartholomew, Prince of Omura <note>Ōmura Sumitada, the first Christian daimyo</note>, whose nephew by his sister was Protasius, the King of Arima, with this inscription:
> With raised hands I reverently offer these letters to the most holy Pope Our Lord, Vicar of the highest God. <note>original: "Sublatis manibus offero haſce literas reuerenter ſanctissimo Papæ D. N. Vicario ſummi Dei."</note>

The signatures of the first letter perform the same act of obedience:
Prostrate on knees at the most holy feet of your beatitude, Francis, King of Bungo. <note>original: "In genua prouolutus ad pedes Sanctiſſimos veſtræ beatitudinis Franciſcus Rex de Bugno."</note>
In the other:
[The servant] of your Holiness who falls on his knees at his feet, Lord Protasius. <note>original: "Sanctitatis veſtræ qui in genua procumbit ad pedes ſuos Dominus Pro-taſius."</note>
The third in the same style.
