» they write, and in the writing itself: they write letters in one way, and books in another, of which they have a great number, both in prose and in very elegant verse. Furthermore, they use characters such that each signifies a certain thing, or even several words, in the manner of the Egyptians <note>A reference to hieroglyphics, which early modern scholars often compared to East Asian characters</note> and the Chinese. Finally, in the view of our people—who are no mean judges of things—this Japanese language is to be preferred to Latin, whether for its style, or for its richness and abundance. For this reason, it requires great labor and a long time to be learned and spoken.

André Thevet, in Book 12, Chapter 16 of his *Universal Cosmography* <note>original: "Coſmographie vniuerſelle"; a major 1575 work by the French royal cosmographer</note>, writing of these Japanese people, states that they write from top to bottom, and not from left to right as we do. The reason they give for this—which is rather thin—is that just as a walking man keeps his feet down and his head up, so too must one begin writing at the top and end at the bottom.

Here then is the simple Alphabet of China and Japan, whose writing proceeds from top to bottom, arranged in columns from the right hand toward the left, in the Hebrew fashion. This was shared with the public through the grace and beneficence of His Majesty, the late King Henry III, by means of the late Count of Bouchage <note>Henri de Joyeuse (1563–1608), a nobleman who famously left the royal court to become a Capuchin monk</note>, while he lived as a Capuchin Father. This was done at the request of the no less eloquent than very learned late reverend and devout Father, Monsieur Edmond Auger of the Society of the name of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note>, who brokered this gift for us, as certified by the late Sieur de Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a diplomat and cryptographer famous for the "Vigenère cipher"</note> in his *Treatise on Ciphers*.

Finally, according to our own people—who are by no means crude judges of such matters—this Japanese language is to be preferred to Latin, whether for its style, or for its richness and abundance. A. Thevet <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a French Franciscan explorer and writer who served as the royal cosmographer</note> in book 12, chapter 16 of his *Universal Cosmography*, writing of these Japanese people, records that they write from top to bottom, and not from left <note>original: "feneſtre," an archaic variant of *senestre*</note> to right <note>original: "dextre"</note> as we do. The reason they give for this is rather thin: that just as a man, when walking, keeps his feet below and his head above, so too must one begin writing at the top and finish at the bottom.

Here then is the simple alphabet of China and Japan, whose writing proceeds from top to bottom, in columns arranged from the right hand toward the left, in the Hebrew fashion. This was shared with the public through the grace and beneficence of the Majesty of the late King Henry III, by means of the late Count of Bouchage <note>Henri de Joyeuse (1563–1608), a high-ranking noble and soldier who later became a Capuchin friar</note> during his life as a Capuchin Father; at the request of the no less eloquent than highly learned late reverend and devout Father Emond Auger <note>A prominent Jesuit (1530–1591) and confessor to King Henry III</note> of the Society of the name of JESUS, who secured this benefit for us, as the late Sieur de Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a diplomat and author famous for his work on cryptography</note> certifies in his *Treatise on Ciphers*.

Furthermore, these Japanese have a book composed in their Chinese language <note>The author refers to *Kanbun*, the classical Chinese used for scholarly and religious texts in Japan.</note>, named *Fouqueque* <note>The *Hokke-kyō*, or Lotus Sutra, one of the most influential scriptures in East Asian Buddhism.</note>, formerly created and composed by *Xaca* <note>Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha.</note> whom they say was the son of one of their Kings, and a very learned personage. > » their writing, but they do not understand them when speaking, which is

Some modern authors have remarked that on this island of Japan, several words are noted in the language of the inhabitants that conform to those of the Icelanders, as a sign of the ancient commerce that may have formerly existed between these two nations; a claim repeated by the Lord of la Popelinière in book 1 of *The Three Worlds* <note>Lancelot Voisin, Sieur de La Popelinière (1541–1608). This theory of a linguistic link between Japan and Iceland is a historical curiosity of early modern ethnography.</note>.

## Of the Indian Philosophers.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.

Strabo <note>An ancient Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC–24 AD).</note> in his works, speaking of the Indian philosophers, writes that there were two sorts: the Brachmans <note>Brahmins.</note>, otherwise called Brachmanes, and the Germans <note>A corruption of the Greek *Garmanes* or *Sarmanes*, referring to the Shramanas, wandering ascetics of ancient India.</note>: and that these Brachmans or Brachmanes were more excellent than the others, because their opinions were closer to reason and truth than those of the Germans (whom Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note>, in book 4 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, calls Samaneans <note>Shramanas.</note>). Also, from the moment these Brachmans were conceived, says the aforementioned Strabo, they had learned men who took care of them; these men, coming to the mother, used I know not what charms and words over the mother and the fruit of her womb, wishing and promising her happiness and good success for the future. But there are some who say that they spoke only of good things to the mother, preaching to her sobriety and continence: and they esteemed as happy those mothers who heard them with a good heart, whom they said would be abundant in lineage. Once the children were brought into the light, they were given instructors, sometimes one, sometimes another: but when it happened that they were grown,

it was then that they were given the most learned and excellent of their school as masters. These Philosophers lived within the woods, which were those closest to the cities, and stayed there assembled together as **Religious** <note>Meaning monks or members of a religious order.</note> do in their monasteries, living very soberly, sleeping on mattresses and animal skins, eating no meat of any kind (as they still do not) and abstaining from women (which they now take no care to observe), speaking only of serious things, and communicating heartfully with those who came to approach them as if desirous both to learn and to make their knowledge known and understood by others. And the disciples practiced great reverence and modest respect when before their masters, it not being permitted for them to speak, cough, or spit; and if it happened that anyone did so, he was suddenly chased away for that day from the company and esteemed a man of little honesty, lacking sobriety and continence.

They lived for a period of thirty years under this discipline and subjection, and then each of the disciples retired to his own house, it being permitted for him to live a little more freely than was customary: for they could dress in subtle and delicate linen, wear rings on their fingers, and bracelets, and jewelry hanging from their ears, but all with discretion and modesty, and without any excess or superfluity. Similarly, they were not permitted to eat the meat of animals other than those that are helpful to man; and meanwhile, sauces and meats that were very sharp and biting, such as garlic, onions, and spices, were forbidden to them. They also had license to marry several wives to have lineage, saying that from a great number there would also come a multitude of good children. It is true that they never philosophized among their wives, so that if they were foolish and fickle, they would not publish the secrets of their school and doctrine; and if they were good, having tasted this knowledge, they might not withdraw from their company. For those who despise both death and pain, who care for neither pleasure, nor ease, nor life itself, who wish to be subject to no one but rather defend their liberty—such a person is esteemed good by them; and the wise and virtuous woman, if their wives embraced such opinions, would also no longer wish to live under the obedience of their husbands.

Regarding their opinions on natural things, they held several views following the opinion of the Greeks, saying the world had a beginning and that it will one day have an end, and that its shape is spherical and round, and that God, being the author and former of it, also fills it all by his power and penetrates it, and runs through it in a single blink of an eye. They held that there are several and diverse principles of things, but that the world had its source and original beginning from water. They established (like Aristotle) beyond the four elements a certain *Entelechy* <note>original: "Entelechie"; from the Greek *entelecheia*, referring to the realization or full expression of a thing's potential.</note>, or *quintessence* <note>The "fifth essence" or element, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire, thought to compose the celestial bodies.</note>, of which the heavens and the stars were composed, and that the earth is placed in the middle of the Universe; and several other things, some true, others approaching the truth, and some fabulous, so that it seems either that Plato fished his doctrine from them, or else that they are Platonists.

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note> in book 7, chapter 2, and Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler.</note> in chapter 65, describe another sort of Philoso—

<note>original: "phes..." - continuing the word "Philosophes" from the previous page</note> ...phers among these Indians, who are called <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>From the Greek *gymnos* (naked) and *sophist* (wise man); a name given by the Greeks to Indian ascetics who wore little to no clothing.</note> because they practiced philosophy while standing completely naked in the sun, sitting or crouching on their haunches like a monkey or an ape, and sometimes standing upright to devote themselves to contemplation. Concerning these, the aforementioned Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman compiler.</note> speaks in this manner, having drawn it from the aforementioned Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History.</note> as he did the rest of his works: "The Indians (he says) have philosophers they call <term>Gymnosophists</term>, who from the morning when the sun rises until the evening when it sets, remain attentively fixing their eyes upon the burning and brilliant globe of the sun, considering certain secrets within it; and they do not mind spending the entire day standing on one foot, and that foot completely naked upon the burning sand, heated by the violent warmth and rays of the sun." Philostratus, in Book 2, Chapter 4 of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, says that these <term>Gymnosophists</term> keep themselves, as has been said, in the sun: they pray to and adore it, and their prayers intend that the hours it measures by its courses and revolutions might be converted and accommodated for the safety of the Indians and for the fertility of their land. And because he maintains that these philosophers possess some kind of fire that they draw from the most brilliant rays of the sun, he adds further that once night has fallen, they pray to it again not to be angry, even though the night veils its beautiful face, but that it might please the sun to remain with the Indians, just as they retain it among themselves. Many and infinite other things concerning the ways of acting and the beliefs of these Indian philosophers are deduced by the aforementioned Philostratus in Book 6 of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*. For the rest, we shall note that under the word <term>Gymnosophist</term> is comprised the generality of Indian doctors and philosophers, because they all went completely naked while they were in their school. Of this, Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> bears witness in Book 4 of *On Sacrifices* <note>Original: "des sacrifices" — referring to Porphyry's "On Abstinence from Animal Food."</note>: that Apostate <note>A term used by Christian writers for Porphyry because of his intellectual opposition to Christianity.</note> who, to embrace the doctrine of Plato too foolishly, renounced Christianity; for he says there were two kinds of <term>Gymnosophists</term>: namely the <term>Brahmins</term>, who attained holiness and integrity through a certain succession of race <note>Meaning it was a hereditary caste.</note>, and the <term>Samaneans</term> (whom Strabo calls <term>Garmanes</term>) <note>Likely referring to Shramanas, non-Vedic ascetics including Buddhists and Jains.</note> who simply made a profession of this doctrine of their own will, without being received into the number of the others who were the most perfect.

The same Strabo cited above divides the <term>Garmanes</term> of whom we spoke before, with some being more perfect than others, insofar as the word <term>Garman</term> is general; and there is another name, which is the <term>Hylobians</term>, which is a Greek word <note>original: "Hylobies" from *hylobios*</note> meaning "living in the woods," and feeding themselves on the fruits gathered from trees, with whose bark they clothed themselves, caring neither for intoxicating drink nor for the company of women. These were honored by Kings, who sought their counsel on divine things, and they were instructed in how it was necessary to revere and perform service to God. In addition to these <term>Hylobians</term>, there were among the <term>Garmanes</term> certain physicians, who took care to debate in the same way about man—that is to say, about what pertains to the body—as the others did regarding what touched the soul. And these lived very frugally, but not in the fields, nor in the woods, nor in the wind like the others, eating...

...rice, and flour: there being no one who would refuse them if they asked, or who would not lodge them lightheartedly in their house if they requested to be received. This was because it was believed to be in their power to make women fruitful and fertile, and that through their drugs and medicines, they had the means to cause the procreation of males and females. Now, they held the opinion that the best medicines were those taken while at rest, and not merely as a matter of habit; and if it were necessary to take them otherwise, it was through ointments, frictions, and poultices, because in these there lay no risk of witchcraft. These physicians and the forest philosophers or <term>Hylobies</term> <note>From the Greek *hylobios*, meaning 'living in the woods.'</note> were very constant in enduring all labor and suffering, even to the point of remaining every day steadfast in the same way of life, without softening any of their severity.

There was a third type of these <term>Sarmanes</term> <note>original: "Germans." In early modern French texts, this was a common corruption of the Greek *Garmanes* or *Sarmanes* (from the Sanskrit *Shramana*), referring to non-Brahminical ascetics.</note> who were charmers, sorcerers, and enchanters, who were not ignorant of anything said regarding the apparitions of the dead, nor of the science practiced by means of the bodies and shadows of the deceased. Furthermore, there was another sort, more civil and courteous than those named above, people who frequented the cities and villages without being so scrupulous about meats or company. These were also not ignorant of the science of <term>demons</term> <note>The author uses this in the classical sense of *daimones*—spirits or intermediate beings—who were thought to bridge the gap between nature and humanity.</note> in which, to tell the truth, most of the philosophers were skilled. Wanting to know the secrets of nature, they considered malevolent spirits to be "Genies," messengers of nature who gave them this knowledge.

The aforementioned <term>Strabo</term> <note>A famous Greek geographer and historian who provided one of the most detailed ancient accounts of India.</note> mentions yet another kind of philosopher, whom he calls <term>Pramnae</term>. He says they are a contentious people and great debaters, who mocked the <term>Brahmins</term> because they busied themselves with the science of the stars and the attempt to judge men by their <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging a person's character or future from their facial features.</note>; they called them fools and vain predictors of uncertain things. Thus, one can see how much vanity was imprinted on the hearts of these people, and yet they did not lack a natural, good, and noble disposition, given their social order, knowledge, and their fairly civil and reformed life. For this reason, one should not be astonished if several great and learned ancient personages traveled as far as India to speak to these <term>Gymnosophists</term> and <term>Brahmins</term>, since even today they have a reputation for knowledge, though they do not come close to those of ancient times.

Those who wish to see several other fine and extensive discourses concerning the life, manners, and customs of these Indian philosophers should read: <term>Diodorus Siculus</term>, Book 7, on the deeds of Alexander, mentioning the letter from the Brahmin King to Alexander the Great; <term>St. Augustine</term>, Book 13, Chapter 17, and Book 15, Chapter 20 of *The City of God*; <term>Fulgosus</term> <note>Battista Fregoso, an Italian author known for his collection of memorable facts.</note>, Book 8, Chapter 11 of his *Rhapsodies*; <term>Caelius Rhodiginus</term> <note>An Italian scholar whose *Lectiones Antiquae* (Ancient Lessons) was a massive encyclopedia of classical knowledge.</note>, Book 13, Chapter 25, and Book 18, Chapter 31 of his *Diverse Lessons*; <term>F. de Belleforest</term>, Book 2, Chapter 8 of his *Universal History*, and Volume 2, Book 3, Chapter 14 and following of his *Universal Cosmography*.

Modern travelers and navigators, in their voyages and sailings describing the customs and ways of the East Indians, report that throughout the East Indies today there are many <term>Brahmins</term>, who are like the priests and philoso...

...sophers, or Doctors of the Idolaters: especially as they serve before the idols and are entrusted with the governance of the temples, of which they have a great number. Some of these are endowed with land and income, while in others the **Brahmins** must live on alms. In these temples, they have statues of stone, wood, and all kinds of metals; they celebrate festivals there and perform grand ceremonies, sounding instruments, singing, using incense, and lighting a great number of oil lamps, for wax is not much in use there. They hold the number three in great reverence and confess a single God, Creator of all the world and the things contained within it, and that his divinity is one in three persons. However, their error is that they believe there are other Gods in great number who govern as deputies of the Great One in this world, whom they pray to and adore. When all is said and done, they make God out to be ceasing and idle, as if he had grown weary making the world, and that these others, being fresher, have now taken up the charge. It is easy to see that these people once had a taste of **Christianity**, as much for this belief in the Trinity and unity of persons, as for the fact that when they enter the Churches of the Christians (who are found in quite good numbers in these Indies), they pray there willingly, revere them, and honor the images of the Saints. Furthermore, <term>Duarte Barbosa</term> <note>original: "Odouard Barbosse." A Portuguese explorer (c. 1480–1521) whose travelogues provided Europe with some of its first detailed descriptions of Indian society.</note> says in his travels that these people always inquire about our Lady, the glorious **Virgin Mary**, as if having heard of her. As for me, I think the lack of Christianity among them resulted from the fault of the **Ministers** <note>The author refers to priests or missionaries.</note> who ceased to admonish the people. Thus it is that these people still say there is hardly any difference between their religion and ours, but they are greatly mistaken: for we give no companion to God; in him alone we hope, and we pray to and honor him in his saints, without making him idle or giving the charge of the world to false gods, nor raising an altar or sacrifice to anyone but this God, who by his word created all that exists in this Universe. Thus, it is impossible to place in the same rank of religion things as different as **Christianity** and **idolatry**. These Brahmins also go entirely naked above the waist, but over the shoulder they wear a cord of three threads with silk tassels, which is the sign to recognize them from the <term>Baucani</term> <note>Likely a corruption of the "Bania" or "Vania," a prominent merchant and banking caste in Gujarat.</note>, who make up the second rank of the Gujarati gentiles. These latter involve themselves in the traffic of merchandise and also do not eat anything whatsoever that has blood; likewise, they kill no animal of any kind on the earth, in the air, or in the waters. They observe ablutions and washings, believing this to be the salvation of their souls. Both these Brahmins and the *Baucani* marry as we do, that is to say, without practicing a plurality of wives as the <term>Mahometans</term> <note>original: "Mahometistes." A historical European term for Muslims.</note> and other idolaters do; and they consider it a sin to fly to second marriages. This lasts for several days, with a great assembly being held, everyone being dressed very richly to honor the married couple. To avoid <gloss>lechery</gloss> <note>original: "paillardise"</note>, they marry very young, both men and women. On the wedding day, the spouses stay upon a bed, richly dressed and laden with jewels and precious stones, and before them is a small table upon which is an idol covered in flowers, surrounded by a quantity of lit lamps, toward which idol...

->LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE. 927<-

The husband and wife must keep their eyes fixed from morning until evening, without drinking, eating, or saying a single word to any living person. Meanwhile, the guests feast and rejoice with their songs, balls, dances, and musical instruments, just as they also set off fireworks for the pleasure and pastime of the company. And should it happen that the husband dies, the woman is no longer permitted to remarry; she succeeds, along with the children, to the inheritance of the deceased. It is also to be noted that the **Brahmins** do not take wives from anywhere else but from among the **Brahmins**, so as not to defile or mix their lineages and families. 

Of these, there are two kinds: some are of high quality and the most respected, being those who have charge of the temples and who offer the sacrifices; others are of a lower condition and serve as messengers and couriers for those who employ them. This is because, wherever they go, there is no one who would cause them trouble or annoyance, even if war is ignited on all sides. Truly, even thieves, upon meeting them on the road, respect them so much that they make way for them and honor them, whereas they rob others. 

Throughout the entire country of the **Deccan**, and in the regions of **Cambay**, **Goa**, and the surrounding lands, there are many of these **Brahmins**, the greatest and most honored of whom are those called <term>Patamares</term> <note>In this context, Patamares refers to Brahmin couriers who were granted safe passage through various territories due to their sacred status.</note>, because they are esteemed to be descended from the royal blood of the Princes of **Cambay**, especially since in this country it was formerly required that Kings be **Brahmins**, as is still practiced today in **Malabar**. These men are so highly esteemed that merchants passing through the country, even if they fall into the hands of brigands and thieves, are as safe as if they were in their own home provided they have one of these **Brahmins** in their company. There is no one so bold as to dare rob them; and if it happens that there are some so wild as to show no respect, and who pillage and rob the poor merchants, the **Brahmin** accompanying them immediately either kills himself or wounds himself with a dagger. The others then take his blood to stain certain images, which they drag through the streets until justice has been done for the wrong the merchants received, and vengeance taken for the spilled blood of their companion. One is constrained to do this both for the reverence held for them and to avoid irritating the people, who love and revere them strangely, inasmuch as they hold them to be holy and believe that if justice were not done for them, they themselves would be punished for having denied it. 

Regarding the **Brahmins** of **Malabar**, the aforementioned modern travelers and navigators identify four types: those who are strictly **Brahmins**, then the <term>Patamares</term>, the <term>Nambudaires</term> <note>original: "Nambudaires." Likely the Nambudiri, the high-caste Malayali Brahmins.</note>, and the <term>Nabures</term>, who are the least valued. The race of these people is very ancient; they come from blood more illustrious than the <term>Nairs</term> <note>The Nair or Nayar are a group of Indian castes from the state of Kerala, traditionally known as a martial nobility.</note>, and they are in charge of performing prayer and possess the understanding of all that concerns their **Religion**. The most honorable among them stay with the King, as they do in **Calicut**, and they eat nothing that has life, nor does the King, who must be taken from this **Brahmin** race. They never kill cows on pain of death, this being a law of their ancestors; because they live on the milk, butter, and cheeses of these animals, they consider it parricide to kill one.

Among the Gentiles <note>A term used by the author for Hindus</note> of the great Kingdom of the **Deccan** in the aforementioned Indies, there are **Brahmins** whom some claim to be of the ancient race of the **Brahman Gymnosophists** <note>Literally "naked philosophers," a term used by the Greeks for Indian ascetics</note>, of whom we spoke above. When their bodies die, they are burned, and with them their wives; those who refuse to do this are shamefully blamed, as specifically reported by the aforementioned **Duarte Barbosa** in his summary of the Indies. Whoever wishes to see many other things worthy of remark and consideration concerning the life, manners, and conduct of these Brahmins, should read **Ludovico di Varthema**, book five of his voyages; **Duarte Barbosa** in his voyages, the chapter on the Kingdom of **Gujarat** in India, and the chapter on the **Brahmins** and their customs; the author of the summary of the Kingdoms, cities, and peoples of the East, speaking of these Brahmins who have succeeded the **Gymnosophists** of the ancient Indians; **Garcia de Orta**, the Portuguese, in several places in his books on spices; **André Thevet**, book 11, chapter 16 of his *Universal Cosmography*; **Paolo Morigia**, book 3, chapters 10 and 11 of his history of all Religions; and more learnedly and excellently than those mentioned above, **Otto Heurnius** in his *Antiquities of Barbarian Philosophy* <note>original: "Antiquitate Philosophiae Barbaricae"</note>, in the treatise entitled *Indian Matters* <note>original: "Indicus"</note>, in the chapter *On the various kinds of ancient Indian philosophers* <note>original: "de Priscorum Indorum Philosophorum variis generibus"</note>, and the chapter *On the various kinds of modern Indian philosophers* <note>original: "de recentium Indorum Philosophorum variis generibus"</note>.

Beyond the aforementioned **Brahmins**, there are also found among the Indies certain individuals originating from the Kingdom of **Delhi**, who stay only a short time in one place. Being called *Yogis* by the people of **Delhi**, they call themselves in their own language **Coamez**, which is to say, <gloss>servants of God</gloss>. Their goal and end is to be placed in the rank of those they call **Abdutes** <note>Likely *Avadhutas*, a type of radical Hindu ascetic who has "shaken off" worldly concerns</note>, an order among them most prized and esteemed of all. They travel in bands, much like the **Egyptians** and **Bohemians** <note>Historical terms for the Romani people</note> of our lands, throughout all the Indies, being everywhere very welcome and cherished by all the **Gentiles** and **Pagans**. They eat all meats without scruple and associate with all kinds of people, neither practicing the customary and superstitious washings of other Indians, nor devoting themselves to the worship of Idols. As for this name **Yogi**, it comes from the Kingdom of **Yoghé**, the inhabitants of which are vagabonds just like these **Coamez**. See **L. Varthema** <note>Ludovico di Varthema, an Italian traveler</note> book 4, chapter 2 of his travels, and the Portuguese **Duarte Barbosa** in his travels, the chapter on the Kingdom of **Delhi**. Also **P. du Jarric** book 1, chapter 4 of his histories of the East Indies.

The Chinese call their Priests in their language **Hoxiones**, **Mandarins**, **Tutans**, and **Loytias** <note>These are early European phonetic transcriptions of Chinese administrative and religious titles like *Heshang* (monk) and *Laodie* (venerable father)</note>.

As for the Priests and Philosophers of the Island of **Japan** named **bonzes** or **bonzies**, there are several kinds. Three of these are like our Monks, whom the Japanese call in their language **Lequixil**, and there are women who are like our Nuns and Religious sisters, whom the aforementioned call in their said language **Hamacata**. They have monasteries just like the Monks in our lands, both inside and outside the cities. Those who stay in the cities never marry, live on alms, have their heads and beards shaved, and wear long robes with wide sleeves. In winter they have their heads covered, and for the rest of the year they have them bare. They eat together like our Religious orders and fast several times during the year. These Monks do not eat any animal whatsoever, so as to appear thin and to rid themselves of the stings of sin. This penance is common to every kind of Monk on the aforementioned Island. It is said that they rise at midnight to pray, and that they perform their oraison by singing for the space of half an hour, then return to bed until the dawn of day, when they rise again for prayer. They do the same at sunrise, at noon, and in the evening; and then they make a sign which, upon hearing, all the people kneel, and joining their hands, lift them to Heaven and all pray. It is these **Lequixil** who preach and exhort the people; they are well-heard, and they weep while preaching, inducing the audience to weep as well, so expert are they in their oratory. As for their doctrine, some hold that they confess one God, creator of all things, which may well be, since the beginning of their superstition and Idolatry took its source from a **Brahmin** and **Gymnosophist** <note>A term from Greek meaning "naked philosopher," used by Europeans to describe Indian ascetics</note> of the Kingdom of China, according to the report of **Baltasar Gago** in his letter sent to his brothers in the year 1563, inserted in book 4, letter 2 of the *Letters from Japan*. And yet, this knowledge of a God is greatly obscured for them by the rest of their faith, their ways of acting, and their ceremonies. ## *Of the language of the Javanese.*

### CHAP. LXXVIII.

The Islands of **Java**, situated in the Indian Sea, are of very great and ample extent, the smallest of which contains 500 leagues in circumference—taking four miles to the league—and possesses eight Kingdoms or Provinces, each being commanded by its own King and using its own particular language, different from the languages of the others, according to the account of **Marco Polo the Venetian**, book 3, chapter 10 of his travels.

## *Of the Region of the West Indies.*

**Abraham Ortelius**, in his *Synonyms* and *Geographical Treasury*, spoke thus of the **West Indies**, or the New World: <note>original: "Atlantis Insula, cuius Plato meminit, & Ammianus Europæ orbe potiorem scribit: Mercator & alij nonnulli volunt hodie Americam esse."</note> The Island of **Atlantis**, which **Plato** mentions, and **Ammianus** writes is larger than the circuit of Europe: **Mercator** and several others believe today that this is **America**. <note>original: "Hæc quarta pars orbis numeratur, & Hispani Indiam vocant, sed falsò & impropriè cum vera India, quæ Asiæ Regio est, ab insigniore fluuio Indo nominatur."</note> This is counted as the fourth part of the world, and the **Spanish** call it **India**, but falsely and improperly, since the true India—which is a region of **Asia**—is named after the more famous river **Indus**. <note>original: "Si verò hanc partem ab eius flumine primario nomen indere libuisset Amazoniam, vel Orelianam potius, quàm Indiam indigitassent."</note> If indeed one had wished to give this part a name from its primary river, they would have designated it **Amazonia**, or rather **Orellana** <note>Named after Francisco de Orellana, the first European to navigate the Amazon River</note>, instead of **India**. <note>original: "Ne hanc tamen cum vera India confunderent, eam Occidentalem aut Hispanicam cognominauerunt; cum altera & vera Orientalis aut Lusitanica vulgò vocatur: ab orbis plagis, & regibus nempe, quibus subsunt, nomenclaturis."</note> Yet, lest they confuse this with the true India, they named it the **West** or **Spanish [Indies]**; while the other and true one is commonly called the **East** or **Portuguese [Indies]**: names derived from the regions of the world and from the kings, of course, to whom they are subject. <note>original: "Hanc Atlanticam Plutonis Insulam vocat Tertullianus de Pallio, Æon quem locum etsi suspectum censet Turnebus, approbat & retinet Pamelius."</note> **Tertullian**, in *On the Pallium*, calls this the **Atlantic Island of Pluto**; although **Turnebus** considers this passage suspect, **Pamelius** approves and retains it. <note>original: "Hanc eandem puto à Plutarcho de facie in orbe Lunæ, sub nomine μεγάλη ἤπειρος Magnæ continentis describit."</note> I believe this same place is described by **Plutarch** in *On the Face in the Moon*, under the name of <gloss>the Great Continent</gloss> <note>original Greek: "μεγάλη ἤπειρος"</note>.

**Globe of the Earth** <note>Original Latin: *Pila Terrae*, literally "Ball of the Earth"</note>: used by Varro at the beginning of his work for the World, and by others. **Gerard Mercator**—who, if any other after Ptolemy has deserved well of Geography, it is he—has excellently divided this into three continents. The first he makes that in which are Europe, Africa, and Asia. (I call this the **Ptolemaic** continent). The second he calls **America**. Others also name it thus, though the common people call it the **West Indies**. There are those who call it the **New World**, which I can bear, but those who call it **America**, I do not like as well. For we know that it was first detected within the memory of our fathers by **Christopher Columbus**. If it were to be named after its discoverer, it should be named after him, and not after **Amerigo Vespucci**, who ten years after Columbus discovered that part of it which lies toward the South. I would prefer the true glory of both to be consulted: that the northern part be called **Columbia**, and the southern part **America**. For nature itself distinguishes this continent into two nearly equal parts and connects them by an intermediate Isthmus.

The third continent, according to the said Mercator, is the **Southern tract** <note>The theoretical southern continent *Terra Australis Incognita*</note>, which has not yet been fully surveyed; **Guillaume Postel**, a man of rare learning, labels this **Chafdia**. One might not absurdly name its inhabitants the **Hypernotians** <note>A term coined to mean "those far to the south," the southern equivalent of the northern "Hyperboreans"</note>.

He notes that they were simple in their speech, which they uttered very loudly and clearly between their teeth and their lips, and that their languages every hundred leagues <note>A league was a historical unit of distance, usually about 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers</note> were entirely diverse and dissimilar, without one being understood by the other in any form or manner whatsoever. This is asserted after **Amerigo Vespucci** in Book 1 of his *Voyages* to **René, King of Sicily**; by **Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo** in the final chapter of his *Summary of the Indies*, and Book 7, Chapter 13 of his *General History of the Indies*; and by **José de Acosta** in Book 6, Chapter 7 of his *Natural History of the Indies*.

In this regard, it is held that these Indians, at the time they were first discovered by the **Spanish**, would not approach the **Copey** trees <note>Species of the genus *Clusia*, whose thick leaves can be etched with a stylus</note> growing in their country, fearing that they would reveal their secrets to the aforementioned Spanish. The Spanish wrote their letters and missives with the point of an iron tool upon the leaves of this tree, by which they communicated their affairs to one another; being ignorant of this, the aforementioned Indians believed that the leaves of said trees spoke for the Spanish.

**Francisco López de Gómara**, a Spaniard, in Book 2, Chapter 75 of his *General History of the Indies*, writes that the inhabitants of **New Spain** <note>The colonial territory primarily comprising modern-day Mexico</note> used—when they were first discovered—certain letters made in the form of specific figures, with which they marked, noted, and understood all things. By means of these letters, they preserved the memory and remembrance of ancient and past events. These letters resembled the **Hieroglyphics** of the **Egyptians**, although they did not contain such a profound meaning, nor did they pronounce them as we do ours. As for the most copious, elegant, pure, and excellent language of this New Spain, it is the language named **Nahuatl** <note>Original: "Ynathual"</note> in that country. The "amorous thieves" and robbers of said country use certain whistles and signs in their behavior, with which they understand each other as easily as if they were pronouncing and speaking a true, pure, and entire language. In this regard, the narrations of the **West Indies** report that at **Tenochtitlan** <note>Original: "Themiftian," the Aztec capital</note>, during its conquest by **Hernán Cortés** for the Emperor **Charles V**, certain records or scrolls <note>Original: "pancartes"</note> were found containing figures of animals, trees, plants, herbs, birds, and fish—and by their limbs and parts, the gestures and deeds of the Kings of this region. These were knotted in the manner of prayer beads <note>Original: "patenoftres"</note> of various colors, according to the things these Indians wished to represent. > To begin with the division and calculations of time that the Indians made (in which one can certainly recognize one of the greatest signs of their liveliness and good understanding), I will first say in what manner the Mexicans <note>Referring to the Aztec or Nahua people of central Mexico</note> counted and divided their years, their months, their calendar, their counts, their centuries, and ages. They divided the year into eighteen months, to each of which they attributed twenty days, by which the 360 days are completed, without including in any of these months the 5 days that remain from the surplus, making the completion of the entire year. But they counted them separately and called them the days of nothing <note>original: "iours de rien"; referring to the *Nemontemi*, the five "unlucky" or "empty" days added to the end of the 360-day solar cycle</note>, during which the people did nothing, and did not even go to their temples; instead, they occupied themselves only with visiting one another, thus wasting time, and the priests of the temple also ceased sacrificing. After these five days passed, they began again their count of the year, of which the first month and the commencement was in March, when the leaves began to turn green again, even though they took three days from the month of February; for their first day of the year was like the 26th day of February, as it appears by their Calendar, within which even the leap year is included and employed with a very ingenious artifice, and was made by the ancient Indians who knew the first Spaniards. I have seen this Calendar, and I still have it in my possession; it well deserves to be seen to understand the discourse and the industry of the Mexican Indians. Each of these 18 months had its own name and its own picture, which it took commonly from the principal feast held in that month, or from the diversity of the weather that the year causes in them. They had in this Calendar certain days marked and destined for the feasts they observed, and counted the weeks of thirteen days, marking the days by zeros <note>likely referring to the circular dots used in Aztec numerical notation</note> which they multiplied up to thirteen, and immediately began again.

For one must know that their wheel, which was like a century to them, contained four weeks of years, each week being thirteen years, which together completed fifty-two years. They painted a Sun in the middle of this wheel, from which four arms or lines came out in a cross reaching to the circumference of the wheel, and they made their turn in such a way that the circumference was divided into four equal parts, each of which, with its arm or line, had a particular color different from the others; and the four colors were green, blue, red, and yellow. Each of these four portions had thirteen separations, which all had their particular signs or figures of house, or rabbit, or reed, or pebble, signifying by each sign one year; and at the head of this sign, they painted what had happened that year. This is why I saw in the Calendar I mentioned the year the Spaniards entered Mexico, marked by a painting of a man dressed in red in our fashion, for such was the dress of the first Spaniard sent by Hernán Cortés <note>original: "Fernand Cortez"</note> at the end of the fifty-two years when the wheel closed and was completed. They used a pleasant ceremony, which was that on the last night they broke all the vessels and utensils they had, and extinguished all fires and all lights, saying that the world was to come to an end at the completion of one of these wheels, and that by chance it might be the one in which they found themselves. For, they said, since the world must then end, what more need is there to prepare meat or to eat? This is why they had no more use for vessels or fire. Upon this opinion, they passed the whole night in great fear, saying that perhaps day would never come again, and they all watched very attentively to see when the day would come; but seeing that the dawn began to break, they immediately beat many drums and sounded trumpets, flutes, and other instruments of rejoicing and joy, saying that God was lengthening their time by another century, which was fifty-two years. And then they would begin another wheel; on this first day and beginning of the century, they took new fire and bought new vessels and utensils to prepare meat, and they all went to fetch this new fire from the High Priest, having previously made a solemn procession of thanksgiving for the coming of day and the prolongation of another century. Such was their fashion and manner of counting years, months, weeks, and centuries.

### HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

...were cast into the fire. Since then, not only have the Indians recognized that this was a mistake, but also those curious Spaniards who desired to know the secrets of the country. Those who have wished to diligently inform themselves about them have found there many things worthy of consideration. One from our Company of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note>, a very wise and experienced man, assembled in the province of Mexico the elders of Texcoco, Tula, and Mexico, and conferred at great length with them; they showed him their histories, their books, and calendars, which were things very worthy of seeing because they had their figures and hieroglyphs, by which they represented things in this manner: those which had a form or shape were represented by their own images, and those which had none were represented by characters that signified them, and by this means they depicted and wrote what they wished. 

And to mark the time when something occurred, they had these painted wheels, where each one contained a century, which was 52 years, as has been said above <note>The "Calendar Round," a 52-year cycle used by the Aztecs and other Mesoamerican cultures</note>; and beside these wheels, they painted with these figures and characters, at the place of the year, the memorable things that happened in it. For instance, they noted the year that the Spaniards entered their country by painting a man with a hat and a red tunic at the sign of the "reed" <note>The Aztec year-sign "Acatl"</note> which was then current. And likewise for other events. 

But because their writings and characters were not as sufficient as our letters and script, they could not express the words as closely, but only the substance of the concepts; and since they were accustomed to reciting by heart speeches and dialogues composed by their ancient Orators and Rhetoricians, and many songs <note>original: "chapas," likely referring to "cuicatl" or ritual poems</note> composed by their poets (which was impossible to learn through hieroglyphs and characters), the Mexicans were very careful that their children learned these dialogues and compositions by memory. 

For this reason, they had schools, and something like Colleges or seminaries, where the elders taught the children these orations and many other things, which were preserved among them by tradition from one to another as completely as if they had been set down in writing. Especially the most renowned nations took care that their children (who had an inclination to be Rhetoricians and exercise the office of Orators) learned these harangues word for word. So much so that when the Spaniards came to their country and had taught them to read and write our letters, many of these Indians then wrote down these harangues, as is testified by several serious men who read them. This is said because those who read such long and elegant speeches in the history of Mexico will easily believe they are invented by the Spaniards and not actually taken and reported from the Indians. But having known the certain truth, they will not fail to place faith, as is reasonable, in their histories. They also wrote these same speeches in their own fashion, using images and characters; and I have seen, to satisfy myself on this point, the prayers of the Our Father <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>, the Hail Mary <note>original: "Aue Maria"</note>, the Creed <note>original: "Symbole"</note>, and the General Confession written in this Indian manner. And in truth, whoever sees them will marvel at them:

...to signify these words (*I, a sinner, confess*), they painted an Indian kneeling at the feet of a monk <note>The original term "Religieux" refers to a member of a Catholic religious order, such as a Franciscan or Jesuit</note> as one who confesses; and then for this one (*to God Almighty*), they painted three faces, with their crowns, in the manner of the Trinity; and for (*the glorious Virgin Mary*), they painted a face of Our Lady, and the half-body of a small child; and for (*Saint Peter and Saint Paul*), heads with crowns, a key, and a sword. Where images failed them, they used characters, such as for (*wherein I have sinned*), etc. From this, one can recognize the liveliness of the intellect of these Indians, since this way of writing our prayers and matters of the faith was not taught to them by the Spaniards, nor could they have done it if they did not have a particular understanding of what they were being taught. I have seen in Peru a confession of all his sins that an Indian brought to confess, written with the same kind of paintings and characters, by painting each of the Ten Commandments in a certain way, where there were certain marks, like ciphers, which were the sins he had committed against that commandment. I do not doubt that if many of the most skillful Spaniards were employed in making records of similar things through their images and marks, they could not achieve it in one year, nor even in ten.

->The same in chapter 8.<-

Before the Spaniards came to the Indies, those of Peru had no kind of writing, whether by letters, characters, ciphers, or figures like those of China and Mexico; however, they did not fail to preserve the memory of their antiquities nor to maintain the order of all their affairs of peace, war, and policy, because they were very diligent in passing traditions from one to another. The young people learned and kept as a sacred thing what their superiors told them, and taught it with the same care to their successors. In addition to this diligence, they supplemented the lack of writing and letters partly through painting, like those of Mexico (though those of Peru were quite crude and heavy in this regard), and partly, and most commonly, by <term>Quipus</term> <note>Original: "Quippos"; these are ancient Andean mnemonic devices made of knotted strings</note>. These Quipus are memorials or registers made of branches <note>likely referring to the main cord from which strings hang</note>, in which there are various knots and various colors that signify different things; and it is a strange thing what they have expressed and represented by this means. For the Quipus are worth as much to them as books of history, laws, ceremonies, and the accounts of their business. There were officers appointed to guard these Quipus (whom today they call <term>Quipucamayos</term> <note>Original: "Quippocamayos"; the trained specialists who kept and read the knotted strings</note>), who were obliged to keep and render account of each thing like the scriveners <note>Original: "tabellions"; public notaries or clerks</note> do here.

That is why they were given entirely full faith and belief; for according to the various sorts of business—such as war, policy, tribes, ceremonies, and lands—there were different Quipus or branches, in each of which there were many knots, small and large, and attached strings, some red, some green, some blue, and others white. And finally, so much diversity that, just as we derive an infinity of words from twenty-four letters by arranging them in different ways, so they derived innumerable meanings...

Before the Spaniards came to the Indies, those of Peru had no sort of writing, whether by letters, characters, ciphers, or figures like those of China and Mexico. Nevertheless, they did not fail to preserve the memory of their antiquities nor to maintain the order of all their affairs of peace, war, and governance, because they were very diligent in oral tradition from one to another. The young people learned and kept as a sacred thing what their superiors told them, and taught it with the same care to their successors. In addition to this diligence, they supplemented the lack of writing and letters partly through painting, like those of Mexico (although those of Peru were quite crude and heavy in this), and partly, and most commonly, by <term>Quipus</term> <note>A system of knotted and colored strings used by the Inca to record information</note>. These Quipus are memorials or registers made of strands, in which there are various knots and various colors that signify different things; and it is a wondrous thing, what they have expressed and represented by this means. For the Quipus serve them as much as books of history, laws, ceremonies, and accounts of their affairs. There were officers appointed to keep these Quipus (whom today they call <term>Quipucamayocs</term> <note>Inca officials specialized in reading and maintaining the quipu records</note>), who were obliged to keep and render an account of each thing, much like the <term>notaries</term> <note>original: "tabellions"</note> here.

This is why they were granted entire faith and credit, for according to the different sorts of affairs—such as war, governance, tribes, ceremonies, and lands—there were different Quipus or strands, in each of which there were many knots, small and large, and attached threads, some red, others green, others blue, and others white. And finally, there were so many variations that just as we derive an infinity of words from twenty-four letters by arranging them in different ways, so they derived innumerable meanings from these strands.

The aforementioned *Francisco López de Gómara* <note>Spanish historian (1511–1566) who wrote the "General History of the Indies" despite never traveling to the Americas.</note> in book 6 of his said general history of the Indies, chapter 11, reports that in the Region of Nicaragua in these Indies there are five languages, all different and dissimilar: namely *Coribicien*, which is highly praised; *Ciorotegua*, which is the native language of the country and the oldest, and which is used by those who have the right of succession and who can use *Cacao* <term>Cacao: used here to refer to cacao beans, which served as currency throughout Mesoamerica.</term>, which is the money of their land, which is made of a mixture of various metals having the shape of an almond; the third language is named *Ciondale*, and this one is used by the coarse people and villagers; just as *Oroieuga* is specific to small children; but the principal one is the language of *Mexico* <note>Referring to Nahuatl, the lingua franca of the Aztec Empire.</note>, even though this country is more than one hundred and fifty leagues from Mexico, as confirmed by *François de Belleforest* <note>French prolific author and translator (1530–1583).</note> in book 4, chapter 15 of his universal history, saying that these Nicaraguans use and employ the same characters of letters as those of the Mexicans, because they long ago originated and descended from the aforementioned Mexicans.

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF THE

...looked at and watched, they will not fail to fall upon them and massacre them. The same is noted in chapter 9 following.

The *Ausermians* <note>Likely referring to a group in the Andes or Chile, possibly the Araucanians (Mapuche), as described by early Spanish chroniclers like Gómara.</note>, just as they are different from other Indians in their customs and displays of bravado, also have a language that is diverse from all others in Peru. The same in chapter 14 following.

The people of the Region of Nicaragua boast of being descended from the Mexicans, saying that in the land of *Ananac* <note>Anahuac, the Nahuatl name for the Valley of Mexico.</note>, which is New Spain, the inhabitants left their country and came by the South Sea <note>The Pacific Ocean.</note> to inhabit Nicaragua; this is quite plausible, seeing that their language closely approaches that of *Chemistitan* <note>Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital.</note>, and the characters they use to signify what they wish to say are similar to the others. They write these on very poorly made parchment, or on certain tanned skins using azure, gold, and other beautiful and rich colors; and above all, they record from memory the high deeds of their captains and the wars they have fought against their neighbors.

The same author, in chapter 17 following, reports that the Mexicans use a type of writing which is made in various forms of animals, birds, and others, just as the Hieroglyphic letters of the Egyptians once were. He holds that these Mexicans have among them, among other books, one titled *Xehutonali* <note>Xiuhpohualli, the Aztec "count of years" or solar calendar.</note>, that is to say, the book of the accounts of years, in which they divide the year into four seasons, as we do—Summer, Autumn, Spring, and Winter—which they name *Tochtli*, *Acatl*, *Tecpal*, and *Calli*, which is to say South, East, North, and West <note>These are the four "year-bearers" of the Aztec calendar: Rabbit, Reed, Flint, and House, which were associated with these cardinal directions.</note>. Each of these seasons has six <note>original: "ci-" (likely *six*), though the Aztec calendar actually used eighteen 20-day months.</note> months, one half of the year being rainy and hot, and the other dry and cold. Each cycle is worth 52 years and has four "weeks" <note>The author uses "hebdomades" (weeks) to describe the 13-year periods that make up the 52-year cycle.</note>, which each contain 13 years; each year has 18 months, and each month 20 days. They begin their first cycle at *Tochtli*, and once that is completed, they move to *Acatl*, and so on from cycle to cycle until they have returned to *Tochtli*. While the first 13-year period lasts, they count one, two, three, up to thirteen, and then afterward they begin counting from one again, just as we do here when counting to one hundred, and once one hundred is finished, we begin counting from one again: so that according to their calculation, the year returns to 365 days.

Some modern travelers and navigators assert that in this Mexican country, there are several and diverse languages, which cause a very great annoyance to those who navigate and travel along its coasts, although there is a common language <note>NahuatI, which served as the lingua franca of the Aztec Empire and surrounding regions.</note> which is understood and spoken across an extent of more than 400 leagues of land, a fact repeated by *F. de Belleforest* <note>François de Belleforest (1530–1583), a French historian and cosmographer.</note> in chapter 5 of his Universal History and in volume 2 of the Cosmography of *Sebastian Münster*.

### LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE

<meta>catchword: OF THE</meta>

> *Forgive us our offenses as we forgive those who have offended us. Do not let us fall into temptation. Deliver us from all evil.* <note>Original: "Araiauion ore remiouzimeengcori oreué...". This is a translation of a portion of the Lord's Prayer into a Tupian language, likely Tupi-Guaraní, as recorded by early French explorers.</note>

->*So be it, Jesus.* <note>Original: "Emona né toico, Ieſus," the Tupi equivalent of "Amen."</note><-

See the aforementioned André Thevet, Book 21, Chapter 8, of his *Cosmography*. Jean de Léry, in Chapter 20 of his *History of America*, deduces that the difference between the languages of these Indians is such that the **Tupinambá**, **Tupiniquim**, **Touaiaire**, **Temiminó**, and **Carijó** <note>These are various subgroups of the Tupi people inhabiting the coast of Brazil in the 16th century.</note> speak the same language, or at least there is little difference between them in their way of speaking or otherwise. The **Karajá** have another way of acting and speaking; the **Goitacá** differ in language and also in their customs from both of the other parties; the **Waukau** likewise have an entirely different way of acting and speaking. The language of the Kingdom of **Cuzco** in **Peru** <note>Referring to Quechua, the administrative language of the Inca Empire.</note> is the most beautiful and eloquent language of all the other languages in the provinces of Peru, and it is the one most spoken and used throughout the mainland of the country.

To be brief, we will hold to the common opinion of modern authors who have been to these West Indies: that regarding the language of these Western Indians in general, it is brief and obscure, but much easier to learn and understand than the Arabic or Turkish languages, or other Levantine tongues. As for their speech, it is harsh and has little grace in its accent; they reiterate it often, repeating the same thing, taking pleasure in such harshness and barbarity, and delighting in speaking indistinctly and poorly forming their words. All these Western Indians are very talkative, and are always recounting the victories and triumphs they have achieved over their adversaries, as the aforementioned André Thevet noted in Book 21, Chapter 9, of his *Cosmography*.

On this subject, Pietro Maffei <note>Original: "P. Maſſee," an Italian Jesuit and historian.</note>, in Book 2 of his *General History of the Indies*, speaking of these Indians in **Brazil**, writes that their language is not so difficult to learn, and that it is nearly the same for all those well known to us so far, except for the names of some things which are used differently by the women of that nation. Three letters of our Alphabet—**F**, **L**, and **R**—are not used at all among them; this is because (as some have noted quite curiously) it happened to them by divine inspiration, inasmuch as they have no **Faith** (*Foy*), no **Law** (*Loy*), nor **King** (*Roy*). <note>This "No F, L, or R" claim was a famous mnemonic used by 16th-century Europeans to characterize indigenous Brazilians as being without religion, government, or social order.</note>

We have been well assured by persons worthy of trust that today one may see a book of **Annals** from the country of **Mexico**, entirely painted and illustrated with the figures we previously described, in the **Vatican Library** in Rome; in this book, the entire history of the deeds and gestures of the Kings of that country, and other memorable things, are described in these figures, as if in **Hieroglyphic** letters. <note>This likely refers to the Codex Vaticanus A (also known as the Codex Ríos), an Aztec manuscript held in the Vatican since the 16th century.</note>

## OF THE INDIAN PRIESTS OF THE
### *East Indies.*

### CHAP. LXXX.

André Thevet, in Book 22, chapters 11 & 15, and Book 23, chapter one of his *Universal Cosmography*, writes that on the Island of Haiti <note>original: "Hayty"</note> in these West Indies, the Priests are named by the Indians *Baitas*, otherwise *Boitij* or *Tequira*, or *Boithij* or *Tequina*. At Cabo Frio <note>A region in Brazil</note> these are named *Pagez*, in Peru *Piaches*, in Culhna <note>Likely referring to the Culiacán region of Mexico</note> *Chichimegues*, in Florida *Iauars*, and on the Island of Japan *Bongies* or *Bonzies* <note>Historical terms for Buddhist monks, from the Japanese "bonzo"</note>. Generally, all their gods, Lords, Priests, and Doctors are named by these Indians as *Monans, Maires, Caraibes, Piaches, Pagees, Iugues, Cemis, Tuiras, Chichimeques, Iarnares, Paracoussi* or *Paraousti, Iaonas, Cudragny*, or *Aruagny*.

---

## OF THE LANGUAGE OF NEW
### *Guinea.*

### CHAP. LXXXI.

Modern navigators in their voyages, speaking of the Province or Region of the Papuas, or otherwise New Guinea—which has already been discovered across seven hundred leagues of coast and divided into four kingdoms, namely Mian, Missel, Oguer, and Noton—report that the inhabitants of these all use the same language, and that they are very civil people with a noble spirit. Pierre du Jarric, Book 2, Chapter 29, of his *History of the East Indies*.

## OF THE WEST INDIES AND THE NEW
### *Lands of New France, Bacaleos, &*
### *the Country of Canada.*

The great King Francis I, amidst the difficulties of his affairs, desired to expand the Christian and French name. In the year 1524, he gave his first commission to a certain Italian Captain from the city of Florence named Giovanni Verrazzano <note>original: "Iean Verazzano"</note> to discover the lands of the West Indies on this side of the Tropic of Cancer, following Christopher <note>Referring to Christopher Columbus</note>, the first author of the discovery of the aforementioned Indies beyond the said Tropic. In execution of this commission, Verrazzano sailed along the entire coast from the new land of Florida up to the 40th degree, as we can see in the account of Verrazzano’s voyage addressed to the said King Francis. Later, in the year 1534, Jacques Cartier, Captain from St. Malo, undertook new voyages under the authority of the same King. He left accounts of these voyages to serve mariners and geographers, and he gave names to the Islands, ports, straits, gulfs, rivers, Cape

This being assumed, I say that both sides of the said river are Canada, and thus the river rightly bears that name, rather than Hochelaga <note>The Iroquoian settlement at present-day Montreal</note> or Saint Lawrence. I have said that Canada is properly the name of a Province. And for this reason, I cannot agree with the Lord of Belleforest <note>François de Belleforest (1530–1583), a prolific French historian and geographer</note>, who says it signifies "Land," nor hardly with Captain Jacques Cartier, who writes that Canada signifies "town." I believe that both were mistaken, and the deception arose because (as it was necessary to speak by signs with these peoples) when one of the Frenchmen asked the Savages what their country was called, while they pointed to their villages and huts, or a circuit of land, they replied that it was "Canada"—not to signify that their villages or the Earth were called so, but the entire extent of the Province. This same Belleforest, speaking of the peoples who live around the Bay or Gulf of Chaleur <note>Located between the Gaspé Peninsula and New Brunswick; "Chaleur" means "Heat"</note>, calls them the people of Labrador, contrary to all geographers universally. In this he was mistaken, seeing as the country of Labrador is at sixty degrees, and the said Gulf of Chaleur is only at forty-eight and a half. I do not know who his author is; but as for Captain Jacques Cartier, he makes no mention of Labrador in his accounts. It would have been better if the said Lord of Belleforest had situated the country of Bacaleos where he placed Labrador, rather than placing it at sixty degrees. For in truth, the greatest fishery for Cod, which we said are called *Bacailleos* <note>A term derived from the Basque and Portuguese words for cod (*bacalhau*), often used to refer to Newfoundland and the surrounding regions</note>, is carried out in the vicinity of the Bay of Chaleur, such as Tregate, Misamichi, and the Bay of Cods.

->*On the color of these Western Indians.*<-

### CHAP. LXXXII.

The aforementioned Lord Marc Lescarbot <note>A French lawyer and author who lived in Acadia from 1606–1607</note> in Book 3 of the aforementioned history, Chapter 10, writes the following regarding the color of these Indians:

> These Indians are all of an olive color, or at least tanned like the Spaniards; not that they are born such, but being naked most of the time, they grease their bodies and sometimes anoint themselves with oil to protect themselves from the flies, which are very troublesome—not only where we were, but throughout this New World, and even in Brazil. Thus, it is no wonder if Beelzebub <note>Original: "Beelzebud." This is a play on the biblical name Beelzebub, which in Hebrew means "Lord of the Flies."</note>, prince of flies, holds a great Empire there. These flies are of a color tending toward red, like tainted blood, which makes me believe that their generation comes only from the rotting of the woods. And indeed, we experienced that in the second year, being a bit more in the open...

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE <note>Although the header mentions "Languages," the text on this page focuses on the physical agility and natural habits of different nations, a common structural quirk in early modern encyclopedic works.</note>

...others, participating more in the nature of fire than those who are distant from it. This is why Pliny, speaking of the Gorgons and the Gorgonides Islands (which are those of Cape Verde), says that the men there are so light in flight that one can hardly follow them with the eye, so much so that Hanno the Carthaginian <note>A Carthaginian explorer (5th century BC) famous for his naval expedition along the African coast.</note> was unable to catch any of them. He even gives an account of the Troglodytes <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>Literally "cave-dwellers," a term used by ancient writers for various tribes in Africa and the Red Sea coast.</note>, a nation of Guinea, whom he says are called "Therotoeans," because they are as swift at hunting on land as the Ichthyophages <term>Ichthyophages</term> <note>Literally "fish-eaters," a name given by ancient Greeks to various coastal peoples.</note> are quick at swimming in the sea, where they tire almost as little as a fish. And Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian who wrote about the Portuguese missions in the Indies.</note>, in his histories of the Indies, reports that the Nairs <note>The Nairs (or Nayars) are a military and noble caste from the Malabar Coast of India (modern-day Kerala).</note> of the Kingdom of Malabar are so agile, and have such a promptness that it is incredible, and they handle their bodies so well at will that they seem to have no bones, so that it is difficult to engage in a skirmish against such people, especially since with this agility they advance and retreat at their pleasure. But to make themselves such, they assist nature; they stretch their tendons from the age of seven years, which they afterwards fatten and rub with sesame oil. What I say can even be recognized in animals: for a Spanish jennet <note>A small, agile breed of Spanish horse.</note> or a Barb is more gallant and light in the race than a nag or a short-tailed horse from Germany, and an Italian horse more so than a French horse.

Now, although what I have said is true, there are still nations outside the Tropics who, through exercise and artifice, acquire this agility. For Holy Scripture makes mention of an *Israelite named Hazael*, of whom it testifies in *2 Samuel, chapter 2*, that he was light of foot as a wild roe in the fields. And to come to the Northern peoples, the *Heruli* <note>An East Germanic tribe who migrated across Europe during the 3rd to 5th centuries.</note> are celebrated for being swift in the race, by this verse from *Sidonius* <note>Sidonius Apollinaris (c. 430–489 AD), a Gallo-Roman poet and bishop.</note>:

> *The Herulian in the race, the Hun in the javelins, and the Frank in swimming.* <note>original: "Cursu Herulus, iaculis Hunus, Francusque natatu."</note>

And by this lightness, the Germans formerly gave much trouble to *Julius Caesar*. Likewise, our *Armouchiquois* <note>An Indigenous group encountered by early French explorers in the coastal regions of modern-day Maine and New Brunswick.</note> are as well-disposed as greyhounds, as we have said above, and the Savages <note>As noted previously, "Sauvages" refers to people living in a natural, forest-dwelling state.</note> yield very little to them, without however violating nature or using any artifice to run well. But like the ancient Gauls, being devoted to hunting—for it is their life—and to war, their bodies are nimble and so little burdened with fat that it does not prevent them from running at their ease.

Now, the dexterity of the Savages is recognized not only in running, but also in swimming. This is something they all know how to do, but it seems that some do it more than others. As for the Brazilians, they are so born to this craft that they will swim for eight days in the sea if hunger did not press them, and they fear more that some fish might devour them than perishing from exhaustion; it is the same in Florida, where men will follow a fish into the sea and catch it if it is not too large. *Joseph Acosta* <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600), a Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist who wrote "Natural and Moral History of the Indies."</note> says the very same of those of Peru. And as for breathing, they have a certain trick of inhaling water and rejecting it, by means of which they easily remain within it for a long time. Women likewise have a marvelous disposition for this exercise: for the *History of Florida* reports that they can cross great rivers by swimming while holding their children on one arm; and they climb very nimbly to the tops of the highest trees of the country.

See what the same author cited above writes in chapter 11 regarding the paintings, marks, incisions, and body ornaments of these West Indians, and in chapter 12 following, regarding the external ornaments of the body, such as bracelets, carcanets <note>A carcanet is an ornamental collar or necklace, often made of gold or jewels.</note>, earrings, etc.

In this, he writes that the Indians of Brazil, having no care for clothing like other Indians, take pleasure in decorating and variegating themselves with bird feathers. They take the downy feathers that we use for bedding and chop them as finely as mincemeat; they then dye these red with their Brazil wood <note>The brazilwood tree (Paubrasilia echinata) produced a valuable red dye and gave the country of Brazil its name.</note>. After rubbing their bodies with a certain gum that serves as glue, they cover themselves with these feathers, creating a garment all of one piece. According to Jean de Léry <note>Jean de Léry (1534–1613) was a French Protestant pastor and author who wrote a famous account of his time in Brazil.</note> in his *History of America*, this led the first explorers who went there to believe that the men called "savages" were naturally shaggy or hairy, which is not the case. For it is certain that these people, in whatever part they may be, have less body hair than we Europeans.

Those of Florida also use this method with down feathers, but only on their heads to make themselves appear more terrifying. In addition to what is mentioned above, the aforementioned Brazilians also make headbands of feathers which they tie and arrange in all colors. These headbands resemble, in their fashion, those "raquettes" or "ratepenades" <note>The term "ratepenade" is an old word for a bat; here it likely refers to a bat-wing shaped headpiece or fan popular in European fashion at the time.</note> used by ladies in our regions, the invention of which they seem to have learned from these people. As for those of New France <note>The French colonial territory in North America, primarily along the Saint Lawrence River.</note>, on their solemn days of rejoicing and when they go to war, they wear a crown around their head made of the long hair of the Moose <term>Ellan</term> <note>Original: "Ellan." The French term "élan" refers to the moose (Alces alces).</note> dyed red, glued or otherwise attached to a leather band three fingers wide, such as Jacques Cartier <note>The French explorer (1491–1557) who claimed what is now Canada for France.</note> says he saw on the King or Lord of the savages he found in the town of Hochelaga <note>A fortified Iroquoian village on the site of present-day Montreal.</note>. However, they do not use as much featherwork as the Brazilians, who make robes, caps, bracelets, belts, cheek ornaments, and bucklers <note>Small round shields.</note> for their lower backs in all colors.

The people are divided by language: indeed, within the same province there are different languages, no more and no less than in Gaul where Flemish, Lower Breton, Gascon, and Basque do not agree with one another. For the author of the history of Virginia <note>Likely referring to Thomas Harriot or the accounts found in Theodor de Bry's "Great Voyages."</note> says that there, each *Wiroan* <note>An Algonquian term for a leader or commander.</note> or Lord has his own particular language. For example, let it be that the chief or Captain of Quanton <note>This may refer to a specific settlement or perhaps a corruption of a name like Agouhanna's territory; the text notes that Jacques Cartier and René Goulaine de Laudonnière frequently used European titles like "King" for these leaders.</note> (whom our historians Jacques Cartier and Laudonnière qualify as King) is called in Canada, *Agohanna*; among the Souriquois <note>Now known as the Mi'kmaq.</note>, *Sagamos*; in Virginia, *Wiroans*; in Florida, *Paraousti*; in the Islands of Cuba, *Cacique*; the Kings of Peru, *Incas*, etc.

I have left out the Armouchiquois <note>A term used by early French explorers for Indigenous groups in present-day New England, likely the Abenaki.</note> and others whom I do not know. As for the Brazilians, they have no Kings, but the elders whom they call *Pcoreroupicheh*, because of their experience of the past, are those who govern, exhort, and order everything. Languages themselves change, just as we see that here we no longer have the language of the ancient Gauls, nor that which was in the time of Charlemagne (at least it is very different); the Italians no longer speak Latin, nor the Greeks ancient Greek—especially on the maritime coasts—nor the Jews ancient Hebrew. Thus, Jacques Cartier <note>Jacques Cartier (1491–1557), the first European to map the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.</note> left us a sort of dictionary of the language of Canada, which our Frenchmen who frequent it today do not understand at all: and for that reason I did not wish to insert it here; I only found this word *Caraconi* for "bread," and today they say *Caracona*, which I believe to be a Basque word <note>Basque whalers were very active in the region, leading to a "Basque-Algonquian pidgin" used for trade.</note>.
