In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified and praised. 

“ Furthermore, the Lord Christ promises in Mark 16 to those who believe in his name that they shall speak in new tongues. He fulfilled the promise of this matter by sending the most abundant Holy Spirit into the assembly of the disciples. For as he was about to send legates <note>A "legate" is an official messenger or representative, here referring to the Apostles.</note> to the kings and peoples of all languages and nations—not to build Babylons, nor to seize for themselves the seats of kingdoms and empires, nor to plot or devise anything against the knowledge of God, but rather to draw the whole world into the consensus of the Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "whole" church, from the Greek *katholikos*.</note> religion, and to build the city of the living and true God—he equipped them perfectly for that task. 

“ The foundation, head, cornerstone, and prince of this city is Christ himself, the Lord of Glory. He equipped them not with hammers, trowels, plumb-lines, axes, or iron; nor with the sword, the javelin, the pike, or bronze engines of war; but with the Holy Spirit, with knowledge of divine things, with holiness of life, with virtues of every kind, and with skill in languages <note>original: "linguarum peritia"</note>. Thus, it is a wonderful and stupendous thing to say: men who were previously unrefined and illiterate, and who were almost like infants in their own native speech, suddenly spoke in the languages of all peoples and nations among whom they were to preach the Gospel. 

“ Making a beginning at Jerusalem, the city situated on Mount Sion (as Isaiah and Micah predicted in chapters 2 and 4), they announce that Christ—the Son of God, the Word, Wisdom, Power, and Justice—has come to earth, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of a virgin from the house of David, died on the cross, and has risen and ascended into heaven, from whence he shall come as the Judge of the living and the dead. He whom the Israelite Church heard preaching on Mount Sinai is now heard by the whole world (contracted, as it were, into a compendium at Jerusalem) preaching on Mount Sion through the Apostles, now clothed in the true flesh of man. Thus, in that multitude which had flowed together from the entire world, each person heard the legates of Christ discoursing in their own native and vernacular speech. 

“ Truly, the early times of the Christian Church required that miraculous and stupendous work. This abundantly proves that the knowledge of languages is a tool that is both useful and necessary for preserving and enlarging the Christian commonwealth, and is a gift of divine munificence that is by no means trivial. The Apostle Paul teaches this in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, and the Church confesses it in its solemn prayer, praying in this manner: "Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love. You who, through the diversity of all languages, have gathered the nations into the unity of faith." This is the first and foremost thing to be sought with holy vows from the heavenly Father, from whom proceeds whatever is rightly judged as good; and the doctrine and instruction of languages should not be despised...

We possess reason, the maker of truly human and celestial works; we possess speech, through which we may moderately discuss matters and reasoning among ourselves; we possess the tongue, an excellent organ, let it be fitted to its proper end; we possess the pen, the stylus, and paper, which fulfill the role of the tongue and of speech. Regarding the Hebrew, judgment has already been passed previously based on Jerome; indeed, they began to use the idioms of other languages. # LANGUAGES OF THIS WORLD

...one speech became confused and mixed through the incursions of nations into the Roman provinces. This also occurred in the German language.

The second cause is the change of Empire and affairs, where necessity forces the introduction of new things. Regarding Empire, Augustine speaks thus in Book 19 of *The City of God*: 

<margin>cc</margin>
> Effort was given so that the imperial city <note>Rome</note> might impose not only its yoke but also its language upon the conquered nations through the peace of society, through which a wealth of interpreters would not be lacking, but rather abound.

To which L. Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist</note> added from Roman histories: The Romans took care that many in the provinces spoke Latin, so that they made Spain and Gaul entirely Latin, the old languages of those nations having been abolished. And in the Senate, they heard no ambassadors except those speaking Latin. Truly they were attempting a most beautiful thing, and most useful to the whole human race—for whatever purpose they did it—so that there might be one single language by which all nations might understand each other. To the people of Cumae <note>An ancient Greek settlement in Italy</note>, a gift was granted by the Roman people as a reward: that they might speak Latin publicly, and that their public criers might have the power to sell and conduct auctions in Latin. But on the contrary, among the Carthaginians, it was decreed that no one should learn Greek letters or the Greek idiom, since they understood that the secrets of their language had been betrayed to Dionysius through trade and hidden conversations; thus necessity demanded either to use foreign words or to not shrink from introducing new things. 

This happens not rarely in matters touching religion. Ulpian <note>A famous 3rd-century Roman jurist</note>, the legal expert, also warns that it is the nature of things that there are more transactions than there are words. And Celsus <note>Another prominent Roman jurist</note> teaches that one must act with prescribed words when common and usual names for legal actions are lacking. I will immediately set down Tully's <note>Cicero's</note> opinion on this matter.

The third cause can be seen as the instruction, study, and rivalry of some teacher. Just as Aeschines <note>A famous Greek orator</note> brought a new kind of speaking to the people of Rhodes. And the speech of theologians who have shaped themselves according to the schools of [Duns] Scotus and Albert [the Great] <note>Key figures in Scholastic philosophy</note> and similar authors is far different from those who emulate Augustine, Jerome, Cyprian, Ambrose, and those ancient theologians. The followers of Apuleius speak and write one way, and the followers of Cicero another. I believe it is a matter of both necessity and discipline that different professions have their own particular kind of speech. For anyone who reads a poet, even a good one, notices that they diverge so far from common speech and prose that they think they are dealing with a foreign dialect. "And the poet," he says, "Our people speak thus in the country." It will not be foreign to my purpose if I transcribe here M. Tully's <note>Cicero's</note> words from the 3rd book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*.

<margin>cc</margin>

->“The chief among them was not so much an inventor of things as he was a creator of new words. If in the Greek language—which most consider to be richer—it was permitted for the most learned men to use unusual terms for matters that were not commonly known, then how much more should this be granted to us, who are now daring to touch upon these subjects for the first time? As we have often said (and indeed with some complaint, not only against the Greeks but also those who wish to be considered more Greek than our own), we must strive not only to avoid being surpassed by the Greeks in the abundance of words but even to be superior in that regard. We should achieve this not only in our own arts but also in theirs. Nonetheless, those words which we use as Latin according to the custom of the ancients—such as **Philosophy**, **Rhetoric**, **Dialectic**, **Grammar**, **Geometry**, and **Music**—even though they could have been expressed in Latin terms, we consider them our own since they have been adopted through common usage.”<-

Thus speaks Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator</note> regarding the naming of things. Customs and character also bring about great fluctuations, as idleness, negligence, frivolity, affectation, and insolence change much in common speech. “Sanctity,” says Fabius <note>Quintilian (c. 35–100 CE), a Roman rhetorician</note>, “and manliness must be sought from the ancient writers, since we have declined into all the vices of luxury in our manner of speaking as well.” There is also a type of secret and mysterious speech used to hide secrets, such as in magic, or in the loves of cheats and vagabonds, which our common people call *Rotwelsch* <note>original: "Rotuuelsch"; a German cant or thieves' argot used by travelers and the underworld</note>, which some have even taught in published books. But now we draw from the dregs of the **Babylonian confusion** <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel, where languages were said to have been first divided</note>. Let us therefore move on to the change of letters and writing.

The Jews also possess an ancient script which Moses and the Prophets used for their secrets; they say it should not be rashly revealed to anyone. They claim the letters we use today were found and handed down by Ezra <note>Ezra the Scribe (5th century BCE) is traditionally credited in Jewish law with introducing the "Square" script (Ashurit) to replace the older Paleo-Hebrew script (Ivri) after the Babylonian Exile.</note>. However, because Saint Jerome <note>D. Hieron. - St. Jerome (c. 347–420 CE), the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> also believed that the ancient letters of the Hebrews were changed by Ezra—and this is accepted as certain by great men—I will add a quote or two from that supreme theologian. The Samaritans also write the Pentateuch of Moses with the same number of letters, differing only in their shapes and flourishes. And it is certain that Ezra the Scribe and teacher of the Law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple under Zerubbabel, discovered other letters which we now use; for up to that time, the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews were the same."

In the Book of Numbers, this same calculation is shown mystically under the census of the Levites and Priests. And we find the name of the Lord, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter divine name, YHWH</note>, expressed in ancient letters even today in certain Greek volumes. Moreover, Psalms 36, 110, 118, and 144, although written in different meters, are nevertheless woven from an alphabet of the same number <note>These are acrostic Psalms, where each line or stanza begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>. So too are the Lamentations of Jeremiah and his prayer. At the end of the Proverbs of Solomon, from the place where he says, "Who shall find a valiant woman?", the same alphabets or divisions are reckoned.

Furthermore, there are five double letters among the Hebrews: **Caph**, **Mem**, **Nun**, **Phe**, and **Tzade**. For they are written one way at the beginning and middle of words, and another way at the end. For this reason, five books are considered "double" by many: Samuel, Malachim <note>Kings</note>, Dibre Hayamim <note>Chronicles</note>, Ezra, and Jeremiah with his *Cinoth* <note>Lamentations</note>. Just as there are twenty-two elements through which we write in Hebrew everything we speak, and the human voice is encompassed by their beginnings, so twenty-two volumes of scripture are counted. By these, as if by the first letters of learning, the tender and still-nursing infancy of the righteous man is instructed in the doctrine of God.

In these sayings of that most learned man, it is established by several reasons that there are twenty-two elements of the Hebrews, which is entirely clear. To this, he asserts that the shapes of the letters were changed by Ezra, and that five letters are marked with a double figure; finally, he mentions the flourishes <note>original: "apicum" - the small strokes or "horns" on Hebrew letters.</note>. Regarding what I think of these things, and the reasons that compel me to think so, I shall explain at length in my commentaries on the Hebrew language. Indeed, I have also observed this variation in the ancient and common script: that formerly, the remaining letters of a word were moved from the end of a line to the beginning of the next line, just as is the custom among the Arabs. Today, however, if a line cannot contain the entire word, one or two letters are placed to fill the space, and the whole word is moved to the head of the following line. Regarding the corrupt pronunciation of the Hebrew language, it will be discussed in a more suitable place.

From the letters of the Hebrews, as we have already said several times, the public [scripts] were derived...

# HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF LANGUAGES

» ...the letters of all peoples and nations. For it would be an endless task to pursue those which men devise for themselves privately; it is a feat granted to no man and a labor of little use. It is my pleasure, therefore, to arrange the Hebrew, Phoenician—or rather Arabic—Greek, and Latin letters in such a way that it may be apparent to eyewitnesses to what extent they agree, or how the three literatures <note>The author uses "literatures" here to refer to the alphabetic systems themselves.</note> originating from the Hebrew have departed from their first source in the number of letters, their order, their shape, or even their sound and power. First, I shall place the Hebrew letters in their proper order, repeating also the names of the letters that have a double power, such as **Pe** and **Phe** <note>This refers to the "dagesh" system where a single Hebrew letter can represent a hard "p" or a soft "f".</note>. Beneath these, I will place the Punic <note>Phoenician or Carthaginian.</note> letters, from which I believe the Greek letters were born, since the Greek names are more intact than the Punic ones. Indeed, the order of the alphabet, which the learned Arabs call the *Abuget* <note>original: "Abuget". This is the *Abjad*, the traditional mnemonic order of the Arabic alphabet: Alif, Ba, Jim, Dal.</note>, is the same as that of the Hebrews. But because they have five additional letters—not in shape, but in power—such as **He**, **Che**, **Dhel**, **Thad**, and **Gaim**, I will join them to the Hebrew letters to which they are related. I have drawn the Arabic characters as best I could, not being a particularly skilled artist in the painting of letters. I thought it better to indicate that the Phoenician letters flowed from the Hebrew rather than to pass over that matter in total silence. Therefore, the best Arabic letters are those that most closely approach the Hebrew. I have also added the ancient Greek letter **Hetha** <note>Heta</note>, which later writers assigned to the long vowel **E**, calling it **Etha** <note>Eta</note>; they noted the aspiration itself by a small mark placed over the letters. We have also added the **Vau** or **Vu** of the Germans, which some nations use for **F** or the consonant **V**. First, therefore, the names shall be placed, and then the shapes.

» Eliph, Be, Ghim, Del, He, Vau, Ze, He, Te, Ie, Cheph, Lem, Mim, Ul'nun, Nun, Sim, Hain, Phe, Kezad, Raph, Re, Ssin, The.

### Greek.

» Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Epsilon, Upsilon, Zeta, Heta, Theta, Iota, Kappa, Lambda, My, Ny, Sigma, Omicron, Phi, Omega, Psi, Rho, Tau.

### *The forms of the Hebrew, Arabic, Greek, and Latin letters ought to be taken from those which we have written above.*

» In this diagram, we can see that the Hebrews have only two vowels besides **A** (which they have doubled as **Aleph** and **Ain**). The latter of these is expressed so that the voice resounds in the throat, just as if it were pronounced "gain." For **i** and **e**, they are content with a single vowel, just as the ancient Romans used the letters **i** and **e** indifferently. -># LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE<-

...but in its place, they put V. As Priscian relates from Pliny, they have a double aspiration <note>The "aspiration" refers to the breathy 'h' sound or "breathing" in phonetics.</note>, one thin and the other thicker. The Arabs have a triple one, as do the Indians. They also have a unique letter **Shin** [Schin] which is more a syllable than a letter or basic element. For if, according to Aristotle, "**Ge**" is a syllable, why not also **Sh**, **st**, **ps**, **gs**, **ch**, **gh**, **ph**, and similar sounds? Also, what else are **Zain** and **Tzade** in their phonetic power than **ds** and **ts**? The Germans could also represent the double-V [W] or **bb** with the consonant **V**, just as the Hebrews do with **Vav**. Some Greeks used the **Digamma** <note>original: "Digamma". An archaic Greek letter (Ϝ) that looked like an 'F' but sounded like a 'W'.</note> for words like *Var*, or *Vuar*, *Vetus*, *Ved*, *Vuend*, *heu*, or *heuu*. But let us now touch upon some matters regarding the Greeks and Latins separately, as there are many arguments that the ancient writing has been changed.

We previously indicated from Pliny that there were only sixteen Greek letters in the beginning, and that Palamedes added four, and Simonides added four more. Plutarch testifies to the same. The order of the letters differs somewhat from the order of the Hebrew letters; for instance, **Theta** is placed earlier and **Tau** in a later position. For the order is reversed among the Hebrew letters, because more correctly <margin>$\odot$</margin> **Theta** would correspond to the Hebrew **Tav** [Thau], and the Greek **Tau** to the Hebrew **Teth**. <note>The author is debating the phonetic alignment between the Greek and Hebrew alphabets.</note> Furthermore, proverbs testify that the ancients also maintained an order where **Alpha** held the first place and **Omega** the last, such as the expression "the Alpha of the cloak-wearers" <note>A Greek idiom meaning the first or best of a particular group.</note>. And in the Revelation of the Lord Christ it is said: "I am the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end." Plutarch also uses various reasons to explain why Alpha is the first of the letters. The Greeks also used letters to denote numbers, a system that requires the position of the letters to remain firm and stable. This is seen in how the 24 books of Homer, that most ancient poet, are organized by letters, and how Galen arranged his interpretation of the ancient terms of Hippocrates and others.

Pliny and other reliable authors judge that the shapes of the Greek letters have changed, as they remember the ancient letters; inscriptions from ancient times testify to this very fact. For example, Terentius Scaurus writes regarding the letters **C** and **K**, saying: "I would argue that **C** is more redundant than **K**, since **K**, as used among the Greeks, sufficiently expresses the power of the letter **C**." However, some were deceived by the shape, because this letter was used not only by us [Latins] but even among the ancient Greeks, as evidenced by the treaty of Greece engraved on a bronze camel in the gardens of Caesar, outside the temple of Fortune. The ancients wrote the aspiration [the 'h' sound] directly in the line of verse in the Latin manner; for example, the Boeotians wrote *muha* instead of *musa*. Later writers divided this into two marks: the mark for the smooth breathing and the mark for the rough or "thick" breathing, as Priscian also teaches in his first book. Scaurus also asserts that **h** is a letter and was written in the verse by the Greeks, and that the people of Attica used it to mark *hecatum*, which means one hundred.

We still see this mark today among the Greeks. In "improper" diphthongs, they did not place a dot under the vowels **α, η, ω**, but placed the letter beside them on the right side as **αι, ηι, ωι** <note>This refers to the "iota adscript," where the 'i' is written next to the vowel, whereas modern readers are more familiar with the "iota subscript" written underneath.</note>. Nor did the ancient Greeks possess so many diphthongs. They also did not use signs to mark prosody—long and short vowels, or acute, grave, and circumflex accents—as is done now. Most ancient monuments testify to this, such as the poems of Callimachus, which Angelo Poliziano <note>A famous Italian Renaissance humanist.</note> includes in chapter 80 of his *Miscellanea* [Centuria], introducing them with these words: "But lend your ears now to the verses of Callimachus..."

Reason proves this, and **Erasmus of Rotterdam** sufficiently showed it in his small book *On the Pronunciation of the Greek and Latin Languages*.

> The same reasoning applies to Latin writing. For at first there were only 16 letters among the ancients, just as many as **Cadmus** brought into Greece; and just as there were no more than sixteen letters among the most ancient Greeks, so the Latins, having received them, preserved that antiquity perpetually, as **Priscian** <note>A famous Latin grammarian from the 5th century AD.</note> testifies. To the sixteen ancient Greek letters, two were later added and accepted from them: **F**, the Aeolic **Vau** <note>Also known as the Digamma, which sounded like 'w'.</note>, and **X**. **Ypsilon** [Y] and **Z** were also adopted for the sake of Greek names. **Varro**, **Macer**, and **Censorinus** judged that **H**, **k**, and **Q** should not be included in the number of letters. **Diomedes** also relates in his second book that some believe there are seventeen letters in the Latin language. For they say two are Greek, **y** and **z**, while **k** and **q** are superfluous; **x** is a double letter, and **h** is actually a mark of aspiration. **Servius** also notes that the Greeks have this mark of aspiration, **Ͱ**, which they call *daseian* <note>original: "daseian". The "rough breathing" mark indicating an 'h' sound before a vowel.</note>; in imitation of this... <note>original: "phile l Ͱ"</note>. By joining these, we made the mark of aspiration **H**. But it is much more likely that the Greeks changed the aspirated letter **H** (or **h**) into the mark for the long vowel **Eta**, and having divided it **Ⱶ ⱶ**, transformed it into the marks for smooth and rough aspiration. These are marked with different signs in a line of verse among the Hebrews.
> 
> Certainly, in the commentaries of **Nonius Marcellus** on his *Compendious Doctrine* organized by the order of letters, only 18 letters are placed. However, in the commentaries of **Sextus Pompeius Festus**, with another letter added, 19 Latin letters are approved: **a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, l, m, n, o, p, q, r, s, t, v**. **Cicero** testifies in his second book of *On the Nature of the Gods* that the *Annals* of the poet **Ennius** were written with these, using these words: "The *Annals* of Ennius were composed of twenty-one forms of letters." Here it appears we should read "one from twenty" <note>original: "vnius de viginti", meaning 19. The author is correcting a possible scribal error in Cicero's text.</note>. **Claudius Caesar**, as **Suetonius** records, devised three new letters and added them to the number of the ancient ones as if they were most necessary. While still a private citizen, he had published a volume on their logic, and soon as Emperor, he obtained without difficulty that they be in common use. Such writing exists in many books, daily records, and titles of works; however, **Priscian** testifies that Caesar’s authority was not long-lasting. For writing about the letter **F**, he says: "For the **Vau** or **digamma**, Caesar wanted to write this figure **Ⅎ**." Although this seemed right to him, ancient custom prevailed. And regarding the <term>antisigma</term> <note>A letter shaped like a reversed C (Ↄ).</note> invented by the same Claudius, he writes: "It is placed before the letter **s**, and serves in place of the Greek **ψ** [psi], for which **Claudius Caesar** wanted this figure **Ↄ** to be written." But no one dared to change the ancient writing, although it seems not without reason that this double letter was also added by the Greeks. Furthermore, the books of the ancients following the order of letters—such as those of **Nonius Marcellus** and **Festus Pompeius**, as we mentioned before—indicate that the order has been preserved since ancient times: starting from **a**, then **b**, then **c**, then **d**, and so on in this manner until **z**. **Pliny** also, in chapter 10 of his last book, teaching about certain gems through the order of the alphabet, proceeds from **a** to **z**, and the word <term>Abecedary</term> <note>A term for the alphabet or an alphabetical list.</note> was formed from there. For instance, Bishop **Epiphanius** shows the marks observed by **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184 – 253 AD).</note> in the distinctions of the sacred books, which later generations have neglected. We shall speak briefly about other scripts, which are commonly called "barbaric." Since there are 22 Hebrew letters, from which (as from parents) the letters of all nations have been generated, some nations have adopted more and some fewer. While their shapes may more or less resemble the originals, they are sometimes called "letters" when they are actually more like syllables—just as children count symbols like **&** and various abbreviations <note>original: "9 tr. pro &, con, tur, rum"; common Latin scribal abbreviations.</note> among the letters of the alphabet. Thus, the **Punic** people <note>The Carthaginians.</note> are said to have 28 letters and elements, though they actually have only 17 letter shapes; by adding accent marks, they vary the sound and power so much that they reach 30 or more. Furthermore, **Lam Eliph** <note>The Arabic ligature of the letters Lam (L) and Alif (A).</note> is placed among the letters, which is actually a symbol or what is commonly called an abbreviation. The **Ethiopians** have greatly disrupted the order of the Hebrew letters; they have 26 letters in number, which at first glance differ greatly from the Hebrew ones. However, a careful observer will not find it difficult to trace them back to their origin.

> Not only have virtues been present in our men, but also sciences equal to those of the ancients. For letters also have their own cycle, such that first, in certain places, through the experience and labor of talented men, the arts arise. Then they grow, and after flourishing for a time in a stable state, they eventually weaken from their own old age. Finally, they gradually die away and are buried in a long oblivion—either by the long-lasting calamity of wars, or because excessive abundance (an evil greatly to be feared in these times) usually brings satiety <note>A feeling of being over-satisfied or bored by having too much of something.</note> to every fickle mind, or because God exacts just punishment from those who turn beneficial sciences <note>original: "scientias salutares"</note> to human destruction. For when the sciences among the Greeks had gradually matured until they were believed to have reached their peak, such a great change followed that Greece itself, where it is now, seems as if it never existed. What of the Latins, among whom there was such a wealth of talent that at almost the same time they surpassed all peoples in military glory and the excellence of all sciences? Yet, by a similar fate, they began to slide back into their former Barbarism when the hordes of Scythians <note>A term often used broadly for northern "barbarian" invaders like the Goths or Huns who contributed to the fall of the Roman Empire.</note> flowing into Italy burned the most crowded libraries and all monuments of antiquity nearly everywhere. This monstrous deed caused such great ruins in all sciences that they lay prostrate for about a thousand years without any value, and seemed about to perish entirely, unless Al-Mansur <note>original: "Mensor"; likely referring to the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mansur or the general patronage of learning by Arab rulers in North Africa and Spain, which preserved Greek texts during the European Middle Ages.</note>, the African and Spanish Prince of the Arabs, had excited the talents of men with great rewards for the Restoration of Letters. I omit how many philosophers, geometers, and astrologers Egypt, India, and Ethiopia produced; how many noble mathematicians there were among the Chaldeans before there were any letters in Greece. I return to our own times, in which—long after letters had rested in almost the entire world—such a great brilliance of all sciences suddenly shone forth, and such fertility of talent existed, that it was never greater in any age. And even the Goths themselves have not lacked most excellent talents lately, as Olaus Magnus <note>A Swedish historian and cartographer (1490–1557) who wrote about the history and geography of the Nordic peoples.</note> witnesses, as Holsterus <note>Possibly a reference to a Northern scholar or a Latinization of a contemporary name.</note> witnesses, and many others, as if nature had decreed that the wounds of the sciences should now be healed by those very people by whom they were once inflicted. For while in a previous age they still followed the custom of their ancestors and ordered learned men to leave the Senate by the voice of a herald (for so we have it recorded in their history), they have now become accustomed to summoning letters from everywhere. This is that certain turning <note>original: "conuersio"</note> of all things, such that no one should doubt that the same thing happens in the minds of men as in the fields, which usually return the favor of rest with greater fertility. But someone will say, "those ancients were the inventors of the arts; the glory is owed to them." Truly, they discovered many sciences beneficial to mankind—and especially the power of celestial things and the fixed courses of the spheres—yet they did not know all the miraculous trajectories of the fixed stars and those which are called wandering <note>Planets.</note>. Furthermore, they diligently noted the obscurity of nature and explained many things accurately; yet they left many of them incomplete, which are now passed down to posterity as perfected by our own people. And no one who looks deeply into the matter can doubt that the inventions of our people ought to be compared with the inventions of the ancients... “

Therefore, those who say that everything was encompassed by the ancients sin no less than those who would strip them of their ancient possession of many arts. Nature possesses innumerable treasures of knowledge which can be exhausted by no ages. Since these things are so, and since by a certain eternal law of nature, the revolution of all things seems to return as if in a circle—just as vices follow virtues, ignorance follows science, the shameful follows the honorable, and darkness follows light—those who think the human race always turns out worse than itself are mistaken. And since old men are in that error, it is believable that this happens to them because they mourn the loss of the flower of their youth, which by itself breathes joy and pleasantness. When they see themselves deserted by every kind of pleasure, and instead of delights they suffer the bitterest pains, and instead of healthy senses, the weakness of all their limbs, it happens that they are overwhelmed by the most sorrowful thoughts. Deceived by a false image of things, they think that faith and friendship among men have perished; and as if having set out from a long voyage, they tell of the golden ages and the golden era to the young. But it happens to them just as it does to those who sail out from a port into the deep: they think the houses and cities are receding. Thus they imagine that enlightenment, humanity, and justice are flying away to heaven and deserting the lands.

Having previously argued that the "Moderns" have surpassed the "Ancients" in technology and geography, Bodin here addresses the "vicissitude" or constant change of languages throughout history.</meta>

Polybius writes that the treaties between the Carthaginians and the Romans <note>original: "Pœnos & Romanos"</note>, which he himself calls "ancient," could scarcely be understood; indeed, the songs used in sacred rites according to old formulas were understood by very few. Thus, we see that gradually all the languages of all peoples change in one way or another. A second cause of this change lies in the mixing of colonies and peoples among themselves. An example of this is Italy and Greece, which for so many centuries had maintained the purity of the Greek and Latin tongues and spread them throughout the whole world; yet after the Scythians and Goths invaded both lands, such a great change followed that it seems as if Latin and Attic Greek never even existed in the places where they are now spoken. Similarly, the colonies of the Etruscans <note>original: "Tuscorum"</note> who were driven from Italy by the Gauls, and the Gauls who once migrated into the deserted lands of Germany, forged a third type of speech different from both originals. The colonies of the English led into Britain and the Saxons into Belgium by Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolo magno"</note>, as well as those of the Gauls into Saxony, gave birth to a variety of speech. In the same way, the Parthians corrupted the Persian tongue; the Arabs corrupted the Punic and Parthian; and the Turks, Tartars, and Slavs corrupted the Greek, just as the Latins corrupted the Gallic and Hispanic speech.

The final cause for the changing of a language is found in the very nature of the region itself. For it is characteristic of all peoples who live further toward the North to produce harsh, clashing consonants, or to draw vowels from deep within the chest with frequent aspirations. This is due to the great force of their internal spirits and the impetus of their natural heat. Thus, the Saxons and those living near the Baltic Sea almost everywhere pronounce "middle" sounds instead of "thin" ones, and aspirated sounds instead of "middle" ones, such as in these examples: they say *th* for *f*, and they use *p* and *f* sounds uniquely <note>The author is describing phonetic shifts—like Grimm’s Law—whereby northern Germanic tribes used breathier or harder consonant sounds compared to southern Europeans.</note>. Those in the South, however, who have a tempered heat and weaker spirits, pronounce words very softly—women even more softly, because they have less spirit and heat than men. This is easily understood in the colony of Saxons that Charlemagne settled among the Belgians. For while the Saxons call a horse *Pfert*, the Flemish, raised under a milder sky, pronounce it *Pert*. I will pass over the inherent nature of each place’s water, which can alter voices and languages; for example, in the Labdano region of Narbonnese Gaul, everyone stammers with a "Labdacism" <note>original: "Labdacismo"; a speech habit or "lisp" involving the excessive repetition or specific pronunciation of the letter L.</note>, as they do in Valedoca among the people of Turin. Likewise, the ancient Sabines used to say *fedum* for *hedum* (goat) and *fircum* for *hircum* (he-goat), just as Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro was an ancient Roman scholar and grammarian.</note> writes; and among us, the Gascons say *hocum* for *focum* (fire) and *hilium* for *filium* (son). Similarly, the people of Paris and Orléans, following the custom of the ancient Etruscans, use *Valerius* and *Furius* in place of the older forms <note>Bodin is noting the historical shift where 's' between vowels became 'r' (rhotacism), comparing French habits to ancient Latin evolution.</note>.

From these three primary causes, therefore, arise the great differences between so many languages. Yet, they can never be so completely abolished that they do not perpetually retain clear traces of the old tongue. For instance, the ancient Celtic language was largely Greek in its foundation, because our ancestors drew their origin from them. Bovelles, Picart, and Périon <note>Renowned 16th-century philologists: Charles de Bovelles, Jean Picart, and Joachim Périon.</note> have extracted nearly infinite words—though not all—from Greek sources into their own language, and they did so without the hardship or violence seen in the work of Lazius <note>Wolfgang Lazius, a contemporary scholar known for more eccentric linguistic theories.</note>, but rather with great ease and sometimes no change at all. However, I do not think there is as much weight in individual words as there is in the actual modes of expression that we share with the Greeks, as well as the elegant use of participles, infinitives, and articles. these sufficiently prove that the origin of the Gauls is owed to the Trojans, or the Greeks, or both, since both used the Ionic tongue.

Louis Le Roy, in Book 1 of *Of the Vicissitude or Variety of Things*, in the chapter on the change and variety of languages, discusses this most excellently in a similar fashion: "Likewise, languages, words, writings, and characters change continually, being of no better condition than other human things..."

" which are ordinarily changed along with their words—namely, public and private ways of living, customs, foods, laws, clothing, buildings, weapons, machines, and instruments. Others, after having been long abolished, are restored. ->The same author in the following second book.<- <note>Likely referring to Jean Bodin's *Methodus* or Louis Le Roy's own subsequent volume.</note>

" Moses recounts in Genesis how the first language of the world and of all the earth was confounded during the building of the Tower of Babel, from which came the division of nations, and the beginning of the diversity of languages proceeded from the pride and presumption of men. Truly, it is a punishment for sin to have so many [languages], which change incessantly according to the appetite of the common people, always forging new words; by the birth of which it is necessary that the preceding ones perish. No more and no less than the seasons of the year strip the earth of flowers and fruits, then clothe it anew with others. Similarly, time makes words decay, and usage makes new ones recognized, giving them favor until, being consumed little by little by old age, they also come to die: because in the end, both we and all our things are mortal. Such mutation and variety ordinarily proceed from the mixing of diverse nations and from great fairs and armies, where people of diverse languages meet, who, by gathering and communicating together, perpetually forge new words, lasting or failing according to whether they are received or rejected by custom. Now, although speech is natural to men, they do not speak except artificially <note>meaning "by art" or learned skill rather than instinct</note>, learning it only by hearing others speak—first mothers and nurses, then the common people. Therefore, it was necessary that the first who assigned names to things, having no others from whom they could learn them, learned them miraculously in a language where the nature and truth of things agreed with their origins and etymologies: which people strive to seek even now in all languages through the meanings of words. The Hebrews give this honor to their language, which they estimate to be the first and most ancient in the world. Herodotus recounts that Psammetichus, King of Egypt, wanting to know which was the first language, gave two newborn children, born of simple folk <note>original: "issus de personnes bestes"—likely meaning uneducated or common people to ensure no linguistic bias</note>, to a shepherd to be raised, forbidding him from saying any word in their presence. Instead, they were to be kept apart, and at certain hours, goats were to be presented to them to be suckled. He did this out of a desire to hear what word these children would pronounce first after their initial wailing. And it happened that after two years had passed, as the shepherd opened the door to enter to the children, they both fell at his feet, and stretching out their hands, pronounced "Bec," which is equivalent to saying "bread" in the Phrygian language. And thus it was found that the Phrygians were more ancient than the Egyptians, and their language was the first.

This same author holds that languages acquire a reputation through their own unique character, elegance, and sweetness; through the sciences written in them; through the power and grandeur of Empires; and through religions. By these means, they are extended into many countries and last for a long time, just as they are also lost and annihilated by their opposites—a point he clearly proves through the examples of the Greek, Latin, and other languages.

Then he continues to say,

> Languages are of no better condition than other human things; rather, just as buildings, clothing, manners, customs, laws, magistrates, and both public and private ways of living, weapons, machines, and instruments change, so too do words and languages. These perish in the long run, leaving no trace of their writing through the succession of time. We have no knowledge of the Oscan <note>An extinct Indo-European language of southern Italy.</note> or Etruscan languages. The Romance—or Provençal—tongue, once celebrated by noble writers, is no longer understood by the people of Provence today; the ancient Gaulish, Spanish, Persian, and Punic <note>The language of ancient Carthage.</note> languages are lost.
> 
> Now, like all human things, languages have a beginning, progress, perfection, corruption, and an end. They are at first coarse, then they become polished alongside the civility of manners and knowledge; after having lasted for some time in purity and elegance, they are corrupted, and finally perish, leaving no trace of their writing through the succession of time.
> 
> The Greeks were very unrefined at the beginning, as Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle say. The first among them to become civilized were the Athenians, who polished their language and brought it to perfection. Yet it did not remain there long; instead, it was corrupted and lost along with the liberty of the country, supplanted by the Macedonians, Romans, and other foreigners who ruled there. Consequently, the innate character and true elegance of the Greek spoken by Plato, Aristotle, Isocrates, Demosthenes, and Aeschines could never again be restored. In place of that language, which one could say was the most beautiful in the world, there has come in the long run another language currently used in Greece and the neighboring islands, mixed with several other tongues. This language is likewise being lost under the Ottoman Empire <note>Original: "l'Empire du Turc"</note>, where the country has remained miserably oppressed for more than a hundred years.
> 
> If the earliest Roman writings survived until now, we would see that Evander and Turnus <note>Legendary figures from the founding of Rome.</note> and the other Latins of that time spoke differently than the later Roman Kings and the first Consuls did afterward. The verses sung by the Salian Priests <note>An ancient college of priests dedicated to Mars; their hymns were famously archaic even to Romans of the 1st century BC.</note> were hardly understood; but because they had been ordained by the first founders, they were not changed out of reverence for religion. Polybius writes that this language was so changed from the first Punic War until the second that one could only understand with great difficulty the treaties made previously between the Romans and Carthaginians. And it remained coarse for about 500 years, having no writer worthy of memory. From then on, people applied themselves to letters and some became learned, though they remained harsh in their speech, praised only for...

armies using and speaking diverse and dissimilar languages. These people, meeting and communicating often, perpetually form new words that either endure or vanish depending on whether they are accepted or rejected through common usage. This same thing occurs through the power and force of certain peoples and nations who, having conquered others and established a new Monarchy, Empire, Kingdom, or Principality, strive to completely destroy and extinguish the natural and mother tongue of others to introduce their own. Just as the Greeks, Latins, and Romans did in ancient times to the languages of many peoples and nations they brought under the force of their arms. And like the Saracens <term>Saracens: A term used in the Middle Ages and early modern period to refer to Arab Muslims.</term>, who, extending their language through arms along with their religion, came to destroy the Persian language and other languages of Asia, burning the books written in them by order of their Caliphs <term>Caliphs: The religious and civil leaders of the Islamic world.</term>. They believed that the Persians and other Asians, deprived of their own specific books, would more easily yield to the Muhammadan superstition <note>The author uses the term "superstition" here to reflect the common European Christian perspective of the time toward Islam.</note>. Then, passing into Egypt, they exterminated the Greek language and its disciplines from Alexandria, and the Latin language from Africa—just as the Latins or Romans before them had done to the African language and its letters.

Thus, it is a certainty that as peoples and nations move from country to country and region to region, they change and alter languages and writing, along with the morals and ways of life of other peoples and nations. We see this in what the Turks did some time ago to the Christians, and in the past with the Goths, Visigoths, Alans, Huns, Vandals, Suebi <term>Suebi: A collective name for various Germanic tribes.</term>, Heruli, Bulgarians, Lombards, and others. These groups, conquering various lands and regions at different times, disdained the languages they did not understand or know how to read; they corrupted, altered, and changed them, creating new ones by mixing their own with those they found. The poor people remaining after such changes and mutations were constrained and forced to learn the language of the cruel and inhuman victors and usurpers, in order to communicate with them and make themselves more agreeable subjects.

Furthermore, these Barbarians, relating everything to war and showing great scorn and contempt for the sciences and literature, burned all the books found in libraries, so that a great ignorance fell upon the world for some time. This caused the transition from grammatical Greek to the vulgar tongue; from Latin proceeded Italian, as well as the French and Spanish of today—in which many Saracenic and Arabic words are found due to the long occupation of the Spains by the Saracens and Arabs. Similarly, from grammatical Arabic came the vulgar Turkish and Moorish tongues.

and the Franks <note>The Germanic people who settled in Gaul and gave France its name.</note> in Belgic and Celtic Gaul; through their interaction, the Latin language was altered and corrupted. From this corruption primarily proceeded the Italian, French, and Spanish languages. Similarly, it happened that several peoples and nations, through a certain envy and emulation, sought to shift, change, and corrupt—even in times of peace—the ancient and original languages of others. They did this so that through such disguise, they might make posterity believe that they retained nothing from their ancestors and predecessors. Thus did the Chaldeans do with the language of the Hebrews; the Syrians and Arabs, coming long after, with that same language; the Armenians with that of the Chaldeans; the Greeks with the Samaritan, Assyrian, or Phoenician; and the Romans and Slavs with that of the Greeks. Likewise, the Goths, Lombards, Germans, Franks, Spaniards, and others did the same with the language of the Romans.

Sometimes it also happened that certain learned and scholarly figures, desiring in their own age to enrich, illustrate, and embellish their mother tongues, delighted in imitating the most articulate and eloquent authors—both ancient and modern—of other older, more delicate, and more well-spoken languages in their writings. Or, they invented new terms themselves as properly and elegantly as they could, which they rendered as if they were their own natural speech. This is what Dante, Cino <note>original: "Cyne"; referring to Cino da Pistoia, a legal scholar and poet who influenced Petrarch.</note>, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Ariosto, and other modern Italians have done for their Italian tongue; Guevara, Boscán, Garcilaso de la Vega, Granada, and Montemayor for the Spanish tongue; and Ronsard, Jodelle, Du Bellay, Belleau, Amyot, Vigenère, and other Frenchmen for our own French language.

But whatever one may say of these alterations and mutations of languages in general or in particular, they must be referred or attributed to three principal causes.

The first is that languages, following the fatal course and order of nature—as do all things in this Universe—after being born, used, and practiced for some time, come through the length of time and years to wither and perish. This has happened to infinite languages that flourished since the beginning of the World, which are now entirely lost and abolished.

The second is that the confusion and multiplicity of colonies or migrations <note>original: "Peuplades"</note> of diverse nations and languages—who have moved from country to country and region to region—have mixed and associated with other tongues. This has always caused a different kind of language, or a third genus, beyond the two natural or mother tongues of the original groups. This is what the Northern peoples did: when they came to these lands, they completely exterminated the pure Greek and Latin languages by introducing a certain jargon <term>jargon: The original text uses "Barragouin," a pejorative term for confused speech or gibberish.</term>, which was quite confused and lasted for some time.

The third and final cause is that the region and situation of certain places produces this effect: for example, peoples who live closest to the North are accustomed by their nature to pronounce their words and speech very rudely and harshly with a great many consonants, being almost unable to express the vowels; and

# LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.
LIIIII

...this is due to the great force and impetuosity of their internal heat, which ultimately causes them to corrupt <note>In this context, "corrupt" refers to the natural linguistic drift or "decay" of a language from its original form over time.</note> the proper words of languages, turning them into harsh and unrefined sounds at last, which gain enough favor and currency to form an entire language. The air and the Waters are sometimes such that they can alter and change voices and tongues, just as we see in an infinite number of peoples and nations today who cannot pronounce their words and speech correctly except by stuttering; others cannot express several consonants, others several vowels. For the reasons and occasions mentioned above, the Characters <note>Writing systems or alphabets.</note> of languages are all diverse and dissimilar: those of the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Syrians, numbering twenty-two, are all different in the forms of their letters and points, as I have demonstrated before. Those of the ancient Phoenicians, numbering twenty-four, do not relate to any of the others mentioned above; those of the Arabs, numbering thirty-one, are completely different from those of other nations; those of the Greeks, numbering twenty-four, are of other various fashions; those of the Latins, numbering twenty-two, have other forms. Those of the Armenians, numbering thirty-eight; those of the Slavs <term>Slavs: likely referring here to the Glagolitic or early Cyrillic scripts</term> and Jacobites <note>Syriac Christians; the author is likely referring to the West Syriac alphabet</note>, numbering thirty-two; those of the Abyssinians and Ethiopians, numbering twenty-seven; those of the Japanese, numbering forty-seven—none of these have anything similar or approaching one another when taken at face value.

These same Hebrews, Chaldeans, Syrians, Arabs, and generally the Asians and Africans write from right to left, saying that in this they imitate the daily movement of the Heavens which moves from right to left, and is most perfect according to the Philosophers; on the contrary, the Greeks, Latins, Slavs, Armenians, Abyssinians, and Ethiopians, Indians of Malabar, and other Europeans write from the left side to the right; the Indians, Cathayans <note>People of Cathay, an old name for Northern China.</note>, Chinese, Japanese, Brahmins, and Gymnosophists <note>Ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and "nakedness."</note> from top to bottom, saying that in this they follow the order of nature, which gave men high heads and low feet, as I have clearly demonstrated before. See what is written on this matter by H. Cardan <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath.</note> in the twelfth book of his *On Subtlety*, and the seventeenth book, ninety-fifth chapter of *On the Variety of Things*; Leo Africanus <note>original: "Iean Leon"; a Moorish diplomat and author famous for his descriptions of African geography.</note> in the first book of his *Description of Africa*; G. Collange in the second book of the *Polygraphy* of Abbot Trithemius; and Lord Fauchet in his collection on the origin of the French language and poetry.

> *Every language changes, whether it be that trade,*

> *Desirous of glory, strikes with new coins*
> *Things and deeds—or at the very least gives*

It is just like the leaves of a wood,

Shone here and there in eloquent speech,

Shamefully stay under the roofs of a lowly hamlet:

Running without bit, without eyes, where the fickle people
Go rushing it headlong; the other, walking enclosed
Within the barriers of art, arranges its words well.
One, already aging on the doorstep of its infancy,
Has the verse for its tomb; the other resists
The threads of the years; one lives unfortunate,
Confined forever in a narrow valley:
The other, bold among the learned, makes itself heard

Greek, as having in its learned writings
Every kind of knowledge eloquently comprised:

## ON THE SOUNDS, VOICES, NOISES, LANGUAGES,
### or tongues of Animals and Birds.

### CHAP. LXXXIX.

Latin authors attribute very specific and appropriate names and verbs to most of the sounds, voices, noises, or languages of animals. They said that Bulls low <note>original: "mugire." A term specifically for the mooing of cattle.</note>. Titus Livius <note>The Roman historian Livy.</note> says on this subject: *when some cows, being driven along, lowed for those they had left behind* <note>original: "cùm actæ boues quædam ad defiderium relictarum mugissent."</note>. The poet Virgil, in the second book of the *Georgics*, writes: *the lowing of cattle* <note>original: "Mugitúsque Boum."</note>. Asses bray <note>original: "rudere."</note>; the poet Ovid in the third book of *The Art of Love*:
> *And the ugly she-ass brays at the rough millstone.* <note>original: "Et rudit à scabra turpis Asella mola."</note>

And in the first book of the *Fasti*:
> *Behold the braying donkey, carrier of hoarse Silenus.* <note>original: "Ecce rudens rauco Silleni vector Asellus."</note>

Lions roar <note>original: "rugire."</note> or growl <note>original: "fremere."</note>.
The author of the *Philomela* <note>A poem about the nightingale, formerly attributed to Ovid.</note>:
> *Untamed tigers snarl, and lions roar.* <note>original: "Tigrides indomita rancant, rugiuntque Leones."</note>

Diomedes <note>A 4th-century Latin grammarian.</note> in his first book, and Nonius, interpreting the ancient verb *grundire* for *grunnire* [to grunt], cite the words of Quintus Quadrigarius:
> *The swine-herd grunted heavily; the mares, whinnying among themselves, kicked up the earth with their heels; the asses bray, the dogs snarl, the chicks peep, the bulls low, the lions roar.* <note>original: "Grundibat grauiter pecus suillum, Equæ hinnibunda inter se spargentes Terram calcibus, Asini rudunt, Canes ganniunt, Pupilli pipant, Tauri mugiunt, Leones rugiunt."</note>

Marcus Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> in some part of his works:
> *The pig, fed on sweet milk and sacrificed at the mill, grunts; the ox lows, the sheep bleats, the horses whinny, the hen peeps.* <note>original: "Grunnit lepido lacte fatur mola mactatus Porcus, mugit Bos, Ouis balat, Equi hinniunt, Gallina pipat."</note>

The learned Joseph Scaliger <note>A prominent Renaissance scholar of the 16th century.</note> in his *Conjectures on the sixth book of M. Varro* speaks very well on this matter. These same Latins also said that dogs bark <note>original: "latrare."</note>; foxes yelp <note>original: "gannire."</note>; camels bellow <note>original: "blaterare."</note>; elephants trumpet <note>original: "barrire."</note>; wild boars gnash their teeth <note>original: "frendere."</note>; leopards growl <note>original: "fremere."</note>; bears groan <note>original: "gemere."</note>; sheep bleat <note>original: "balare."</note>; geese cackle <note>original: "strepere."</note>; crows croak <note>original: "crocitare."</note>; storks clatter <note>original: "crepitare."</note>; and cicadas chirp <note>original: "stridere."</note>. The poet Ausonius in his 75th Epigram:
> *You mimic the barking of pups, the whinnying of horses,*
> *the goatish flock, and the wool-bearing herds*
> *with their bleating; you would say asses braying*
> *when you wish to mimic the Arcadian beast, Marcus.*
> *The crowing of roosters, and crows rejoicing in their throats,*
> *and whatever voices such a beast possesses.*
> *Since you imitate everything so truly that they could not be called fake,*
> *you cannot have the sound of a human voice.*
<note>original: "Latratus Catulorum, hinnitus fingis Equorum / Caprigenumque pecus, lanigerósque greges / Balatu adsimilas, asinos quoque rudere dicas, / Quum vis Arcadicum fingere Marce pecus. / Gallorum cantus, & ouantes gutture Coruos, / Et quicquid vocum Bellua talis habet. / Omnia cùm similes ita vere, vt ficta negentur / Non potes humana vocis habere sonum."</note>

The author of the *Philomela*, whom some say is the same poet Ovid:
> *Come, sweet friend, providing the comforts of night,*
> *for among the birds none is like you:*
> *You, Philomela, can produce a thousand distinctions of voices,*
> *yourself can repeat a thousand varied measures.*
> *For although other birds attempt melodies,*
<note>original: "Dulcis amica veni noctis solatia præstans, / Inter Aues enim nulla tibi similis: / Tu Philomela potes vocum discrimina mille, / Mille potes varios ipsa referre modos. / Nam quamuis aliæ volucres modulamina tentent," Philomela is the poetic name for the nightingale.</note>

Nothing can equal your melodies;
Besides, while other birds chatter only during the day,
You can sing by both night and day.
For though the titmouse <note>original: "Parus"</note> chirps <note>original: "tinnitet"</note> all through the night,

The blackbird <note>original: "Merulus"</note> also joins in with such beautiful odes,

In the warmth of spring, the owl <note>original: "Acredula." This term is debated; it often refers to a small bird or a type of owl that sings at night.</note> composes new songs,

The wood-pigeon <note>original: "Palumbes"</note> claps its wings, calling from the leafy branch,
And the duck <note>original: "Anas"</note>, swimming in the rivers, perhaps quacks <note>original: "tetrinit"</note>.
The crane calls <note>original: "gruit"</note>, and the swans trumpet <note>original: "drenfant"</note> in the river bends,
The hawk pipes <note>original: "pipat"</note>, and the kite cries with open mouth <note>original: "lipit"</note>.
The rooster is accustomed to crow <note>original: "cucurrire"</note>, the hen cackles <note>original: "gracillat"</note>,
The peacock screams <note>original: "pupillat"</note>, the wandering swallow twitters <note>original: "trinsat"</note>,
While eagles scream <note>original: "clangunt"</note>, the vulture is known to shriek <note>original: "pulpare"</note>,
The raven croaks <note>original: "crocitat"</note>, and the jackdaw chatters <note>original: "frigulat"</note>.
The stork clatters <note>original: "clotorat"</note> its huge beak from the tower,
But the wretched sparrow chirps <note>original: "pipit"</note> sadly with its weeping.
The parrot utters human speech with its voice,
And sounds "hello" or "goodbye" to its master.
The talkative magpie mimics various voices from its throat
And repeats whatever it hears with a scurrilous noise.
And the cuckoos call "cuckoo" <note>original: "cuculant"</note>, the hoarse cicada chirps <note>original: "fritiuit"</note>,
The bee hums <note>original: "bombilat"</note> as it gathers the gifts of honey,
The horned owl <note>original: "Bubo"</note> hoots <note>original: "bubulat"</note> a terrifying song,
Bringing grim fate to the human race.
The night screech-owl <note>original: "Strix"</note> and the bat shriek <note>original: "stridunt"</note>,
The little owl <note>original: "Noctua"</note>, fleeing the light, hoots <note>original: "cucubat"</note> in the darkness.
But the owls <note>original: "Vlulæ"</note> howl <note>original: "ululant"</note>, singing with mournful voices,
And the bittern <note>original: "Butio"</note> booms <note>original: "bubit"</note> in the marshy waters.
The goldcrest <note>original: "Regulus"</note>, the bee-eater <note>original: "Merops"</note>, and the red-breasted swallow <note>original: "Procne"</note>
Know how to twitter <note>original: "zinzillulare"</note> with a similar rhythm.
The nightingale <note>original: "Philomela"</note>, who surpasses all birds in song,
Has compelled me to write down these voices of birds.
But now, of my own accord and without compulsion,
I shall follow the distinctions of the voices of four-legged animals.
Untamed tigers snarl <note>original: "rucant"</note>, and lions roar <note>original: "rugiunt"</note>,
The panther growls <note>original: "caurit"</note> when in love, the leopard snarling with mouth agape <note>original: "felit"</note>.
While lynxes howl and growl <note>original: "orcando fremunt"</note>, the wild bear growls <note>original: "uncat"</note>,
The wolf itself howls <note>original: "ululat"</note>, and the wild boar mashes its teeth <note>original: "frendet" - literally to gnash or grind.</note>.

->*And the elephant <note>original: "Barrus"</note> trumpets <note>original: "barrit"</note>, the deer bell <note>original: "glocitant"</note>, and the wild asses <note>original: "Onagri"</note> cry,*<-

->*And their sounds; therefore, who could speak them all?*<-
->*All things bring forth their gifts of praise to their Lord,*<-
->*Whether they remain forever silent, or are able to make sound.*<-

Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist.</note>, a Greek author, in Book 5, Chapter 13 of his *Onomasticon* <note>A thesaurus of Greek terms organized by subject.</note>, has left us in writing that the Greeks, in place of the Latin names and verbs declared above, used Greek names and verbs that were just as elegant and excellent. Specifically: to low or bellow <note>original: μυκᾶσθαι</note>, to bray <note>original: ὀγκᾶσθαι</note>, to roar <note>original: βρυχᾶσθαι</note>, to grunt <note>original: γρυλλίζειν</note>, to neigh <note>original: χρεμετίζειν</note>, to whimper <note>original: κνυζᾶσθαι</note>, to chirp or peep <note>original: πιπίζειν ou στρουθίζειν</note>, to chatter <note>original: βαβάζειν</note>, to talk <note>original: λαλεῖν</note>, to bark <note>original: ὑλάκτειν</note>, we stammer <note>original: ψελλίζομεν</note>, a roaring <note>original: βρύζημα</note>, I roar <note>original: βρυζέω</note>, I roar or rage <note>original: βρεμέω</note>, I groan or sigh <note>original: στενάζω</note>, to bleat <note>original: βληχᾶσθαι</note>, I make a noise <note>original: ψοφέω</note>, or to spit <note>original: πτύειν</note>, to chatter or talk idly <note>original: στωμύλλειν ou φλυαρέω</note>, I caw <note>original: κρώζω</note>, a croaking <note>original: κρώγμω</note>, with a noise <note>original: ψόφω</note>, or I make a noise <note>original: ψοφέω</note>, I spit or hiss <note>original: πτύζω</note>, or to be like <note>original: ἐοικεῖν</note>, and others with which the Greek Comic Poets are principally filled. Rodolphus Galterus <note>Rudolf Gualther (1519–1586), a Swiss Reformed pastor and scholar.</note>, the Latin translator of this author’s Greek words, wrote the following regarding them:

The voices of animals are as follows. For dogs, indeed, barking <note>original: "Latratus"</note>, to bark, barking, and to yelp or whine <note>original: "gannire"</note>. You shall also say *deazein* and *deazontes* <note>Greek: "to bark" or "to revile"</note> to rail and railing, and also to mourn and mourning. According to Xenophon, however, it is also called a clangor, for he speaks of them as "shouting." Some of the poets have also called the sound of dogs *bauzein* <note>Greek: to bark/bow-wow</note>, and *knyzan* when they make a sound while sleeping. For wolves, there is the howl <note>original: "ululatus"</note>, to howl, howling. For lions, the roar <note>original: "rugitus"</note>, to roar, roaring. For horses, the neigh <note>original: "hinnitus"</note>, to neigh, neighing, or neighing at [another]. Some have also spoken of "fremitus" regarding horses, and that horses snort <note>original: "fremere"</note>, though they all gnash their teeth <note>original: "frendere"</note>. For pigs, however, the voice is a grunt <note>original: "grunnitus"</note>, to grunt, grunting, to squeal <note>original: "quirritare"</note> and squealing. Some have also said *gruditus* for to grunt and grunting. For cattle, the bellow <note>original: "mugitus"</note>, to bellow, bellowing. For sheep, the bleat <note>original: "balatus"</note>, to bleat, bleating. For goats, the mutter <note>original: "mutius"</note>, to mutter, muttering. Homer also called goats <margin>bleating <note>original: μηκάδας</note></margin> "bleaters." It seems, however, that the proper term for goats is "fremitus," to snort, snorting. Just as Herodotus is mistaken when speaking of the kids of the Phrygians, when he thinks that goats bleat <note>original: "balare"</note>. For asses, the bray <note>original: "ruditus"</note>, to bray, braying. You shall say the same for mules. But they are also called "Oncantes" <note>From the Greek word for braying</note>. And some of the Poets have called asses "Onciatores" <note>Brayers</note>. It should be noted further that for other brute animals for which specific names do not exist—such as the Bear, Leopard <note>original: "Pardale"</note>, Panther, and others—they are said to roar <note>original: "rugire"</note>; furthermore, for smaller animals such as foxes, jackals <note>original: "thois"</note>, and wolves, they are said to bark and roar.

Connected to these is the human voice: Clamor, voice, talkativeness, sound, shouting, and speech, regarding which one may shout, call, chatter, sound, exclaim, and speak. Indeed, the names for voice, clamor, sound, talkativeness, and speech have already been mentioned: but let there be added to these, from shouting, 'shouter' <note>original: "clamator"</note> and 'fellow-shouter' <note>original: "conclamator"</note>."

Most of these Latin and Greek names and verbs cannot be conveniently turned or rendered word-for-word into our French language, which is less copious and abundant in these words, and others, than the Latin and Greek languages, as I have demonstrated previously when speaking of the Greek language compared with the Latin.

Whatever the case may be regarding these sounds, voices, noises, or languages of animals, we shall say in this place that it is a most marvelous thing to see the docility of certain birds, and principally of Parrots, who alone among those of their kind are very well-suited to imitate and mimic human voices, words, and languages, as the great Aristotle well noted in book 8, chapter 12 of his *History of Animals*. Pliny, in book 10, chapters 40 and 43, writes that these birds, in his time, pronounced the greetings of the Roman Emperors in the Latin language; this is confirmed by Solinus (his imitator) in chapter 55 of his *Polyhistor*; Aelian in book 13, chapter 18 of his *History of Animals*; and Suidas after him in his works; and Plutarch in the treatise *On the Cleverness of Animals*.

> *And taught magpies to attempt our words?*
Statius, in book 7 of the *Silvae*:
> *Parrot, leader of birds, eloquent delight of the gods;*
> *Parrot, skillful imitator of the human tongue.*

Girolamo Cardano, in book 15, chapter 82 of *On the Variety of Things*, asserts having seen one sing the musical notes *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. ...description of the parrots of the West Indies which learn in those regions to ask in the Indian tongue for flour, for food, and for drink, and that it is necessary to go to war against their enemies to capture and eat them. See Cesare Maucini <note>original: "Cæsar Maucini"</note> treating the manner of raising, feeding, healing, and teaching birds to sing and speak.

What has been considered above has moved a very great dispute among the most learned Hebrew, Greek, and Latin personages: namely, to know and understand if these birds have certain and assured judgment, reasoning <note>original: "ratiocinations"</note>, understanding, and speech. Porphyry, in Book 3 of *On Abstinence* <note>original: "des sacrifices"; Porphyry's work "On Abstinence from Animal Food" argued for the rationality of animals.</note>, writes that every soul—which we can more properly call life—being endowed with sense and memory (functions which are indubitably in these birds, because they learn human voices so accurately, and the things that are taught to them), is by the same means reasoning and accompanied by internal and external speech. This author asserts that birds participate in this, as do other animals whose speech, he says, if not commonly understood by men, is no wonder, seeing that men think foreigners—whose mother tongue is not known to them—do nothing but moo, bray, or babble. In fact, this Author asserts that there were men in ancient times who perfectly understood the voices, warbling, sounds, and words or languages of these Birds: namely Melampus, Tiresias, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>original: "Apollonius Thianelis"; a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>, of whom Philostratus recounts wonders in his biography in these words.

...and the power of the air, which has the energy by its force to disturb the confused parts of their vital functions with a movement of passions—confused signs as much of pain, sadness, and anger as of love, joy, and gladness. This is very well confirmed by the poet Virgil:

> *Indeed, I do not believe they have a divine spirit <note>original: "Haud equidem credo quia sit divinitus illis / Ingenium"</note> or a greater foresight of things granted by fate; but when the weather and the shifting moisture of the sky have changed their paths, and the wet South wind thickens what was just now thin, and thins what was thick, the impressions of their minds change, and their hearts conceive different motions now than when the wind was driving the clouds: hence that chorus of birds in the fields, the joyful cattle, and the crows exulting in their throats.*

The Lord of Pimpont <note>A 16th-century French scholar and commentator on Virgil.</note> in his commentaries on this poet reports several fine Greek passages concerning this matter, which I will not report in this place to advance my subject. Cicero, in his first book *On Duties* <note>original: "Offices"</note>, speaking of these things says: *Insofar as they are moved by sense, they adapt themselves only to that which is near and present, feeling very little of the past or future; man, however, since he is a participant in reason, etc.* <note>original: "tantum quantum sensu mouentur ad id solũ quod adeſt, quodque præſens eſt ſe accommodat, paululum admodum ſentientes præteritum aut futurum, homo autẽ quoniã rationis eſt particeps &c."</note>

To make it short, we will say that Plutarch, in the treatise on which animals are the most clever, reports that Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Plato, and Diogenes asserted that brute beasts participated in reason, but that they did not use this reason freely because it was weak and clouded within them—neither more nor less than an eye that is darkened and tarnished—and this because of their bad temperament, called by the Greeks <term>dyskrasia <note>original: δυσκρασία; a medical term for an imbalance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which was thought to affect character and health.</note></term>. This author repeats this in Book 5, chapter 20 of his *Opinions of the Philosophers*. Porphyry, in Book 2 of <term>On Abstinence from Living Things <note>original: περὶ ἀποχῆς τῶν ἐμψύχων; a Greek work advocating for vegetarianism and discussing animal souls.</note></term>, concerning the difference between animate things, has left in writing that Aristotle, Empedocles, and Democritus said and asserted as much in this regard, affirming that these brute beasts have <term>participation in the rational power <note>original: μετοχὴν τῆς λογικῆς δυνάμεως; the idea that animals share in a basic form of logic or reasoning.</note></term>, and that Tiresias, Melampus, and Apollonius of Tyana asserted in their lives that birds could be understood in their languages, which Pliny confirms in Book 10, chapter 49, under the authority of Democritus, as I noted above; which will seem at first glance to many to be entirely impossible. But so that I may repeat here what has seemed so to many great and excellent persons: it is a great and strong argument to prove that these brute beasts use some reason to see that they have memory of past things, know present ones, and seem to predict future ones. In fact, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who often walked while teaching.</note> attribute memory and imagination to brute beasts, except for insects, but not long-lasting memory—as if most men did not also have memory that is just as unstable and fleeting! Truly, did the dog of Ulysses not show that he had a firmer and more stable memory than that of his servants, by recognizing his master even though he had been absent from him for the space of twenty years? This his domestic servants could not do. And did the dogs of the Portuguese and Spanish who went to the conquest of the West Indies, named Bezeril <note>Likely Becerrillo, a famous and feared Spanish war dog in the Americas.</note> or Berezzil, and Leoncico <note>The famous dog of the explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa, said to be able to distinguish between hostile and friendly natives.</note>, not recognize very well the fleeing Indians—

For this reason, we will not believe that these brute beasts have no reason simply because men seem to have more of it. Furthermore, what would cause dogs, horses, foxes, and other brute beasts to go mad, if there were not in them some part of reason that was spoiled and corrupted? For there can be no privation of a thing in that which has no capacity for it. <note>A philosophical argument: you cannot "lose" reason (go mad) unless you possessed reason to begin with.</note> And it is a certain and assured thing that when this happens, these brute beasts are not only destitute of "common sense," which we call <term>phantasy</term> <note>In the psychology of the time, "phantasy" or "imagination" was the faculty that processed sensory data.</note>, but it is necessary that some other spiritual part be altered in them—namely the "ratiocinative" power which the Greeks call <term>λογικὴν δύναμην</term> <note>original: "logikēn dynamin"; the power of logic or reason.</note>. Yet if we judge that brute beasts perform all their actions by the sole force of nature, why then—nature being their guide—do they not build cities, castles, and houses, seeing as that same nature has shown them the way to construct their nests, dens, and lodges? All of the above will give us a perfect knowledge and interpretation of the following excellent verses from one of the greatest poets of this time: <note>The poem describes the experiment attributed to the Egyptian King Psammetichus, who isolated two children to see what language they would speak first.</note>

> In times past, the Phrygians, and those whom the Nile
> Feeds, soul-nourishing with a fruitfully fertile flood,
> Desirous to know which of their two languages
> Was first in being: they unwisely committed
> The right of Eloquence to an evil stuttering,
> And made judges of those who have no judgment,
> Namely, two small children, whom their mute mothers
> Nourished in the terror of most solitary places,
> Without any human’s enchanting voice
> Resonating nearby for thrice twelve months;
> They were led into the midst of the people of Xanthus
> And the Egyptians, with a powerless breath
