<header>LANGUAGES OF THIS UNIVERSE.</header>

*They cry "Bec" several times; "Bec, Bec" is the only word*
*That their tongue forms, and that their mouth expresses,*
*Therefore the Phrygians, knowing that in their heart*
*“Bec” means bread, they paint from their heart* <note>The original French uses "courage," which in this period often refers to the inner heart, spirit, or disposition.</note>
*Joy upon their brow for having had such luck*
*To obtain from nature a judgment in their favor.*
*Fools, who did not think that the bleating flocks* <note>The author suggests the children were merely imitating the "baaa" of the sheep they were raised with, rather than speaking an innate language.</note>
*Which grazed upon the flowers of the nearest hills*
*Were teaching them this term; and that the words of Gauls,*
*Memphians, Greeks, Hebrews, Trojans, Latins, English*
*Are not born within us; rather, each language*
*Is learned both by habit and by long usage,*
*The aptitude for speaking remaining only*
*Natural to humans, like that other Ornament*
*Which, richly diverse, makes them all unlike*
*The stupid herds of miserable beasts.*
*For if you consider that the bull bellows,*
*The slow ass brays, and the lion roars*
*Now high, now low, and that by such languages*
*They seem to us, eloquently, to reveal their hearts,*
*These are not words, but rather expressions*
*Of the muddled movement of a few passions:*
*Confused signs of pain, of sadness,*
*Of ire, thirst, hunger, love, or joy.*
*One can say the same of those winged Singers*
*Who upon the green branches of the distant bushes*
*Warble in the morning. For though it seems*
*Two by two, three by three, they share together,*
*Though their voice bends in a hundred thousand ways,*
*Though they boldly carve out a hundred dainty songs,*
*Though Apollo might have been a disciple in their school,*
*It is a sound without subject, notes without words,*
*A song repeated a thousand times in a day,*
*A discourse which, being mute, is lost within the woods.*
*But man alone can discourse of temperance,*
*Of strength, of equity, of honor, and of prudence,*
*Of God, of Heaven, of water, of the Earth, and of the Airs,*
*With chosen, meaningful, and diverse terms:*
*Developing his Heart, not through a single language,*
*But like Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), one of the greatest scholars of the Renaissance, renowned for his mastery of numerous ancient and modern languages.</note>, the wonder of our age,*
*The Sun of the learned, who speaks eloquently*
*Hebrew, Greek, Roman [Latin], Spanish, German,*
*French, Italian, Nubian, Arabic,*
*Syriac, Persian, English, and Chaldean,*
*And who, a Chameleon, can transfigure himself*
*Into any author he wishes—O rich, O supple Spirit!*
*Dignified son of the great Julius <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a famous physician and scholar.</note>: and dignified brother still*
*Of Sylve his eldest, whom Gascony honors:*

<meta>This page concludes the author's argument regarding the distinction between human reason-based speech and animal mimicry, following the discussion of the "first word" (Bec) and the polyglot achievements of scholars like Scaliger.</meta>

<header>HISTORY OF THE ORIGIN OF LANGUAGES, &c.</header>

*But as for parrots, who, making their home*
*In a dwelling open on all sides to the light of day,*
*Contend with us for the palm of eloquence,*
*Recite at full length the Christian Creed,*
*And speak the Lord's devout prayer,*
*Calling by name every member of the household:*
*They are like the voice that, daughter of our own voice,*
*Through hollow valleys, prattles importunately* <note>The author is comparing the parrot’s speech to an echo.</note>
*Without knowing what it says. In vain they beat the air,*
*And speaking without understanding themselves, they speak without speaking,*
*Deaf to their own voice: inasmuch as language*
*Is nothing but a resonant image of the spirit,*
*Even when it is brief, when it is ornate, when it is sweet,*
*And such as it was known to all before Nimrod.* <note>Nimrod is the biblical figure traditionally associated with the construction of the Tower of Babel; "before Nimrod" refers to the time when humanity supposedly shared a single, primordial language.</note>

To bring an end to this work, we shall say that we have seen and heard with our own eyes, both in Paris and in this city of Moulins about three years ago, a certain person of handsome body and face, aged about twenty-five years, with fair hair, calling himself the <term>Sieur de la Volte</term> <note>Lord of La Volte; likely a stage name for a performer or virtuoso.</note>, who, by a strange or rather marvelous industry, counterfeited or completely imitated the sounds, voices, noises, languages, and <term>warblings</term> <note>original: "deſgoiſements," referring to the rapid, melodic chirping of birds.</note> of all animals and birds, solely through the governance and conduct of his tongue, mouth, and throat; which is one of the strangest and most admirable wonders that one can see, tell of, or hear recounted in this century.
